units.la: Etsi tot jam extāt, nō in Psalmos modò, sed & in cæteros omnes sacros libros meditationes, ut non valde operæpreciū videri possit, nouas aliquas in luce emittere, tamē ut in artibus & scientiis [?] perpoliendis non effæta natura neq; exhausta, sic & multò magis sacrarū literarū fontes inexhaustos & perenes aquas videre, & gratū esse debet, & tam est utile, quā quod utilissimū. Mundi quidē senecta hæc est, si lapsos & præterlabētes annos spectes: sin verò dona S. Sancti in multis, viridis certè iuuēta est vel constans ætas. Hoc sic præfari libuit, adolescētes studiosi, quia hoc ipsū luce clarius cōspicitur, vel in unius Psalmi expositione, quam, non illa quidē nostra, quasi in nostra officina natā, & fabricatā, sed nostram, quia nobis data dicatáque est, nunc in luce edimus, cōmunémque vobis facimus. Non eo quidē ab authore consilio data nobis est, ut ederetur, sed ut priuatim esset mutui & perpetui inter nos amoris monimentum: at nunc non solùm vobis, sed studiosis omnibus facta communis,quòd eam inter nos pri-vatim author esse voluit, erit multò magis, mutui, inquam, & perpetui inter nos, imò & totā Ecclesiam, amoris monimentum.
units.tr: Although so many meditations now exist, not only on the Psalms but on all the other sacred books, that it may hardly seem worthwhile to bring out some new ones, still, just as nature is not worn out or exhausted in refining the arts and sciences, so much more should we see the sources of sacred letters as inexhaustible and their waters as perennial. Such a thing ought to be welcome, and it is as useful as anything could be. If you count the years that have slipped by and passed, this is indeed the old age of the world; but if you look at the gifts of the Holy Spirit in many people, it is surely a green youth, or at least a steady age. I wished to preface things this way, studious young men, because this very point is clearer than light in the exposition of a single Psalm, which we now bring out into the light. It is not ours, as if it were born and made in our own workshop, but it is ours in that it has been given and dedicated to us, and we now make it common to you, and to all students of the same kind. The author did not give it to us with the intention that it be published, but so that it would be a private monument of mutual and lasting love between us. Now, however, since it has been made common not only to you but to all students, and since the author wished it to be private between us, it will be a far greater monument of mutual and lasting love, I say, between us, and indeed for the whole Church.

units.la: Habetis ergo, id etiam, quod apud me re-posìtum cùm sciretis, totū iam fere quinquen-nium postulare & flagitare plerique vestrū non destitistis: eòque certè avidius, quòd hæc in publicis concionibus vernacula lingua tra-ctata non leuè omnibus doctrinæ existima-tionem, vobis certè, vt & cætera omnia au-thoris eiusdem, summâ admiratione merito concitarunt. Vos igitur cæteris in Psalmis a-liisque Sacræ Scripturæ libris explican-dis (quādo etiā huic vos muneri vouistis) iisdē quæ vobis hoc in Psalmo indicantur vesti-giis privatim & publicè, vt cuiq; dabit Deus, insistite: hanc enim ob causam in eius editionem consensi, hancque adeò ob causam authorem (quæ est ipsius gratia) mihi amicissimum, quidquid hīc à me eo inconsulto aut etiā invito præstitum est vestrorum studiorum gratia, æqui boníque facturum, confido. Valete in Christo Iesu. Ex Musæo nostro. Cal. Mart. 1578.
units.tr: So you have that which, since you knew it was set aside by me, most of you have not ceased to demand and press for, now for nearly five years. You have done so all the more eagerly because these meditations, when treated in public sermons in the vernacular, have deservedly won no small esteem for learning among everyone, and certainly among you, with the greatest admiration, just as all the other works of the same author have. So, in expounding the other Psalms and the other books of Holy Scripture (since you have also devoted yourselves to this office), follow privately and publicly, as God gives to each of you, the same footsteps that are shown to you in this Psalm. It is for this reason that I consented to its publication, and for this reason I trust that the author, who is most friendly to me, will take in good part whatever I have done here for the sake of your studies, without his knowledge and even against his will. Farewell in Christ Jesus. From our Museum, the Kalends of March 1578.

units.la: MEDITATIONES IN PSALMVM XXXII.
units.tr: Meditations on Psalm 32.

units.la: Præclarè à veteribus dictum est, peccatū onus esse omnium longè grauissimum: quandoquidem peccato tāquam onere homines adeò premuntur, ut in terrā proni nunquam in cœlum suspiciant, nisi porrecta Dei manu, ad vitæ melioris cogitationē erigantur. Quæ sententia confirmatur etiam ab ipso Christo cum ad se vocat eos qui graui peccatorū pondere fatigātur. Veruntamen adeò sunt homines peccato dediti, ut etiam non parū peccet in ipso peccato rectè sentiendo. Quidam enim ea sunt stupiditate, ut sub onere tanto deficientes, onus tamen ipsum non sentiant, sed sibi potius in illo miserrimo labore gratulentur, sibi placeant, & peccata peccatis quotidie cumulates, noua semper onera coaceruent, alij nimio peccati pondere opprimuntur. Utrique morbo remedium allaturus est David hoc Psalmo quem tractandum suscepimus.
units.tr: The ancients rightly said that sin is by far the heaviest of all burdens, since people are so weighed down by sin, as by a load, that they bend to the ground and never lift their eyes to heaven unless God stretches out his hand and raises them to thoughts of a better life. Christ himself confirms this saying when he calls to himself those who are worn out by the heavy weight of their sins. Yet people are so given over to sin that they sin not a little even in how they feel about sin. Some are so stupid that, though they collapse under so great a burden, they do not feel the burden itself, but rejoice in that most wretched toil, take pleasure in themselves, and, piling sin upon sin each day, keep heaping up new burdens. Others are crushed by the excessive weight of sin. David, in this Psalm which we have undertaken to treat, will bring a remedy for both diseases.

units.la: Nam ille suo exemplo proposito docebit quatenus sentiendum onus peccati, & quonam modo ab humeris nostris excutiendum sit: docebit, inquam, nobis esse vera fide ac pœnitentia ad Dei misericordiam recurrendum,ut ab ea peccatorum veniam im-petremus.Ergo cum tantus præco misericor-diæ Dei & remissionis peccatorum se nobis offerat, æquum est ut eius vocem audientes, in hac excellenti atque adeò omnium maximè necessaria doctrina acquiescamus.
units.tr: For by his own example he will teach how far the burden of sin is to be felt and how it is to be shaken off our shoulders. He will teach, I say, that we must have recourse, with true faith and repentance, to God's mercy, so that we may obtain forgiveness of sins from it. Therefore, since so great a herald of God's mercy and of the remission of sins offers himself to us, it is right that we listen to his voice and acquiesce in this excellent and altogether most necessary teaching.

units.la: *Hoc autem in Psalmo vates noster tria po-tissimum videtur præstare. Primùm enim doctrinam proponit de remissione peccatorum, docetque eam à nobis tanti esse faciendam, ut vel ipsam fœlicitatem in illa constituere debeamus. Deinde confirmat præclaram illam sententiam, non alienis & longè petitis rationibus,sed suo ipsius exemplo: enar-rátq; quibus doloribꝰ prope fuerit cõfectus, cùm à peccati stimulis urgeretur, in quos fletus eruperit,quæ fuerint ipsius preces,quæ agnitio ac cõfessio peccati,denique quis fuerit istius confessionis fructus, nempe remis-sio & venia quâ à Domini misericordia consecutus est. Postremò totus est in cohorta-tionibus,ut ipsius exemplo cõfirmati,sanctis precibus Dei favorem ac salutem adipiscamur:ac ne in vitiis obdurescamus, proponit cum Dei iudicium in obstinatos,tum eius misericordia erga pios ac fideles, qui dum certa fide syncerísque animis peccatorum remissio nem amplectuntur, habent unde gaudeant & exultét in Deo,à cuius liberalitate tantum beneficium acceperunt. Summa est: primo loco poni sententiam de remissione peccatorum. torum.Secundo eius sententiæ confirmatio-nem adscribi. Tertio cohortationes adiun-gi, ut rectè nobis usum istius sententiæ ap-plicemus.
units.tr: In this Psalm our prophet seems chiefly to do three things. First, he sets forth the doctrine of the remission of sins and teaches that we must hold it in such high esteem that we should place our very happiness in it. Next, he confirms that excellent saying not by foreign and far-fetched arguments but by his own example. He recounts with what griefs he was almost worn down when the goads of sin pressed him, into what weeping he burst, what his prayers were, what acknowledgement and confession of sin he made, and finally what fruit that confession bore, namely the remission and pardon he obtained from the Lord's mercy. Lastly, the whole passage is made up of exhortations: that, strengthened by his example, we may obtain God's favour and salvation through holy prayers; and that we may not harden ourselves in vices, he sets before us both God's judgement against the obstinate and his mercy towards the pious and faithful. Those who embrace the remission of sins with sure faith and sincere hearts have cause to rejoice and exult in God, from whose generosity they have received so great a benefit. The sum is this: first, the saying about the remission of sins is put forward; second, its confirmation is added; third, exhortations are joined, so that we may apply the use of that saying rightly.

units.la: Atque ut ad illud quod primo loco poni-tur accedamus, testatur ipsa Psalmi inscriptio hic agi de re maximi momenti, & cuius co-gnitio nobis summopere necessaria est. In-scribitur enim hic Psalmus Maskil, id est, e-rudiens: quasi dicat in hoc Psalmo doctrinâ scitu dignissimam contineri, ut ita reddamur attentiores & diligentiores ad eam edisce-ndam: quod etiam aliqui ex veteribus agnove-runt. Hoc autem vocabulum postea repetet in versu 8. cùm aperte doctoris partes su-scipiet.
units.tr: To come to what is placed first: the very inscription of the Psalm shows that the matter treated here is of the greatest importance and that knowledge of it is most necessary for us. This Psalm is inscribed Maskil, that is, "instructing", as if to say that this Psalm contains a doctrine most worthy to be known, so that we may be made more attentive and diligent in learning it. Some of the ancients also recognised this. David will repeat this word later, in verse 8, when he openly takes up the part of a teacher.

units.la: Et certè non sine ratione doctrina de re-missione peccatorum hic appellatur scientia in qua erudiri debeamus, cùm satis constet (si modò rem ita ut decet expendamus) nullam omnino scientiam, quæcunque tandem sit, cum hac nostra esse comparandam. Veniant enim in medium veteres omnium Philoso-phorum greges, ex quorum fontibus varios scientiarum riuulos esse diducendos doctissi-mi plerique censuerunt, & indè rerū omnium cognitionem hauriendam: cedò quot quan-tósque[?] labores susceperunt in earum rerum indagatione quarum cognitionem aut nun-quâ sunt adepti, aut certè si adepti sunt, eam vanam esse atque inutilem ratio tandem & experientia comprobauit? Nimirum verum est quod aliquando fuit à Chrysostomo ra-ditum, subtiles Philosophorum disputatio-nes nihil aliud esse quàm tenues aranearum telas, quæ quidem ab aura leuissima statim di-scerpuntur & euanescunt. vt enim scripta Phi-losophorum prima fronte subtilia ac splen-dida videantur, attamen postquam diu mul-tumque laborantes, sursum ac deorsum co-gitationum leuitate volitarunt, quid tandem aliud quàm aranearum telas contexuerunt ar-gutis disputationibus, quibus leuiorum homi-num ingenia possint irretire? Nonne de illis merito dici potest quod aliquando dicebat Augustinus, eorû argumenta esse vitrea, quæ lucet subtilitate & franguntur vanitate? Quis non miretur Philosophos miseros de fœlici-tate, ignaros de scientia, mendaces de vero, improbos de virtute in suis libris tam acutè disputantes? Sed quid illos accuso quòd non potuerint assequi ratiocinando, quæ sit vera virtus, quæ vera scientia, cùm ne suam quidem ignorantiam intellexerint, nec vnquam sci-uerint, quid sit peccatum, vnde manarit, quas-tas tenebras offuderit hominum mentibus& quanta in corruptione hominû natura versa-tur. Hæc, inquam, adeò nesciuerunt, vt contra existimarint eam demum esse sapientiam, siquis omnia in se posita esse cōsideret. Nihil ergo mirum si celebris hæc doctrina, de remissione peccatorum, fuerit iis incognita qui vim & effecta peccati,imò ipsum peccatū nunquam cognouerunt. Atque dum semper quæreret, quid sit bene beatéque viuere, nunquam illi bene nec beatè vixerunt. Cùm verò plurimæ sint artes atque scientiæ quibus vita hominū continetur, possumus affirmare illas omnes scientias ad hanc nostrā de qua agimus nihil esse, atque adeò si ab ea separentur, esse non tātum inutiles,sed etiā perniciosas. Et quem-admodum Augustinus dicere solebat,esse a-liquam doctam ignorantiam, nos contra dicere merito possumus, quamlibet scientiam indoctam esse, si ab hac nostra vera scientia fuerit sciuncta. Cùmque (vt ait Bernardus) multi scire velint, vt sciantur: meminerimus eam demum veram esse scientiam, quæ nos efficiat non solùm doctiores verumetiā me-liores. Nam si Mathematicas disciplinas con-sideres,quæ in numerorum scientia,in dispi-ciendo mundi ordine,in cognoscendo syde-rum cursu & in dimetiedis terrę partibus ver-satur: Quorsum,obsecro,illa omnia,dum te intimum innumerabiles aculei cōfodiunt & ipse peccati sensus conuincit te & cœlo& terra indignum esse ? Quid tibi syderum cursus, quid cœlestium orbium cognitio profutura est, si te peccatum ad inferos vsque detruse-rit? Quid te iuuabit sanandorum corporum scientia, si tuus animus lethali morbo, id est, peccato laboret? Cur iactas iurisprudentiam, cùm tua te accusět cōscientia, téque iniustifsimum esse pronuntiet?Itaque dicendum est omnes disciplinas fore nobis inutiles, nisi hæc sancta de remissione peccatorum scientia simul accesserit. Et quemadmodum ægris corporibus amara videntur ea quæ tamen natura dulcissima sunt, atque illis nihil suave est, nihil iucundū quandiu morbo detinētur: ita nobis existimādum est, nullam nos ex ul-lis rebus utilitate ac lætitiam posse percipere, donec verā animi valetudinem, id est, cognitionē fiduciamque de peccatorum remissio-ne simus assecuti. Quod ne cui mirum videa-tur, intueamur Dauidem, qui partes doctoris suscepit, ut nos in hac excellentissima doctrina erudiat, non tātum verbis, sed etiam exe[?]-plo. Quantus enim fuit ille sumus Dei vates? quot artibus instructus? qua varia rerū cognitione imbutus? Ille tamen hic fatetur se nulla alia in re, quam in hac de remissione peccatorum scientia unqua acquiescere potuisse. Au-diamus etiam S. Dei Apostolum profitetem se nihil iam scire quam Christum pro se crucifixum, quæ vnica est remittendorum peccatorum ratio. Atque ex his omnibus conclu-damus, scientiam hanc quam Dauid traditu-rus est, longe esse cæteris omnibus antepo-nedam. Hanc pueri, fœminæ & cuiuscunque generis opifices, hanc agricolæ & quotquot sunt literarum expertes, possunt sine labore, sine vigiliis, sine sumptu, vel horæ momen-to & cum summa animi delectatione perdiscere Atque vt id fiat, iam ipsa Dauidis verba attente audiamus.
units.tr: Certainly not without reason is the doctrine of the remission of sins here called a science in which we ought to be instructed, since it is quite clear (if we weigh the matter as it deserves) that no science whatever, of whatever kind, is to be compared with this one of ours. Let the ancient throngs of all the philosophers come forward, from whose springs most learned men have judged that the streams of the various sciences are to be drawn, and from which the knowledge of all things is to be drawn. How many and how great were the labours they undertook in investigating those things whose knowledge they either never attained or, if they did attain it, which reason and experience have at last proved to be empty and useless? It is true, as Chrysostom once said, that the subtle disputations of the philosophers are nothing but thin spiders' webs, which are torn apart and vanish at the lightest breath of air. For although the writings of the philosophers look subtle and brilliant at first sight, yet after labouring long and hard, flitting up and down with the lightness of their thoughts, what else have they woven but spiders' webs, with clever disputations by which the minds of lighter men may be ensnared? Can it not rightly be said of them what Augustine once said, that their arguments are like glass, which shines with subtlety and is shattered by vanity? Who would not marvel at these wretched philosophers, ignorant of happiness, ignorant of science, liars about truth, wicked about virtue, who dispute so sharply in their books? But why do I accuse them for failing to grasp by reasoning what true virtue is and what true science is, when they did not even understand their own ignorance, and never knew what sin is, whence it springs, what darkness it has cast over human minds, and how deep the corruption is in which human nature is involved? These things, I say, they so little knew that, on the contrary, they thought wisdom consisted in considering everything as placed within oneself. Nothing is surprising, then, if this celebrated doctrine of the remission of sins was unknown to those who never knew the power and effects of sin, indeed sin itself. And while they were always seeking what it is to live well and happily, they never lived well or happily. Since there are very many arts and sciences by which human life is sustained, we can affirm that all of them are nothing in relation to this one of ours, and that if they are separated from it they are not only useless but even harmful. Just as Augustine used to say that there is a learned ignorance, we can rightly say on the contrary that any science is unlearned if it has been cut off from this true science of ours. And since, as Bernard says, many wish to know in order to be known, let us remember that the true science is the one that makes us not only more learned but also better. For if you consider the mathematical disciplines, which consist in the science of numbers, in surveying the order of the world, in knowing the courses of the stars and in measuring the parts of the earth: to what end, I ask, are all those things, while innumerable goads pierce you within and the very sense of sin convicts you that you are unworthy of heaven and earth? What will the course of the stars or knowledge of the heavenly spheres profit you, if sin has thrust you down even to the depths? What will the science of healing bodies help you, if your soul labours under a deadly disease, that is, sin? Why do you boast of jurisprudence, when your conscience accuses you and declares you most unjust? Therefore we must say that all the disciplines will be useless to us unless this holy science of the remission of sins comes alongside them. Just as to sick bodies those things seem bitter which are by nature most sweet, and nothing is pleasant or agreeable to them as long as they are held by disease, so we must judge that we can perceive no usefulness or joy in anything until we have attained true health of soul, that is, knowledge of and trust in the remission of sins. Lest this seem strange to anyone, let us look at David, who takes up the part of teacher to instruct us in this most excellent doctrine, not only by words but also by example. How great was that prophet of God? How well equipped with arts? How steeped in varied knowledge of things? Yet here he confesses that in no other matter could he ever find rest except in this science of the remission of sins. Let us also hear the holy Apostle of God professing that he now knows nothing except Christ crucified for him, which is the only way of remitting sins. From all these things let us conclude that this science which David is about to hand down is far to be preferred to all others. Children, women and craftsmen of every kind, farmers, and all who are unlearned in letters, can learn it without toil, without vigils, without expense, in a single hour, and with the greatest delight of mind. So that this may come about, let us now listen attentively to David's own words.

units.la: 1. verf. Beatus ille est cui transgressio (sua) remissa, & cuius peccatum tectum est.
units.tr: 1. verse: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, and whose sin is covered.

units.la: HAnc de peccatorum remissione senten-tiam proponit Dauid, cuius postea confirmationem subiiciet: Sed hic proponendi modus est ἐμφατικώτερος[?]. Nam videtur,si propius intuearis, continere exclamationem in quam Dauid erupit post multas ac varias cogitationes (libenter enim in eorum sententiam discesserim, qui Psalmum hunc a Daui-de compositum fuisse existimant, cum a Dei Spiritu persuasus est de adulterij & homicidij venia impetrata.) Ergo postea quam diu multumque pugnauit aduersus aculeos peccati quibus assiduè pungebatur, & tandem amplexus Dei misericordiam, prostratis peccati viribus, euasit superior: tum sensit dulcissimam quietem in animo, cum eius pacata & tranquilla fuit conscientia. Quare exclamans quàm, inquit, fœlices sunt ij, qui sunt certi de peccatorum remissione! quod perinde est ac si diceret: quàm præclare mecum actum est, quem Dominus ab arctissimis peccati vinculis summa misericordia liberauit! Me antehac impuræ vitæ recordatio, me meorum peccatorum stimuli confoderunt, mihi ob oculos versata est fœda illa ingratitudo, qua summam Dei erga me liberalitatem contempsi, me anteactæ vitæ pudor, me præteritæ libidinis[?] memoria propemodum confecit: audiebam sacrosanctæ legis latam in mesen[?]tentiam, videbā animo ipsos inferos, in quos iusto Dei iudicio mox essem detrudendus. Quid multa? nihil mihi præter horrore mortis occurrebat. Verum in mediis illis tenebris mihi misericordiæ divinæ fulgor obortus est, & me collabentem clemens & benignus ille pater confirmauit, suíque Spiritus efficacia persuasit, omnia mihi peccata esse condonata. Tunc vidi cœlum ipsum quodammodo apertum, audiui mei Patris vocem dulcissimam, qua mihi peccatorum veniam largitus est. Ergo possum merito exclamare, Eos demum esse fœlices, qui vera fide apprehendunt peccatorum remissionem. Hic est sensus verborum Dauidis.
units.tr: David sets forth this statement about the forgiveness of sins, and he will later add its confirmation. But this way of putting it is more emphatic [ἐμφατικώτερος]. For if you look at it more closely, it seems to contain an exclamation that broke from David after many and varied thoughts. (I would gladly agree with those who think that David composed this Psalm after he had been persuaded by the Spirit of God that the pardon for adultery and murder had been obtained.) So after he had long and hard struggled against the stings of sin by which he was constantly pricked, and at last, embracing the mercy of God, had overcome the strength of sin and prevailed, he then felt the sweetest rest in his mind, when his conscience was calm and tranquil. Therefore, exclaiming, he says, "How happy are those who are certain of the forgiveness of sins!" This is as if he were saying: "How splendidly has it gone for me, whom the Lord, by his supreme mercy, has freed from the tightest bonds of sin! Before this, the memory of an impure life, the goads of my sins, pierced me; that foul ingratitude was before my eyes, by which I had despised God's great generosity toward me; the shame of my past life, the memory of my former lust, almost wore me out. I heard the sentence of sacred law pronounced, I saw in my mind the very depths into which I was soon to be thrust down by the just judgment of God. Why say more? Nothing but the horror of death met me. But in the midst of those darkness a gleam of divine mercy arose for me, and that gentle and kind Father steadied me as I was collapsing, and by the efficacy of his Spirit persuaded me that all my sins had been pardoned. Then I saw heaven itself somehow opened, I heard the sweetest voice of my Father, who granted me the forgiveness of my sins. Therefore I can rightly exclaim that those are at last happy who grasp the forgiveness of sins with a true faith. This is the sense of David's words."

units.la: Ex quibus nobis colligendum est, in quo nostra sit constituenda fœlicitas: nempe in illa Dei gratia, quæ nostris animis inscribit certam de remissis peccatis fiduciā. Quod quàm verum sit, facile constabit, si naturam ipsius fœlicitatis consideres. Nam eā esse stabilem, fixam & perpetuam atque summa voluptate perfusam necesse est, vt vere suo nomini respondeat. Iam videamus quidnam reperiri possit eiusmodi, vt & perpetuum sit, & vera voluptate expleat hominem. Certè si res omnes creatas oculis animi lustremus, si totius orbis partes, si varia hominum studia exactè [?]intueamur[?], nihil se offeret vbi fœlicitas possit fit ; tanquam in sua sede, collocari. Testes sunt illi ipsi Philosophi, quos adeo exercuit summi boni investigatio, ut nunquam inter omnes constiterit, ecquänam in re summum bonum aut quæri debeat, aut possit inveniri.
units.tr: From these words we must gather where our happiness is to be founded: namely, in that grace of God which writes on our minds a sure confidence concerning sins that have been forgiven. How true this is will be easily established if you consider the nature of happiness itself. For it must be stable, fixed and everlasting, and filled with the greatest pleasure, if it is truly to answer to its name. Now let us see what can be found of such a kind that it is both lasting and fills a person with true delight. Certainly, if we survey with the eyes of the mind all created things, if we closely examine the parts of the whole world and the various pursuits of men, nothing will present itself where happiness could be placed, as in its proper seat. The philosophers themselves bear witness, who were so troubled by the search for the highest good that they never agreed among themselves what the highest good ought to be sought in, or whether it could be found at all.

units.la: Testes sunt etiam varij hominum conatus & labores, quos frustra suscipiunt, ut tandem fœlicitatem adipiscantur. Mirum est sane hoc omnibus propositum esse, ut sint fœlices: eo omnes aspirare, eo sua studia dirigere:& ta-men tam paucos esse, vel qui fœlicitatem no-rint, vel qui ipsam ita ut decet amplectantur.
units.tr: The various efforts and labours of men also bear witness, which they undertake in vain in order at last to attain happiness. It is indeed remarkable that everyone has this purpose, that they should be happy; everyone aims at this, directs their pursuits to this; and yet there are so few who either know happiness or embrace it as it ought to be embraced.

units.la: Quod ut fiat dilucidius, fingamus nos esse in fœlici- media hominum turba, qui variis studiis cu-riisque distrahuntur, & singulos rogare, ecquem ad scopum colliment & dirigant suæ vitæ cursum. Auare, quid tandem spectas in immensis illis laboribus, curis, vigiliis & in summa illa cupiditate, quæ te dies noctesque solicitat? qui fit ut ad rem tantopere sis attentus? ut domos domibus, agros agris, nummos denique nummis semper adiungas? Cedo, si quis hac oratione uteretur, nonne statim audiret auarum respondentem se tot labores suscipere ad congerendas divitias, quia in il-lis fœlicitate esse sitam arbitratur? Age, pro-grediamur ulterius, rogemus eos qui flagrant honoris & gloriæ cupiditate, quam tandem ob causam tot pericula adeant, ut sibi possint nominis splendorem & celebritatem compa-rare: quid aliud responsuros existimamus, quàm se fœlicitatem in hominum gloria con stituisse? Quid porrò diƈturi sunt ij qui nihil non tentant vt voluptatibus perfruantur?nón ne putát eos esse fœlices qui suam libidinem explent, & vt in cœno, ita in voluptate corporis volutantur? Itaque auari, ambitiosi & voluptatibus dediti huc habent fine propositu,vt fœlices fiant: sed quàm miserè fallatur, ipsa tandem docet experientia. Nam diuitiæ (vt ait Solomo) sunt alatæ & velocissimo cur su e nostris manibus euolant: suntque (vt ait Chrysostomus) quouis seruo fugitiuo infideliores. (Atque vtinam diuitias perdamus potius quàm diuitiæ nos perdant.) Quid porrò possis in diuitiis spectare quod ad fœlicitatè accedat? magnus est labor dum acquiruntur, maior metus dum possidetur, maximus dolor cùm amittuntur. Nù ergo in labore, in metu, in dolore fœlicitatè hominis cõstituas? Quid dicā de gloriæ vanitate: cuius splêdore Psaltes ait statim euanescere, quamque Nazianzenus cõparat cũ nauis vestigiis ὡσπερ πόα δὲ χαρασσο-μένοις [?] καὶ ἀλλυμένοις [?] ὁμοίως [?]. Quid denique de voluptate censendũ est, quam in luctum desinere Solomo pronuntiat, & quam aliquis ex veteribus, funus in viuo corpore, non minùs verè quàm eleganter appellauit? Quæ cùm ita sint, nobis concludendum est, nihil in rebus humanis vbi fœlicitatem collocemus, posse reperiri: audiendúmque esse Dauidem cùm affirmat, fœlices esse eos quorum peccata sunt remissa. Cùm enim Dauid rex essēt & omnium rerum copia circumfluere ret,non tamen dixit.eos esse fœlices qui sce-ptra gerunt, qui longè lateque dominantur, qui honoribus, qui diuitiis, qui voluptatibus abundant: sed potius: O fœlices eos, inquit, quibus Dominus peccata condonauit! Nam hac in re nobis idem statuendum est quod solet in ædificanda domo obseruari. Vt enim si firmum est fundamentum, non dubium est quin ea quæ fuerint superstructa, duratura sint,alioqui fundamenti vitio breui tempore collapsura:ita si fœlicitatem in rebus terrenis &caducis opinionis errore nobis finxerimus, quid mirum si euerso fundamento vana il-la fœlicitas statim corruat? Quod si eam fun-demus in Deo atque in eius misericordia,quę potissimum elucet in nostrorum peccatorum remissione, tunc certè affirmare poterimus fœlicitatem firmissimo fundamento nixam, fore constantem atque sempiternam. Quis enim vnquâ,nisi assentator, vel Pharaonem, Nabuchadnezarem,vel Neronè & eiusmodi potentissimos reges ac imperatores fœlices appellauit? Nos autè Prophetas,Apostolos, Martyres,tot denique sanctos homines fœli-ces ac beatos prædicamus:Nempe quia spre-tis diuitiis, honoribus & voluptatibus,men-tes in vno Deo defixas habuerunt,& accepta peccatorum remissione, in sola eius miseri-cordia conquieuerunt.Quis autem Lazarum medicum, ulcerosum, ad fores alienas proie-ctum illi diviti superbo, induto purpura & omni voluptatū genere diffluéti non facile anteponat? quis nostrum ex iis quæ consecuta sunt, non illum fœlicem, hunc autem miserrimum esse credat? Itaque cum Davide exclamemus Beatum esse non avarū, non ambitiosum, non voluptarium, non eum quem vulgò beatum prædicant: sed cui transgressi [?] sua remissa, & cuius peccatum tectum est.
units.tr: To make this clearer, let us imagine that we are in the middle of a crowd of men, who are pulled apart by various pursuits and cares, and we ask each one to what goal they direct the course of their life. Miser, what are you looking for in those immense labours, cares, watchings, and in that great greed which harasses you day and night? How does it happen that you are so intent on the matter? That you always add house to house, field to field, and finally money to money? Tell me, if someone asked this, would he not at once hear the miser answer that he undertakes so many labours to heap up riches, because he thinks happiness lies in them? Come, let us go further, let us ask those who burn with the desire for honour and glory, for what reason they undergo so many dangers, so that they may acquire for themselves the splendour and renown of a name: what else do we think they will answer, than that they have placed happiness in the glory of men? What again do those intend who attempt everything so that they may enjoy pleasures? Do you not think that those are happy who satisfy their lust, and wallow in bodily pleasure as in filth? So the greedy, the ambitious and those given to pleasures have this end in view, that they may become happy; but how wretchedly they are deceived, experience itself finally teaches. For riches (as Solomon says) have wings and fly swiftly out of our hands; and they are (as Chrysostom says) more faithless than any runaway slave. (Would that we might lose our riches rather than that riches lose us!) What, moreover, can you look for in riches that comes near to happiness? Great is the labour while they are acquired, greater the fear while they are possessed, greatest the grief when they are lost. Will you then place the happiness of man in labour, in fear, in grief? What shall I say of the vanity of glory, whose splendour the Psalmist says quickly fades away, and which Nazianzen compares to the traces of a ship [ὡσπερ πόα δὲ χαρασσομένοις καὶ ἀλλυμένοις ὁμοίως], like grass that is withered and perishes alike? What finally is to be judged of pleasure, which Solomon declares ends in mourning, and which one of the ancients called, no less truly than elegantly, a funeral of the living body? Since these things are so, we must conclude that nothing can be found in human affairs in which to place happiness; and we must hear David when he affirms that those are happy whose sins are forgiven. For although David was a king and overflowed with an abundance of all things, he did not say that those are happy who hold sceptres, who rule far and wide, who abound in honours, in riches, in pleasures; but rather, "O happy are they," he says, "to whom the Lord has forgiven their sins!" For in this matter we must hold to what is usually observed in building a house. For just as, if the foundation is firm, there is no doubt that what has been built upon it will endure, but otherwise, through the defect of the foundation, it will soon fall, so if we have imagined happiness in earthly and perishable things through an error of opinion, what wonder if, the foundation being overthrown, that empty happiness collapses at once? But if we found it in God and in his mercy, which shines forth above all in the forgiveness of our sins, then we can certainly affirm that happiness, resting on the firmest foundation, will be constant and everlasting. For who ever called Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, or Nero and such most powerful kings and emperors happy, except a flatterer? But we proclaim the prophets, apostles, martyrs, and finally so many holy men, happy and blessed: namely because, having despised riches, honours and pleasures, they kept their minds fixed on the one God, and, having received the forgiveness of sins, rested in his mercy alone. And who would not readily prefer Lazarus, the sick man, lying full of sores at another's door, to that proud rich man clothed in purple and flowing with every kind of pleasure? Which of us, from what followed, would not believe that the former is happy and the latter most wretched? Therefore, with David, let us exclaim: Blessed is not the greedy, not the ambitious, not the pleasure-seeker, not the one whom people commonly call blessed; but he whose transgression is forgiven, and whose sin is covered.

units.la: Sed hoc loco nobis occurritur à duplici hominū genere, quorum alij existimant fœlicitatem hominis non extra ipsum hominē, sed in eius meritis & operibus esse ponendam: ita ut illi demum futuri sint fœlices, qui sanctis operibus fœlicitatem fuerint promeriti. Alij vero non possunt adduci ut credant nomen fœlicitatis iis competere, qui tot miseriis & afflictionibus in hac vita perpetuò iactantur. Ergo utrorumque rationes à nobis expendendæ sunt & refellendæ.
units.tr: But here we meet two kinds of people. Some think that a person's happiness is not located outside the person, but must be sought in his merits and works, so that only those who have earned happiness by holy works will be happy. Others cannot be brought to believe that the name of happiness belongs to those who are constantly tossed about by so many miseries and afflictions in this life. So the arguments of both must be weighed and refuted by us.

units.la: Qui fœlicitatem statuunt in bonis operi-bus, Primùm in hoc falluntur quòd bona o-pera humanis viribus & meritis attribuunt. Recte siquidé Augustinus: Quisquis, ô Domine, inquit, enumerat tibi merita sua, quid enumerat nisi munera tua? Et Cyprianus: Dei est, Dei est, inquâ, omne quod possumus. Deinde ipsa bona opera à Dei Spiritu profecta, manet ni-hilominus imperfecta nostro vitio. Porrò affirmamus Davidis interprete ipso Apostolo meliorem meliore adhiberi non posse, qui in Epist. ad Rom. 4. Romanos colligit ex his verbis quę nunc tractamus hominē non iustificari suis operibus: Et concludit nostram iustitiam in operibus multo modo quaerendam esse. Neque nos mouet quod alibi dicitur, hominem esse beatum, qui sanctitatem colit & legem Domini dies noctesque meditatur. Nam utrumque verum est, sed diuerso respectu. Nec enim causa pugnat cum suis effectis, sed potius haec ad illam referenda sunt: ita tamen ut conueniens adhibeatur distinctio. Exempli gratia: si dicam hominem viuere qui videt, audit, ambulat, & reliquas corporis actiones exercet, verum proculdubio dixero. Sed quum ad vitae causam propius accedo, iam intueor ipsam animam, cuius vires & effecta elucent in exterioribus illis actionibus. Ita dicendum est, eos esse foelices qui sancte viuunt, non quod suam foelicitatem in suis operibus collocent, sed quia vitae sanctimonia effectu est illius iustificationis, quam iam fide apprehenderunt in Christo, quemadmodum egregie disserit Apostolus. Itaque ut facilius explicemus haec Dauidis verba, beatos esse quibus peccata sunt remissa, sic accipienda sunt: foelicitatem hominis in sola Dei misericordia residere: hanc autem misericordiam delere peccata propter Christum & imputare iustitiam, quod beneficium a nobis non alia ratione quam fide percipitur. Quare quum Dauid hic agit de remissione peccatorum, necessario infert imputationem iustitiae & reconciliationem cum Deo, sine qua nullum bonum, nedum felicitas, nobis potest obvenire. Quod etiam fuse persequitur Paulus in praeclaro illo loco Epistolae ad Romanos. Iam si David tot tantisque virtutibus exornatus, non alibi quam in remissione peccatorum felicitatem constituit, quid de nobis miseris hominibus dicendum erit, si in operum nostrorum mercede felicitatem quaesierimus? Porro si tanta fuit Davidis fiducia, cum nondum exhibitus esset Christus, per quem solum peccata nostra remittuntur: quanto maiori fiducia ac spe esse debemus, qui tanta Christi luce sumus illustrati?
units.tr: Those who place happiness in good works are first deceived in this, that they attribute good works to human powers and merits. Augustine rightly says: "Whoever, O Lord, enumerates his merits to you, what does he enumerate but your gifts?" And Cyprian: "It is God's, it is God's, I say, all that we are able to do." Moreover, the good works themselves, though they proceed from the Spirit of God, nonetheless remain imperfect through our fault. Furthermore, we affirm, with the Apostle himself as the interpreter of David, that no better interpreter can be found. In the Epistle to the Romans, Rom. 4., he gathers from these very words that we are now treating that man is not justified by his works, and he concludes that our righteousness must be sought in a quite different way than in works. Nor are we moved by what is said elsewhere, that the man is blessed who cultivates holiness and meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. Both statements are true, but in different respects. Nor does the cause contend with its effects; rather, the effects must be referred to the cause, provided that a fitting distinction is applied. For example, if I say that a man lives who sees, hears, walks, and performs the other actions of the body, I will doubtless have spoken truly. But when I come closer to the cause of life, I now look at the soul itself, whose powers and effects shine forth in those outward actions. So it must be said that those are happy who live holily, not because they place their happiness in their works, but because holiness of life is the effect of that justification which they have already apprehended by faith in Christ, as the Apostle expounds excellently. Therefore, so that we may more easily explain these words of David, "Blessed are those whose sins are forgiven," they must be understood thus: man's happiness rests in God's mercy alone. This mercy blots out sins on account of Christ and imputes righteousness, a benefit which we receive by no other means than faith. Wherefore, since David here treats of the remission of sins, he necessarily infers the imputation of righteousness and reconciliation with God, without which no good, much less happiness, can come to us. Paul also pursues this at length in that famous passage of the Epistle to the Romans. Now if David, adorned with so many and such great virtues, placed happiness nowhere but in the remission of sins, what shall be said of us wretched men, if we seek happiness in the reward of our works? Moreover, if David's confidence was so great when Christ, through whom alone our sins are remitted, had not yet been revealed, with how much greater confidence and hope ought we to be, who have been illumined by so great a light of Christ?

units.la: Atque ut posteriorem obiectionem diluamus, ad eos accedendum est, qui nullum quidem Scripturae testimonium praetexunt errori suo, sed sensum & iudicium carnis asse-runt, cui videri non possunt qui patiuntur, es-se felices. Audiamus enim ea quae ipsi dictita resolent, quoties exagitant nostram in Christo conditionem. Itane tandem, inquiunt, felices estis, cum nulla pars vitae vestrae dolorum vacua sit, sed potius omnibus laborum molestiarumque generibus expositi? Infan-tes videmini iam simul cum lacte fugere ipsa calamitatum primordia, & crescentibus an-nis vestrae itidem miseriae crescere videntur. Vos mundus odit, terra expellit, flammae exu-runt, runt, aquæ submergunt. Vos cæteri homines iam homines esse non patiuntur: vos patria cæteris dulcissima non agnoscit, cognati reiiciunt, amici deserunt, hostes trucidat, omnia denique pericula insectantur: ita ut in angulum compulsis & redactis, vix vobis liceat respirare. Vos igitur beati? imo ne inter vivos quidem estis recensendi, qui vitam vitalem (vt ille dicebat) nunquam vivitis. Hæc illi, non tam argumenta quam maledicta, non tã obiiciunt quam euomunt adversus piorum conditionem: quæ tamen omnia non tanti sunt momenti ut nobis eripiant fructū bonæ con-scientiæ, & nos quasi de ipsa fœlicitatis pof-sessione deiiciant. Quid autem si vel ea quibus nos adoriuntur, nostrã etiam fidem confirment? Nos terra, nos mundus, nos cæteri homines abigunt (hoc enim obiicitis.) Ita sit sane: nonne propterea infœlices esse concludetis? Atqui illa ipsa sunt illustrissima nostræ fœlicitatis insignia. Ecquos enim fœlices Dominus pronunciat? eosne qui suis deliciis indormiunt? Minime, sed eos qui persecutio-nem patiuntur. Eosne quibus homines blandiuntur? Imo quibus homines maledicunt. Eosne qui risu & voluptatibus diffluunt? imo eos qui lugent. Ergo si apud nos pluris esse debet sacrosancta illa vox Domini nostri, quam vana hominum ludibria & petulantes linguæ maledicorum: Non est cur ineptas illas obiectiones moremur. Si terræ exosi sumus, at nos cœlum approba t: si nos homi-nes reiiciunt, at nos Deus rec ipit: si negamur ab amicis, a Deo agnoscimur: si vita hæc no-stra multis calamitatibus obn oxia est, habe-mus spem melioris vitæ quæ lab orum dolo-rumque omnium expers futura est. Nihil i-taque mirum est, si mundus nobis aduersatur: non enim in illo fœlicitatem no st ram consti-tuimus. Nam cur a mundo infœlicissimo fœ-licitatem expectemus? Sed hoc nobi s satis su-perque est, quòd in mediis angustiis a Dei vo-ce & ab eius promissionibus certissimis su-stentamur. Ex quo fit ut in media miseria fœ-licitatem, in doloribus lætitiam, in laboribus quietem, in morte denique vitam a pprehen-damus. Non terrena est nostra fœlicitas, sed cœlestis: non ab hominibus pendet, sed a Deo: non exterior est, sed intus ab ipso Dei verbo concipitur, alitur, perficitur. Non cõ penetrat infidelium oculi quos vanus rerum præ-sentium externarúmque fulgor perstringit: Sola est, sola, inquam, est fides quę puris ocu-lis fœlicitatem nostram intuetur, & tota in eius contemplatione acquiscit. Valeant er-go impuri illi homines quibus vera fœlicitas placere nõ potest, eò scilicet miseriores quòd gaudeant suis miseriis atque adeò ipsam mi-seriam fœlicitatem esse existiment. Nam quid de Abrahamo, Isaaco, Iacobo dicturi sunt quos in continuis prope laboribus versatos esse sancta commemorat historia? Christū-ne etiam infœlicem audebunt dicere, quē mundus spreuit, quem reiecit, quem denique cruce & acerbissimis doloribus affecit? Itaque dicendum est, eos esse beatos, non qui hominum, sed qui Dei iudicio beati pronuntiantur: nec audiendos esse qui fœlicitatem in rebus fluxis & caducis statuunt, eósque miseros appellitant, qui ab illarum desiderio ac fiducia animos auocarunt. Audiamus potius nostrum Dauidem exclamantem, eos esse fœlices quibus Dominus peccata condonauit.
units.tr: To answer the latter objection, we must turn to those who put forward no testimony of Scripture for their error, but assert the sense and judgment of the flesh, which cannot see those who suffer as happy. Let us hear what they keep repeating whenever they assail our condition in Christ. "Are you then truly happy," they say, "when no part of your life is free of sorrows, but you are exposed to every kind of toil and trouble? Even in infancy you seem to flee from the very beginnings of calamity, along with your milk, and as the years grow, your miseries seem to grow too. The world hates you, the earth expels you, flames burn you, waters drown you. The other men no longer allow you to be men. Your fatherland, sweetest to others, does not acknowledge you; relatives cast you off, friends desert you, enemies slaughter you; in short, every danger pursues you, so that, driven into a corner and cramped, you can scarcely draw breath. Are you then blessed? Nay, you should not even be counted among the living, you who never live the living life, as that man used to say." These are not so much arguments as curses, not so much objections as vomit against the condition of the godly. Yet none of these things is of such weight as to snatch from us the fruit of a good conscience and cast us down, as it were, from the very possession of happiness. But what if the very things by which they assail us also confirm our faith? You object that the earth, the world, and other men drive us away. Very well. Will you therefore conclude that we are unhappy? Yet these very things are the most illustrious marks of our happiness. For whom does the Lord pronounce happy? Those who slumber in their pleasures? By no means, but those who suffer persecution. Those whom men flatter? No, those whom men curse. Those who dissolve in laughter and pleasures? No, those who mourn. Therefore, if that most holy voice of our Lord should carry more weight with us than the empty mockeries of men and the wanton tongues of slanderers, there is no reason to dwell on those silly objections. If we are hateful to the earth, heaven approves us; if men reject us, God receives us; if we are disowned by friends, we are acknowledged by God; if this life of ours is exposed to many calamities, we have the hope of a better life, which will be free of all toil and sorrow. Nothing is therefore strange if the world opposes us, for we have not placed our happiness in it. Why should we expect happiness from the most unhappy world? But it is enough and more than enough for us that, in the midst of straits, we are sustained by God's voice and by his most certain promises. From this it follows that in the midst of misery we grasp happiness, in sorrows joy, in labors rest, and in death itself life. Our happiness is not earthly but heavenly; it depends not on men but on God; it is not external, but is conceived, nourished, and perfected within by the very Word of God. It does not penetrate the eyes of unbelievers, whom the empty glitter of present and external things dazzles. Faith alone, faith alone, I say, looks upon our happiness with pure eyes and rests wholly in its contemplation. Let those impure men fare well, for whom true happiness cannot be pleasing, all the more wretched because they rejoice in their miseries and even think misery itself to be happiness. For what will they say of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom sacred history records as having lived in almost continual labors? Will they dare to call even Christ unhappy, whom the world despised, rejected, and finally afflicted with the cross and the most bitter sorrows? Therefore it must be said that those are blessed who are pronounced blessed by the judgment of God, not by the judgment of men. Nor should we listen to those who place happiness in fleeting and perishable things, and call wretched those who have turned their minds away from the desire for and trust in such things. Let us rather hear our David exclaiming, that those are happy whose sins the Lord has forgiven.

units.la: Nam vt hæc doctrina nobis accommode-tur, quæ tanta potest esse fœlicitas, quàm si de Dei misericordia & summo erga nos fauore sinus persuasi? Quod vt melius intelligamus, expendamus quaeso, & serio expendamus peccatorum nostrorum grauitatem. Quanta enim fuit nostra ingratitudo aduersus Dei beneficentia? quanta stupiditas in consideradis eius erga nos meritis? quàta leuitas in obliuiscendis? quàta peruicacia in reiiciendis? quàta porrò incredulitas? quot concupiscetiæ? quæ perfidia? Atque vt vno verbo dicā, quanta vitiorum omnium colluuies? Quid ergo restabat, nisi vt nosDominus procul eiiceret à suo vultu & in æternę mortis voragine præcipites daret? Quinetiam vt nobis somnū excuteret, videamus quot & quantas plagas nobis infli-xerit. Collapsæ variis in locis orbis Christiani iacent Ecclesiæ, iacet præclarus ille ordo qui in sanctis illis cœtibus relucebat, iacent piorū cadauera, vel potius non iacet, sed insepulta varie a fluctibus iactantur. Hęc autē omnia a iusto Dei nobis irascetis[?] iudicio profecta sunt. Quis ergo nostrum non exhorrescat? quis non tremat ad tāta Dei iudicia? quis non gemat in tot tātisque doloribus? Hic igitur nobis occurrere debet pręclara hæc Dauidis sentętia, quæ nos in mediis angustiis & in tanta dolorū acerbitate sustentet: fœlices, in-quit, sunt ij, quibus peccata remissa sunt. Ergo si ex animo peccata nostra agnoscimus, si supplices ad Dei misericordiā confugimus, si gemitus, si lacrymas ad summum eius tribunal profundimus, non dubium est quin ista vox dulcissima in animis nostris resonet: vobis vestra transgressio remissa est & vestra peccata sunt tecta. Itaq; summa hanc Patris nostri misericordiā amplectamur, atq; jam una cum Dauide profitemur nos esse fœlices, in quorum animis Dominus inscripserit fiduciam certissimā de peccatorum nostrorum remissione. Ergo ad eius thronum per Christum cum vera fide accedamus, freti verissimis eius promissionibus: ipsum ex animo colamus, reuereamur, adoremus: ut ita pacatis conscientiis placida quiete in animis nostris sentiamus. Hæc igitur omnia nobis cogitāda sunt cum hęc Dauidis verba meditamur: Beatus est ille cui transgressio (sua) remissa est.
units.tr: For how can this doctrine be applied to us? What happiness can be as great as to be persuaded in our hearts of God's mercy and his highest favor toward us? That we may understand this better, let us weigh, I beg, and weigh seriously, the gravity of our sins. How great was our ingratitude toward God's beneficence? How great our stupidity in considering his merits toward us? How great our levity in forgetting them? How great our obstinacy in rejecting them? How great, moreover, our unbelief? How many our lusts? What treachery? And, to say it in one word, what a sewer of all vices we are! What then remained, except that the Lord should cast us far from his face and hurl us headlong into the abyss of eternal death? Moreover, let us see how many and how great the blows he has inflicted on us, to shake sleep from our eyes. The churches of the Christian world lie collapsed in various places; that famous order which shone in those holy assemblies lies prostrate; the corpses of the pious lie there, or rather do not lie, but are tossed about unburied by the waves in various directions. All these things have proceeded from the just judgment of God. Who among us then does not shudder? Who does not tremble at such great judgments of God? Who does not groan under so many and so great sorrows? Here, then, this famous saying of David ought to meet us, to sustain us in the midst of distress and in such bitterness of sorrow: "Happy," he says, "are those whose sins are forgiven." Therefore, if we acknowledge our sins from the heart, if we flee as suppliants to God's mercy, if we pour out groans and tears before his supreme tribunal, there is no doubt that this sweetest voice resounds in our souls: "Your transgression is forgiven you, and your sins are covered." Let us therefore embrace this mercy of our Father, and now, with David, let us profess that we are happy, in whose minds the Lord has written a most certain confidence in the remission of our sins. Let us therefore approach his throne through Christ with true faith, relying on his most true promises. Let us worship, revere, and adore him from the heart, so that with consciences at peace we may feel a calm quiet in our minds. All these things must be thought over by us when we meditate on these words of David: Blessed is he whose transgression (his) is forgiven.

units.la: Postquam ex superioribus intelleximus quanti sit nobis facienda hæc doctrina de peccatorum remissione, utpote in quas summum hominis bonum & cumulata fœlicitas collocari debeat, refutatis iis qui existimat aliunde quam ex hoc fonte fœlicitatem esse hauriendam: iam aliud etiam se offert considerandum in his nostri Prophetę verbis: Nempe remissionem peccatorum nobis debere ef[?] fio pecca-se certò persuasam, vt animi nostri in hac certa & indubitata fiducia, tanquam in suauissi-ma tranquillitate conquiescant. Si enim pec-catorum remissio fœlicitatem nostram com-plectitur, si porrò nulla merito dici potest hominis fœlicitas, nisi ab homine sentiatur: quis non videt, aut remissionem peccati nul-lam fœlicitatem præstare, aut certè eam sen-tiendam, &, vt extensis manibus, sic vera & certissima fide esse prehendendam? Et, quod totius rei caput est, nisi adsit illa de qua agi-mus certitudo, nónne necesse est miseras cō-scientias in perpetuo dolore versari? Nec enim possumus dubitare an remissa sint nobis peccata, nec-ne, quin grauissimos cruciatus secum afferat illa dubitatio. Quandoquidem metus æternæ mortis & horror iudiciorum Dei nobis semper obuersabitur, qua cogitatione nihil accidere potest acerbius, nihil mi serabilius, nedum vel tantulum sensum fœlicitatis habeamus. Nempe verum est quod dici solet, nullam esse voluptatem in expectatione alicuius boni, si adiunctus est mali contrarij metus. Quod si summa improborum hominū infœlicitas vel in eo maxime consistit quòd peccati aculeis urgentur, quòd Deum[?] iratum sentiunt, & ad eius tribunal contremiscut: quis merito negarit piorum fœlicitatem in eo maximè elucere, quòd suis peccatis à Dei misericordia condonatis, paternum Dei fauorem persentiunt? Atqui tantum bonum, sublata ista quam tractamus certitudine, nobis contingere nullo modo potest. Ergo, ut res tota paucis conficiatur, cùm nulla sit fœlicitas nisi quis ea perfruatur (alioquin erit adumbratum potius simulachrum, quàm verum & solidum corpus fœlicitatis) cúmque nemo fœlicitate frui possit, quin eam sentiat: nemo sentire, quin habeat: nemo habere, qui de ea dubitet: Efficitur profectò tunc demum nos esse fœlices, cùm de remissione peccatorum certi sumus. Atque ut hoc ad res alias translatum magis elucescat, num, cedò, aliquis dici potest frui diuitiis, qui an habeat diuitias nec ne, incertus sit? num regiis honoribus ille fruitur, qui dubitat an eos unquam sit adepturus? Ita nec existimandum est ullam esse in remissione peccatorum fœlicitatem, si absit certa & indubitata remissionis fiducia. Quocirca in hoc Psalmo Dauid nō dubitat affirmare se venia peccati à Domino fuisse confecutū: quod etiā significat in Psal.51. cùm petit à Domino lætitiam salutis & spiritum verè liberum: quæ omnia nō possunt alia ratione quàm hac certa fiducia, de qua agimus comparari. Quid quòd ipse Christus toties remissa esse peccata multis affirmauit? Sic enim affatur Paraly-ticum illum apud Matthæum: fili, inquit, sis bono animo: peccata tua tibi sunt remissa. quibus verbis respondetur extra omnem con-trouersiam. Constat enim Christum voluisse persuasionem veniæ isti paralytico omnino impressam esse, ut ex illa fiducia animum re-ciperet. Dulcis etiam est hæc vox apud Iohan{1}nem: Filioli, vobis, inquit, scribo quoniam re-missa sunt vobis peccata. Quemadmodum etiam Apostolus pronuntiat nos tunc demum vera frui pace conscientiæ, quando certi su-mus de nostra per Christum iustificatione: quam idem Apostolus alio loco comprehen-dit nomine remissionis peccatorum. Atque si exemplis locus iste illustrandus esset, ille i-pse Apostolus nobis occurreret, cuius fides & persuasio de Dei erga se & pios omnes a-more, tanta fuit, ut vel auderet morti ipsi in-sultare. Mihi, inquit, persuasum est neque mortem, neque vitam, neque Angelos, ne-que principatus, neque potestates, neque in-stantia, neque futura, neque sublimitatem, ne-que profunditatem, neque vllam rem aliam creatam posse nos separare à charitate Dei quæ est in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. At fieri non potest, ut quis sibi recte persuadeat amari se à Deo, quin etiam eadem fiducia re-missionem peccatorum amplectatur. Quan-diu enim peccata nostra vigent coram oculis Dei, necessario accendunt eius iram, nec nos unquam amare potest nisi cum peccatorum nostrorum remissione. Statuamus ergo, cum tanta sit Dei erga nos liberalitas tantusque fauor, ut nobis in unico Filio Domino nostro veniam offerat, nostras esse partes eam vera & certa fide recipere, ut accepta remissione felices simus quemadmodum docet noster vates.
units.tr: Having seen from what has gone before how greatly this doctrine of the remission of sins is to be valued, since in it the highest good of man and his fullest happiness must be placed, and having set aside those who think happiness is to be drawn from any source other than this one, there is another matter to consider in the words of our Prophet. We ought to be firmly persuaded that our sins are forgiven, so that our minds may rest in this sure and unshakeable confidence, as in the sweetest tranquillity. For if the remission of sins embraces our happiness, and if no one can rightly be called happy unless he feels it, who does not see that either the remission of sin brings no happiness at all, or else it must be felt and grasped by a true and certain faith, as one grasps with outstretched hands? And, which is the heart of the whole matter, unless that certainty of which we are speaking is present, must not wretched consciences necessarily remain in constant grief? For we cannot doubt whether our sins have been forgiven or not without that doubt bringing very grievous torments with it. Since the fear of eternal death and the dread of God's judgements will always confront us, and nothing more bitter or more miserable can come to mind than this thought, we cannot even have the slightest sense of happiness. It is indeed true, as is commonly said, that there is no pleasure in expecting some good when the fear of the contrary evil is attached to it. If the chief unhappiness of the wicked lies especially in this, that they are pricked by the goads of sin, that they feel God to be angry and tremble before his judgement seat, who could rightly deny that the happiness of the godly shines forth chiefly in this, that, with their sins pardoned by God's mercy, they perceive the fatherly favour of God? But such a great good can in no way come to us if the certainty we are discussing is taken away. Therefore, to bring the whole matter to a conclusion in few words: since there is no happiness unless one enjoys it (otherwise what we have would be a shadow of happiness rather than its true and solid body), and since no one can enjoy happiness without feeling it, and no one feel it without possessing it, and no one possess it who doubts it, it follows surely that we are then at last happy when we are certain of the remission of our sins. And to make this clearer by applying it to other things: can anyone, I ask, be said to enjoy riches if he is uncertain whether he has riches or not? Does he enjoy royal honours who doubts whether he will ever obtain them? So neither ought we to think that there is any happiness in the remission of sins if a sure and undoubting confidence in that remission is lacking. Hence in this Psalm David does not hesitate to affirm that he obtained pardon of his sin from the Lord; which he also signifies in Psalm 51, when he asks the Lord for the joy of salvation and a spirit truly free; and all these things cannot be obtained by any means other than this certain confidence of which we speak. What of the fact that Christ himself often affirmed that sins were forgiven to many? For so he addresses the paralytic in Matthew: "Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you." By these words it is answered beyond all controversy. For it is plain that Christ wished the persuasion of pardon to be fully impressed upon that paralytic, so that he might take heart from that confidence. Sweet too is this voice in John: "Little children, I write to you, because your sins are forgiven you." In the same way the Apostle declares that we then truly enjoy the peace of conscience when we are certain of our justification through Christ, which the same Apostle elsewhere calls by the name of the remission of sins. And if this place were to be illustrated by examples, that very Apostle would meet us, whose faith and persuasion of God's love towards himself and all the godly was so great that he dared to mock death itself. "I am persuaded," he says, "that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." But it cannot happen that someone rightly persuades himself that he is loved by God without also embracing the remission of sins with the same confidence. For as long as our sins stand before the eyes of God, they necessarily kindle his anger, nor can he ever love us except with the remission of our sins. Let us therefore establish this: since God's generosity and favour towards us is so great that he offers us pardon in his one Son our Lord, it is our part to receive it with a true and certain faith, so that, having received the remission, we may be happy, as our prophet teaches.

units.la: Obiiciunt Pontificij qui huic nostrae de certa fiducia doctrinae, id est verae felicitati & conscientiarum tranquillitati bellum inferre dixerunt: Non decere Christianum hominem illam iactare fiduciam, quam aiunt non procul abesse, aut a superbia aut sane a temeritate: nosque iubet perpetuis dubitationum fluctibus agitari: quasi vero ista dubitatio sit magis consentanea humilitati ac mansuetudini Christianae. Atqui (ut illis respondeamus) dum humiles esse volunt, in summam perfidiam incidunt, qua nihil dici potest arrogantius. Hoc enim est in dubium revocare veritatem promissionum Dei & eum (ut ait Iohannes) mendacij arguere. Praeterea ecquid-nam profitetur se credere in Symbolo, quando dicunt se credere remissionem peccatorum? Respondent, hanc se remissionem credere generalem quidem, non autem eam quę unicuique privatim concedatur. At nihil unquam dici potuit absurdius. Quodnam enim, obsecro, est primum verbum Symboli? Credo, inquiunt: cur ergo non dicunt plurali numero, credimus? Nónne ipsa luce clarius est, hunc huius verbi sensum esse, nos debere nobis ipsis accomodare ea omnia quæ in Symbolo continentur? Cuius autem erit impudentiæ aut potius infidelitatis, te credere aliis peccata sua remitti, non autem tibi? Quod perinde est ac si quis se diuite esse credat, eo-quod permulti diuitias possident: se satiari, quia alij manducant, se videre, quia alij oculos habent. Falleris, mi homo, tibi enim pro-fitendæ sunt propriæ, non alienæ diuitiæ, tuo ore tibi manducandum, tuis oculis tibi videndum, id est, ut ait Propheta, tibi tua fide vi-uedum est. Cur enim dicimur habere pignus & arrhabonē sancti Spiritus in cordibus no-stris, nisi quia unicuique fidelium obsignan-tur promissiones generales, ita ut de illis dubitare non liceat? Quod etiam ut expressius significaret Dominus, instituit sua Sacramen-ta quæ piorū unusquisque percipit, ut ita per suum habeat, promissiones eas quæ verbis generalibus conceptæ sunt ad se etiam priua-tim pertinere. Contra vero cùm de dubita-tione Scriptura loquitur, eam adeò reiicit, ut Iacobus asserat eos qui dubitanter precantur, nunquam obtinere quod postulant: quo in loco egregiè istam dubitationem exagitat & eam comparat cum maris fluctibus à vento agitatis. Sed hoc vel unum argumentum debet sufficere, quòd dubitatio sit prorsus fidei contraria, adeò, ut hæc cum illa coniungi nulla ratione possit. Ergo scitè Hebraei: apud quos idem verbum & cōfidere & recumbere atq; inniti significat: vt videre licet apud Solomonem. Ex quibus omnibus concludendum est Pontificiorum doctrinam de dubitatione nobis fine dubitatione repudiandam, fiquidē nostro vati vel potius Spiritui fanǰto volumus assentiri.
units.tr: The Papists, who have declared war on this doctrine of ours concerning certain confidence, that is, on true happiness and the tranquillity of consciences, object that it is not fitting for a Christian man to boast of that confidence, which they say is not far removed either from pride or at least from rashness; and they bid us be tossed about by the perpetual waves of doubt, as if that doubt were more in keeping with Christian humility and gentleness. Yet (to answer them) while they wish to be humble, they fall into the greatest faithlessness, than which nothing can be said to be more arrogant. For this is to call into question the truth of God's promises and (as John says) to charge him with lying. Moreover, what do they profess to believe in the Creed when they say they believe in the remission of sins? They answer that they believe this remission to be general, but not that which is granted to each individual privately. Yet nothing more absurd could ever be said. For what, I beg you, is the first word of the Creed? "I believe," they say: why then do they not say in the plural, "we believe"? Is it not clearer than light itself that the meaning of this word is that we ought to apply to ourselves all the things which are contained in the Creed? But whose shamelessness, or rather faithlessness, would it be to believe that sins are remitted to others but not to yourself? This is just as if someone should believe himself rich because many possess riches, or be satisfied because others eat, or see because others have eyes. You are mistaken, my friend: for it is your own riches, not another's, that you must profess; you must eat with your own mouth, and see with your own eyes; that is, as the Prophet says, you must live by your own faith. For why are we said to have the pledge and earnest of the Holy Spirit in our hearts, unless because the general promises are sealed to each one of the faithful, so that it is not lawful to doubt them? To signify this more plainly, the Lord also instituted his Sacraments, which each of the godly receives, so that he may thus possess for himself those promises, couched in general terms, as pertaining to himself privately as well. On the other hand, when Scripture speaks of doubting, it so rejects it that James asserts that those who pray doubtingly never obtain what they ask; in that passage he vigorously assails that doubt and compares it with the waves of the sea stirred by the wind. But this one argument ought to be enough, that doubt is utterly contrary to faith, so much so that the two can in no way be joined. Hence the Hebrews rightly note that the same word signifies both to trust and to lean upon and rest on, as may be seen in Solomon. From all these things it must be concluded that the Papists' doctrine of doubt is without doubt to be rejected, if we wish to assent to our prophet, or rather to the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Iam videamus quonam pacto nobis hæc doctrina accommodanda fit. Omninò duo sunt hominum genera quibus hæc in primis doctrina inculcanda est. Vnum est eorum qui nullo peccati sensu tanguntur: alterum eorum qui nimio peccati sensu & diuini iudicij terrore opprimuntur. Ergo de illis prioribus agamus. Dici non potest quam fit periculosus ille stupor quo peccata nostra non sen-timus. Et sanè (vt initiò diximus) mirum est Satanam ita hominibus posse illudere, vt o-nusti atque etiam obruti peccatorum pondere,non tamen sentiat onus illud grauiffimu, sed tāquam expediti & onere leuati exultent. Tu flagitiis omnibus deditus, tu peccatis omnibus immersus es,& in medium mare conjectus, mare non fentis? Tu carnis & concupi-fcentiae subiectis facibus totus deflagras,& tamen in media libidinum flāma, flammam non fentis? Iam instant Dei iudicia, iam apertae sunt inferorum fauces, iam ipsius mortis telum vibratum est,& obstupescis? Te grauis[?]mae Dei minae non commouent? non percellunt? cellunt? [?] Tibi tot iudiciorum Dei exempla praeterita, tot poenae iam inflictae, tot rursus, nisi resipiscas, infligendae, tot damna, angustiae, calamitates, tot denique mortis genera tibi stu-poris somnum non excutiunt? O infoelicem illam hominum vitam quae mortis aeternae materia est, & in qua sic ad aliquod tempus viuitur, vt moriendum sit in aeternum! Ergo nobis exorandus est Deus, vt abiecta omni stu-piditate, serio peccatorum nostrorum sensu ita afficiamur, vt nos ipsi damnemus, nobis displiceamus, ad ipsius horrenda iudicia tremamus, & ad summam eius misericordiam nobis in Christo exhibitam per ipsum Christum vera fide recurramus.
units.tr: Let us now see how this doctrine is to be applied to us. There are two kinds of people to whom this teaching above all must be pressed. One is those who are touched by no sense of sin; the other is those who are crushed by a great sense of sin and by terror of God's judgment. Let us deal first with the former. It cannot be said how dangerous that stupor is by which we do not feel our sins. And indeed (as I said at the beginning) it is remarkable that Satan can so deceive people that, though they are loaded and even overwhelmed by the weight of their sins, they do not feel that very heavy burden, but rejoice as if they were unencumbered and relieved of the load. You are given over to every shameful deed, you are plunged into every sin, and thrown into the middle of the sea: do you not feel the sea? You are wholly ablaze, with the torches of the flesh and desire set alight: and yet in the midst of the flame of lust, do you not feel the fire? Now the judgments of God are at hand, now the jaws of hell are open, now the very shaft of death has been hurled: and do you stand amazed? Do the most grievous threats of God not move you? Do they not strike you down? Do the many judgments of God in past times, the many punishments already inflicted, and the many more still to be inflicted unless you repent, the many losses, distresses and calamities, and finally the many kinds of death, not shake the sleep of stupor from you? O unhappy human life, which is the material of eternal death, and in which one lives for a time in such a way that one must die for ever! Therefore we must pray to God that, casting off all stupidity, we may be so affected by a serious sense of our sins that we condemn ourselves, are displeased with ourselves, tremble at his dreadful judgments, and with true faith flee to his supreme mercy offered to us in Christ, through Christ himself.

units.la: Qui vero peccatorum sensu adeo perculsus est, adeo prostratus, vt eius fides sit quodammodo labefactata & se in desperationem propemodum coniiciat, au- diat hac Dauidis vocem suauissimam: O beatum illum cui sua transgressio remissa est! existima Dauidem non procul abesse, sed tecum verba facere, te consolari, tibi manum porrigere, vt te ex tetra illa desperationis spelunca sal-uum educat. [?]
units.tr: But whoever is so struck down and so prostrated by the sense of sin that his faith is in some way shaken and he almost casts himself into despair, let him hear this most sweet voice of David: O blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven! Imagine David not far off, but speaking with you, consoling you, stretching out his hand to you, that he may lead you safely out of that foul cave of despair.

units.la: Te miserrimum esse conqueraris, at ille te beatissimum esse praedicat: tu peccatorum tuorum numerum & onus (vt ille dicebat) Aetna gravius ostendis, ille peccata tua deleta & te a peccatis liberatum esse pronuntiat. Quid est igitur quod te auertat a tanta consolatione recipienda? Annon satis idoneus videtur esse testis summus hic Dei seruus,cuius ore Spiritus sanctus locutus est? Sed age, attende ad vocem tui Redemptoris audi quibus te verbis ad se reuocet Dominus & Seruator noster Iesus Christus: Venite, inquit, ad me omnes qui onerati estis, qui defatigati estis, quorum animus deficit sub ingenti & grauissima mole peccatorum. Tu vero quid ad hæc dicturus es? Si te peccatorem agnoscis, peccatores ad se vocat Christus: si plurimis peccatis onustus vix spiritum ducis, ergo ille ipse es ad quem paterna illa vox Seruatoris dirigitur: ergo accede ad Christum & peccatorum remissionem quam tibi offert amplectere. Ille in se receptis tuis peccatis, in te iustitiam suam confert & propria morte persolutis tuorum peccatorum poenis, te facit suæ quietis participem. Hæc igitur nobis occurrant quoties Satan in animos nostros quasi desperationis faces iniiciet, ut eas certa fide & apprehensione misericordiæ Dei restinguamus, atque recepta peccatorum remissione nos iam esse felicissimos vna cum Dauide constanter affirmemus.
units.tr: You complain that you are most wretched, but he proclaims you most blessed; you point to the number and burden of your sins, heavier (as he said) than Aetna, but he pronounces your sins blotted out and you freed from sin. What is it then that turns you away from receiving so great a consolation? Does not this chief servant of God, through whose mouth the Holy Spirit spoke, seem a sufficient witness? But come, attend to the voice of your Redeemer, and hear with what words our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ calls you back to himself: "Come to me," he says, "all you who are burdened, who are weary, whose spirit fails under the huge and crushing weight of sins." And what will you say in reply? If you acknowledge yourself a sinner, Christ calls sinners to himself; if you are so weighed down by many sins that you scarcely draw breath, then you are the very one to whom that fatherly voice of the Saviour is directed. Therefore come to Christ and embrace the forgiveness of sins that he offers you. He, having taken your sins upon himself, confers his righteousness upon you, and by his own death, having paid the penalties of your sins, makes you a partaker of his rest. So let these thoughts meet us whenever Satan throws into our minds, as it were, the torches of despair; let us quench them with a sure faith and a grasp of the mercy of God, and, with the forgiveness of sins received, steadfastly affirm with David that we are already most blessed.

units.la: Iam tempus est verba ipsa Dauidis propius inspicere, ut inde etiam nobis aliqua constet utilitas. Beatus, inquit, cui transgressio remissa & cuius tectum est peccatum.
units.tr: Now it is time to look more closely at David's own words, so that some profit may also be gained from them. "Blessed," he says, "is he whose transgression is forgiven, and whose sin is covered."

units.la: vers. 2. Beatus homo cui Æternus non imputabit iniquitatem.Meminit igitur transgressionis remissæ, peccati tecti, & iniquitatis non imputatæ. De ipsa remissione iam tractauimus:nunc de peccato tegendo, deque iniqui-tate non imputata nobis agendum est. Ac primum cum Dauidi non satis fuit vti vno sio peccā[?] verbo, sed rem eandem voluit verbis pluri-bus explicare, eo nos voluit admonitos istam remissionem de qua agit, maximi momenti & esse, vt ad quam explicandam nulla sufficere possit oratio. Deinde illam esse absolutam & perfectā, ne forte suspicemur peccata nobis tantum ex parte condonari. Quae dubitatio si-quādo inualuerit, non tatum nobis omnem fiduciam salutis excutiet, verumetiā coniiciet in acerbissimos dolores atque cruciatus. Ita-que docet vates peccata omnino nobis con-donari, nequid superest dubitationis. Remit-titur, inquit, transgressio, tegitur peccatum, non imputatur iniquitas, quae gradatio nobis est obseruanda: videtur enim priora a sequen-tibus fusius & facilius explicari. Nam si dubi-tem quid sit, transgressionem remitti, docet id fieri, quia tegitur coram Deo ne illius oculis pateat. Rursus si nec id quidem mihi satis facile videatur, subiicit, Deum illam non mi-hi imputare, id est, me perinde haberi ac si non fuerim ipsius legem transgressus.
units.tr: Verse 2: "Blessed is the man to whom the Eternal will not impute iniquity." He therefore speaks of forgiven transgression, covered sin, and iniquity not imputed. We have already treated the forgiveness itself; now we must speak of covering sin and of iniquity not imputed to us. First, since David was not content to use one word for sin, but wished to explain the same thing with several words, he meant to warn us that the forgiveness he is speaking of is of the greatest importance, so that no speech can be sufficient to explain it. Next, he means that it is complete and perfect, lest we perhaps suspect that our sins are pardoned only in part. If such doubt should ever gain ground, it would not only shake from us all confidence of salvation, but would also throw us into the bitterest pains and torments. So the prophet teaches that our sins are wholly forgiven, so that no room for doubt remains. "Transgression," he says, "is forgiven, sin is covered, iniquity is not imputed"; this order is to be observed, for the earlier terms seem to be explained more fully and more easily by those that follow. For if I doubt what it means that transgression is forgiven, he teaches that this happens because it is covered before God, so that it is not exposed to his eyes. Again, if even this seems to me not easy enough, he adds that God does not impute it to me, that is, that I am regarded just as if I had never transgressed his law.

units.la: Sed me fortasis peccatorum grauitas ab hac fiducia retardauerit cogitantem toties & tam grauiter peccasse, vt mihi ad Dei miseri- cordiam ipsa mea peccata viam intercludat: Ergo, ne ista cogitatio in animos nostros ir- repat, obseruemus Dauidem' pluribus vocabulis expressisse peccatum, cùm modò trans-gressionem, modò peccatum,modò etiam i-niquitatem vocat,ut hac ratione doceat,qua-lecunque tandem sit peccatum, illud nobis à summa Dei misericordia remitti.
units.tr: But perhaps the gravity of my sins will hold me back from this confidence, as I think that I have sinned so often and so grievously that my very sins block my way to God's mercy.
