So, lest such a thought creep into our minds, let us observe that David expressed sin by many words: at one time he calls it transgression, at another sin, and at another iniquity, so that he may teach by this means that, whatever sort of sin it may be, it is forgiven us by the supreme mercy of God.

units.la: Cæterum verbum tegendi & occultandi minus fortasse consentaneum videri possit. Constat enim omnia esse Dei oculis exposi-ta, quibus etiam patent ipsæ cogitationes in intimis sensibus delitescentes,nedum peccatum possit vlla ratione occultari.
units.tr: Moreover, the word "covering" and "hiding" may perhaps seem less fitting. For it is agreed that all things are laid open to the eyes of God, to whom even the thoughts hidden in the innermost feelings are open; much less can sin be hidden in any way.

units.la: Respondeo solius esse Dei ea vocare quæ non sunt,ac si essent(ut ait Apostolus)& contra, facere, ut quæ sunt, perinde censeatur ac si non essent. Quare cùm dicimus peccata esse tecta, non in eam partem accipimus, quasi aliquid possit Deum latere, cuius oculis omnia sunt conspicua, atque adeò ipsæ profundissimæ abyssus apertæ sunt atque peruiæ, quæ admodum merito Psaltes exclamabat, Quò fugiam à facie tua? Sed quia Deus ipse tegit & occultat peccata, quando illa delet ac remit-tit habetque pro non commissis. Itaque huc proferendi sunt illi loci qui disserunt de hac ipsa remissione & affirmat peccatorum me-moriam coram Domino penitus aboleri. Delebo, inquit, peccata tua instar nubis, quæ sci-licet statim euanescit: Abiiciam ea in fundum maris, ea procul remouebo quemadmodum Oriens distat ab Occidente: Si rubuerint in-star coccini, albescent instar niuis: Et alij loci consimiles, quibus nihil aliud significatur quàm quod alibi dicitur, Deum non fore me morem peccatorum nostrorum,&hîc,peccata tegi,id est,prorsus deleri. Cùm enim nihil coram Deo tegi possit, efficitur id amplius non esse, quod coram Deo tectum esse dicitur. Quod etiam aliquomodo significare voluit Dauid ipsa vocabulorum allusione nepe[?] Nasuj & Casuj: quasi dicat, peccata tecta esse quæ remissa sunt. Et certè genus illud loquendi mirum in modum efficax est, vt magis exprimat quàm sit illorum misera conditio quibus peccata non sunt condonata, cùm videlicet semper exposita sint acerrimis Dei oculis, ex quo necessarium est consequi poenas gra-vissimas, vt iam antè exposuimus. Quò fit vt cùm Propheta conqueritur de multis ac variis Israëlitarum afflictionibus, dicat Domi-num posuisse eorū peccata in conspectu suo.
units.tr: I answer that to call those things that are not as if they were (as the Apostle says) belongs to God alone, and, on the other hand, to make things that are be regarded as if they were not. Therefore when we say that sins are covered, we do not take it in the sense that anything can be hidden from God, to whose eyes all things are visible, and indeed the most profound abysses are open and penetrable, as the Psalmist rightly cried out, "Whither shall I flee from your face?" Rather, God himself covers and hides sins when he blots them out and forgives them, and holds them as not committed. Accordingly, those passages are to be cited here which treat of this very forgiveness and affirm that the memory of sins is wholly abolished before the Lord. "I will blot out your sins," he says, "like a cloud," which of course vanishes at once; "I will cast them into the depths of the sea, I will remove them far off, as the East is distant from the West"; "if they are red like scarlet, they shall become white as snow." And other similar passages, which signify nothing else than what is said elsewhere, that God will not remember our sins; and here, that sins are covered, that is, utterly blotted out. For since nothing can be covered before God, it follows that what is said to be covered before God no longer exists. David also wished to express this by a play on words, namely Nasuj and Casuj, as if he said that sins are covered which have been forgiven. And certainly that manner of speaking is wonderfully effective, to express more fully the miserable state of those whose sins have not been pardoned, since they are of course always exposed to the most piercing eyes of God, from which it necessarily follows that they suffer the gravest punishments, as we have already explained above. Hence it is that when the Prophet complains of the many and various afflictions of the Israelites, he says that the Lord has set their sins in his sight.

units.la: Quid ergo de iis dicendum est qui existi-mant peccata sua occulta esse, modò fuerint hominibus insciis admissa? quasi verò pluris fit hominum quàm Dei scientia. Quî fit igi-tur vt hominum conspectum verearis, nec tetamen Dei vultus à peccado deterreat? Quid tibi proderit homines latuisse, cùm summus ille iudex oculis omnia peruestigantibus tua peccata animaduerterit? imò cur non potius, quantum in te est, detegis, vt vulnera, ita pec-cata tua coram summo illo & clementissimo medico, vt iis medeatur? Quis æger vnquam texit sua vulnera, ac non potius explicuit coram medico remedium aliquod allaturo? Explica igitur vulnus: tunc enim erit vere tectum, cum erit sanatum. Præclarè sanè à veteribus dictum est neminem sine teste peccare, quia conscientia est instar mille testium: cuius conscientiæ definitio rem etiam ipsam satis declarat: arguit enim te ita peccare ut peccatum tuum non possit occultari, cum vel tu tibi ipse tui criminis sis conscius. Quinetiam si te ipse audies, eris tuus & accusator & iudex. Et sanè in ipsa conscientia insculpta sunt manifesta diuini iudicij vestigia, cum te ipsa redarguat peccantem & intus accuset [?] coram summo illo iudice ad cuius tribunal te stit. Itaque concludendum est, peccatum reipsa detectum esse & apertum, quanuis hominibus incognitum fuerit: tunc autem dici potest tectum & occultum, quando coram Deo tegitur, id est, ut iam sæpius diximus, quando remittitur à Deo.
units.tr: What then should be said about those who think their sins are hidden, provided they were committed without men knowing? As if men's knowledge were greater than God's! How is it, then, that you fear the sight of men, yet the countenance of God does not deter you from sin? What will it profit you that men did not notice, when that supreme judge, whose eyes search out everything, has seen your sins? Why not rather, as far as you can, disclose them, just as you show your wounds, before that supreme and most merciful physician, so that he may heal them? What sick man ever covered his wounds rather than showing them to a doctor who was about to bring a remedy? Lay open the wound, then: it will truly be covered when it has been healed. The ancients rightly said that no one sins without a witness, because conscience is like a thousand witnesses. The very definition of conscience makes the point clear enough: it convicts you of sinning in such a way that your sin cannot be concealed, since you yourself are aware of your crime. Moreover, if you listen to yourself, you will be both your own accuser and your own judge. Indeed, the clear traces of divine judgment are engraved in conscience itself, since it convicts you while you sin and accuses you inwardly before that supreme judge before whose tribunal you stand. We must therefore conclude that sin is in fact disclosed and open, even if it is unknown to men. It can then be called covered and hidden when it is covered before God, that is, as we have said many times, when it is forgiven by God.

units.la: Sunt etiam alij qui conatus quidem omnes adhibent ad peccata sua coram Deo tegeda, sed eius rei nō rectam rationem ineunt, cum peccata humanis satisfactionibus tegi posse sibi persuadeant, atque ita, quid proprie sit peccatū, ignorant. Num enim, obsecro, leue est Deum offendere, cum necesse fuerit sacrū illum Domini nostri sanguinem semel effundi di ad peccatorum nostrorum sordes abluendas? Nimirum sumus Adami primi omnium parentis perquàm similes, qui post peccatum seipsè foliis tegere conabatur. Cum igitur miseros & cæcos illos homines huc & illuc curritantes video, ut conscientiæ vulneribus aliquam faciant medicinam, id est, ut suæ tur-pitudini consuant vana foliorum integumen-ta, aut (vt ait Nazianzenus) luto lutum pur-gent: cùm video & viuos & mortuos inuo-cari, superstitionem addi superstitioni, tem-pla idolis extrui, pœnas ipsis corporibus in-fligi & alia id genus plurima (quis enim om-nes idololatrarum errores enumeret?) mihi certè videre videor insanos homines ligni struem ingentem in ignem coniicientes, ut scilicet ipsum ignem extinguant. Atqui quo[?] plus ligni congeris, eo maiorem vim flam-marum excitas eóque fiunt maiora incen-dia. Ita etiam cum peregrinaris, cum missis decantandis opes & operam insumis & per-dis, cum surdas idolorum aures vanis precum susurrationibus solicitas, quid, cedò, aliud quàm noua peccata semper congerens, accensam in te iram Dei magis ac magis inflam-mas? Porrò cum te nihilominus conscientiæ stimulus urgeat, satis magno argumento esse debet, peccata tua tecta non esse. Audiendus est enim Iohannes, si conscientia, inquit, nos arguit, Deus est maior nostra conscientia. Teneamus igitur, nulla alia ratione tegi posse peccata nostra quàm sola Dei remittentis misericordia.
units.tr: There are also others who make every effort to cover their sins before God, but do not take the right course in this, since they persuade themselves that sins can be covered by human satisfactions, and so they do not know what sin properly is. For, I beg you, is it a light matter to offend God, when it was necessary for that sacred blood of our Lord to be shed once for all to wash away the stains of our sins? We are indeed very like Adam, the first parent of all, who after sinning tried to cover himself with leaves. So when I see those wretched and blind men running here and there to apply some remedy to the wounds of conscience, that is, to sew on the vain coverings of leaves for their shame, or (as Nazianzen says) to cleanse mud with mud; when I see both the living and the dead invoked, superstition added to superstition, temples built for idols, bodily punishments inflicted, and very many other things of this kind (for who could list all the errors of the idolaters?), I seem to myself to see madmen heaping a huge pile of wood onto a fire, evidently to put the fire out. Yet the more wood you heap on, the greater the force of the flames you kindle, and the fiercer the blaze becomes. So too when you go on pilgrimages, when you spend money and effort on sung masses and waste them, when you importune the deaf ears of idols with vain whisperings of prayers, what, I ask, are you doing but always piling up new sins, and inflaming more and more the anger of God that is kindled against you? Furthermore, when the sting of conscience nonetheless presses upon you, this should be strong evidence that your sins are not covered. For John must be heard: if our conscience condemns us, God is greater than our conscience. Let us hold, then, that our sins can be covered by no other means than the mercy of God who forgives them.

units.la: Sed hic fortasse à nobis quæri possit, qua-tenus debeamus peccatorum à nobis admis-sorum esse memores. Et num adeo illa tecta sint, vt debeant etiam à nobis perpetua obli-uione sepeliri. Quam quæstionem vt dissolua-mus, repetendum est quod sæpe fuit à veteri-bus vsurpatum, nempe tunc peccata nobis re-mitti, quando nos ipsos coram Deo accusa-mus: tunc nos iustificari, cùm nos ipsos damna-mus[?]: tunc peccata tecta esse, cùm ea detegi-mus & agnoscimus coram Deo. Debemus igitur nostra peccata reuocare in memoriam non vt de ipsorum remissione dubitemus, sed vt illa recordatio nos reddat magis gratos er-ga Deum, &, ne peccemus in posterum, pru-dentiores. Iuuat etiam illa præteritorum pec-catorum memoria ad retundendam super-biam siquando nos illa inuaserit: vt omittam nos inde etiam reddi fratribus peccantibus æquiores.Hæc omnia & pleraque alia confi-milia obseruanda sunt quando differimus de peccatis nostris coram Deo tegendis.
units.tr: But here perhaps someone may ask us how far we ought to remember the sins we have committed, and whether they are so covered that we too must bury them in perpetual oblivion. To resolve this question we must repeat what the ancients often said: that sins are forgiven us when we accuse ourselves before God; that we are justified when we condemn ourselves; that sins are covered when we disclose and acknowledge them before God. We ought therefore to call our sins to mind, not so that we doubt their forgiveness, but so that this remembrance may make us more grateful towards God and, lest we sin again, more prudent. The memory of past sins also helps to beat down pride, should pride ever assail us; and I say nothing of the fact that it makes us more lenient towards brothers who sin. All these points, and many others like them, are to be observed when we discuss the covering of our sins before God.

units.la: Quid autem de hominibus dicendum est? an etiam optandum erit vt peccata nostra tecta sint coram humanis oculis? Respondeo, id non simpliciter posse definiri. Fieri enim potest, vt ipsa coram hominibus detectio & confessio peccatorum seruiat Dei gloriæ & Ecclesiæ ædificationi: qua in re detegenda sunt peccata ingenuè, & omnis fugienda est tergiuersatio: quemadmodum videmus vsuvenisse Achano Israëlitæ qui dedit gloriam Deo, cum peccatum coram omnibus, hortante & iubente Iosua, confessus est. Quod si potius detrimentum passuri sint proximi, si peccata nostra foras efferantur, tunc rogandus est Dominus, ut ea & coram se & coram hominibus tegat. Sed semper meminerimus nobis Deo non hominibus obsequendum esse, neque nos propterea iustos fore, si nos homines iustificent, sed si Deus ipse non nobis imputet peccatum, quemadmodum hic Dauid testatus est his verbis:
units.tr: But what should be said about men? Is it also to be wished that our sins be covered from human eyes? I answer that this cannot be settled simply. For it can happen that the very disclosure and confession of sins before men serves the glory of God and the edification of the Church. In such a case sins are to be disclosed openly, and all evasion must be avoided, just as we see was done by Achan of Israel, who gave glory to God when he confessed his sin before everyone, at the urging and command of Joshua. But if our neighbours are rather going to suffer harm should our sins be brought out into the open, then the Lord must be asked to cover them both before himself and before men. Yet let us always remember that we must obey God rather than men, and that we shall not be righteous merely because men justify us, but only if God himself does not impute sin to us, as David testifies here in these words:

units.la: Beatus homo cui non imputabit Dominus iniquitatem: Quæ significat peccatum statim reos nos agere coram Deo, ita ut si nobis Dominus peccatum imputet, id est, æstimet tanti quanti est, necesse sit penitus interire. Sic enim alibi: Si iniquitates obseruaueris, ô Æ-terne, quis subsistet? Sed, dicat aliquis, cum Deus summè sit iustus, qui fit ut peccatum non imputet? Nimirum propter Christum mediatorem qui pertulit pœnas nostris peccatis debitas atque ita in causa est quo minus peccata nobis imputentur. Deus (inquit Apostolus) erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputando eis peccata ipsorum. Superest ut Deum ex animo precemur, ut tot crimina a nobis admissa, tantam ingratitudinem, tot tantasque vitæ sordes pro summa sua misericordia condonet: idque propter Christum Redemptorem nostrum. Ut autem eius sanguine in cruce semel effuso peccata nostra sint & remissa & tecta & non imputata, det nobis clementissimus ille Pater veram fidem, qua tantum in Christo beneficium amplectamur. Sequitur apud Davidem:
units.tr: Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute iniquity. This means that we are at once guilty before God, so that if the Lord should impute sin to us, that is, reckon it at its true worth, we must perish utterly. So he says elsewhere: If you mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But someone may say: since God is supremely just, how does it come about that he does not impute sin? Surely on account of Christ the Mediator, who bore the punishments due to our sins, and so is the reason why sins are not imputed to us. God (says the Apostle) was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them. It remains for us to pray to God from the heart that, in his supreme mercy, he would pardon so many crimes committed by us, such great ingratitude, and so many and such great defilements of our life, and that he would do so on account of Christ our Redeemer. And that our sins, by his blood once shed on the cross, may be forgiven, covered and not imputed, may that most merciful Father give us true faith, by which we may embrace so great a benefit in Christ. There follows in David:

units.la: Et non est in Spiritu eius dolus: id est, Beatus ille est in cuius spiritu fraus nulla reperitur. Quae verba hunc habet sensum, foelicem illum esse qui remissionem peccatorum ita ex animo & sine simulatione perceperit, vt a peccato deinceps abhorreat, omninoque studeat iustitiæ atque pietati. Ergo hæc Davidis verba proprie diriguntur aduersus hypocritas, qui licet extrinsecus virtutem colere videantur, intus tamen in animo ipsam oderunt. Præclarè Basilius illud Platonis dictum probat, extremum hunc esse iniustitiæ terminum, eum videri iustum qui non sit iustus: contraque damnat illud Euripidis: Cupio bonus videri, magis quam esse. Et profecto hæc Davidis sententia apte cum superiori cohæret.
units.tr: And there is no guile in his spirit: that is, blessed is the one in whose spirit no fraud is found. These words have this sense: that he is happy who has received the forgiveness of sins so sincerely and without pretence that he thereafter abhors sin and earnestly strives after righteousness and godliness. Therefore these words of David are rightly aimed against hypocrites, who, although they seem outwardly to cultivate virtue, nevertheless inwardly hate it in their heart. Basil well approves that saying of Plato, that the extreme point of injustice is to seem just when one is not; and conversely he condemns that saying of Euripides: I wish to be good rather than to seem good. Indeed, this sentence of David coheres aptly with the preceding one.

units.la: Agebat enim Davidde remissione peccatorum vera fide apprehendenda: nunc pronuntiat necessarium esse vt hypocrisis abesset à nostris animis, siquidem ita vt decet, peccatorum veniam fide sumus adepturi. Quod perinde ac si Davidipse ita nobiscum verba faceret: Hæc foelicitas quam ego vobis tantopere commendo, non in eos cadit qui vana quidem externaque pietatis specie relucent, sed interim impurum animum intus gerunt: Absit à nobis hypocrisis, absit omnis simulatio. Nã hæc nostra fœlicitas candorem mentis requi-rit: ibi moratur, ibi hæret: odit ac refugit frau-dulentas & tenebricosas hypocritarum late-bras, atque in purissima fidei luce versatur. I-taque duæ doctrinæ videntur ex hoc loco no-bis esse colligendæ. Prior est, fidei cum hy-pocrisi nullam esse societatem. Posterior au-tem, ita demum remissa nobis esse peccata, si huius nostræ remissionis & veniæ fructus, id si socie-tas est, pietatis virtutisque studia consequantur.
units.tr: For David was speaking earlier of grasping the forgiveness of sins by true faith; now he declares that hypocrisy must be absent from our minds, since we shall obtain pardon of sins by faith only if we do so as we ought. It is as if David himself were speaking to us in this way: This happiness which I commend to you so earnestly does not fall to those who shine with vain and outward appearances of piety while carrying an impure mind within. Far from us be hypocrisy, far from us be all pretence. For this happiness of ours requires purity of mind: it dwells there, it clings there; it hates and shuns the fraudulent and dark hiding-places of hypocrites, and it lives in the purest light of faith. Thus two teachings seem to be drawn from this passage. The first is that faith has no fellowship with hypocrisy. The second is that our sins are forgiven us only if, as the fruit of this forgiveness and pardon, zeal for godliness and virtue follows, if that can be called a fellowship.

units.la: Atque ut de hypocrisi agamus, nihil repe-rias magis alienum à fidei natura quàm simu-lationem. Ut enim ignis depictus longè dif-fert ab igne vero, cùm ignis solam speciem non etiam effecta & vires habeat: ita hypo-crisis habet quidem aliquam virtutis similitu-dinem, sed si propius accedas, tum reperies i-gnem pictum & adumbratum cuius nec lu-cem videre nec calorem sentire unquam pos-sis. Enimuerò fides sedem habet in corde, hypocrisis in vultu: fides in hoc tota incum-bit ut Deo placeat, hypocrisis ut ab homini-bus approbetur: denique fides viva est, effi-cax, sibíque constans atque perpetua, hypo-crisis autem celeriter tanquam flosculus deci-dit & detracto vano pietatis fuco & colore, inanis iacet & marcescit: ita ut verissimè di-ctum sit à Nazianzeno, nihil quod fictum est, firmu & solidum esse posse, πᾶν ὁ ἀρετῶν-τῶν, inquit, ἀλλὰ μόνιμον. Virtutem enim quo melius cognoscis, eo magis amas: at hypocri-fis simulatque cognoscitur, interit, & jam hy-pocrisis esse definit. Itaque ille ipse Nazian-zenus elegantissimè comparabat hypocrisin cum histrionicis meretricibus quæ natiua pul-chritudine carentes, pigmentis utuntur & fiunt, inquit, ob venustate invenustiores. Sed nihil dici potest aptius quàm quod Dominus Pharisæis hypocritis obiicebat, nempe quòd essent similes sepulchris dealbatis. Nam licet extrinsecus ornamenta quædam appareant, intus tamen nihil est præter ossa mortuorum & immunditiam. Qua similitudine nihil dici potuit accommodatius. Recte siquidem hypocritæ ad sepulchra remittuntur, qui revera mortui sunt, quantùvis vana specie vitam e-mentiantur. Quare non est difficile judicare eum resprorsus abhorrentes & contrarias velle coiungere, qui existimat hypocrisi cum fide aliquod esse commercium. Ex quo factum est, ut eam non immerito Dauid excluserit, differens de peccatorum remissione, quæ à fide separari nullo modo potest. Scite vero nomine fraudis ac doli hypocrisin significare voluit: quandoquidem hypocrita adeò fallax est ut non tantùm alios, sed seipsum etiam imprimis decipiat. Atque idem mihi facere videtur, ut siquis summa in rerum inopia constitutus, nullam ad res necessarias comparan-das adhibeat diligentiam, sed satis habeat mo-dò vulgò diues habeatur & interim jactet se egregiè
units.tr: But to speak of hypocrisy: you will find nothing more alien to the nature of faith than pretence. As a painted fire differs greatly from a real fire, since it has only the appearance and not the heat and power, so hypocrisy has indeed some likeness of virtue, but if you come nearer you will find a painted and shadowy fire, whose light you can never see and whose heat you can never feel. Faith has its seat in the heart, hypocrisy in the face. Faith devotes all its effort to pleasing God, hypocrisy to being approved by men. Finally, faith is living, effective, constant and lasting in itself, but hypocrisy quickly falls away like a little flower, and once the empty colour of feigned piety is stripped off, it lies there worthless and withers. So it was truly said by Nazianzen that nothing feigned can be firm and solid: [πᾶν ὁ ἀρετῶντων, ἀλλὰ μόνιμον]. For the more closely you know virtue, the more you love it; but hypocrisy, as soon as it is recognised, perishes, and it ceases to be hypocrisy at all. Hence the same Nazianzen aptly compared hypocrisy to stage harlots who, lacking natural beauty, use cosmetics and become, he says, less attractive for their charms. But nothing can be said more fittingly than what the Lord objected to the hypocritical Pharisees, namely that they were like whitewashed sepulchres. For although some ornaments appear on the outside, within there is nothing but the bones of the dead and uncleanness. No comparison could be more suitable. Indeed hypocrites are rightly sent back to the sepulchres, since they are in truth dead, however much they pretend to live by a vain show. Therefore it is not difficult to judge that he is wholly mistaken who thinks that hypocrisy has any fellowship with faith, when the two are utterly opposed and contrary. This is why David rightly excluded hypocrisy when he spoke of the forgiveness of sins, which can in no way be separated from faith. Wisely, too, he meant hypocrisy by the name of fraud and deceit, since the hypocrite is so deceitful that he deceives not only others but, above all, himself. And he seems to me like someone who, in great want of goods, takes no care to obtain what is necessary, but is content merely to be thought rich by the common people, and meanwhile boasts that he is splendidly

units.la: egregie aliis imponere. Equidem fateor me falli, qui te diuitem esse putem, sed quanto grauius tibi ipse imponis, qui falsa diuitia‐rum vmbra contentus ad veras diuitias ani‐mum non adiungis? Videmus igitur quàm proprie hypocrisin vates noster dolum ap‐pellauerit.
units.tr: splendidly imposing on others. I admit that I am deceived if I think you rich; but how much more gravely do you deceive yourself, who, content with the false shadow of riches, do not join your mind to true riches? We see, then, how aptly our poet called hypocrisy deceit.

units.la: Venio nunc ad id quod posterius affirma‐bam, videlicet remissionem peccati vere & ex animo apprehensam, necessario, vt fructum, sic pecca‐ta pietatis studium producere. Quemadmo‐dum enim eam demum arbore viuere & fer‐tilem esse dicimus, quæ fructus suos edit, a‐lioquin stipitem & truncum mortuum appel‐laturi: ita vbi semel fiducia remissionis pecca‐torum in animis nostris radices egit, statim um pra‐diffundit suas vires & in altum crescens, no‐uos quotidie progressus facit, ita vt inde sum‐ma pietatis studia efflorescant, maximaque charitatis officia, tanquam fructus vberrimi proferantur. Nam qui fieri potest vt ex ani‐mo sentias tibi peccatum esse condonatum, quin vicissim ex animo peccatum horreas? quin refugias? quin ad virtutis studium ani‐mum appellas? Ergo dicendum est illis re‐mitti peccata, qui peccata sentiunt, sentien‐do oderunt & fugiunt, atque ea fugiendo ad virtutem contrariam toto animi impetu fe‐runtur. Sic enim (vt ait Apostolus) libera‐mur à peccato, vt iustitiæ seruiamus, id est, vt animus noster tanquam emeritis stipen‐ diis peccati, se totum dedat pietatis & sanctimoniæ studio: quemadmodum etiam alibi dicitur, nullam esse condemnationem iis qui sunt in Christo & qui secundum spiritum, non autem secundum carnem incedunt. Semper autem meminerimus nos agere de veris iustificationis fructibus, qui quidem ab ipsa cordis radice producuntur: quam ob causam Psaltes spiritum ipsum nominauit, non quòd piorum sanctificatio ita conclusa in animo teneatur vt foras nō prodeat, sed quia illa demum opera recta sunt quę ex recto atque integro corde proficiscuntur.
units.tr: I come now to what I said last, namely that the forgiveness of sin, truly and from the heart laid hold of, necessarily produces the zeal of piety as its fruit. For just as we say that a tree is alive and fruitful only when it bears its fruit, and otherwise we would call it a dead stump and trunk, so when confidence in the forgiveness of sins has once taken root in our minds, it immediately spreads its strength, and growing upward it makes new progress every day, so that from it the highest zeal for piety flowers and the greatest acts of love are brought forth as the most abundant fruit. For how can you feel from the heart that your sin has been pardoned without in turn hating sin from the heart? Without shrinking from it? Without turning your mind to the pursuit of virtue? Therefore it must be said that sins are forgiven to those who feel their sins, and in feeling them hate and flee them, and in fleeing them are carried with the whole force of their minds toward the contrary virtue. For thus (as the Apostle says) we are freed from sin, that we may serve righteousness, that is, that our mind, like a soldier discharged from the service of sin, may devote itself wholly to the study of piety and holiness. Just as elsewhere it is said that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ and who walk according to the Spirit, not according to the flesh. But let us always remember that we are speaking of the true fruits of justification, which indeed spring from the very root of the heart. For this reason the Psalmist named the spirit itself. Not that the sanctification of the godly is so shut up in the mind that it does not come forth outwardly, but because those works are right which proceed from an upright and sincere heart.

units.la: Hoc autē loco nobis refellenda est eorum opinio qui existimant essentiale iustitiā in nobis inhærere, ex qua iusti simus: atque hanc Dauidis sententiam detorquent ad suum errorem confirmandum, cùm ait eum esse fœlicem cui peccata ita remissa sunt, vt in eius spiritu non sit dolus, id est, in cuius animo residet integritas.Ex quo efficiunt non Christi, id est, alienam iustitiam, sed propriam nobis imputari, vt iusti simus. Verùm homines isti longè sanè resiliunt à Dauidis mente, neque tenent rectam de iustificatione doctrinam. Non enim iustificatio cum effectis iustificationis confundenda est. Quis enim tam excors tamque demens fuerit, vt riuulos ipsi fonti & origini opponat, ac nō potius ab ipsa diducendos existimet? Ita etiam statuendum est, imputatam nobis Christi[?] iustitiam esse instar fontis perennis & abundantissimi ex quo si quae in nobis sunt iustitiae & sanctitatis guttulae, emanarunt.
units.tr: Here we must refute the opinion of those who think that righteousness inheres in us essentially, and that by it we are righteous. They twist this saying of David to confirm their error, when he says that he is happy whose sins are so forgiven that there is no deceit in his spirit, that is, in whose mind there is integrity. From this they conclude that not the righteousness of Christ, that is, an alien righteousness, but our own is imputed to us, so that we are made righteous. But these men stray far from David's meaning, and they do not hold the right doctrine of justification. For justification must not be confused with the effects of justification. For who would be so foolish and so mad as to set streams against the fountain and source itself, and not rather think they must be separated from it? So we must likewise maintain that the righteousness of Christ imputed to us is like a perennial and most abundant fountain, from which any drops of righteousness and holiness that are in us have flowed.

units.la: Praeterea quum satis constet ex Apostolo nos fide iustificari: iustificatio autem duas habeat partes, nempe remissionem peccatorum & iustitiae imputationem, ecquonam modo fiet vt essentiali iustitia in nobis inhaerente iusti simus, quum mortificatio ordine sequatur iustificationem? Rursus hoc etiam considerandum est, nos non posse iustos censeri ab ea iustitia quae tantum inchoata, sed quae perfecta sit & absoluta.
units.tr: Moreover, since it is sufficiently clear from the Apostle that we are justified by faith, and justification has two parts, namely the forgiveness of sins and the imputation of righteousness, how can we be made righteous by an essential righteousness inhering in us, when mortification follows justification in order? Again, this must also be considered: we cannot be counted righteous by that righteousness which is merely begun, but only by that which is perfect and complete.

units.la: Age vero proferant vel unum ex Adami posteris (excepto Christo) in quo possit eiusmodi iustitia reperiri. Quod si nequeant, fateantur profecto, nobis esse Christi iustitiam imputandam vt iustificemur. Illa enim demum iustitia perfecta est & omnibus numeris absoluta. Quo fit vt Apostolus affirmet Christum nobis factum esse iu- stitiam. At enim, inquiunt, non potest Deus habere pro iustis qui revera iusti non sunt. Quasi vero non simus re vera iusti, si imputatione iustitiae iusti simus. Quid enim, obsecro si cum soluendo non esses, aliquis tuo nomine creditori tuo satisfecerit? Nonne re vera liber es ab obligatione, licet ipse non perfoluveris? Quid? nonne re vera redempti sumus? nonne re vera sumus cum Deo reconciliati? Atqui summū illud beneficiū non nobis ipsi, sed Christus propria morte cōparauit. Non enim mortui sumus in cruce, non poenas nostris peccatis debitas persoluimus, non iram Dei pertulimus, denique non illius iudicio satisfecimus: sed in his omnibus necessario ad imputationem recurrēdum est. Verum prae-stat hūc locum verbis Apostoli quàm nostris concludere: Quemadmodum, inquit, per vnius hominis inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per obedientiam vnius, iusti constituuntur multi. Quibus verbis apertissimè docemur, Christi iustitia nos esse iustos coram Deo, cuius tamē iustificationis hoc effectum sit, ut in nobis gignat iustitiæ & pietatis studium & nos ad amorē virtutis & obedientiæ erga Deum incendat. Quia verò noster ille conatus ad iustitiam adhuc est imperfectus, semper ad perfectam Christi iustitiam recurrendum est, ut & nos & nostra omnia Dominus in suo dilecto amplectatur acceptaque habeat. Hunc autē esse sensum nostri Dauidis iam satis ante à nobis expositū est. Quin-etiam ipsum doli & fraudis vocabulum quo utitur rem satis explicat. Non enim eum dicit esse foelicem in cuius operibus nihil de-sideratur: sed cuius remissa sunt peccata & a-nimus vacat omni simulatione, quemadmo-dum supra diximus. Nimirū eò respexit Ambrosius, cùm diceret: Non gloriabor, inquit, quia iustus sum, sed quia redemptus sum: non quia vacuus sum peccato, sed quia remissa sunt mihi peccata: non quia profui aut mihi quisquam profuit, sed quia pro me Aduocatus apud Patrē Christus est, quia pro me sanguis Christi effusus est. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Come now, let them produce even one of Adam's posterity (except Christ) in whom such righteousness can be found. But if they cannot, they must surely confess that the righteousness of Christ must be imputed to us so that we may be justified. For that righteousness alone is perfect and complete in every respect. Hence the Apostle affirms that Christ was made righteousness for us. But, they say, God cannot hold as righteous those who are not really righteous. As if we were not really righteous when we are righteous by the imputation of righteousness! For what, I ask, if someone had satisfied your creditor on your behalf when you were not able to pay? Are you not really free from the obligation, even though you yourself have not paid? What? Are we not really redeemed? Are we not really reconciled to God? Yet Christ, not we ourselves, procured that supreme benefit by his own death. For we did not die on the cross, we did not pay the penalties owed for our sins, we did not bear the wrath of God, and finally we did not satisfy his judgement: but in all these things we must necessarily have recourse to imputation. Indeed it is better to conclude this place in the words of the Apostle than in our own: As, he says, through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many are made righteous. By these words we are most clearly taught that we are righteous before God by the righteousness of Christ; yet the effect of this justification is that it begets in us a zeal for righteousness and piety, and inflames us to love virtue and to obey God. But because that effort of ours toward righteousness is still imperfect, we must always have recourse to the perfect righteousness of Christ, so that the Lord may embrace us and all that is ours in his beloved, and hold it acceptable. Now we have already explained earlier that this is the meaning of our David. Moreover, the very word for deceit and fraud which he uses explains the matter well. For he does not say that he is happy in whose works nothing is lacking, but whose sins are forgiven and whose mind is free from all pretence, as we said above. Surely Ambrose had this in view when he said: I shall not glory because I am righteous, but because I am redeemed; not because I am free from sin, but because my sins are forgiven; not because I have profited or anyone has profited me, but because Christ is my Advocate with the Father, because the blood of Christ was poured out for me. So he.

units.la: Quæri tamen non immerito poterit, an homines à Deo sanctificati & iustitiæ Christi participes animū habeat prorsus ab hypocrisi & simulatione vacuum. Respondeo: ea quę in sanctis vel purissima sunt, labe tamen non ca rere. Sed certum est Dauidem agere non de iis peccatis in quibus sancti sibi displicent & quibus obsistunt, sed de improbitate & malitia in qua sibi hypocritæ blandiuntur, & ei solum aliquam virtutis & honesti speciē præte xunt. Atque hanc esse Dauidis mentem satis indicat Hebraica dictio, qua vtitur: conuenit enim peruersis illis hominib<bl>qui</bl> dolo & fi au de, tanquā iaculo ex insidiis emisso, proximos cōfodiunt. Itaq; non sunt verba Dauidis accommodanda sanctorum næuis & iis peccatorum reliquiis quæ semper hærent vel in sanctissimis hominibus quandiu hic degunt.
units.tr: It may still fairly be asked whether men sanctified by God and partakers of the righteousness of Christ have a mind entirely free from hypocrisy and pretence. I answer that even those things in the saints that are most pure are not free from some stain. But it is certain that David is not speaking of those sins over which the saints are displeased with themselves and which they resist, but of the wickedness and malice in which hypocrites flatter themselves, and which put on a show of some virtue and honesty. The Hebrew word he uses makes clear that this is David's meaning: it fits those perverse men who, with deceit and fraud, stab their neighbours as with a javelin thrown from an ambush. Therefore David's words should not be applied to the blemishes of the saints or to those remnants of sin that cling even to the holiest men as long as they live here.

units.la: Superest vt hanc doctrinam nobis applicemus & procul ab animis nostris simulationem, dolos & fraudes remoueamus: ac potius candorem atque integritatē colamus: neque simus duplici corde, quemadmodū Scriptura loquitur, sed ex animo & sine hypocrisi pietati iustitiæque studeamus. Iam videamus quid nos amplius vates doceat.
units.tr: It remains for us to apply this teaching to ourselves, and to remove far from our minds pretence, deceit and fraud, and rather to cultivate candour and integrity. Let us not be of a double heart, as Scripture puts it, but let us pursue piety and righteousness sincerely and without hypocrisy. Now let us see what else the psalmist teaches us.

units.la: ver.3. Quādo tacui, inquit, consenuerunt offa mea in rugitu meo toto die. Hactenus sen-tentia proposuit de foelicitate hominis in re-missione peccatorum constituenda:nunc se-quitur illius sententiae confirmatio ab exem-plo ipsius Dauidis,quam esse secundam huius Psalmi partem initio diximus. Hæc autē ver-ba prima specie videntur habere aliquam dif-ficultatem.Nam rugitus contrarius est silen-tio, ita ut nemo vere tacuisse dici possit qui per totum diem rugitum,id est,ingetem cla-morem ediderit præ dolore.Itaque sic a qui-busda explicatur hic locus, ut repetendū sit illud,consenuerunt offa mea, quasi dicat: siue tacitus dolore corde premerem, siue prorū-pere in gemitus&clamores,semper manebat summus ille & grauissimus dolor qui me inti-mum coficiebat & propemodu ipsas ossium medullas exhauriebat.Ergo ad Domini misericordiam recta pœnitentia & syncera pecca-torū confessione cofugi,ex quo factum est ut dolore sim leuatus, apprehensa peccatorum remissione. Quæ interpretatio veram doctri-nam continet: sic enim ante oculos ponūtur grauissimi illi dolores, quos tandiu patimur dum iram Dei aduersus peccata nostra accen-sam persentimus,ut iam aliquoties à nobis di-ctum est. Alij vero sic exponunt Dauidis ver-ba:Quia tacui,id est,quandiu,inquit,non cō-fessus sum coram Deo peccatum meum, consenuerunt offa mea præ gemitu meo quoti-diano. Nam me Dei manus quotidianis ictibus identidem vrgebat. Quare apud me decreui fateri peccatum & tanquam vlceris mei saniem coram medico explicare, vt aliquod remedium meis vulneribus afferret. Quæ expositio videtur apte conuenire. Nam notanda est coniunctio quotidianarum plagarum cum quotidiano rugitu. Deinde cum ante peccati confessionem Dei percutientis manus non cessarit (quod colligere possumus ex hoc loco) cumque Deo percutiente Dauid testetur se totum diem rugiisse, id est, vocem præ doloris acerbitate sustulisse, quis non videt silentium de quo loquitur posse commodissimè referri ad peccatum, de quo tandiu siluisse dicitur, quandiu illud coram Deo ex animo confessus non est? Ait igitur: Quia tacui, consenuerunt ossa mea. Hæc rectè cum superioribus cohærebūt si dicamus transitum fieri à generali doctrina ad Dauidis hypothesin.
units.tr: Verse 3: "When I kept silent," he says, "my bones wasted away through my groaning all the day long." Up to this point the psalm has set out the happiness of man as resting on the forgiveness of sins. Now follows the confirmation of that statement from the example of David himself, which at the beginning we said is the second part of this psalm. These words, at first sight, seem to present some difficulty. For groaning is the opposite of silence, so that no one could truly be said to have kept silent who through the whole day uttered a groan, that is, a loud cry, from pain. So some explain this passage in such a way that the phrase "my bones wasted away" must be repeated, as if he said: whether I was silent and pressed down the pain in my heart, or whether I broke out into groans and cries, that highest and most grievous pain always remained, which consumed me inwardly and nearly drained the very marrow of my bones. Therefore I fled to the mercy of the Lord by true repentance and sincere confession of sins, and as a result I was relieved of my pain once the forgiveness of sins was grasped. This interpretation contains true doctrine, for it sets before our eyes those most grievous pains which we suffer for as long as we feel the wrath of God kindled against our sins, as we have said on several occasions. Others, however, explain David's words in this way: "Because I kept silent," that is, as long as, he says, I did not confess my sin before God, my bones wasted away because of my daily groaning. For the hand of God pressed upon me with daily blows again and again. Therefore I resolved in my own mind to confess my sin and to lay open the matter of my wound before the physician, so that he might bring some remedy to my sores. This explanation seems to fit well. For the connection between the daily plagues and the daily groaning should be noted. Further, since before the confession of sin the hand of God striking him did not cease (which we may gather from this passage), and since David, with God striking him, testifies that he groaned all day long, that is, that he raised his voice because of the bitterness of his pain, who does not see that the silence of which he speaks can most suitably be referred to the sin about which he is said to have been silent for as long as he had not confessed it before God from his heart? He says, therefore: "Because I kept silent, my bones wasted away." These words will fit well with what precedes if we say that there is a transition from the general doctrine to David's particular case.

units.la: Nam postquam remissionem peccatorum commendauit adeò vt etiam in illa collocarit hominis fœlicitatem: Ne, inquit, aliquid vobis dubitationis superfit, volo meipsum proponere in quo istius sententiæ veritatem, tanquam in speculo, possitis intueri. Cum meorum peccatorum grauitate accensus Dei furor me summis & quotidianis cruciatibus afficeret, nullum vnquam aliud remedium potui tot tatisque doloribus adhibere, quàm si supplex ad Dei misericordiā cōfugere & tanquā ad summæ illius Maiestatis pedes prouolu-tus, peccata mea agnoscerem, ipsorumque veniam deprecarer. Hoc igitur Dauidis exe-plo docendi sumus, ea Dei dona quæ singulis hominibus conferuntur, debere ad omnium utilitatem accommodari. vt enim in corpore videmus tantam esse membrorum coniun-ctionem, vt singula quicquid habent, conferant in communem totius corporis vsum & conseruationem: ita quoque nobis faciendum est, siquidem ad Ecclesiæ corpus vnusquisque nostrum vere pertinet.
units.tr: For after he had commended the forgiveness of sins so highly that he located in it the happiness of man, he says, lest any doubt remain for you, I wish to set myself forward, in whom you may see the truth of this statement as in a mirror. When the Lord's wrath, kindled by the weight of my sins, afflicted me with the highest and daily torments, I could never find any other remedy for such great and heavy pains than to flee as a suppliant to the mercy of God, and, prostrate at the feet of that supreme Majesty, to acknowledge my sins and beg for their pardon. Therefore we are to be taught by this example of David that the gifts of God which are bestowed on individual men ought to be used for the benefit of all. For just as we see in the body that the members are so joined together that each contributes whatever it has to the common use and preservation of the whole body, so we too must act, since each one of us truly belongs to the body of the Church.

units.la: Hoc vel profani agnouerunt cum docerent nos nobis non esse natos, sed partem nostri patriā, partem parētes, partem amicos vendicare: quod quantò melius ac verius de Ecclesia dicendum est? Quā-obrem demus operam ne collata in nos Dei beneficia ingrato silentio cōsepulta iaceant in tenebris, sed potius communi cæterorum vtilitati salutíque possint inseruire.
units.tr: Even pagans recognised this when they taught that we are not born for ourselves, but that our country claims one part of us, our parents another, and our friends another. How much better and more truly must this be said of the Church! Therefore let us take care that the benefits of God bestowed upon us are not buried in ungrateful silence and lie in darkness, but may rather serve the common usefulness and salvation of others.

units.la: Poterat Dauid tacere summū illud beneficium quod acceperat à Domino, poterat solus & tacitus illo frui: sed noluit rem tanti momenti non esse cum aliis communicatam. Sciebat enim homines sæpissime incidere posse in eiusmodi cruciatus: ne igitur aliis deesse videretur, idem præstitit quod factitant ij qui ab aliquo graui morbo conualuerunt, cum eos qui in eundem morbū incidunt docet quibusnam remediis sit vtendum: & (vt Nazianzeni simi-litudinem vsurpem) solent qui à serpentibus fuerunt idi dare consilium iis qui idem vul-nus acceperunt, & quibus est, inquit, <bl>ἔρως</bl>, ξύω ὁρ κακὸν ἄλλος ὁ μοιον: quod & a-pud Profanū Poëtā illa intellexit, quæ haud ignara mali miseris succurrere didicerat.
units.tr: David could have kept silent about that supreme benefit which he had received from the Lord; he could have enjoyed it alone and in silence. But he was unwilling that a matter of such importance should not be shared with others. For he knew that men very often may fall into such torments; so that he might not seem to be lacking to others, he did the same thing that those do who have recovered from some grave illness, when they teach those who fall into the same disease which remedies are to be used. And (to borrow the comparison of Nazianzen) those who have been bitten by serpents are accustomed to give counsel to those who have received the same wound; and, as he says, [ἔρως, ξύω ὁρ κακὸν ἄλλος ὁ μοιον], which the heathen poet also understood, who, not unacquainted with evil, had learned to help the wretched.

units.la: In primis autem considerandum est quis-nam se morbo nostro remedium allaturum esse profiteatur. Is est Dauid: Dauid, inquā, & rex & Propheta qui tot tantisque donis ex-celluit, vt de illo difficile dictu sit, vtrum rex fortior, an propheta sanctior fuerit. Ille ta-men qui opibus, qui gloria, qui virtute ac san-ctimonia inter cæteros eminebat, non dubi-tauit hoc in loco partes doctoris suscipere, aut potius fungi medici officio, vt aliqua morbis nostris solatia ac fomenta possit ad-hibere. Atque quod mireris magis, vt nos reddat ad remedia suscipienda promptiores, ipse cicatrices suas ostendit, & tanquam digi-to commonstrat qua parte vulnus acceperit, & quánam ratione conualuerit, id est, inge-nuè fatetur peccatum, atque ipsam confes-sionem scriptis tradidit ad hominum memo-riam sempiternam. Quid? adeóne tui obliui-sceris, ô Dauid, vt tam male tui nominis cele-britati & famæ velis esse cósultum? Mihi, in-quit, sufficit dum gloria Dei sanantis in meo detecto vulnere reluceat. Huc igitur oculosconuertamus, vt tanti viri nos exemplum do-ceat, nō esse quòd nos pudeat ingenuè fatericulpam nostram etiam coram omnibus, si nostra illa confessione gloria Dei illustretur & aliquid utilitatis accedat Ecclesiae. Hoc idem fecit Psal.51.& passim aliās. Hoc praestitit Daniel & suo & totius Ecclesiae Israeliticae nomine, cuius peccata coram posteritate testatus est. Sed in primis urget regis persona: nā his temporibus eò res rediit, ut qui sunt potentiores, adeò priuatae gloriae sint addicti, ut eam & honori Dei & utilitati publicae non dubitent anteferre. Quinetiam plerique ita vanis opinionibus inflantur, quasi homines esse desierint simulatque reges exti- titerunt. Imperare (inquit Chrysostomus) est ars omnium artium maxima. Et profecto ita est. Ex quo efficitur Regum & po- tentiorum peccata longe cæteris esse gra-uiora. ut enim si quando ab iis peccetur qui malos scandunt, qui cursitant per foros, qui remigant, non tantum erit periculi, quam si peccet is qui clauum tenet: ita Regum & Ma-gistratuum peccata maximi sunt momenti & sæpe attrahunt summam rerum omnium perturbationem. Ne igitur sceptrum, ne in-fulas, ne gloriosa Magistratus insignia peccatis unquam praetexito: illa enim non mi-nuunt, sed augent peccata, & quo sublimior es atque potentior, eo peccata tua sunt periculosiora, cum non tantum noceas peccato, sed etiam exemplo. Quod cum Dauid perspectum haberet, non veritus est hanc sui peccati confessionem mandare literis, ut eam exciperent omnes anni consequentes. Itaq; cùm eam lego, mihi audire videor Dauidem ita loquentem. Sciant posteri (hoc enim quanta potero vocis contentione proclamabo) Sciant, inquam, posteri me peccasse, me Dei clementissimi Patris liberalitatem spreuisse, me ingratum, me terræ carnisque cupiditatibus deuinctum in crassis tenebris iacuisse: Hæc vox, hæc confessio, hæ lacrymæ meam culpam coram Deo atque hominibus testentur. Sed hoc sit summæ Dei misericordiæ & paterni fauoris perpetuum monimentum, quòd me miserum & iacentem porrecta manu erexerit, quòd meorum peccatorum confessionem admiserit, quòd preces & gemitus meos exaudierit, & suo Spiritu mihi in animo peccatorum meorum veniam obsignârit. Ita Dauidis exemplum non priuatis modo, sed etiam iis qui summos gerunt & amplissimos Magistratus proponendu est, vt saluteпublicâ suæ gloriæ & priuatis rebus omnibus anteponant.
units.tr: First of all, however, we must consider who it is that promises to bring a remedy for our disease. It is David: David, I say, both king and prophet, who excelled in so many and such great gifts that it is hard to say whether the king was stronger or the prophet holier. Yet he who stood out among the rest in wealth, in glory, in virtue and in holiness did not hesitate in this passage to take up the role of a teacher, or rather to discharge the office of a physician, so that he might be able to apply some comfort and fomentation to our diseases. And, what you may marvel at even more, in order to make us readier to accept remedies, he displays his own scars and, as it were, points with his finger to the part where he received the wound and the manner in which he recovered; that is, he candidly confesses his sin and has handed down the confession itself in writing to the everlasting memory of men. What? Have you forgotten yourself so much, O David, that you wish to be so poorly provided for in the celebration and fame of your name? "It is enough for me," he says, "if the glory of God, the healer, shines forth in my exposed wound." Let us therefore turn our eyes here, so that the example of so great a man may teach us that there is no reason for us to be ashamed to confess our fault openly, even before all, if by that confession the glory of God is made illustrious and some benefit accrues to the Church. The same thing was done by David in Psalm 51 and elsewhere in many places. Daniel did the same, both in his own name and in the name of the whole Israelite Church, whose sins he bore witness to before posterity. But the person of the king presses especially upon us, for in these times things have come to such a point that those who are more powerful are so devoted to private glory that they do not hesitate to put it before the honour of God and the public good. Indeed, many are so puffed up by vain opinions that they seem to think they have ceased to be men as soon as they have become kings. "To rule," says Chrysostom, "is the greatest of all arts." And truly it is so. From this it follows that the sins of kings and the powerful are far more serious than those of others. For just as, if someone sins who climbs the masts, who runs about the marketplaces, who rows, there is not as much danger as when he sins who holds the helm, so the sins of kings and magistrates are of the greatest importance and often draw down the greatest disturbance of all affairs. Therefore never shelter your sceptre, your mitres, or the glorious insignia of magistracy behind your sins: for these do not diminish but increase sins, and the higher and more powerful you are, the more dangerous your sins are, since you harm not only by sin but also by example. Since David clearly understood this, he did not shrink from committing this confession of his sin to writing, so that all the following years might receive it. Therefore, when I read it, I seem to hear David speaking thus: "Let posterity know (for I will proclaim this with all the strength of my voice) let posterity know, I say, that I have sinned, that I have spurned the generosity of the most merciful Father God, that I, ungrateful, bound by the desires of earth and flesh, lay in thick darkness. Let this voice, this confession, and these tears bear witness before God and men to my fault. But let this be a perpetual monument of God's supreme mercy and fatherly favour, that when I was wretched and lying low he stretched out his hand and raised me up, that he admitted my confession of my sins, that he heard my prayers and groans, and sealed in my mind, by his Spirit, the pardon of my sins." Thus the example of David is to be set forth not only to private persons but also to those who hold the highest and most distinguished magistracies, so that they may put the public safety before their own glory and all private interests.

units.la: Sed hic possit suboriri quæstio de silentio Dauidis: Quia tacui, inquit, consenuerunt ossa mea: An enim Dauidem tacuisse, nec peccatum statim confessum fuisse dicemus? Certè tantum virum in peccato suo obstupuisse aut illud voluisse silentio tegere idque coram Deo, videtur maximè alienum. Cur igitur ait hoc loco se tacuisse? Cui sic responsum esse velim, vt dicamus, absurdum non esse Dauidem nō statim ad peccati confessionem fuisse adductū. Cuius rei magnum est argumentum quòd adulterium commis-sum cum Bethsabea amplius nouem men-sēs etiam coram Deo tacuit. Non. quòd omnino obduruisset in peccato, sedquia obdormiscebat donec excitatus est grauis-fima Nathani obiurgatione. Qui locus indicat Satanam in primis conari,non tantum nos in peccatum pellicere, verumetiam no-stris oculis peccati ipsius tenebras offudere, ne illud videamus neque sentiamus, ut ita paulatim serpens nos tādem totos possideat. Atque ita fit ut homines quo sunt morti propinquiores, eo minus mortem videant, mi-nus sentiant. Aduertamus igitur ne in tātum periculum incidamus & caueamus insidias Satanæ qui sensim virus peccati in animos nostros instillat, donec illud tandem in per-niciem nostrā redundet.
units.tr: But here a question may arise about David's silence: "Because I kept silent," he says, "my bones grew old." Shall we say that David kept silent and did not at once confess his sin? Surely it seems quite out of character for so great a man to have been stupefied in his sin, or to have wanted to hide it in silence, and that before God. Why, then, does he say here that he kept silent? My answer would be this: it is no absurdity that David was not at once brought to confess his sin. A strong proof of this is that he kept silent before God for more than nine months after he committed adultery with Bathsheba. This was not because he had become utterly hardened in sin, but because he was asleep until he was roused by Nathan's severe rebuke. That passage shows that Satan above all tries not only to entice us into sin, but also to cast the darkness of sin before our eyes, so that we neither see it nor feel it, and so the serpent gradually possesses us entirely. And so it happens that the nearer men are to death, the less they see death and the less they feel it. Let us therefore take care that we do not fall into so great a danger, and let us guard against the snares of Satan, who little by little instils the poison of sin into our minds, until at last it overflows to our ruin.

units.la: Sunt igitur tria tempora considerāda: Unum, cùm in peccatis quodammodo indormimus. Secundum, cùm in nobis peccati sensus excitatur & nostras cōscientias suis stimulis urget. Tertium, cùm ad veram peccati confessionem adducti simul etiā amplectimur peccati remissionem in Christo. Itaque Dauid hoc in Psalmo duo posteriora tempora videtur potissimum de-scripsisse, quando commemorat summos illos dolores quibus affectus fuit donec ad misericordiam Dei refugiens certa & vera fide apprehendit peccati remissionem.
units.tr: There are therefore three times to be considered. The first is when we are in some sense asleep in our sins. The second is when the sense of sin is awakened in us and urges our consciences with its goads. The third is when, brought to a true confession of sin, we at the same time embrace the remission of sin in Christ. Accordingly, in this Psalm David seems chiefly to have described the last two times, when he recalls those great sorrows with which he was afflicted until, fleeing to the mercy of God, he laid hold with a certain and true faith on the remission of sin.

units.la: Hinc autem obseruemus veram poenitentiam esse Dei donū, neque à nostris viribus vlla ratione pendere, vt non abs re dixerit Apostolus: Si Deus, inquit, dederit illis poenitentiam. Nam si Dauid ipse nō statim sensit pàcatam conscientiam, sed diu multumque versatus est in mediis illis doloribus, quos sine dubio iudicii diuini apprehensio & legis terror infligebant, quid de nobis sperādum est qui tam procul absumus à Dauidis integritate? Rursus cùm poenitentia sine fide, fides autem sine Dei Spiritu esse non possit, quis non facilè censeat donum istud poenitentiae non comparari nostris viribus, sed à Dei liberalitate & misericordia conferri?
units.tr: From this we may observe that true repentance is a gift of God and in no way depends on our own powers, so that the Apostle rightly said: "If God," he says, "should give them repentance." For if David himself did not at once feel a pacified conscience, but was long and greatly troubled in those midst of sorrows, which undoubtedly the apprehension of divine judgment and the terror of the law inflicted, what ought we to hope, who are so far removed from David's integrity? Again, since repentance cannot exist without faith, and faith cannot exist without the Spirit of God, who would not readily judge that this gift of repentance is not acquired by our own powers but is bestowed by the generosity and mercy of God?

units.la: Quis igitur illos homines ferat, qui secure doctrinam poenitentiae & quasuis cohortationes obiurgationesq; despiciūt atque semper procrastinăt, quasi donum poenitetiæ in manibus habeant & liceat quoties voluerint poenitere? longè sanè fallūtur. Nec enim temerè est quòd toties Prophetae hunc locum vrgent in suis cōcionibus: Resipiscēdum esse dum tēpus fert, nec expectādum peccatoribus dum poenitentiae fores occludātur: quod etiā elegātissima Virginū parabola Christus expressit. Praeterea non omittendū est certos esse poenitentiae gradus. Primùm enim excutitur ille stupor, quo naturā in peccatis obdurescimus: deinde serio sesu[?] peccati afficimur:
units.tr: Who, then, can bear those men who, in their security, despise the doctrine of repentance and all exhortations and rebukes, and always put off repentance, as though they held the gift of repentance in their hands and might repent whenever they pleased? They are greatly mistaken. For it is not without reason that the Prophets so often press this passage in their sermons: that one must repent while time allows, and that sinners must not wait until the gates of repentance are shut. Christ also expressed this in the most elegant parable of the ten virgins. Moreover, it must not be overlooked that there are certain degrees of repentance. For first that stupor is shaken off by which we grow hard in sins by nature; then we are seriously affected by the sense of sin.

units.la: d.j. Tum nos terret propositu Dei tribunal, terrent eius minæ, & legis Diuinæ sententia animos consternat: pungunt etiam pœnarum morsus quibus sæpe Dominus nos peccatorum commonefacit. Sed omnium acerrimus est ille dolor qui ex cõscientiæ stimulis proficiscitur: quò tandem vbi ventū fuerit, nobis est summopere cauendum ne ad illos pauores adhærescamus, sed longius progrediendū est, nempe ad Dei promissiones & ipsius misericordiam nobis plenissimè in Christo patefactā: atque hæc postrema cogitatio dulcis-sima est & tanquam medicina conscientiæ. Hinc aùt exoritur lucta quædā spiritualis inter metum & fiduciā, atq; inter desperationē & spem: vt quodāmodo mors cum vita, minæ cū promissionibus, Lex cum Euangelio, ipsi denique inferi cum cœlesti gloria certare videantur. Cùm autē fides armata promissionibus Euangelicis & vndique meritis Christi nixa & suffulta victrix euadit: tum ouans erumpit in veram confessionem peccati cuius simul remissionem percipit in Christi passione & eius perfectissima obedientia quam nostro nomine Deo præstitit: ita vt vera peccati confessio sit velut fidei victricis trium-phus.Hæc igitur omnia possumus in Dauide tanquam in speculo contemplari vt iam su-pra annotauimus. Iam discutiamus ipsa Da-uidis verba. Consenuerunt, inquit, offa mea in rugitu meo quotidie: his verbis non vulgare, sed extremum dolorem significat & eum qui ipsas quodammodo medullas peruadens, animum vehementissimè torquebat, atque id consensescendi verbo declaratur. Nam quod ait Solomo verissimum esse constat, aegritudinem animi exsiccare offa: quemadmodum etiam Propheta coqueritur in Psal.102. offa sua præ mœrore arefacta & adusta esse: & noster Dauid in Psal.6.&31. exclamat, oculos suos quasi vetustate cośumptos, ossaque ipsa exesa esse atque putrefacta, quòd sese tot tantisque angoribus dedidisset. Quæ omnia significantissimè exprimunt vim doloris. Scimus enim ita natura coparatum esse, ut qui affecta sunt ætate, longè sint quàm antea imbecilliores: nâ humore natiuo exarescete, & ficciora fiũt corpora & infirmiora. Itaq; scriptura solet vitâ hominis cum flore coparare. Videmus autè marcescetis floris cotracta & sicca esse folia. Quamobrem apposite noster vates adhibuit verbum cõsenefcendi, ut signi-ficaret doloris acerbitatem & vehemetiam: quasi dicat: Quemadmodum homines prope acta iam ætate decursaque, corpus effœtu senti unt ossaque ipsa exsiccata & medullis propemodum exhausta: ita me tot curæ doloresq; conficiunt, ut in ipso ætatis flore decrepitam ætatem iam repræsentare videantur.
units.tr: Then the tribunal of God set before us terrifies us, his threats terrify us, and the sentence of the divine law dismays our minds. The stings of punishments also prick us, by which the Lord often reminds us of our sins. But the most bitter of all is that pain which arises from the goads of conscience. When one has come to this point, we must take the greatest care not to cling to those terrors, but must press on further, namely to the promises of God and his mercy most fully revealed to us in Christ. This last thought is most sweet and serves as a medicine for the conscience. From this there arises a certain spiritual struggle between fear and confidence, and between despair and hope, so that, as it were, death seems to contend with life, threats with promises, the Law with the Gospel, and finally hell itself with heavenly glory. But when faith, armed with the Evangelical promises and leaning and supported on all sides by the merits of Christ, comes forth victorious, then it breaks out exultantly into a true confession of sin, and at the same time receives the remission of it in the passion of Christ and in his most perfect obedience, which he rendered to God in our name. So a true confession of sin is, as it were, the triumph of victorious faith. We can contemplate all these things in David as in a mirror, as we have already noted above. Now let us examine David's own words. "My bones," he says, "grew old through my roaring every day." By these words he signifies not an ordinary grief, but an extreme sorrow, one which, penetrating as it were to the very marrow, tormented his spirit most violently, and this is expressed by the verb "to grow old." For as Solomon says, it is certain that a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones; so too the Prophet complains in Psalm 102 that his bones were dried up and burnt by grief; and our David in Psalms 6 and 31 cries out that his eyes were consumed as if by age, and his very bones were eaten away and rotten, because he had given himself over to so many and such great anguishes. All these things express most forcibly the power of grief. For we know that nature has so ordained that those who are advanced in years are much weaker than before, for their natural moisture dries up, and their bodies become drier and feebler. So Scripture is accustomed to compare the life of man with a flower, and we see that the leaves of a withering flower are shrivelled and dry. Therefore our poet aptly used the verb "to grow old," to signify the bitterness and vehemence of his grief, as if he were saying: just as men, when their age is nearly spent, feel their body worn out by age and their very bones dried up and almost emptied of marrow, so cares and sorrows wear me down, so that in the very flower of my age they seem to represent a decrepit old age.

units.la: Hæc ergo fuit mens Dauidis ut suũ dolorem distinguat à doloris simulatione. Multi enim dolet ubi nihil est op*, hic ubi opus est, non dolent. Nam quotusquisque est qui ita ut decet doleat propter admissa peccata & eorum vero sensu afficiatur? Multi sane præ se ferunt eiusmodi dolorem, sed saepe accidit ut sola lingua doleant, ita ut illis merito conueniat quod dici solet, cito lacrymam exa-rescere. Dauid autem ossa ipsa commemo-rat ut magis significet dolorem suum in ipsis præcordiis infixum & quodámodo inustum esse. Huc etiam pertinet dictio Rugitus, qua significat luctum nō mediocrem fuisse, cùm in magnos clamores eruperit, ducta si-militudine à leonibus quorum rugitus lon-gè latéque exaudiri solet: qua similitudine suos dolores Iobus etiam exprimebat. Præterea cùm ait luctu illum fuisse quotidianū & assiduum, facit ut longè etiā grauior esse vi-deatur. Itaq; crescit eleganter oratio, dū[?] insequens dictio antecedenti vim addit. Primùm non leuis est dolor, qui penetrat usque ad i-pfas ossium medullas. Deinde magnus est dolor qui non solitos clamores, sed horribiles exprimit, ita ut non tā vox hominis quā rugitus leonis censeri debeat. Postremo summus est ille dolor qui nulla tèporis[?] intermissione relaxatur. Itaque si illa omnia simul congeras, facile videbis Dauidis dolorem amplificari quanta fieri potuit orationis ef-ficacitate.
units.tr: This, then, was David's intention, to distinguish his sorrow from the pretence of sorrow. For many grieve where there is nothing to grieve about; here, where there is cause, they do not grieve. For how few are there who grieve as they ought over the sins they have committed, and are truly affected by the sense of them? Many indeed display such grief outwardly, but it often happens that they grieve only with the tongue, so that the saying rightly applies to them, that the tear dries up quickly. But David mentions the bones themselves to signify more clearly that his sorrow was fixed in his very heart and, as it were, branded there. To this also pertains the word "roaring," by which he signifies that his mourning was no small one, since it broke out into great cries, the comparison being drawn from lions, whose roar is wont to be heard far and wide; Job also expressed his sorrows by this comparison. Moreover, when he says that his mourning was daily and continual, he makes it seem even much heavier. Thus the expression grows elegantly, as the following word adds force to the preceding one. First, it is no slight grief that penetrates to the very marrow of the bones. Second, it is great grief that wrings out not customary cries but horrible ones, so that it should be judged not so much the voice of a man as the roaring of a lion. Lastly, it is the greatest grief that is never relaxed by any interval of time. So if you gather all these things together, you will easily see how David's sorrow is magnified with all the force of expression that could be achieved.

units.la: Verùm hic quædam possit emergere dubitatio. Nam ecquónam pacto conueniunt personæ Davidis ea quæ de tanto luctu deq; tam immoderato dolore dicuntur?Dicendū est, non hanc esse Davidis metem ut se cum brutis animantibus comparatum esse velit, ut quasi laxis habenis totus feratur in luctum & impatientiam. Sed hoc Poetice dictum est, ad exprimendam doloris acerbitatem: quemadmodum sæpe aliàs hæc dictio Rugitus usurpatur in eum finem. Quædam igi-tur dicamus de luctu & iis doloribus qui in pios homines cadunt: atque videamus quatenus illis hac in re vel possit vel debeat indulgeri. Primum omnium constat mulie-bres illos ciulatus in quos improbi solent erumpere quoties in rerum asperitate versantur, nulla ratione probari posse, cum nō tantum hominem dedeceant, verumetiam solent ab impatientia & desperatione proficisci. Quin etiam ipsi Philosophi molles eiusmodi & eneruatos animos ne hominis quidem nomine dignos esse censuerunt: quo fit ut flebiles istas Tragicorum voces vehementer improbarint:Hæc omnia vidi inflamari: Ité ἑτέρῳ δ᾽ ἀφ᾽ ἑτέρων κακά[?]. Atque ut in nostrum campum revertamur, flevit quidem Esau, sed ille fletus non fuit acceptus Deo. Saul summam animi ægritudinem sensit. Iudas etiam à mœrore absorptus est. Quid plura? Christus ipse dum inferorum cruciatus describit, ubi, inquit, est fletus & stridor dentium. Habent igitur, habent, inquam, impii suos dolores, sed a quibus longè abes-se debent piorum fletus. Nam impij gemunt quia affliguntur: pij vero quia iram Dei in se prouocarunt. Impij in suis fletibus mur-murant aduersus Deum: contrà pij offerunt Deo suos fletus, vt ab ipso consolationem accipiant. Impiorum lacrymae ex impatien-tia, piorum lacrymae ex poenitentia procedunt: impiorum dolores sunt initia aeter-ni illius cruciatus quem sunt tandem persensuri, piorum vero dolores eo spectant ne doleant in aeternum. Recte igitur Paulus tristitiam, quae secundum Deum est, longè aliam esse docet ab ea quae est huius se-culi tristitia. Ergo flent pij, vt consolationem accipiant: patiuntur, vt gaudeant: cruciantur, vt tandem aeternae quietis sint participes. Atque huius insignis differentiae haec causa poterit assignari, quod ij dolores quibus afficiuntur reprobi proficiscuntur ab ira Dei: piorum vero dolores promanant a Dei, castigantis quidem, sed tamen Patris misericordia: quod eleganter expressit Nazianzenus cum suas afflictiones vocat amaras sagittas emissas ex dulci manu Domini ἐν γλώσ-ης ταλαιπώρης οἰκτρᾶς[?]. Concludamus igitur fletum piorum ab impiorum lacrymis & stridore distare quamplurimum, quanuis in speciem nihil discriminis esse videatur.
units.tr: But here a certain doubt may arise. For in what way do those things that are said of such great mourning and of such immoderate grief agree with the person of David? It must be said that David's intention was not to make himself like the brute animals, so that, as if with loosened reins, he was carried wholly into mourning and impatience. Rather, this is said poetically, to express the bitterness of his sorrow, just as this word "roaring" is often used to that end elsewhere. Let us therefore say something about mourning and those sorrows that fall upon godly men, and let us see how far, in this matter, they may or ought to be indulged. First of all, it is established that those women's wailings into which the wicked are wont to break out whenever they are in adversity cannot be approved in any way, since they not only disgrace a man but are usually born of impatience and despair. Indeed the philosophers themselves judged that spirits of this soft and enervated kind were not even worthy of the name of man; hence they strongly disapproved of those tearful voices of the tragedians: "All these things I saw set ablaze" [Hæc omnia vidi inflammari], and "one evil after another" [ἑτέρῳ δ᾽ ἀφ᾽ ἑτέρων κακά]. But to return to our own field: Esau did weep, yet that weeping was not acceptable to God. Saul felt the deepest distress of spirit. Judas also was swallowed up by sorrow. What more? Christ himself, when describing the torments of hell, says: "Where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth." So the wicked have their sorrows, indeed they have them, I say, but the tears of the godly ought to be far removed from these. For the wicked groan because they are afflicted; the godly, because they have provoked the wrath of God. The wicked in their weeping murmur against God; on the contrary, the godly offer their tears to God, that they may receive consolation from him. The tears of the wicked come from impatience, the tears of the godly from repentance. The sorrows of the wicked are the beginnings of that eternal torment which they will at last feel, but the sorrows of the godly look to this end, that they may not grieve for ever. Rightly, therefore, Paul teaches that the sorrow which is according to God is very different from the sorrow of this world. So the godly weep that they may receive consolation; they suffer that they may rejoice; they are tormented that at last they may be partakers of eternal rest. And the cause of this remarkable difference can be assigned as follows: the sorrows with which the reprobate are afflicted proceed from the wrath of God, but the sorrows of the godly flow from the mercy of God, who indeed chastises, but is still a Father. Gregory Nazianzen expressed this elegantly when he called his afflictions "bitter arrows shot from the sweet hand of the Lord" [ἐν γλώσσης ταλαιπώρου οἰκτρᾶς]. Let us therefore conclude that the weeping of the godly differs very much from the tears and gnashing of the wicked, although in outward appearance there seems to be no difference at all.

units.la: Praeterea refellendi sunt ex hoc loco stu-pidi quidā homines, qui nescio quā indolentiam in Ecclesiam inuehere voluerút & Stoi corum errores ex inferis excitare. Nec enim sancti sunt habendi tanquam Marpesia cau- tes (vt ille dicebat) ita vt sensu careant: quod si esset, nulla certe patientia, nullaque patien tiæ corona sanctis hominibus tribueretur.
units.tr: Moreover, some stupid men must be refuted on the basis of this passage. They wish to introduce a kind of insensibility into the Church and to revive the errors of the Stoics from the dead. The saints are not to be regarded as Marpesian rocks, as that man used to say, so that they lack feeling. If that were so, no patience would be credited to holy men, and no crown of patience would be laid up for them.

units.la: Vbi enim quæso virtus patientiæ si nihil pa- teris? si non doles? si non afficeris sensu af- flictionum quas Dominus immittit? hoc er- go est hominem ex homine tollere. Neque suscipio veterum Philosophorum errores re- futados, qui adductis athletarum exemplis, ho mines ad animi magnitudine cohortabatur.
units.tr: For where, I ask, is the virtue of patience if you suffer nothing? If you do not grieve? If you are not affected by the feeling of the afflictions which the Lord sends? This is to take the man out of man. Nor do I take up the errors of the ancient philosophers to be refuted here, who, citing the examples of athletes, urged men to greatness of spirit.

units.la: Illi enim frequeti vsu adictus ita obdurue- rant, vt saepe (siquidem fides habenda est Philo sophis) multis vulneribus acceptis, tame sine clamore, sine lacryma, sine gemitu animam exhalaret. Atqui stuporis potius qua constan tiæ nomine illud appellarim. Nā ille demum constans existimadus est, qui dolores quidem percipit, sed eos tandē superat vera patietia, cū Dei misericordiam amplectitur & suam ipsius ad Dei voluntatem flectit. Vt enim e- quus laudabitur qui admotos stimulos per- sentiens, redditur proptior ad ingrediedum illud iter quo ducitur a sessore, nō qui aduer- sus stimulos calcitrans, restitat & præfractè obnititur: ita de homine dicedum est, eū esse constantem, nō qui spernit verbera, qui ob- duruit ad dolores, sed qui doloribus cōmouē tur & incitatur ad eam viam ineunda quam Dominus commonstrat. Dicamus ergo do-lere fideles posse quoties percutiuntur à Dei manu, sed adhibendum esse modum ne patientiæ metas transiliant, alioquin constantia degeneraret in impatientiam & querelam adversus Deum, quod improbi factitat. Et certè fatendum est, ut cæteri affectus naturales qui in sanctos cadunt, inquinati sunt à peccato, ita & à sanctis hominibus peccari in hac dolorum tolerantia. Aut enim non satis, aut plus æquo dolent. Sed hic naevus, hæc imperfectio separanda est vel à stupore, vel à desperatione improborum. Quod si quis roget quam ob rem dolere debeant pij in suis afflictionibus, sic habeat: duplicem esse doloris causam. Una est naturalis, videlicet sensus pœnæ quam patiuntur: Altera adventitia quæ à pœnitentia ducitur, quando dolet sanctis hominibus Deum offendisse. Prior ille dolor ut communis est omnibus, ita nihil habet quod Deo peculiariter sit acceptum. Neque etiam per se peccatum est, quemadmodum neque cæteri naturales affectus. Quia tamē natura per peccatum corrupta est, ideō quoties etiā ipsi naturales affectus in nos cadūt, fieri nō potest ut careat prorsus omni labe. Jā quod attinet ad eū dolore qui manat à pœnitentia, ille Deo gratus est & instar sacrificij spiritualis ipsi offerendus. Quamobrē Apostolus cōmedat tristitiā Corinthiorū eo quòd fuerint redditi diligentiores tiores & ad peccatum agnoscendum & ad ea præstanda quæ conferebant ædificationi totius Ecclesiæ. Hic ergo dolor nobis vehementer probandus est, quo magis dolemus quòd Deum offenderimus, quàm quòd pœnas ipsas à iudicio Domini inflictas sentiamus.Porrò cùm Dauid loquatur de quotidiano dolore, hinc discamus non ad horæ mo-mentum nobis sentiedum peccati dolorem. Ne igitur illos imitemur quibus si semel pro-pter admissum peccatum vel lacrymula excussa, vel gemitus forte expressus fuerit, iam præclarè se officio defunctos esse arbitratur. Atqui pœna nostris peccatis debita, æterna est ne ergo tam leviter prætereamus quod foret alioquin æternum, nisi summa Domini misericordia intercederet.
