Imitemur potius Dauidem qui diu in luctu & squalore versatus est propter sensum peccati quo dies noctésque afficiebatur, queadmodu significauit his verbis consenuerunt ossa mea, inquit, in rugitu meo quotidiano. Ac ne cui dubium fit quam ob causam adeò excruciaretur subiungit.
units.tr: For those men, hardened by frequent practice, became so insensible that often (if we may trust the philosophers) they breathed out their souls, even after receiving many wounds, without a cry, without a tear, without a groan. Yet I would rather call that stupor than constancy. For a man is to be judged truly constant not when he feels no pain, but when he feels the pain and at length overcomes it through true patience, embracing God's mercy and bending his own will to the will of God. As a horse is praised not for kicking against the goads and stubbornly resisting the rider, but for feeling the spurs and becoming more ready to go along the road to which the horseman leads it, so it must be said of a man that he is constant not because he scorns blows and has grown hard to pain, but because he is moved by his sufferings and stirred to take up the way that the Lord shows. Let us say, then, that the faithful can grieve whenever they are struck by the hand of God, but that a measure must be observed, lest they leap over the bounds of patience. Otherwise their constancy would degenerate into impatience and complaint against God, which the wicked practise. And certainly it must be admitted that, just as the other natural affections that fall upon the saints are tainted by sin, so the saints also sin in this endurance of pain. For they either grieve too little or grieve more than is right. But this blemish and imperfection must be kept apart both from the insensibility and from the despair of the wicked. And if anyone asks why the godly ought to grieve in their afflictions, let him understand this: there is a twofold cause of grief. One is natural, namely the sense of the punishment they suffer. The other is adventitious, arising from repentance, when the holy grieve that they have offended God. The former grief, as it is common to all, so has nothing in it that is especially acceptable to God. Nor is it in itself sinful, any more than the other natural affections are. Yet because nature has been corrupted by sin, therefore, whenever even the natural affections fall upon us, it cannot happen that they are wholly free from stain. But as for the grief that flows from repentance, it is pleasing to God and is to be offered to him as a kind of spiritual sacrifice. Therefore the Apostle commends the sorrow of the Corinthians because they were made more diligent both in acknowledging their sin and in doing those things which contributed to the edification of the whole Church. This grief, then, must be greatly approved by us, by which we grieve more that we have offended God than that we feel the punishments themselves inflicted by the judgment of the Lord. Furthermore, since David speaks of a daily grief, let us learn from this not to feel the grief of sin only for a moment. Let us not imitate those who, if a little tear has been shaken out or a groan perhaps forced from them on account of a sin committed, think at once that they have discharged their duty admirably. Yet the punishment owed for our sins is eternal. Therefore let us not pass over so lightly what would otherwise be eternal, were it not for the supreme mercy of the Lord interceding. Rather let us imitate David, who for a long time lived in mourning and squalor because of the sense of sin by which he was afflicted day and night, as he signified in these words: My bones have grown old, he says, because of my daily groaning. And lest anyone doubt why he was so tormented, he adds:

units.la: vers.4.
units.tr: Verse 4.

units.la: Nam dies noctésque manus tua gravis fuit super me, versus est humor meus in siccitates æstatis. Explicatio est præcedentis versus. Dicebat enim ossa sua consenuisse propter quotidianos illos rugitus quos magnitudo doloris exprimebat: nunc addit causam ißtius tanti clamoris, nempe Dei percutientis manum: atque ita singula prope verba singulis respondent. Meminerat enim quotidiani gemitus: nunc ait se dies noctesque manum Domini ingrauescetem sensisse, ita vt nullus fuerit quieti locus. Quod autem subiungit humorem suum versum esse in siccitatem, ei respondet quod dixerat de ossibus consenescentibus prae nimio dolore. Manus autem Domini significat in hoc loco eius iudicium & poenas ab eo inflictas(vt recte Hebręi doctores interpretantur) ducta similitudine ab hominibus, qui dum percutiunt solent vehementer manum deprimere, vt grauior sit ictus. Alibi manus Domini significat praesens eius auxilium & summam potestatem qua omnia sibi ipse subiicit, vt quum saepe di-citur Dominus eduxisse Israelitas ex Aegypto, manu potenti. Aliquando denotat gratiam a Domino propositam & oblatam, vt ait per Prophetam se passis manibus rebellem populum reuocauisse. Sed hic manus Dei significat eius iudicia, quemadmodum dixi, vt etiam saepe occurrit apud Prophetas, manum Dei extentam adhuc esse, quum significare volunt iudicia Domini adhuc pergere, nondum esse poenarum finem. Hic est sensus huius loci. Caeterum non explicat genus ipsum doloris, nec est etiam quod nos ea quaestio multum detineat. Potuit certe vel morbo vel alia quavis ratione sentire cruciatum & dolorem etiam in corpore. Quinetiam si solae fuissent conscientiae vulnera & intimi dolores proficiscentes ex apprehensione & horrore iudicij Dei, hoc vnum certè satis superque erat ad hominem prope redigendum ad tabem. Ergo operæpraetium[?] est considerare quid praestiterit Dauid in hoc tanto cruciatu potius quàm in eo describendo & eius causis disquirendis curiosius immorari. Hoc igitur in primis obseruandum est, Dauidem ad Deum ipsum oculos sustulisse in mediis doloribus & ipsius percutientis manum non tantùm sensisse, verùmetiam agnouisse. Nam in hoc homines plerùq; peccare video quòd nolunt agnoscere manum eius à quo percu-tiuntur, vt aliquando Prophetæ Iudæis ex-probrabant: Quorsum, (inquit Esaias) vltra percutiemini? addetis transgressionem. Et Ieremias, percussisti eos (inquit) & non do-luerunt. Nimirùm, vt Esaias alibi dicebat, Populus non reuertebatur ad eum qui se per cusserat. Enimuerò facile est sentire vulnus, sed difficile est oculos couertere ad eam ma-num quæ vulnerat. Plerique omnes fatentur mundū hunc regi prouidentia Dei, nihilque temere accidere: sed vbi ventum est ad rem ipsam, pauci sunt qui in sese agnoscant quod in vniuersum agnouerunt de Dei prouidentia & generali rerum omnium gubernatio-ne. Quippe alij varios rerum euentus & huius vitæ rerumque humanarum incon-stantiam accusant: alij res aduersas imprudenti & temeritati suæ adscribunt, quòd nempe non ante præuiderint, nō cauerint, non hac vel illa ratione sibi consuluerint: alii defixi sunt in suorum hostium improbitate quam solam incusant, solam damnant, solam insectatur: quod quidem est, non sua, sed aliorum peccata confiteri. Sed interim dolores nihilominus recrudescunt. Ergo mihi illi homines similiter facere videntur, ut si quis accepto graui vulnere, non curet vulnus, non ad medicum recurrat, non aliquod remedium comparet, sed modo suam ignauiam accusat quod telum non declinauerit, modo telum ipsum increpitans mordeat, aut aliquid denique eiusmodi faciat, cum sint potius adhibenda remedia quibus vulnus curetur. Ita etiam quoties in afflictionibus & in rebus exulceratis versamur, ne nos ipsos, ne hostes, ne mundum aspiciamus, tanquam inde nostras molestias doloresque leuaturi: sed erigamus oculos ad Deū qui tela ipsa immisit pro summo suo & iustissimo iudicio. Non quidem ut ad-versus ipsum murmuremus, aut aliquid detrahamus de perfecta eius æquitate, sed potius ut misericordiam imploremus, & ab eo ipso qui vulnus inflixit, medicinam requiramus. Sic enim alicubi Nazianzenus dicebat: A te percussus, ad te respicio. Sic etiam fecit hic no-ster vates quia Domino percussus exclamat: Manus, inquit, tua grauis fuit super me. quasi dicat, Agnosco Domine tuam manum: non hæreo in rebus mediis, sed sublatis in cœlum oculis in teipsum intueor, cuius iussu & voluntate iustissima scio me in tantos dolores incidisse. Hoc idem a nobis praestandum erit quoties affligemur, nec erunt imitandi nobis illi Ægyptij qui a Domino percussi exclamabant quidem digitum Dei esse, sed non propterea resipiscebat. Nos autem caueamus ne aut stupore iudicia Dei spernamus, aut impa tientiæ vocem doloris acerbitas nobis extor queat. Hoc enim satis superque esse debet, quod est manus Domini feriētis: & sola haec cogitatio debet frenare impetum doloris, ne nos rapiat extra metas. Est enim manus non hostis perimentis, sed patris castigantis quem nostra peccata propemodum eò adegerunt, vt suam in nos manum depresserit. Igitur ea manus quae nos formauit, quae nos aluit, quae nos ex idololatriae & ipsis inferorum faucibus extraxit, quae toties aperta, nobis summa Dei beneficia porrexit: ea, inquam, manus à nobis prouocata, in nos ingrauescit. Verum tamen ad eam ipsam manum recurramus, eam prehendamus, eam quatumuis ferientem supplices osculemur, neque dubitemus fore quin breui sit manus liberationis, quae manus fuit castigationis. Cæterum cum Dauidem vide- mus graviter diuque afflictu fuisse, discamus patieter ferre afflictiones etsi diutius durare videbuntur. Nam si tatus vir a Domino mul- ta & grauia fuit passus, quid est cur ipsi diutur num laborem longioresque molestias refugiamus? Sit igitur Dauid nobis exemplum fortitudinis & patientiæ nequando vis doloris atque diuturnitas, nos adigat ad desperationem. Ait autem humorem siue succum suum exaruisse instar siccitatum æstatis, vt magis exprimat quod antea dixit de ossibus suis consenescentibus, quemadmodum iam ante dictum est. Summa est, tantum fuisse doloris sensum, vt ab eo pene confectus fuerit. Est certè modus adhibendus, nec probandi sunt ij qui se ita læguori[?] dediderunt, vt non se tantum valetudine priuauerint, sed etiam aliquando morte præmaturam accersiuerint. Ii sunt desperantium non pœnitentium dolores. Veruntamen vix fieri potest, vt serio doleamus, quin illam animi ægritudinem, corporis quoque ægritudo quodammodo consequatur. Itaque constat Dauidem vere & ex animo doluisse.
units.tr: For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my moisture was turned into the drought of summer. This is an explanation of the preceding verse. For he had said that his bones had grown old because of those daily groans which the greatness of his pain drew from him. Now he adds the cause of such great crying: the hand of God striking him. And so almost each word answers to each word. For he had mentioned daily groaning; now he says that day and night he felt the hand of the Lord growing heavier, so that there was no place of rest. As for his adding that his moisture was turned into dryness, this answers to what he had said about his bones growing old through excessive pain. Now the hand of the Lord in this place signifies his judgment and the punishments inflicted by him, as the Hebrew teachers rightly interpret, the image being taken from men who, when they strike, are accustomed to press the hand down hard, so that the blow may be heavier. Elsewhere the hand of the Lord signifies his present help and supreme power by which he subjects all things to himself, as when it is often said that the Lord led the Israelites out of Egypt with a mighty hand. Sometimes it denotes the grace set forth and offered by the Lord, as when he says through the Prophet that he had called back the rebellious people with outstretched hands. But here the hand of God signifies his judgments, as I have said; just as it often occurs among the Prophets, the hand of God being still stretched out, when they wish to signify that the judgments of the Lord are still continuing and that the end of the punishments is not yet. This is the sense of this place. Moreover, the verse does not explain the kind of pain itself, nor is it necessary for us to be much detained by that question. He could certainly have felt the torment and pain even in his body, whether from sickness or from some other cause. Indeed, even if there had been only the wounds of conscience and inward griefs arising from the apprehension and horror of the judgment of God, this alone would have been enough and more than enough to reduce a man almost to wasting away. Therefore it is worth considering what David did in so great a torment, rather than dwelling too curiously on describing it and inquiring into its causes. First of all, then, this is to be observed: David lifted his eyes to God himself in the midst of his griefs, and recognised, not only felt, the hand of the One who struck him. For I see that men commonly sin in this, that they are unwilling to acknowledge the hand of him by whom they are struck. Sometimes the Prophets reproached the Jews with this: Why, says Isaiah, will you be struck any more? You will add transgression. And Jeremiah: You have struck them, he says, and they have not grieved. Indeed, as Isaiah says elsewhere, the people did not turn back to him who had struck them. For it is easy to feel a wound, but difficult to turn one's eyes to the hand that wounds. Nearly all men confess that this world is ruled by the providence of God and that nothing happens by chance; but when it comes to the matter itself, there are few who acknowledge in themselves what they have acknowledged in general about the providence of God and the general government of all things. Some complain of the various outcomes of events and of the inconstancy of this life and of human affairs; others ascribe adverse things to their own imprudence and rashness, because they did not foresee beforehand, did not take care, did not provide for themselves in this or that way; others are fixed upon the wickedness of their enemies, which alone they accuse, alone they condemn, alone they pursue. This indeed is to confess the sins not of oneself but of others. Yet meanwhile the pains break out again nonetheless. So those men seem to me to act like someone who, having received a grievous wound, does not tend the wound, does not hasten to a physician, does not procure some remedy, but now accuses his own sluggishness for not turning aside the weapon, now bites the weapon itself with reproaches, or does something of this kind, when rather remedies by which the wound may be cured ought to be applied. So too, whenever we are in afflictions and in matters that have become like open sores, let us not look to ourselves, nor to our enemies, nor to the world, as if we were to relieve our troubles and pains from there. Rather, let us lift our eyes to God, who sent the very weapons according to his supreme and most just judgment. Not so that we murmur against him, or take anything away from his perfect equity, but rather that we may implore his mercy and seek the remedy from him who inflicted the wound. For thus Nazianzen says somewhere: Struck by you, I look to you. So too our poet here did, for being struck by the Lord he cries out: Your hand, he says, was heavy upon me. As if to say: I acknowledge your hand, O Lord; I do not cling to the intermediate causes, but with my eyes lifted to heaven I look upon you yourself, by whose command and most just will I know that I have fallen into such great griefs. The same thing must be done by us whenever we are afflicted, nor should we imitate those Egyptians who, struck by the Lord, cried out indeed that it was the finger of God, but on that account did not repent. Rather, let us take care either not to despise the judgments of God through stupor, or lest the bitterness of grief force from us a cry of impatience. For it ought to be enough and more than enough that it is the hand of the Lord that strikes; and this thought alone ought to restrain the rush of grief, lest it carry us beyond its bounds. For it is not the hand of an enemy bent on destroying, but of a father chastening, whom our sins have all but driven to lower his hand upon us. Therefore that hand which formed us, which nourished us, which drew us out from idolatry and from the very jaws of hell, which has so often been opened to offer us the greatest benefits of God: that hand, I say, provoked by us, grows heavier upon us. Yet let us nonetheless return to that very hand, take hold of it, and kiss it as suppliants, even as it strikes, and let us not doubt that before long it will be the hand of deliverance, as it was the hand of chastisement. Moreover, when we see that David was grievously and long afflicted, let us learn to bear afflictions patiently, even if they seem likely to last longer. For if so great a man suffered many and grievous things from the Lord, why should we shrink from a longer labour and more prolonged troubles? Let David therefore be an example to us of fortitude and patience, so that the force of pain and its long duration may not drive us to despair. He says that his moisture or sap has dried up like the drought of summer, so as to express more fully what he said before about his bones growing old, as has already been said. The sum is that the sense of pain was so great that he was almost worn out by it. Certainly a measure must be applied, and those are not to be approved who so give themselves over to lethargy that they not only deprive themselves of health but sometimes even hasten an untimely death. Such are the griefs of the despairing, not of the repentant. Nevertheless, it can hardly happen that, when we grieve in earnest, that sickness of mind is not in some measure followed by sickness of body also. Thus it is evident that David truly and from his heart grieved.

units.la: Porrò si, vt quidam existimant, Dauid in hoc Psalmo respexit ad adulterium commissum cum Bethsabæa, non leuiter prætereundum est, merito corpus ipsum pœnas luisse quod fuit instrumentum peccati, & cuius vt libido expleretur, ad tantum scelus vir alioquin sanctissimus prorupit. Merito ergo succus corporis prope exhaustus est, qui antea luxurians materia fuit libidinis & peccati. Similitudo autem petita ab iis rebus quæ ab æstiui solis ardore pene conflagrantes exaruerunt, multum est efficax ad rem ante oculos[?] constituendam. Vt enim res eiusmodi humore suo destitutæ tandem in pulueren redigu̅tur: ita Dauidis corpus à iudicio Dei tâquam flamma cœlesti correptum, videtur penitus exaruisse. Atque obiter hinc discimus, quoties æ̨grotamus eam esse gra-uem afflictionem. Dicebat ille profanus o-ptandam esse sanam mentem in corpore sa-no:nec immerito. siquidem corpus effœtum & inualidum vrgente morbo, propemodum inutile redditur ad res obeundas. Eò spe-stat quod aliquando dicebat Siracides: sani-tatem esse maximum thesaurum. Nihil enim in hac vita vel vtilius est vel optabilius. Nec sine causa morbi numeratur inter eas pœnas quibus Dominus afficit transgressores legis; nam hoc magno argumeto est valetudinem esse maximum Dei beneficium.Sed nihil nobis sæpius vsuuenit quàm abuti tanto & tâ præ- claro Dei dono:queadmodū dicebat Nazian zenus,sultæ valetudinis fructū esse peccatū. ἀσωθέτως ὑγιείας καρπὸς , ἀκαρπία, inquit. Quò sit vt, ea detracta, Dominus nos exer- ceat variis morborū generibus.Si verò in me- diis morbis patientiâ & fortitudine atq; adeò in primis refipiscentiam adhibuerimus, tunc illi morbi fient nobis saluberrimi. Discamus igitur, si sumus sano corpore, Deo habere gratiâ pro hoc tanto beneficio:& robur cor- poris ipsámque valetudinem impendere instari de regno Domini amplificando & promouenda proximorum salute. Sin autem morbo la-boramus, ne hæreamus in causis fecūdis, nec in humorum vitio & corruptione. Sed sta-tim oculos in Deum cõiiciamus, nos vitæ an-tè male actæ pœniteat, cõuertamur ad Deū, defleamus peccata, versemur in sanctis cogi-tationibus mortis, denique vera fide cœleste omníque ex parte fœlicem vitam apprehen-damus. Itaque statuamus, eos in media & ve-geta valetudine ægrotare, qui valetudine abu-tuntur: contrà eos ægrotos bene habere qui ad Deum ex animo conuertuntur, & ab ipsis morbis petunt aduersus peccata medicinam. Hæc omnia sunt obiter consideranda quum Dauidis verba meditamur, quibus conqueri-tur corpus suum deficiente humore prope exaruisse instar siccitatum æstatis. Iam addit: vers.5. Peccatum meum notum tibi feci & iniquitatem meam nō n abscondi.
units.tr: Moreover, if, as some think, David in this Psalm had in view the adultery committed with Bathsheba, we should not pass over lightly that the body itself was rightly punished, since it was the instrument of sin, and it was in order to satisfy its lust that this otherwise most holy man broke out into so great a crime. It is therefore fitting that the moisture of his body was nearly drained away, since before it had been a riotous source of lust and sin. A comparison drawn from things that have been nearly burned up and dried out by the heat of the summer sun is very effective in setting the matter before our eyes. For just as such things, deprived of their moisture, are at last reduced to dust, so David's body, seized by the judgment of God as by a heavenly flame, seems to have been utterly dried up. And in passing we learn from this how grievous a affliction sickness is, whenever we are ill. That profane man used to say that a sound mind in a sound body is to be desired, and not without reason, for a body worn out and weakened by a pressing disease becomes almost useless for carrying out its tasks. To this point belongs what Ben Sira once said: that health is the greatest treasure. For nothing in this life is either more useful or more desirable. Nor without reason is sickness counted among those punishments with which the Lord afflicts the transgressors of his law; for this is a strong argument that health is the greatest gift of God. But nothing happens to us more often than to abuse so great and so remarkable a gift of God; as Nazianzen used to say, the fruit of health squandered is barrenness [ἀσωθέτως ὑγιείας καρπὸς, ἀκαρπία], as he puts it. Hence it comes about that, once health is taken away, the Lord exercises us with various kinds of sickness. But if in the midst of sicknesses we apply patience and fortitude, and above all repentance, then those sicknesses will become most salutary for us. Let us therefore learn, if we are in sound body, to give thanks to God for so great a benefit, and to spend the strength of our body and our very health in advancing [instari de] the kingdom of the Lord and in promoting the salvation of our neighbours. But if we are suffering from sickness, let us not cling to secondary causes, nor to the defect and corruption of the humours. Rather, let us at once turn our eyes to God; if we repent of the life we have led before, let us turn to God, let us lament our sins, let us dwell on holy thoughts of death, and finally, with true faith, lay hold of the heavenly and in every respect happy life. Let us therefore hold that those are sick in the midst of vigorous health who abuse their health, and, on the contrary, that those are well who turn to God from the heart and seek from their very sicknesses a remedy against sin. All these things are to be considered in passing when we meditate on David's words, in which he complains that his body, with its moisture failing, has been nearly dried up like the dryness of summer. Then he adds, verse 5: I have made my sin known to you, and I have not hidden my iniquity.

units.la: Repetendus est ordo totius Psalmi vt fa-cilior nobis constet huius loci expositio. Di-ximus tres esse huius Psalmi partes: nempe Doctrinam de remissione peccatorum, Exem-plum Dauidis propositum ad illius doctrinæ confirmationem, & cohortationem ad resi-piscentiam. Explicata est prima illa pars qua doctrina tradita fuit, ingresíque sumus in ex-positionem exempli Dauidis quod ipse pro-posuit, vt magis inculcet veritatem eius do-ctrinæ quam primo loco posuit. Rursus tria sunt consideranda in Dauidis exemplo videlicet dolor cruciatúsque Dauidis propter pec-catum, deinde confessio peccati coram Deo, postremò peccati remissio. De doloribus Dauidis supra egimus, neque hîc quod iam tractatum est, videtur esse repetendum. Iam ergo sese offert confessio Dauidis nobis explicanda, de qua sic ipse Dauid: Peccatum meum notum tibi feci. Diximus de lucta illa spirituali quæ nobis suscipienda est quoties per pœnitentiam reuocamur à peccato, quan doquidem & mundus & caro & diabolus a-cerrimè pugnant aduersus initia pœniten-tiæ, vt ea siqua fieri possit ratione extinguat. Timor & diffidentia fidem oppugnat, despe-ratio in spem emergentem totis viribus insur-git, vt eam pessundet: Satan autem proponit grauitatem peccati, vim legis horrorémque iudiciorum Dei, quæ omnia adhibet tàquam tormenta bellica quibus peccatorem perter-refactum concutiat ac deiiciat, ne ad miseri-cordiam Dei erigat oculos, sed iaceat in ipsa mortis voragine demersus.Illud igitur certa-men longè est grauissimū neque satis expêdi, imò ne cogitari quidè potest ab iis qui illud semel non susceperint. Sed quod de Martyri-bus dicit Cyprianus, huc rectè accommodari potest: Deum ipsum qui suos coronat, in suis vincere, in suis triumphare. Itaque vbi cle-mentissimus ille pater fidei vires in animos nostros iniecit & proposito misericordiæ vultu, serenissimum fulgorem conspiciendum exhibuit:tum hostibus victis & prostratis euadit victrix pœnitentia freta viribus Spiritus sancti, qui tantam fidei lucem in nobis accendit vt statim discutiantur metus & desperationis tenebræ. Vide autem quan-tum distet Dei iudicium ab humanis ac fo-rensibus iudiciis. Hic enim reus quum primum confitetur, damnari solet: illic vero simulatque reus confitetur, absolutus est. Ista omnia clarissimè videntur in Dauide. Postquam, inquit, diu multumque luctatus sum, tandem multos eosque acerbissimos dolores perpessus, victor euasi. Nam peccatum meum confessus sum coram Deo. Itaque Dauidis ista confessio opponitur silentio cuius ante meminit. Vt enim eum qui in equuleo & tormentis constitutus est, quanuis multos clamores edat, tamen nihil dixisse affirmamus, donec crimen confessus fuerit: ita tunc demum Dauidem locutum fuisse dicimus, quum ad peccati confessionem peruenit. Cuius nomine intelligamus non nudam & simplicem verborum aliquot prolationem aut solam apertionem oris, sed intimam peccati agnitionem & certam indubitatamque apprehensionem remissionis peccatorum. Sic enim Iohannes: Si confiteamur, inquit, peccata nostra, fidelis est ac iustus vt nobis remittat ea & purget nos ab omni iniquitate. Porro hic agitur de peccato coram Deo confitendo, & quod ex Cypriano didicimus hic memoria repetendum est, Deum esse cordis non vocis auditorem. Ergo animus ipse loquatur, gemat, confiteatur necesse est, vt confessio vera & legitima dici possit. Istud à Dauide fuisse obseruatum ille ipse docet his verbis:
units.tr: The order of the whole Psalm must be recalled, so that the exposition of this passage may be easier for us. We have said that there are three parts of this Psalm: namely, the doctrine concerning the forgiveness of sins; the example of David set forth to confirm that doctrine; and an exhortation to repentance. That first part, in which the doctrine was delivered, has been explained, and we have entered upon the exposition of the example of David, which he himself set forth so that he might impress more strongly the truth of the doctrine that he placed first. Again, there are three things to be considered in David's example: namely, David's sorrow and anguish on account of sin; then the confession of sin before God; and finally the remission of sin. We have already dealt with David's sorrows above, and what has already been treated does not seem to need repeating here. Now, therefore, David's confession presents itself to us for explanation, concerning which David himself speaks thus: I have made my sin known to you. We have spoken of that spiritual struggle which we must undertake whenever we are called back from sin by repentance, since the world, the flesh and the devil fight most fiercely against the beginnings of repentance, so that they may, by whatever means possible, extinguish it. Fear and distrust assail faith; despair rises up against the emerging hope with all its strength, so that it may overthrow it; and Satan sets before us the gravity of sin, the force of the law and the horror of God's judgments, employing all these things as siege engines with which to shake and cast down the sinner, terrified, so that he may not lift his eyes to the mercy of God, but may lie sunk in the very abyss of death. That struggle, therefore, is by far the most grievous, and it cannot be sufficiently weighed, nor even adequately conceived, by those who have not once undergone it. But what Cyprian says of the martyrs can be rightly applied here: that God himself, who crowns his own, conquers in them and triumphs in them. Therefore, when that most merciful Father has infused the strength of faith into our minds, and has shown, with a face full of mercy, a most serene brightness to be looked upon, then, with the enemies defeated and laid low, victorious repentance prevails, relying on the strength of the Holy Spirit, who kindles in us so great a light of faith that the fears and the darkness of despair are at once dispelled. But see how far God's judgment is from human and forensic judgments. For here the accused, as soon as he confesses, is usually condemned; but there, as soon as the accused confesses, he is acquitted. All these things are seen very clearly in David. After, he says, I had struggled long and hard, and had at last suffered many and most bitter sorrows, I came out victorious. For I confessed my sin before God. Therefore David's confession is set against the silence that he mentioned before. For just as we affirm that a man who is placed on the rack and in torments, however many cries he utters, has said nothing until he has confessed his crime, so we say that David then at last spoke when he came to the confession of sin. By this term let us understand not the bare and simple utterance of a few words, nor merely the opening of the mouth, but the inward acknowledgment of sin and the sure and undoubting apprehension of the forgiveness of sins. For thus John says: If we confess, he says, our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. But here it is a question of confessing sin before God; and what we learned from Cyprian must here be remembered again, that God is the hearer of the heart, not of the voice. Therefore the mind itself must speak, groan, and confess, so that the confession may be called true and lawful. That David observed this he himself teaches in these words:

units.la: Peccatum, inquit, meum tibi notum fe-ci: id est, vere ad te conuersus sum, ô Do-mine,& coram tuo tribunali ex animo agnoui peccatorum meorum grauitatem, confi-sus tua misericordia.
units.tr: I have made my sin known, he says, to you: that is, I have truly turned to you, O Lord, and before your tribunal I have acknowledged from my heart the gravity of my sins, trusting in your mercy.

units.la: Ergo hic locus postulat vt aliquid de peccatorum confessione dicamus. Eam autem duplicem esse iam supra quodammo-do attigimus. Vnam quæ coram Deo, alteram quæ coram hominibus fiat. Vtraque extat in hoc versu. Nam Dauid testatur se peccatum confessum esse coram Deo. Dein-de non priuatim aliquibus istud dicit, sed edito hoc Psalmo videtur palàm & coram omnibus adeoque coram ipsa posteritate peccatum confiteri & quasi tubæ clangore promulgare. Paucis igitur de vtraque confessione nobis agendum est. Primùm autem existere possit quædam dubitatio, quum Deo patent res omnes ipsæque nostræ in intimis mentibus delitescentes cogitationes eius oculis sint expositæ, quid opus fuerit narrare peccatum illud quod commisimus. Deus enim satis scit nos peccasse, qui longè ante sciebat nos peccaturos. Qui fit ergo vt Dauid dicat se Deo notum fecisse peccatum. Respondeo hoc totum dici ἀνθρωποπαθῶς[?]. Solet enim Scriptura dicere de Deo quæ videmus hominibus contingere. Sic iubemur Deo narrare res nostras, vt illis prouideat. Sic dicitur Deus descendere & intueri res humanas vt cognoscat quomodo se habeant. Sic Deus ipse declarat se fidem Abrahami ex eius obedientia cognouisse, vt omittam quod toties occurrit de piis à Domino tentandis probandisque vt videat quonam pacto sint erga se affecti. Quæ omnia vt rectè intelligamus, ad homines ipsos sunt accommodanda. Nouit quidem Dominus hominum peccata, & quanquam summopere conantur impij sua scelera tegere (tantum abest vt ea fateantur) tamen Dominus ea videt oculis acutissimis qui bus omnia peruestigat & scrutatur & tandem singulorum rationem reposcit. Verum dicitur ea cognoscere peccata quæ ipsi à no-bis explicantur: non quòd ea ignorarit, sed quia vult à nobis narrari, vt ea ratione magis commoueamur. Ergo dicendum est Dauidem notum fecisse peccatum Deo, quando verè atque ita vt decet agnouit peccatum suum esse Deo notum. Sic de precibus dici solet. Quis enim dubitet Deum scire nostra vel penuriam vel afflictionem? videmus tamen pios in suis precibus singula ordine ita recensere quasi res ipsis esset cum eo cui penitus illa omnia essent ignota. Sed, quemadmodum dixi, Dominus hoc vult, non sua, sed nostri causa. Illa enim commemoratio acuit preces nostras & animos reddit ad precandum paratiores. Similiter iudicandum est de peccati confessione. Non enim per eam aliquid Deo dicturus es quod nescias, sed ita testaris teipsum scire & cognitum habere tuum peccatum. Praeterea nullus superest hypocrisi locus. Nam cur peccatorum aliquam partem subticeas coram eo qui te intimum tuaque omnia tam exacte nouit? Sunt igitur omnia candide aperienda & serio agnoscenda. Quid autem (quaerat fortasse aliquis) de impiis censendum est, ut de Caino qui peccati sui grauitatem coram Deo confessus est? Eáne habenda erit syncera confessio? Nequaquam. Nam ea confessio de qua loquimur non est extorta, sed non diffidens, non in Deum ipsum contu-meliosa: sed spontanea, demissa, pia, ab i-psa fide proficiscens & in misericordia Dei recumbens. Atque ut Spiritu Dei praelucen-te peccatum videmus, docente agnoscimus, monente sentimus, inspirante gemimus: i-ta etiam eodem Spiritu dictante & fugge-rente, peccatum nostrum confitemur. Quae Dei pr[?]quum ita sint, concludendum est, confes-sionem peccati non nostris viribus autmeritis (quod Papistae somniant) sed soli gratiæ Dei acceptam esse referendam. Hanc autem de qua agimus confessionem omnino necessariam esse, quis ignorat? Si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere (inquit Iohannes) nobis ipsis imponimus. Accipite (clamat O-feas) verba vobiscum & dicite Deo: Auferi-niquitatem & profer bonum & reddemus vitulos labiorum, id est, gratiarum actionem. Neque sane opus est multa commemorare quibus confirmemus quod egregiè a veteribus fuit usurpatum: confessionè peccati, esse peccati medicinam. Singulis enim paginis innumera occurrunt testimonia quibus docemur confessionem peccatorum & vtilem nobis & in primis esse necessariam. Summa est, illum demum recte confiteri peccata sua coram Deo, qui ex animo se peccatorem miserum & perditum agnoscens, recurrit ad eius misericordiam in Christo exhibitam, & ex illa certam remissionis peccatorum fiduciam concipit.
units.tr: Therefore this passage requires that we say something about the confession of sins. Now, we have already touched above, in a certain way, that there are two kinds of it: one that is made before God, and another that is made before men. Both are found in this verse. For David testifies that he has confessed his sin before God. Then, he does not say this privately to some people, but by publishing this Psalm he appears to confess his sin openly and before all, and so before posterity itself, and to proclaim it as with the blare of a trumpet. Therefore we must deal briefly with each kind of confession. Now, first, a certain doubt might arise: since all things lie open to God, and even our thoughts hidden in the innermost mind are exposed to his eyes, what need is there to tell of the sin that we have committed? For God knows well that we have sinned, he who long before knew that we would sin. How is it, then, that David says he made his sin known to God? I answer that all this is said in human terms [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς]. For Scripture is accustomed to speak of God in terms of what we see happening to men. Thus we are commanded to tell God our affairs, so that he may provide for them. Thus God is said to come down and to look upon human affairs so that he may know how they stand. Thus God himself declares that he has known Abraham's faith from his obedience; to say nothing of how often it occurs that the godly are tested and proved by the Lord, so that he may see in what way they are disposed towards him. All these things, so that we may rightly understand them, must be adapted to men themselves. Indeed, the Lord knows the sins of men; and although the wicked strive most earnestly to cover their crimes (so far are they from confessing them), yet the Lord sees them with the most piercing eyes, by which he searches out and examines all things, and at last demands an account from each one. But it is said that he knows those sins which are explained by us, not because he was ignorant of them, but because he wishes them to be told by us, so that we may be moved more by this method. Therefore it must be said that David made his sin known to God when he truly and as is fitting acknowledged that his sin was known to God. So it is customary to speak of prayers. For who would doubt that God knows our want or our affliction? Yet we see the godly, in their prayers, recount each thing in order, as if the matter were with one to whom all those things were wholly unknown. But, as I have said, the Lord wishes this, not for his own sake, but for ours. For that recounting sharpens our prayers and makes our minds more ready to pray. Similarly, we must judge concerning the confession of sin. For by it you will not tell God anything that he does not know, but you bear witness that you yourself know and have recognised your sin. Besides, there is no room left for hypocrisy. For why should you conceal some part of your sins before him who knows you inwardly and all your affairs so exactly? Therefore all things are to be laid open candidly and acknowledged seriously. But what (someone may perhaps ask) is to be judged of the wicked, such as Cain, who confessed the gravity of his sin before God? Is that to be regarded as sincere confession? By no means. For the confession of which we are speaking is not extorted, but is not distrustful, nor insolent against God himself; it is spontaneous, humble, devout, proceeding from faith itself and resting upon the mercy of God. And just as, with the Spirit of God shining before us, we see sin, recognise it as he teaches, feel it as he warns, and groan over it as he inspires, so also, with the same Spirit dictating and suggesting, we confess our sin. Since these things are so, it must be concluded that the confession of sin is to be referred not to our own strength or merits (as the Papists dream), but to the grace of God alone. Who does not know that this confession of which we are speaking is wholly necessary? If we say, John says, that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. Take with you words, cries Hosea, and say to God: Take away all iniquity and receive what is good, and we will render the calves of our lips, that is, thanksgiving. Nor indeed is there need to recall many things by which we may confirm what the ancients have excellently maintained: that the confession of sin is the medicine of sin. For on every page countless testimonies occur by which we are taught that the confession of sins is both useful to us and above all necessary. In sum, he alone rightly confesses his sins before God who, acknowledging from his heart that he is a wretched and lost sinner, runs to God's mercy exhibited in Christ, and from that conceives a sure confidence of the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: Iam quod attinet ad confessionem coram hominibus, ante aliquid de hac re diximus, cum differebamus de peccatis tegendis. Summa huc redit: si quando eiusmodi peccati confessio cedat in gloriam Dei & ædificationem Ecclesiæ, ea nobis vtendum esse. Huius autem publicæ confessionis (quam veteres ἐξο-μολόγησιν appellarunt) vsus ab Apostolicis temporibus ad Christianam Ecclesiam manauit. Eamque pij maiores sancte ac diligenter coluerunt, donec tandem a Ponti-ficiis [?]ficiis in auricularem confessionem, id est, rem non tantum dissimilem, sed etiam pla-nè contrariam, fuit immutata. Quid enim tam absurdum dici potest, quàm omnium peccatorum catalogum à nobis vel debe-re vel posse recenseri? Quid? tu in immen-sam peccatorum voraginem delapsus ac de-mersus conaris, scilicet, singulas guttas e-numerare, dum te interim infinita vis & copia aquarum obruit atque suffocat. Quantò hic noster melius alio in loco sic exclamat: Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis pur-ga me. Quid porrò tam alienum à gratui-ta peccatorum remissione ( in cuius laudi-bus iampridem versamur ) quàm auricu-lari cuidam susurratione peccatorum veni-am esse alligatam? Quantum, obsecro, la-queum miseris conscientiis hoc pacto Pontificij iniecerunt? Rectè igitur Dauid: Ti-bi, inquit, peccatum meum notum feci. Et rursus: Fatebor transgressionem meam coram Domino. Quibus verbis satis explicat ad quem sit peccatorum nostrorum confes-sio dirigenda, nempe ad Deum solum, cuius etiam solius est parcere atque misereri. Publi-ca vero confessio non in eum finem institu-ta fuit, ut ab ea peccatorum remissio ullo mo-do pendere debeat, sed tantum ut Ecclesiæ sit aliqua ratione satisfactum, & omnes vnius poenitentia confirmentur qui fuerant [?]nius peccatis & scandalis vulnerati. remedio vix ullum aliud reperias & ad arcenda scandala & ad fouendam sacram Ecclesiæ coniunctionem magis accommodatum. Non possum igitur quin earum Ecclesiarum fœlicitatem prædicem, quæ publicæ confessionis usum, sublatis Pontificiis erroribus, in lucem, cum summa piorum utilitate revocarunt. Atenim, dicat aliquis, eâ Pontificij abusi sunt. Certè, & fœdè abusi sunt. Amplius dico: ipso Euangelio abusi sunt, prædicationem Euangelij corruperunt, Sacramenta suis sordibus inquinarunt, rectam Dei invocandi rationem perverterunt, templa innumeris idolis polluerunt. Quid plura? Ipsam propemodum Solis lucem crassissimis errorum nebulis obscurarunt.
units.tr: Now as for confession before men, we said something about this matter earlier, when we were discussing the covering of sins. The sum comes to this: whenever the confession of such a sin tends to the glory of God and the edification of the Church, we are to make use of it. The practice of this public confession (which the ancients called [ἐξομολόγησιν]) came down to the Christian Church from apostolic times. The pious forebears cherished it holily and diligently, until at last it was changed by the Papists into auricular confession, that is, into a thing not merely unlike but plainly contrary. For what can be said to be so absurd as that we are either obliged or able to recount a catalogue of all our sins? What? You, having slipped and sunk into an immense abyss of sins, try, of course, to count the individual drops, while meanwhile the infinite force and abundance of waters overwhelms and suffocates you. How much better our author elsewhere cries out: "Who understands his errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults." What, moreover, is so alien to the free remission of sins (in whose praises we have long been engaged) as that the forgiveness of sins should be tied to a certain whispering of them into the ear? How great a noose, I beg you, have the Papists thrown over wretched consciences by this method! Rightly then David says: "I have made my sin known to you." And again: "I will confess my transgression to the Lord." By these words he sufficiently explains to whom our confession of sins is to be directed, namely to God alone, whose alone it is also to pardon and have mercy. Public confession, however, was not instituted for the purpose that remission of sins should in any way depend on it, but only so that some satisfaction be made to the Church, and all who had been wounded by one man's sins and scandals be confirmed in repentance. You will hardly find any other remedy more suited both to ward off scandals and to foster the sacred fellowship of the Church. I cannot therefore but commend the happiness of those churches which, with the Papist errors removed, have restored the use of public confession to light, with great benefit to the godly. But someone will say, the Papists abused it. Certainly, and shamefully abused it. I add further: they abused the Gospel itself; they corrupted the preaching of the Gospel, defiled the Sacraments with their filth, perverted the right manner of invoking God, and polluted the temples with countless idols. What more? They have all but obscured the very light of the sun with the thickest clouds of errors.

units.la: Veruntamen si hoc satis est ad repudian-dum verum publicæ confessionis usum, quin tu igitur Euangelicæ prædicationi & Sacramentis renuntias, quibus Pontificij abutuntur? Nimirum secernendus est usus à corruptela & abusu. Quid est igitur quòd te pu-deat publicè peccatum ignoscere, quod pu-blicè cum totius Ecclesiæ damno & scanda-lo admisisti? Non puduit Dauidem non tantùm in hoc Psalmo, sed etiam sæpe aliàs sua peccata vel coram posteris omnibus confiteri. Nō puduit Paulū non solùm ore, sed scriptis etiam sempiternis profiteri se blasphemum, se persecutorem, se iniuriosum fuisse: denique fe indignum esse qui vocetur Apostolus. At-que ut ad regia exempla redeamus, non pu-duit praestantissimum Imperatorem Theo-dosium peccatum publicè deflere coram Ec-clesia & veniam à Domino deprecari. Quod quidem factum praeclarissimum pii veteres ad æternam hominum memoriam consecrarunt. Hæc sit igitur summa:verum confessio-nis vsum sublatis omnibus erroribus nobis in primis esse retinendum:nec ipsam confes-sionem, siue soli Deo, siue etiā publicè fiat, unquam esse gratiæ Dei opponēdam,sed totam potius ab ipsa Dei gratia & misericor-dia deducendam. Atque hoc pacto imitabi-mur Dauidis exeplum qui profitetur se pec-catum suum notum fecisse Domino & iniquitatem suam non abscondisse. Verùm cur addit se non abscondisse iniquitatem suam? Perinde enim loquitur ac si penes ipsum fuerit abscondere Deo peccatum. Sed lōge sanè secus est. Iam enim antea confirmauimus fieri nō posse ut peccata Deum lateant. Veruntamen hoc loquendi genere Dauid opponit suam syncē[?]ritatem improborum hominum hypocrisi & tergiversationi. Quoties enim illorū con-scientia pugitur commissorum peccatorum aculeis, solent laborare in quaerendis latebris & diverticulis ut conspectum Dei fugiant. Nam ex primo parente (vt iam ante dictum est) satis constat simul cum peccato natam & Deo quoque fuisse illam hypocrisin, quæ nobis frustra suadet latitare, quoties vox Domini resonat in conscientiis nostris. Demus igitur operam ut profligata illa hypocrisi quæ no-bis naturalis est, nos ingenuè & reuerenter sistamus coram Deo nósque-nudos agnoscen-tes, non à Deo, sed ad Deū potius fugiamus, qui nos induat suæ misericordiæ donis atque adeò meritis cumulatáque Christi iustitia. Hæc & similia meditemur in exemplo Dauidis nobis proposito. Iam addit.
units.tr: But if this is enough to reject the true use of public confession, why then do you not also renounce the preaching of the Gospel and the Sacraments, which the Papists abuse? Clearly the use must be separated from corruption and abuse. Why then should you be ashamed to publicly acknowledge a sin which you committed publicly, to the damage and scandal of the whole Church? David was not ashamed, not only in this Psalm but often elsewhere, to confess his sins even before all posterity. Paul was not ashamed to profess, not only with his mouth but also in writings that will last forever, that he had been a blasphemer, a persecutor and an insulter; in short, that he was unworthy to be called an apostle. And to return to royal examples: the most excellent Emperor Theodosius was not ashamed to lament his sin publicly before the Church and to beg pardon from the Lord. The pious ancients consecrated this most noble deed to the eternal memory of men. Let this then be the sum: the true use of confession, with all errors removed, is above all to be retained by us; and confession itself, whether made to God alone or even publicly, is never to be set against the grace of God, but rather wholly derived from the grace and mercy of God itself. In this way we shall imitate the example of David, who professes that he has made his sin known to the Lord and has not hidden his iniquity. But why does he add that he did not hide his iniquity? For he speaks as if it had been in his power to hide sin from God. But it is quite otherwise. For we have already established earlier that sins cannot escape God's notice. Yet by this manner of speaking David sets his sincerity against the hypocrisy and evasion of wicked men. For whenever their conscience is pricked by the stings of the sins they have committed, they tend to labour in seeking hiding places and byways so as to flee the sight of God. For from the first parent (as has been said before) it is sufficiently clear that along with sin there was born that hypocrisy, which vainly persuades us to lie hidden whenever the voice of the Lord resounds in our consciences. Let us therefore take pains that, this hypocrisy, which is natural to us, having been overthrown, we present ourselves openly and reverently before God, acknowledging ourselves naked; let us flee not from God but rather to God, who may clothe us with the gifts of his mercy and indeed with the merits and the abundant righteousness of Christ. Let us meditate on these and similar things in the example of David set before us. He now adds:

units.la: Dixi confitebor aduersum me transgressionem meam. Id est, constitui apud me operæpretiū esse meipsum serio accusare, nedum subterfugia hæc & illæc quærere: nam transgressus sum legem Domini: quid prodest culpam dissimulare coram eius oculis qui omnia tam acutè circunspicit & perquirit? Itaque ver-bum, dicendi, hoc loco significat delibera-tam & fixam sententiam, ut & Psalm. 31. In te speraui Domine: dixi, Tu es Deus meus. & Psal. 16. Anima mea dic Æterno: Tu es Deus meus. In quibus locis Propheta significat hanc apud se sententiam stare: hoc habere constitutum, ut iam amplius nequeat in dubium reuocari. Hæc est significatio verbi Hebraei hic usurpati. Etenim non so-lum significat loqui, sed etiā cogitare, rém-que decretam & statutam pronuntiare, ut i-ta testemur nos serio illud in animum induxisse. Atque hæc verbi significatio(ut id o-biter dicamus)declarat quàm integra & syncera debeant esse quæcunque loquimur, nè illos imitemur loquaces & futiles homines quorum lingua præcurrit mentem: nec rursus simulatos illos qui aliud gerunt in ore, aliud in pectore.
units.tr: I said, I will confess my transgression against myself. That is, I have resolved in my own mind that it is worth while to accuse myself seriously, far from seeking these and those subterfuges: for I have transgressed the law of the Lord. What good is it to hide the fault before the eyes of him who looks into and searches out all things so keenly? Therefore the verb "to say" here signifies a deliberate and settled judgment, as also in Psalm 31: "In you, O Lord, I have hoped; I said, You are my God," and Psalm 16: "My soul, say to the Eternal: You are my God." In these places the Prophet signifies that this sentence stands in his mind: that he has this as a settled purpose, which can no longer be called into doubt. This is the meaning of the Hebrew word used here. For it signifies not only to speak but also to think, and to pronounce a matter decided and fixed, so that we testify that we have seriously taken it to heart. And this meaning of the word (to say this in passing) shows how sincere and unfeigned whatever we say ought to be, lest we imitate those talkative and frivolous men whose tongue runs ahead of their mind, nor again those pretenders who have one thing in their mouth and another in their breast.

units.la: Est enim iucunda verbi Hebraei analogia cum utrunque significat & loqui & cogitare: ut discamus ea demum proferenda esse quæ cogitantur. Quod nec profanos ipsos latuit. Sic enim Homerus Vlyssem ait vocem expectore misisse. Quò fit ut à nobis longè abes-se debeat omnis hypocrisis & simulatio. Sed ut ad nostrum Dauidem reuertamur: Dixi, inquit, confitebor: quasi dicat, non hoc tantùm lingua quàm cor ipsum pronuntiauit. Hoc semel mihi faciendum esse constitui. Vidi enim hoc mihi necessario præstandum esse, neque me ulla alia ratione posse consolationem adipisci. Quæ omnia si propius inspicias, videbis Dauidem non statim huc deuenisse, sed post multas alias cogitationes.
units.tr: For the analogy of the Hebrew word is pleasant, since it signifies both to speak and to think, so that we may learn that only those things are to be uttered which have been thought. This did not escape even the profane writers. For thus Homer says that Ulysses sent forth a voice from his chest. Whence it follows that all hypocrisy and pretence ought to be far from us. But to return to our David: I said, he says, I will confess: as if to say, not only did my tongue utter this, but my heart itself. I have resolved once for all that this must be done by me. For I saw that this had to be accomplished by me of necessity, and that I could obtain consolation by no other means. If you look more closely at all these things, you will see that David did not arrive at this at once, but after many other thoughts.

units.la: Quinetiam si meminerimus eorum quæ dicta sunt in explicando versu tertio huius Psalmi, usus est Dauid dolore & cruciatu tanquam doctore ac duce ad hanc confessionis viam ingrediendam. Unde colligendum est non abiiciendos esse animos si non statim ea præstamus quæ à nobis Dominus requirit: sed adhibendam esse operam vt superatis omnibus difficultatibus tandem meliores cogitationes primum locum obtineant.
units.tr: Moreover, if we remember what was said in explaining the third verse of this Psalm, David used grief and torment as a teacher and guide to enter this path of confession. From this it is to be gathered that spirits ought not to be cast down if we do not immediately perform what the Lord requires of us, but that effort must be applied so that, all difficulties overcome, better thoughts at length may take the first place.

units.la: Deinde obseruandū est Dauidem reipsa fecisse quod se facturum constituerat, vt eius exemplo eos damnemus qui praeclara & fan-cta quaeque profitetur, nihilque aliud praeferunt quam sanctimoniam atque probitatem: promittunt, iurant, testantur, nunquam autem eorum verba ad rem conferuntur: verum vbi loquentes audieris, omnia quoque videris. Illi enim homines sunt monstri similes, cum toti sint os & lingua, neque manus habeant neque pedes, id est, nihil habeant praeter sermonis iactatiam: non enim opere praestant quae verbis polliciti sunt. Dauid autem cum ait sibi fuisse constitutum confiteri Deo peccatum, simul etiam confessus est, atque adeo his verbis confitetur. Sic in parabola filius ille luxu propemodum perditus, tandem resipiscens, Surgam, inquit, & proficiscar ad patrem meum & dicam ei: Pater peccaui in coelum & aduersum te. Haec ille, quae statim reipsa praestitit: quemadmodum ipsi etiam facere debemus, vt iam dixi. Nunc quod addit Aduersum me, magis exprimit quam syncere & candide versatus sit in peccati confessione, cuius hoc proprium est vt nos ipsi accusemus potius quam adhibita excusationis aliqua specie culpam eleuemus. Aduersum me, inquit, id est, fateor me in culpa esse: volo esse in meipsum testis etiā coram sum-mo iudice, vt implorem paternam eius misericordiam. Quare discamus aduersari nostris
units.tr: Next, it must be observed that David in fact did what he had resolved to do, so that by his example we may condemn those who profess all things splendid and holy, and put forward nothing but sanctimony and uprightness: they promise, swear, testify, yet their words are never brought to the deed; but when you have heard them speaking, you may see everything. For they are like monsters, being all mouth and tongue, having neither hands nor feet, that is, having nothing but the boasting of talk; for they do not perform in deed what they have promised in words. But David, when he says that it had been resolved by him to confess his sin to God, at the same time also confessed, and indeed confesses by these very words. So in the parable that son, almost ruined by dissipation, at last coming to his senses, says: "I will arise and go to my father, and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you." These are the words he immediately carried out in fact, just as we too ought to do, as I have already said. Now as to what he adds, against myself, it expresses more fully how sincerely and candidly he dealt in confessing his sin; this is the mark of confession, that we accuse ourselves rather than lighten our guilt by some pretext of excuse. "Against myself," he says, that is, I confess that I am in fault; I wish to be a witness against myself even before the supreme judge, so that I may implore his fatherly mercy. Wherefore let us learn to set ourselves against our sins and to accuse them, and in some way to summon ourselves to judgment.

units.la: peccatis eáque accusare ,nósque ipsos quo- damodo vocare in ius, ut a misericordia Do- mini absoluamur, peccatorum remissione im- petrata. Quod Dauidi usuenisse ille ipse te- stis est hoc loco, dum addit: Tu remisisti ini- quitatem peccati mei. Quibus verbis aperte declarat quāta animi fiducia fuerit peccato- rum remissionem amplexus: quem locū iam supra tractauimus, ita ut plura de hac re dice re superfluum esse videatur. Certe cum Da- uid etiam ad Deum oratione conuersus hoc tam fidenter ac certo pronuntiat, nullum lo cum relinquit Papisticae dubitationi. Caete- rum ut doceat non leue aliquod crimen suis- se condonatum, utq; Dei misericordiam in hoc tanto beneficio relucentem magis am- plificet, utitur hac loquendi formula, iniqui- tatem peccati, inquit. Nam assentior He- braeis doctoribus qui hac locutione peccatū amplificari existimant, quemadmodum dici- tur terra pulueris, coenum luti & quae sunt e- iusdem generis. Atque inde consequitur eius quod ante diximus luculenta probatio: nempe Dauidem non leui aliquo sensu pec- cati tactu fuisse, sed serio & ex animo agno- uisse peccati grauitatem: quo fit etiam ut ma- gis emineat summa Dei condonantis mise- ricordia.
units.tr: to accuse them, and in a manner to summon ourselves to judgement, so that we may be absolved by the mercy of the Lord, our sins having been forgiven. That David experienced this is attested by the witness himself here, when he adds: You have forgiven the iniquity of my sin. By these words he clearly shows with how much confidence of mind he embraced the remission of sins. We have already treated this passage above, so that it would seem superfluous to say more on this matter. Certainly, when David turns to God in prayer and declares this so confidently and certainly, he leaves no room for Papistical doubt. Moreover, in order to teach that no slight crime had been pardoned, and to magnify more fully the mercy of God shining forth in so great a benefit, he uses this form of speech, "the iniquity of sin," he says. For I agree with the Hebrew teachers who think that by this expression sin is intensified, just as one says "the earth of dust," "the mire of mud," and other things of the same kind. And from this follows a clear proof of what we said before: namely, that David was not touched by some slight sense of sin, but truly and from the heart acknowledged the gravity of sin; and so it also comes about that the supreme mercy of God in forgiving stands out all the more.

units.la: Cur igitur(sic enim debet vnusquisque no- strum sibi doctrinam hac applicare) cur, in- quam, me meorum peccatorum moles, me tot iniquitatum numerus ab amplectenda Dei misericordia retardabit? illa ipsa est misericordia quæ non leuia tantum peccata, non minores tantum iniquitates, sed iniquitates peccatorum, id est, longè maximas solet pœnitentibus condonare: magna est mea culpa, sed misericordia Dei maior est: meam malitiam illius bonitas, meam ingratitudinem illius liberalitas superabit. Hæc igitur nostris metibus[?] subiiciamus quoties nos peccatorum grauitas excruciabit & illi ponamus summam Dei misericordiam, caveamusque ne nos vitiorum numerus à vera confessione & pœnitentia deterreat, sed potius quò maior erit nostra iniquitas, eò sit maior & ardentior illius coram Deo confessio. Quemadmodum hic Dauidem fecisse perspicimus: cuius quæ sequuntur verba iam expendenda sunt.
units.tr: Why then (for in this way each of us ought to apply this teaching to himself), why, I say, should the mass of my sins and the number of my iniquities hold me back from embracing the mercy of God? That very mercy is accustomed to pardon penitents not only slight sins and not merely lesser iniquities, but the iniquities of sins, that is, by far the greatest. My fault is great, but the mercy of God is greater: his goodness will overcome my wickedness, and his generosity my ingratitude. Let us therefore set these things before our minds whenever the gravity of our sins torments us, and let us place over against them the supreme mercy of God. Let us also take care that the number of our vices does not deter us from true confession and repentance; rather, the greater our iniquity, the greater and more fervent let our confession before God be. This is what we see David doing here, and the words that follow must now be weighed.

units.la: ver.6. Idcirco te orabit vnusquisque pius tempore inueniendi: in inundatione aquarum multarum (ipsum[?]) illum non attingent. Posteaquam se vera fide peccatorum remissionem ac veniam apprehendisse declarauit, iam ostendit quinam fructus ex hoc tanto beneficio consequentur. Atque docet istud Dei donum non restringi ad vnum Dauidem, sed instar lucis clarissimæ longè lateque refulgere, quo fit vt ad totius Ecclesiæ vtilitatem pertineat. Cum, inquit, huiusmodi[?] me collati beneficij fama ad alios peruenerit, inde reddentur promptiores & alacriores ad precandum in mediis ærumnis, nec illos sua peccata retardabunt cum tantum diuinæ misericordiæ fulgorem in me relucentem intuebuntur, sed potius quærent auxilium Dei & eo fruentur atque liberabuntur è suis afflictionibus. Hæc est sententia Da-uidis: ex qua colligere possumus quem in fi-nem Dominus sua in nos beneficia conse-rat, nempe vt fructus ad alios etiam por-rigantur (quemadmodum iam ante mo-nuimus) & quæ ab ipsius liberalitate tan-quam ex fonte ad nos defluunt, ea ad com-munem totius Ecclesiæ ædificationem pos-sint redundare. Huc respiciebat ille ipse Dauid cum Psal.51. profitebatur se fore pœ-nitentium doctorem ac magistrum vt illos ab iniquitate revocaret. Quinetiam Apo-{1}stolus testatur se veniam a Domini miseri-cordia fuisse consecutum, vt esset cæteris exemplo quo promptius & alacrius ad miseri-cordiam Dei Patris confugiant. Hic enim idem statuendum est quod de corpore dici solet. Nam si quis annulum induat, quanquis cum digito gerat, dicimus tamen non hunc vel illum digitum, sed totum hominem inde exornari: ita diuinæ liberalitatis ornamenta quæ potissimum in hoc vel illo Ecclesiæ membro refulgent, non illud solum membrum, sed totum corpus illustrant ac universæ Ecclesiæ decus & splendorem asserunt. Rursus obseruandum est nostras esse partes recte ut aliorum exemplis quae nobis ad imitandum proponuntur, ne ad tantam lucem nobis exhibitam caeci simus. Interroga priorem ætatem, inquit ille, quia dies nostri super terram sunt instar umbrae. Sumus igitur aliorum cum doctrina tum exemplis instituendi ut vitam nostram pie & sancte formare possimus. Multa quidem exempla veteres historiae, multa etiam rerum quoti-dianarum experientia nobis suppeditat, sed nescio quomodo ut tantam lucem vndique circunfusam nolimus intueri. Atque ve-terum exemplorum meditatio attentaque consideratio non parum potest ad animos commouendos. Non te mouet iudiciorum Dei metus? Audi Paulum monentem, ne, inquit, Idololatrae sitis sicut quidam Israelitae: ne scortemur sicut eorum quidam scortati sunt & ceciderunt uno die 23.millia. Rursus si te tuorum peccatorum sensus adeo deiicit, ut ad amplectendam Dei misericordiam surgere nequeas: pone tibi ante oculos ipsum Dauidem qui veniam a Domino consecutus est (ut innumerabiles alios praetermittam) & qui hoc Psalmo profitetur tantum beneficium sibi fuisse collatum, ut hoc exemplo caeteri confirmarentur & meliori animo suorum peccatorum veniam postularent. Idcirco, inquit, te orabit vnusquisque: quasi dicat, Multi meo exemplo resipiscent: multi ad te confugient Domine,& ex eodem liberalitatis fonte hau-rient,ex quo me aspergere dignatus es. At-que hic cogor nostrum stuporem incusare. Seipsum Dauid in exemplum proponit, nos docet,monet,incitat,et interim desides ster-timus. Quotus enim quisque est qui Dauidis exeplo in peccatis ingemiscat? qui lacrymas effundat ad Dei pedes prouolutus? qui ad di-uinam misericordiam confugiat? eam implo ret?ea nitatur? qui denique Deo supplicet in tot rebus aduersis quibus vndiq; premimur? Itaque non desunt exepla,sed desunt qui ex- emplis propositis recte vti velint. Quinetiam audire mihi videor vanā excusatione quam multi suæ ignauiæ prætexunt: quid enim?in- quiunt,Sumus-ne cum Dauide comparandi? fas illi sane fuerit diuinam misericordia suis precibus euocare qui tot tantisque benefi- ciis ornatus, tot S.Spiritus donis illustratus fuit: nobis no item,qui ad Dauidis præstan- tiam nihil sumus.Itáne vero? At longè aliter concludit Iacobus: Elias, inquit, homo erat iisdem quibus nos obnoxius, & precatus est ne pluereť, atque adeò nō pluit super terram annos tres & sex menses. Quid ergo sibi vult Iacobus hoc exeplo proposito? num vt nos à precando deterreat cùm tam longè absi- mus ab Eliæ sanctitate? imò potius: Orate, inquit:falluntur enim qui preces ab hominū dignitate vel meritis pendere existimant, cùm earum fructus à sola Dei misericordiā per Christum mediatorem sit expectandus: Enimuero mirari satis nō possum hominum hac in re peruersitatem, qui dum monentur sanctorum hominum exemplis resipiscere, exclamant, indignos esse qui sibi tantam puritatem imitandam proponant. Rursus cum eorum peccata redarguuntur, cum obiiciuntur adulteria & homicidia, cum ipsa Christianæ religionis abnegatio reprehenditur: statim ad Dauidis peccata & ad Petri lapsu refugiunt. Nonne, inquiunt, Deus Dauidi, nonne Petro condonauit? Ita est sane: sed Dauidi pœnitenti, peccatumque ex animo agnoscenti: Petro lacrymanti, non obstinato, nō præ-fracte in vitiis pergenti, condonauit. Vtendū est igitur, non abutendum piorum veterum exemplis, quorū peccata voluit Deus sacris literarum monumentis esse prodita, non ut eorum exemplo peccemus, sed ut eorum potius exemplo resipiscamus. Quod ut melius intelligas, expende quod sequitur in contex-tu: Te orabit, inquit, unusquisque pius. Ecce tibi quales oporteat eos esse, qui sibi Dauidis exemplum imitandum proponent. Quos e-nim, ô Dauid, futuros meliores tuo exemplo dicis? Vnumquemque pium, inquit, id est, benignum, mansuetum, pietatis virtutisque studiosum. Hæc enim est propria verbi Hebraei significatio. Ex quo debet intelligi, eos demum Dauidis exemplo posse proficere qui pij sunt, qui peccati dolore experrecti ex animo peccatum agnoscunt, peccatum sentiunt, pecca[?] tum oderunt: qui summisi[?] atque in seipsis deiecti se totos conferunt ad Dei misericordiam: non autē qui in vitiorum sordibus volutati, altum, & (vt hoc mutuer ab Ethnicis) Endymionis somnum dormiunt. Præclare igitur Dauid hæc duo simul coniunxit, mansuetudinem & precationem, quandoquidem nisi inter precandum mansuetum, humilem ac benignum animum habeas, vana est & irrita precatio. Nec enim abs re Hebraei vocant fideles Chasidim nomine a misericordia ac benignitate deducto, sed vt primum docent nos esse vasa diuinæ misericordiæ in quæ pius ille & clementissimus Pater immensos suæ gratiæ thesauros infundit: deinde vt significent quales ipsi esse debeamus, id est, benigni atq; misericordes, cum in omnibus vitæ actionibus, tum vel maxime in præcādo. Quare in ea precatione qua nobis Dominus noster Iesus Christus dictauit, hoc nominatim profitemur, nos esse odio vacuos & omni vindictæ cupiditate. Quod vtinam ante oculos habeamus, quoties precamur. Tā sæpe enim video hac in re peccari, vt cogar huc locū paulo fusius inculcare. Mutuis odiis & quotidianis prope rixis ac dissidiis laboramus, atque interim volumus fideles pleno ore prædicari. Obsecro, mi frater, cur te fidelem nominas? cur te iactas Deum precari nisi sis misericors? Meminerīs quæso huius loci, vbi Dauid eos ait esse precaturos qui erunt benigni, mansueti, misericordes. Cur te quotidie precibus Ecclesiasticis interesse video postulantem ut tua tibi peccata remit-tantur quemadmodum iis qui te offenderunt remittis? Ecquonam ore istud pronuntias, cum odium in fratres conceptu atque alta mente repositum, te medacij coram Deo coarguat? At enim, inquis, ille me graviter offendit, an ergo ut toties illatam iniuriam obliuiscar? Quid? nónne longe grauius in Deum peccasti? Vide quam sis iniquus rerum aestimator: Vis ti-bi remitti ea quae in Deum aeternum & omni-potentem admisisti: nō aute ea vis remittere quae in te homuncione, in te vermem, in te-cinerem ac puluere admissa sunt. Quamob-rem omnes odij atq; offensionis aculeos hęc una cogitatio excutiat, quod nos quanquam odio dignissimos à Domino in gratia recipi, nos peccatores longe maximos, ab ipso venia impetrare postulamus. Hæc aute ad ritè precandum via est (siquidem Prophetam nostrum audimus) ut benigni, ut mansueti, ut misericordes ad precandum accedamus. Te, inquit, Domine unusquisque mansuetus orabit. Itaq; me-minerimus præclari istius nominis quod nobis à Dei Spiritu in sacris literis inditum est, dum fideles appellantur mansueti, quemad-modum cum ouibus comparari solet. Quin-etiam ubi Esaias prædicit fore cum ex omnibus mundi partibus se homines in Ecclesiam recipient, usurpat similitudinem à columbis ductam,qua etiam usus est Christus cùm iu-bet nos esse simplices instar columbarum. Atque hic locus non solùm reiicit crudeles hostes Euangelij, quos Scriptura similes facit lupis atque leonibus (nec sanè immeritò, cùm eorum rictus piorum cruore aspersos oculis lacrymantibus iam toties Ecclesia viderit) verumetiam vibrandum est hoc telum aduersus eos, qui in media Ecclesia fœnore & quibusuis iniuriis fratres opprimunt, hac præsertim annonæ difficultate. Quis enim non miretur accipitres una cum columbis volare? Absit ergo ab iis qui se colūbas pro- fitentur accipitrum rapacitas, absit à fratri-bus in fratres iniuria, ac potius demus ope-ram ut nostra mansuetudo atque benignitas huic sacro nomini quod nobis Scriptura im-posuit, tandem respondeat. Iam si pij, si fideles haberi volumus, audiamus ex Dauide quodnam sit pij hominis officium: Quilibet, inquit, pius orabit. Nimirum hoc hominis pij officium, hæc in primis cura esse debet, ut precetur: quandoquidem precatio fructus longè uberrimos & ad vitam hanc tutandam & ad futuram asequendam producit. Si- quis enim prematur rebus aduersis, sicui pe-ricula immineant, si quem morbus, si fames, si rerum omnium penuria, si ulla denique calamitas urgeat: quidnam in tanta rerum a-cerbitate facturus est? Orabit. Quid autem si in hostium potestatem venerit & in summo vitæ discrimine versetur? Orabit. Quid porrò si peccati sensus stimulet? si excruciet culpæ contractæ recordatio? si mortis æternæ metu atq; inferorum horrore identidè animus exteratur? Orabit. Hæc una consolatio, una spes, unum perfugium. Quamobrem nunquam satis laudari potest Chrysost. sententia, qui precationem esse animæ ipsius animæ existimauit.
units.tr: Ver. 6. Therefore every godly person will pray to you in the time of finding; in the flood of many waters they will not reach him. After David had declared that he had grasped the forgiveness of sins and pardon by true faith, he now shows what fruit will follow from so great a benefit. He teaches that this gift of God is not restricted to David alone but shines far and wide, like the brightest light, so that it serves the good of the whole Church. "When," he says, "the report of this benefit conferred on me has reached others, they will be made readier and more eager to pray in the midst of their troubles. Their sins will not hold them back when they see the brightness of divine mercy shining in me, but rather they will seek the help of God, enjoy it, and be freed from their afflictions." This is David's meaning. From it we can gather the end for which the Lord bestows his benefits on us: that their fruit should reach others also (as we have already noted), and that what flows down to us from his generosity, as from a fountain, may overflow for the common edification of the whole Church. David himself had this in view when, in Psalm 51, he declared that he would be a teacher and master of penitent sinners, to call them back from iniquity. Indeed, the Apostle testifies that he obtained pardon from the mercy of the Lord so that he might be an example to others, to flee more promptly and eagerly to the mercy of God the Father. For the same thing must be said here as is commonly said of the body: if someone puts on a ring, although he wears it on a finger, we say not that this or that finger, but the whole man is adorned by it. So the ornaments of divine generosity, which shine chiefly in this or that member of the Church, do not illuminate that member alone but the whole body, and they proclaim the glory and splendour of the whole Church. Again, it must be observed that it is our part to be rightly instructed by the examples of others, which are set before us for imitation, lest we be blind to so great a light offered to us. "Ask the former age," he says, "for we are but of yesterday and our days upon earth are a shadow." Therefore we must be instructed by the teaching and the examples of others, so that we may shape our life piously and holily. Ancient histories supply us with many examples, and so does the experience of everyday affairs, yet somehow we refuse to look at a light so abundantly poured round about us. Yet the meditation and attentive consideration of ancient examples can do not a little to move our minds. Does the fear of God's judgments not move you? Hear Paul warning: "Do not be idolaters, as some of the Israelites were; nor let us commit fornication, as some of them did, and fell in one day, twenty-three thousand." Again, if the sense of your own sins so casts you down that you cannot rise to embrace the mercy of God, set before your eyes David himself, who obtained pardon from the Lord (to pass over countless others), and who in this Psalm declares that so great a benefit was conferred on him that others might be strengthened by his example and ask for the pardon of their sins with a better heart. "Therefore," he says, "every godly person will pray to you." As if he said: "By my example many will return to their senses; many will flee to you, O Lord, and will drink from the same fountain of generosity from which you deigned to sprinkle me." Here I am compelled to accuse our own dullness. David sets himself forth as an example; he teaches us, admonishes us, urges us on, and in the meantime we lie idle. For how few are there who, following David's example, groan over their sins, pour out tears prostrate at the feet of God, flee to the divine mercy, implore it, lean upon it, and finally pray to God in the many adversities by which we are pressed on every side? So examples are not lacking, but those who want to use the examples set before them rightly are lacking. Indeed, I seem to hear the empty excuse with which many dress up their laziness: "What then? Are we to be compared with David? It was surely right for him to call on the divine mercy by his prayers, since he was adorned with so many and great benefits and illuminated by so many gifts of the Holy Spirit; but we, who are nothing in comparison with David's eminence, are not in the same position." Is that so? Yet James concludes quite differently: "Elijah," he says, "was a man subject to the same things as we are, and he prayed that it might not rain, and so it did not rain on the earth for three years and six months." What then does James mean by setting this example before us? Is it to keep us from praying, since we are so far from the holiness of Elijah? Rather the contrary: "Pray," he says; for those are mistaken who think that prayers depend on the dignity or merits of men, when their fruit is to be expected from the mercy of God alone, through Christ the mediator. Indeed, I cannot sufficiently wonder at the perversity of men in this matter: when they are urged to return to their senses by the examples of holy men, they cry out that they are unworthy to set before themselves a purity so great to imitate. Again, when their sins are rebuked, when adulteries and murders are thrown in their faces, when even the denial of the Christian religion is reproved, they at once take refuge in the sins of David and the fall of Peter. "Did not God," they say, "pardon David? Did he not pardon Peter?" It is so indeed; but he pardoned David when he repented and acknowledged his sin from the heart, and Peter when he wept, not when he remained obstinate and stubbornly persisted in his vices. The examples of the godly men of old are therefore to be used, not abused: God willed that their sins be handed down in the sacred records of Scripture, not that we should sin by their example, but that we should rather return to our senses by their example. To understand this better, consider what follows in the context: "Every godly person will pray to you," he says. Here you have what sort of people they ought to be who will set David's example before themselves for imitation. For whom, O David, do you say will be made better by your example? "Every godly person," he says, that is, kind, gentle, zealous for piety and virtue. For this is the proper meaning of the Hebrew word. From this it must be understood that those can profit from David's example only who are godly, who, awakened by the pain of sin, truly acknowledge their sin, feel it, and hate it; who, humbled and cast down within themselves, betake themselves wholly to the mercy of God; not those who wallow in the filth of vices and sleep the deep sleep of Endymion (to borrow this from the heathen). Rightly, then, David joined these two things together, gentleness and prayer, since unless you have a gentle, humble and kindly spirit while you pray, your prayer is empty and vain. Nor without reason do the Hebrews call the faithful Chasidim, a name derived from mercy and kindness; first, to teach us that they are vessels of the divine mercy, into which that godly and most merciful Father pours the immense treasures of his grace; then, to signify what we ourselves ought to be, that is, kind and merciful, in all the actions of life, and above all in prayer. Therefore, in that prayer which our Lord Jesus Christ taught us, we openly profess that we are free from hatred and from every desire for revenge. Would that we kept this before our eyes whenever we pray. For I see that this is sinned against so often that I am compelled to press this point a little more fully. We labour under mutual hatreds and almost daily quarrels and disputes, and yet we want to be called faithful with full mouths. I beg you, my brother, why do you call yourself faithful?
