Why do you boast that you pray to God, unless you are merciful? Remember, I pray, this passage, where David says that those will pray who are kind, gentle and merciful. Why do I see you daily taking part in the ecclesiastical prayers, asking that your own sins be forgiven you, just as you forgive those who have offended you? With what mouth do you utter this, when the hatred you have conceived against your brothers and hold deep in your mind convicts you of lying before God? "But," you say, "he has offended me grievously; am I then to forget so many injuries?" What? Have you not sinned far more gravely against God? See how unjust a judge of things you are: you want your sins against the eternal and almighty God to be forgiven, but you do not want to forgive what has been committed against you, a mere man, a worm, ashes and dust. Therefore let this one thought drive out all the stings of hatred and offence: that we, though most worthy of hatred, are received by the Lord into grace, and that we, the greatest of sinners, ask pardon from him. Now this is the way to pray rightly (since we heed our Prophet): that we come to prayer kind, gentle and merciful. "Every gentle person will pray to you, Lord," he says. Let us therefore remember that noble name which the Spirit of God has given us in the sacred writings, when the faithful are called gentle, as sheep are commonly compared with them. Indeed, where Isaiah foretells that men from all parts of the world will be received into the Church, he uses a likeness taken from doves, which Christ also used when he bids us be simple as doves. And this passage not only rejects the cruel enemies of the Gospel, whom Scripture makes like wolves and lions (and not undeservedly, since the Church has so often seen their jaws, stained with the blood of the godly, through her tearful eyes), but this weapon must also be aimed at those who in the midst of the Church oppress their brothers with usury and every kind of injury, especially in this present difficulty of grain. For who would not wonder at hawks flying together with doves? Let the rapacity of hawks be far from those who profess themselves doves; let injury of brother against brother be far away; and rather let us take care that our gentleness and kindness at last correspond to this sacred name which Scripture has given us. Now, if we want to be called godly and faithful, let us hear from David what the duty of a godly man is: "Everyone who is godly," he says, "will pray." Surely this is the duty of a godly man, and this should be his first care: to pray, since prayer produces fruits far more abundant, both for guarding this life and for attaining the life to come. For if someone is pressed by adversities, if dangers threaten him, if disease, famine, want of all things, or any calamity at all presses him, what will he do in so great a bitterness of affairs? He will pray. But what if he falls into the power of enemies and is in the greatest peril of his life? He will pray. What further, if the sense of sin stings him, if the recollection of guilt incurred tortures him, if his spirit is equally terrified by the fear of eternal death and the horror of hell? He will pray. This is the one consolation, the one hope, the one refuge. Therefore the saying of Chrysostom can never be praised enough, who judged prayer to be the very life of the soul.

units.la: Nā adeo est utilis, adeo necessaria precatio, ut per eam anima, salus, vitaque ipsa quodam modo viuere videatur. Quæ cum ita sint, cur, cedo, diutius cunctamur? cur non assiduis precibus ad Deum recurrimus? his, his, inquam, temporibus quibus, si unquam aliās, nobis precandi necessitas incumbit. Afflictæ, vexatæ, prostratæ plurimis in locis orbis Christiani iacent Ecclesiæ: fideles pulsi patria, eversi bonis, egestate, miseria, doloribus obruti, in lacrymis & squalore vitam ægre trahunt. Hæccine siccis oculis intueri & sine ingenti animi acerbitate vel audire possumus, vel cogitare? Cur non ergo votis ardentibus Dei misericordiam supplices deprecamur? Cur non rogamus ut peccatis nostris ignoscat quæ tantum Dei furorem in nos accenderunt? Si conatus hostium Euangelij & eorum potentiam pertimescimus, cur non ab Solomone edocti statim nos recipimus in illam arcem fortissimam vbi salus nostra in tuto collocetur? Sic enim ille: nomen Æterni est instar turris fortissimæ ad quam curret iustus,& exaltabitur. Curtamus[?] igitur: excutiamus stuporem illum quo languetes vix tardo passu ingredimur. Quid enim est quod nobis vnquam metum inferat in sublimem illam ac munitissimam precationis arcem semel receptis? Metum dico? imo vero quis tantus hostis, quae tanta vis vnquam esse possit, quam non valido illo precationis ia-culo configere atque evertere facile possi-mus? Precatio mare diffidit, precatio ma-num Dei percussuri sustinuit, muros Iericho diruit, Solem in medio cursu insistere coegit: Precatione Moses fudit Amalecitarum copias: Iosua euocato e coelo grandine fregit quin-que Regum exercitus: Samuel in fugam ver-tit Palestinos: nec vllis aliis quam sanctarum precum viribus coelum Elias clausit, coelum idem Elias aperuit. Quid plura? Quoties te in-voco, inquit Dauid, hostes mei retrocedunt. His etiam precationis armis Iosaphat Am-monitas Moabitasque superauit, his Asa Æ-thiopas: his Ezechias Assyrios profligauit. Deniq; precatio semper fuit piorum arma, victorie[?], triuphi. Agedum ergo, cunctis improborum hominum furoribus preces opponamus. Quid enim? quae Solis cursu olim sistere potuerunt, nonne minas hostium, nonne conatus furoresq; cohibebunt? quae coelum clauserunt, nonne frenabunt terrenas hominum vires & profusam impiorum audaciam? Itaq; demus operam vt huic Dauidis dicto respodeamus: orabit, inquit, vnusquisque pius. Precemur igitur, siquidem pij & fideles haberi volumus. Atque ut intelligamus non frustrà nos precaturos, subiicit: Tempore, in-quit, inueniendi: quasi diceret, eorum nunquam fore preces irritas, qui ex animo Deo suppli-carint. Hoc autem maxime debet animos no-stros ad preces incedere, quòd quauis Deum à nobis auerterimus peccatis nostris, nunc tã men eum videmus pro sua summa misericordia sese nobis offerre, nos ad se vocare, nos pertrahere, nobis extenta brachia porrigere, nimirum cum nos Euangelicæ prædicationis facit participes. Sic enim Paulus post Prophetam: Tempore, inquit, accepto exaudiui te & in die salutis succurri tibi: Ecce nunc tempus acceptum, Ecce nunc dies salutis. O dulcissimam vocem Apostoli! Ergo, fratres, si vera fide Christi gratia nobis in Euangelio oblatã amplectemur, si in sacrosancto Iesu Christi nomine Deum precemur, si paternis Dei nostri oculis tot ab improbis accepta vulnera detegamus, si toties effusas lacrymas gemitusque in clementissimū eius sinum deponamus: iam audiemus suauissimam illam vocem in animis nostris resonante: Ecce nunc tempus acceptū, ecce nunc dies salutis. Audiemus etiam Dauidem nobis affirmatem hoc esse tempus quo Deum inuenire, & eius gratiam & fauorem assequi possimus. Hactenus in tanta Ecclesiæ tempestate ac procella, rerum aduersarum tetra caligine vndique circunfusa, visus est Deus quodammodo latere, quod plerisque sanctis, adeoque toti Ecclesiae saepe vsuuenisse testes sunt haec voces: Quousque Domine abscondes a me facie tuam? Cur a nobis vultum tuum auertis, o Domine, & permulta similia. Haec est enim natura & vis afflictionis, vt Deum a nobis procul abscedentem & auersum ostendere videatur. Tunc autem debent succurrere egregiae consolationes quae passim occurrunt in sacris literis: Inuocabitis me, quaeretis me & inuenietis, inquit Dominus. Et Christus: Petite, inquit, & dabitur vobis: quaerite & inuenietis: pulsate & aperietur vobis. Ergo Deus precibus quaeritur, precibus inuenitur. Nec enim vt Pontifices solent, incerto animo & dubio precamur: sed potius ita petimus, tanquam certo impetraturi: quae cibus & precibus rimus, tanquam inuenturi: pulsamus tanquam ingressuri. Audiamus enim Apostolum ita praecipientem: Accedamus, inquit, cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae, vt consequamur misericordiam, & gratiam inueniamus ad opportunum auxilium. Quamobrem ita statuamus, Deum semper inueniri, modo vera fide & precibus in Christo fundatis serio & ex animo quaeratur. Sic enim aliquando non minus vere quam eleganter Augustinus, A te petatur: in te quaeratur: ad te pulsetur: sic accipietur, sic inuenietur, sic aperietur. Hoc autem ipsum inueniendi vocabulum vsurpatum a Dauide multum valere debet ad excitandum in nobis precandi diligentiam. Qui enim aurum, qui diuitias quaerunt, nonne summum laborem ac diligetiam adhibent vt eas inueniant? quanto ergo aequius est nos esse esse intentos ac diligentes in Deo quaerendo, quem summum bonum summamque nostram foelicitatem esse scimus? Quo loco redarguenda est nostra socordia, qui quaquam assiduis concionibus admonemur, vt Dei misericordia sanctis precibus imploremus, procrastinamus tamen, & rem semper in aliud tempus differimus. Atqui praesens est necessitas, cur non igitur praesens subsidium comparamus? Qui scis enim an tibi in posterum precari licebit? quid tibi tantum audes de te promittere? Atqui parabola stultarum vir-ginum satis docet, tempus esse redimendum, nec impune laturos eos qui oblatam suo tempore Dei misericordiam recipere neglexerint. Quamobrem pareamus Prophetae i-ta monenti: Quaerite Dominum, inquit, dum inuenitur: inuocate eum dum prope est. Verendum est enim ne si semel occasioni defuerimus, ipsa postea nobis desit occasio. Nam ecce, vbi Dei verbum praedicatur, vbi celebrantur Ecclesiastici coetus, ibi Deus & quaeri debet & potest inueniri. Non inuenitur Deus in deliciis, in ludis, in voluptatibus: non in ebrietate, non in profusis conuiuiis & comessationibus. Hic, hic quaerendus est Deus, quaerendus est in sacris concio-nibus nibus, in publicis precibus, in assidua rerum divinarum meditatione. Sed, proh, dolor, tantum abest ut Deum quaeramus, ut etiam Deum ipsum nos quaerentem averso vultu refugiamus. Dominus accensa in mediis no- stris urbibus pura praedicationis luce, nos quaerit, vocat, excitat, ut salutem oblatam amplectamur: nos autem alias res agentes obsurdescimus, nec audimus ea de quibus toties[?] admonemur: & quasi vercamur[?] ne nobis illuceat Dei Spiritus, neve nos prehendat Dei vocantis manus & deducat ad purio-ris vitæ studium, nos ipsos in mundi tene-bras ultro coniicimus, ac delitescimus in carnis illecebris & cæca hominum voluptate. Quamobrem caveamus ne in nos iure accommodetur hæc exprobratio quæ extat apud Esaiam: Tota die, inquit, exten-di manus ad populum rebellem. Cauea mus, inquam, ne nobis tandem aliquando fœdam istam ingratitudinem ita Dominus exprobret: Vobis porrexi manus quum ad vos misi Euangelij mei præcones, quibus utor tanquam manibus ut homines ad mei cognitionem adducam. Vos eorum voce vocavi: vos eorum opera diligenter quæsivi, ut in meorum cœtum colligerem, ut in æternam fœlicitatem reciperem: At nihilominus in peccatis obduruistis: verbum meum neglexistis: gratiam meam reiecistis: sanctas cohortationes ludibrio habuistis. Ergo, fratres, (no[?] lo enim aliquid grauius dicere) iustam Dei sententiam vera poenitentia anteuertamus. Deum ipsi lacrymis ac precibus quaeramus, aut potius Deo nos quaerenti, nos vocanti, ad nos accedenti obuiam prompti & alacres procedamus. Verumenimuero vt ipsum inueniamus, precemur vt ipse prior nos inueniat: non enim propriis viribus vel Deum quaerere possumus, vel inuenire: sed omnes nostrae salutis partes acceptae referendae sunt Dei misericordiae. Sic Paulus quum dixisset Deum esse Galatis cognitum, statim subiecit, Imo potius, inquit, cogniti & edocti estis a Deo.
units.tr: Prayer is so useful and so necessary that through it the soul, its salvation and its very life seem in some way to live. Since this is so, why, I ask you, do we hesitate so long? Why do we not return to God constantly in prayer? We need to pray now, in these times above all others, if ever there were such times. The Churches of the Christian world lie afflicted, harassed and prostrate in very many places. The faithful have been driven from their homeland, stripped of their goods, and overwhelmed by want, misery and pain, and they drag out their lives with difficulty in tears and squalor. Can we look on this with dry eyes, or hear or think of it without great bitterness of spirit? Why then do we not beg God for his mercy with burning prayers? Why do we not ask him to pardon the sins that have kindled such great wrath against us? If we fear the attempts of our enemies and the power of those who oppose the gospel, why, having been taught by Solomon, do we not at once take refuge in that most strong fortress, where our safety is placed in security? For thus he says: "The name of the Lord is a strong tower; the righteous runs to it and is exalted" (Prov. 18:10). Let us then run, and shake off the stupor that makes us walk so slowly and reluctantly. For what can frighten us once we have entered that high and well-fortified citadel of prayer? Fear, do I say? Indeed, what enemy can be so great, what force can ever be so mighty, that we cannot strike it down and overthrow it with that powerful missile of prayer? Prayer divided the sea; prayer withstood the hand of God as it was about to strike; prayer broke down the walls of Jericho; prayer compelled the sun to stand still in the middle of its course. By prayer Moses routed the forces of the Amalekites; Joshua, calling down hail from heaven, shattered the armies of five kings; Samuel turned the Philistines to flight; and Elijah shut heaven by no other power than that of holy prayers, and the same Elijah opened it again. What more? "As often as I call upon you," says David, "my enemies turn back" (Ps. 56:9). By these same weapons of prayer Jehoshaphat defeated the Ammonites and Moabites, Asa the Ethiopians, and Hezekiah routed the Assyrians. In short, prayer has always been the weapon, the victory and the triumph of the godly. Come then, let us set our prayers against all the rage of wicked men. For what? Will not those prayers that once could halt the course of the sun restrain the threats, attempts and fury of enemies? Will not those that shut heaven curb the earthly strength of men and the unbridled audacity of the impious? Let us therefore take pains to answer this saying of David: "Every godly person," he says, "will pray." Let us pray, then, if we wish to be counted godly and faithful. And so that we may understand that we shall not pray in vain, he adds: "In a time of finding" (Ps. 32:6), as if to say that the prayers of those who have besought God from the heart will never be unanswered. Yet this above all ought to stir our minds to prayer: although we have turned God away from us by our sins, we now see that in his great mercy he offers himself to us, calls us to himself, draws us on, and stretches out his arms to us, especially when he makes us partakers of the evangelical preaching. For thus Paul, following the prophet: "In an acceptable time," he says, "I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor. 6:2). O sweetest voice of the Apostle! Therefore, brethren, if with true faith we embrace the grace of Christ offered to us in the gospel, if we pray in the most holy name of Jesus Christ, if we lay before the fatherly eyes of our God the many wounds we have received from the wicked, if we pour out so many tears and groans into his most merciful bosom, then we shall hear that most pleasant voice resounding in our souls: "Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation." We shall also hear David assuring us that this is the time in which we may find God and obtain his grace and favour. Hitherto, in such a tempest and storm of the Church, with the dark mist of adverse circumstances spread on every side, God has seemed in some way to hide himself. Many holy men, and indeed the whole Church, have often borne witness to this experience in such words as these: "How long, Lord, will you hide your face from me?" and "Why do you turn your face from us, O Lord?" and many similar cries. For this is the nature and force of affliction: it seems to show God as withdrawing far from us and turned away. Then, however, the outstanding consolations that occur everywhere in the sacred letters ought to come to our aid: "You will call upon me, and you will seek me and find me," says the Lord (Jer. 29:12–13). And Christ: "Ask," he says, "and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and it will be opened to you" (Matt. 7:7). Therefore God is sought by prayer and found by prayer. For we do not pray with an uncertain and doubting mind, as the Papists are wont to do; rather we ask as those who are sure to obtain, we seek as those who are sure to find, we knock as those who are about to enter. For let us hear the Apostle giving this command: "Let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help" (Heb. 4:16). Let us therefore lay this down: God can always be found, provided he is sought seriously and from the heart, with true faith and with prayers founded in Christ. For Augustine once said, not less truly than elegantly: "Let him be asked of you, let him be sought in you, let him be knocked upon by you: so he will be received, so he will be found, so he will be opened to you." Moreover, this very word "finding," used by David, ought greatly to avail to arouse in us diligence in prayer. For those who seek gold and riches, do they not expend the utmost labour and diligence to find them? How much more fitting, then, is it for us to be intent and diligent in seeking God, whom we know to be the highest good and our supreme happiness! Here our sloth is rebuked, for although we are admonished by constant sermons to implore God's mercy with holy prayers, we nevertheless put it off and always defer the matter to another time. Yet the need is present; why then do we not prepare present help? For who knows whether it will be permitted you to pray in future? What do you dare to promise yourself for tomorrow? Indeed, the parable of the foolish virgins teaches well enough that time must be redeemed, and that those who neglect to receive the mercy of God offered at its proper time will not go unpunished (Matt. 25:1–13). Therefore let us obey the prophet admonishing us: "Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near" (Isa. 55:6). For we must fear lest, if we once fail the opportunity, the opportunity itself later fail us. For behold, where the word of God is preached and ecclesiastical assemblies are held, there God both ought to be sought and can be found. God is not found in pleasures, in games, in sensual delights; not in drunkenness, not in lavish feasts and revelries. Here, here God must be sought: he must be sought in holy sermons, in public prayers, in constant meditation on divine things. But, alas, far from our seeking God, we even turn our faces away from God himself when he seeks us. The Lord, with the pure light of his preaching kindled in the midst of our cities, seeks us, calls us, and rouses us, that we may embrace the salvation offered; but we, busy with other things, grow deaf and do not hear those things about which we have so often been admonished. And as if we feared that the Spirit of God might shine upon us, or that the hand of the God who calls might seize us and lead us to the pursuit of a purer life, we willingly cast ourselves into the darkness of the world and hide ourselves in the allurements of the flesh and in blind human pleasure. Therefore let us take care lest this reproach, which stands in Isaiah, be justly applied to us: "All day long," he says, "I have stretched out my hands to a rebellious people" (Isa. 65:2). Let us take care, I say, lest the Lord at last reproach us with this shameful ingratitude: "I stretched out my hands to you when I sent to you my heralds of the gospel, whom I use as hands to bring men to the knowledge of me. I called you by their voice; I diligently sought you through their labour, that I might gather you into my assembly and receive you into eternal happiness. Yet nevertheless you hardened yourselves in sin; you neglected my word; you rejected my grace; you made a mockery of my holy exhortations." Therefore, brethren (for I would not say anything more severe), let us anticipate God's just sentence by true repentance. Let us seek God ourselves with tears and prayers, or rather, let us go forward ready and eager to meet God seeking us, calling us, and drawing near to us. Indeed, that we may find him, let us pray that he may first find us; for we can neither seek nor find God by our own strength, but all the parts of our salvation must be referred to the mercy of God. So Paul, when he had said that the Galatians had come to know God, at once added: "Or rather, you have been known by God and taught by him" (Gal. 4:9).

units.la: Et ad Philippenses: Persequor vt apprehendam, cuius rei causa apprehensus sum a Chri-sto: Et Iohannes: In hoc, inquit, est charitas, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ipse nos dilexerit. Ergo vt Deum inuenia-mus, vires a Deo nobis suppeditari necesse est, & quasi manu ad ipsum deduci atque pertrahi, vt in solidum vni Deo gloria tribuatur. Quod si fiet, tunc sentiemus quàm vera sit haec sententia Dauidis quam tractauimus, vnumquemque pium Deū precari inueniendi tempore. Quod etiam vt explicet apertius, subiungit:
units.tr: And to the Philippians: "I press on to lay hold of that for which Christ Jesus laid hold of me." And John: "In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us." Therefore, if we are to find God, he must supply us with strength and, as it were by the hand, lead and draw us to himself, so that all glory is given wholly to the one God. If this happens, we will feel how true is that saying of David which we have considered, that every godly man prays at the time of finding. To make this clearer, he adds:

units.la: In inundatione aquarum multarum (ipsa) illum non attingent. Hic est, inquit, fructus precationis: haec sunt praestantissima eius effecta, quod ab omnibus periculis & malis, fi-deles precantes liberantur. Ergo Dauid magnificè laudes precationis amplificat, simili petito ab aquis longè lateque inundatibus. Non enim dicit preces nos tegere, ne aliquot tātum afflictionum guttulis aspergamur, sed ipsam inundationem in medium proponit. Nec rursus meminit vnius aut alterius fluminis, sed aquarum multarum, adeo ut nullis humanis rationibus possis ex tantis malis emer-gere. Nec porrò affirmat pios non submergi, sed ne attingi quidem: ut nihil quod ad rem illustrandam facere possit, prætermissum esse videatur. Equidem non dubito quin alluserit ad generalem illam inundationem qua semel Dominus vniuersum orbem terrarum atque omnes homines, excepta Noachi familia, demersit. Vt ergo tunc eos demum aquæ non attigerunt, qui se in arcam receperant: ita qui se confert ad precationis præsidium omnia damna atque pericula superabit. Eò spectat etiam egregia illa promissio quam Dominus per Esaiam Ecclesiæ proponit: Cùm transfi-bis, inquit, per flumina, tecum ero, & flumina profunda te transuersum non rapient. Hæc autem aquarum similitudo quanquam generaliter rebus omnibus aduersis conuenit, tamen proprie in hostes Ecclesiæ solet accommodari: quemadmodum sæpe videmus in Pfal-mis, ac eo præsertim loco vbi fideles comparant suos hostes cum aquis inundatibus: Nisi, inquiunt, nobis Deus præsto adfuisset, iam hostes vt aquæ nos inundassent, iam torrens caput nostrum superasset, iam aquae tumidae vitam nostram obruissent. Sic eandem simi-litudinem Esaias eleganter usurpavit, quum praediceret regem Assyrium suas copias infusurum in Judaeam & decem tribus in captivitatem abducturum: Superato, inquit, undique alveo & egressus ultra omnes ripas suas redundabit in Judaeam, refluens & transiens usquedum collum pertingat. Et alibi, dicit Assyrios fuisse instar maris & aquarum alte frementium. Ieremias autem eodem sensu denuntiat erupturas aquas ex Septentrione, quae terram Judaeae inundarent. Aptissima certe similitudo, & quae ad vivum exprimit naturam hostium Ecclesiae. Quantus enim sit aquarum inundantium impetus, quantum periculum, vel ex eo colligitur quod sola fuga vitari possunt. Si exardescat incendium, aquis restinguetur: aquarum autem impetum & furorem sola Dei potentia, solum Dei imperium compescit. Iam si similitudinem ipsam longius persequaris, caetera egregie cōuenient. Namsi ad nostra tempora accedendum est, improbi qui suam rabiem suosque impetus effundunt in Ecclesiam nunquam quiescunt, sed perpetuo motu agitantur: semper fremunt, semper minantur, blasphemi-asque[?] tanquam spumam semper evomunt: Nunquam sibi constant, sed instar torrentis extra rationis alveum ipsaque naturae & humanitatis ripas longe evagantur. Et quemadmodum tū inflatus torrens augetur, cum vndique colle-cti riuuli in vnum confluunt: ita sæpe hostes Ecclesiæ (quod etiam Dauidis tempore accidisse illeipse testis est) vnà con- spirarunt, vt collectis viribus in Ecclesiam impetum facerent. Denique videmus quantum detrimenti aquæ torrentis inundantes afferant, dum magno impetu decurrentes omnia simul secum rapiunt, dumque ipse torrens (vt Poëta dicebat) sternit agros, sternit fata læta, boumque labores: similiter etiam hostes Euangelij magno furore atque impetu Ecclesiam depopulantes omnia vastant, omnia rapiunt, nec ab vllo quàm à solo Deo reprimuntur. Sæpe enim accidit vt quum maximè florerent Ecclesiæ, & essent [?] miles agro cultissimo lætàsque segetes proferenti: quum viderentur (redeundum est enim ad Poëtas) Segetes largiri fruges, florere omnia: tum rapidus hostium torrens longè latèque agrum Ecclesiæ inundans omnia propemodum vastauerit, adeo vt permulti qui antea Euangelium profitentes virere & frugem promittere videbantur, postea inculti & steriles iacuerint, vt limo & cœno, ita idololatriæ sordibus obruti ac demersi. Quid ergo nobis erit in tanta malorum inundatione faciendum? Nempe Dauid est author adhibendus, qui nobis ostendit precationis tutissimum perfugium, vt in eam [?] tanquam in arcam Noachi recepti ab hostium periculis liberemur: atque unusquisque nostrum cum Nazianzeno profitea-tur: ζωτῷ Νῶε κιβωτὸν, ὅπως μόεγν[?] αἰῶν[?] ἀ-λέξω. Quo minus ferendi sunt miseri illi homines, qui, ut suæ salutì consulerent, à suæ salutis præsidio, id est, ab Ecclesia defecerunt. Qui profectò idem mihi videntur fecisse, ut si Noachus inundationis metu se ipse ex arca in medias aquas coiecisset. Verum audio quid sensus carnis obiiciat. Ubinā, inquit, est istius promissionis fructus? annon & sæpe alias & his maximè tèporibus hostium Ecclesiæ conatus non modo attigerunt Ecclesiā, sed eam etiam propemodum euerterunt? Respondeo quod à veteribus eleganter dictum est: Ecclesiam oppugnari, sed non expugnari: iactari fluctibus, sed non demergi. Quid enim obsecro (ut in exemplo proposito maneamus) Noacho putamus accidisse? Num ita tranquillum fuisse super aquas, ut semper immobilis permaneret? ut nullis unquam fluctibus agitaretur? Minimè verò: sed ita Noachus ab aquis iactatus est, ut ab illis obrui nunquam potuerit: nimirum Deo illius salutem protegente. idem igitur piis omnibus continget modo se in arca, id est, in Ecclesia, & in puro Dei cultu contineant. Semper enim verum est quod Dauid alibi cecinit: Deum præsse diluuio. Quanvis ergo nos exterior humanarum rerum aspectus deterreat, permaneamus tamen in arca ubi salus nostra deposita est & Dei vocem potius quàm carnis consilium audia-mus. Quis enim Noachi tempore non existi-massèt alta & immobilia montium iuga fore aduersus aquarum inundationes tutiora arca illa quæ in speciem caduca & fragilis esse vi-debatur? Longè tamen secus euenit: ipsi e-nim summi montium vertices demersi sunt, & sola arca salua permansit. Quinetiâ vt tunc quò magis crescebant aquæ, eò semper altiùs arca euehebatur: ita nunquam ab hostibus e-uerti, nunquam obrui potest Ecclesia, sed quò maiores erunt illorum impetus, eò subli-mior erit Ecclesia, & auxilio Dei suffulta sem-per excelsior eminebit. Itaque (vt locum i-stum tandem absoluamus) recurramus ad Deum ardentibus & assiduis precibus: eius misericordiam & auxilium imploremus, eum ex animo quæramus: neque dubitemus quin ipsius fauorem simus adepturi, quò tot cala-mitates quibus vrgemur & ipsum malorum diluuium per vniuersum propè orbem dissu-sum superare valeamus. Sequitur:
units.tr: In the flood of many waters they shall not reach him. This, he says, is the fruit of prayer: these are its most excellent effects, that faithful people who pray are delivered from all dangers and evils. So David greatly magnifies the praise of prayer, using a comparison drawn from waters that spread far and wide. For he does not say that prayers cover us so that we are sprinkled by only a few drops of affliction, but he sets the flood itself before us. Nor does he mention one river or another, but many waters, so that by no human means could you emerge from so great evils. Nor does he affirm merely that the godly are not submerged, but that they are not even touched, so that nothing that could illustrate the matter seems to have been left out. I do not doubt that he alluded to that general flood by which the Lord once drowned the whole earth and all men except the family of Noah. Just as then only those were not touched by the waters who had withdrawn into the ark, so whoever betakes himself to the protection of prayer will overcome all losses and dangers. To this also looks that remarkable promise which the Lord sets before the Church through Isaiah: "When you pass through the rivers, I will be with you, and the deep rivers shall not sweep you away." Now this likeness of waters, although it applies generally to all adversities, is nevertheless usually applied properly to the enemies of the Church, as we often see in the Psalms, and especially in that place where the faithful compare their enemies with flooding waters: "Unless the Lord had been present with us, the enemies, like waters, would already have flooded us; already the torrent would have passed over our head; already the swelling waters would have overwhelmed our life." Thus Isaiah also elegantly used the same likeness when he foretold that the Assyrian king would pour his forces into Judea and lead the ten tribes into captivity: "The channel having been overflowed on every side, and going beyond all its banks, it will spill over into Judea, flowing back and passing through until it reaches the neck." And elsewhere he says the Assyrians were like the sea and like waters roaring loudly. Jeremiah, moreover, in the same sense foretells waters bursting out from the north which would flood the land of Judea. Certainly a most apt likeness, which expresses to the life the nature of the enemies of the Church. For the force of flooding waters, and how great their danger is, may be gathered from this, that they can be avoided only by flight. If a fire blazes up, it is quenched with water; but the force and fury of waters is restrained by the power of God alone and the command of God alone. Now, if you pursue the likeness itself further, the other points agree remarkably. For if we must come to our own times, the wicked who pour out their rage and assaults upon the Church never rest, but are driven by perpetual motion: they always roar, always threaten, and always spew out blasphemies like foam. They never remain constant, but like a torrent they wander far beyond the channel of reason, and beyond the very banks of nature and humanity. And just as a swollen torrent grows when rills gathered from every side flow together into one, so the enemies of the Church (as David himself bears witness that it happened also in his time) have conspired together so that, with their forces gathered, they might make an attack upon the Church. Finally, we see how much harm flooding torrents do, when, rushing down with great force, they sweep everything away together, and when the torrent itself (as the poet said) lays waste the fields, lays waste the joyful harvests and the labours of the oxen. In the same way the enemies of the gospel, laying waste the Church with great fury and violence, destroy everything, seize everything, and can be restrained by no one but God alone. For it often happens that when the churches were flourishing most, and the field, most well tilled, was bringing forth joyful crops, and when all things seemed (for we must return to the poets) to yield fruits and to flourish, then the swift torrent of enemies, flooding the Church's field far and wide, laid waste almost everything; so that many who before, professing the gospel, seemed to be in leaf and to promise a harvest, afterwards lay uncultivated and barren, overwhelmed and sunk in the filth of idolatry as in mud and mire. What then must we do in so great a flood of evils? Surely we must take David as our guide, who shows us the safest refuge of prayer, so that, received into it as into the ark of Noah, we may be freed from the dangers of enemies; and each of us should profess with Nazianzen: [ζωτῷ Νῶε κιβωτόν, ὅπως μόγις αἰῶνα ἀλέξω]. All the more are those wretched men to be borne with who, in order to look to their own safety, have fallen away from the protection of their salvation, that is, from the Church. These men, surely, seem to me to have done the same as if Noah, out of fear of the flood, had thrown himself out of the ark into the midst of the waters. But I hear what the sense of the flesh objects. "Where," it says, "is the fruit of that promise? Have not the attempts of the enemies of the Church, both often before and especially in these times, not only touched the Church, but almost overthrown it?" I answer with what the ancients have elegantly said: the Church is assailed, but not overcome; tossed by waves, but not sunk. For what, I ask (to remain with the example proposed), do we think happened to Noah? Was the water so calm that he remained always motionless? that he was never shaken by any waves? By no means; but Noah was so tossed by the waters that he could never be overwhelmed by them, God, of course, protecting his safety. The same therefore will happen to all the godly, provided they remain in the ark, that is, in the Church, and in the pure worship of God. For it is always true what David sang elsewhere: that the Lord sits enthroned above the flood. Therefore, although the outward appearance of human affairs terrifies us, let us nevertheless remain in the ark, where our salvation is laid up, and let us listen to the voice of God rather than the counsel of the flesh. For who in Noah's time would not have thought that the high and immovable ridges of the mountains would be safer against the floods of waters than that ark, which seemed frail and perishable in appearance? Yet things turned out very differently: the highest peaks of the mountains were indeed sunk, and the ark alone remained safe. Moreover, just as then the higher the waters rose, the higher the ark was lifted, so the Church can never be overturned or overwhelmed by enemies, but the greater their assaults become, the more exalted the Church will be, and, supported by the help of God, it will always rise higher. Therefore (so that we may at last bring this passage to a close), let us return to God with ardent and constant prayers; let us implore his mercy and help, let us seek him from the heart; and let us not doubt that we shall obtain his favour, so that we may overcome both the many calamities by which we are pressed and the very flood of evils spread almost over the whole world. There follows:

units.la: vers. 7. Tu es latibulum meum: ab angu-stia seruabis me & liberationis canticis me cir-cundabis.
units.tr: vers. 7. You are my hiding place; you will keep me from distress and surround me with songs of deliverance.

units.la: Hic Dauid summa erga se Dei beneficia agnoscit, cùm vt gratias agat Deo, tùm vt se in medium proponat tanquam exemplum in quod omnes debeant intueri. Nec enim dubium est quin talè simus experturi Deum erga nos, qualem Dauid ipse in mediis asslictionibus[?] expertus est, quum ad illius misericordiam & auxilium perfugit. Superiore vero[?] su doctrinam generalem tradidit, quum diceret iis paratam esse salutem certissimam qui ad Dominum sanctis precibus confugient. Nunc id confirmat suo exemplo: Ac ne, inquit, dubitetis ita futurum quemadmodum praedixi, en vobis exemplum illustrissimum divini auxilii, siquidem oculos in me coniiciatis. Quum enim omnia me afflictionum genera, velut armati hostes insequerentur: ego tanquam in latibulum, ita in Dei praesidium me recepi, ut me ille paterno sinu tegeret, ac mihi liceret tuto sub eius alarum umbra delitescere: ille me suo complexu fouit, a me pericula propulsauit & mihi ab hostibus foeliciter liberato maximum dedit gratiarum actionis argumentum.
units.tr: Here David acknowledges God's greatest benefits toward himself, both to give thanks to God and to set himself forward as an example for everyone to look upon. There is no doubt that we shall experience God toward us as David himself experienced him in the midst of afflictions, when he fled to God's mercy and help. In the preceding verses he had set out a general doctrine, saying that certain salvation is prepared for those who take refuge in the Lord with holy prayers. Now he confirms it by his own example: "And lest you doubt that it will happen as I have said, behold an most illustrious example of divine help for you, if you look upon me. For when every kind of affliction pursued me like armed enemies, I withdrew, like one hiding in a shelter, into God's protection, so that he would cover me with a father's bosom and I might lie hidden safely under the shadow of his wings. He embraced me, drove dangers away from me, and, having happily freed me from my enemies, gave me the greatest cause for giving thanks."

units.la: Hæc igitur est sententia huius loci, in quo primum ordo ille quem Dauid secutus est videtur esse observandus. Postquam e-nim egit de remissione peccatorum & hu-ius beneficij a Deo accepti magnitudinem verbis amplissimis illustrauit, iam caetera be-neficia commemorat, atque in primis prae-sidium, salutem, & a periculis omnibus li-berationem. Qui ordo, quemadmodum di-xi, nobis spectandus est. Ita enim statuere debemus, remissionem peccatorum esse in-star fontis uberrimi ex quo caetera Dei beneficia & dona ceu varij riuuli diducuntur. Nam quum eos potissimum beneficiis exornet Dominus quos gratos habet, qui sieri potest vt nos purissimus ille Pater, amore complectatur, nisi prius peccata condonarit? Hinc ergo cætera bona originem ducere necesse est. Quem etiam ordinem serua-uit Paulus in Epistola ad Romanos : vbi, & 8. postquam multis verbis disseruit de gratuita fidei iustificatione & remissione peccatorū, tum subiicit certissimam illam piorum fiduciam qua pericula, qua gladios, qua mortem ipsam negligunt, qua denique tanquam victores insultant etiam inferorum potesta-ti. Quinetiam quum Dauid petit auxilium à Deo in rebus aduersis, solet primùm Dei misericordiam deprecari, vt ita doceat frustrà nos ad Deum recurrere, nisi nos pro summa sua misericordia gratos habeat. Vbi verò certò sumus persuasi de peccatorum remissione, fieri non potest quin simul etiam credamus à Deo nos protegi, Deo nos esse curæ & aduersus omnia pericula fore tutos sub eius præsidio. Semper enim occurret quod ait Paulus, quì fieri potest vt qui pro-prio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omni-bus tradidit cum, non etiam cum eo omnia nobis gratificetur? Quid? qui mihi peccata condonauit, num in posterum mei curam ab iiciet ? qui mihi salutem in Christo dedit, qui mihi cœlum aperuit , qui me iam in æternæ vitæ possessionem introduxit, nónne me ab huius vitæ incommodis, quatenus meæ salutis ratio postulabit, sartum tectúmque tuebitur? qui peccatum, mortem, Satanam propter me vicit, cuertit, conculcauit, non minas hostium meorum, non eorum conatus audaciamque profligabit?Itaque.videmus nobis semper esse à peccatorum remissione incipiendum, vt hoc iacto fundamento, magnam deinde (vt ita loquar) spei, fiduciæ, & fortitudinis molem aduersus hostium impetum extruamus, atque certis & intrepidis animis cum Dauide dicamus: Tu es latibulum
units.tr: This, then, is the sense of this passage, in which the order David followed seems to be observed first. After he had treated the forgiveness of sins and illustrated in very ample words the greatness of this benefit received from God, he now recounts his other benefits, above all protection, salvation, and deliverance from all dangers. As I said, this order is for us to observe. For we ought to hold that the forgiveness of sins is like a most abundant fountain, from which God's other benefits and gifts flow out like various streamlets. For since the Lord especially adorns with benefits those whom he holds dear, how can that most pure Father embrace us with love unless he has first pardoned our sins? Hence the other goods must necessarily derive their origin from this. Paul also kept this order in the Epistle to the Romans, where, in chapter 8, after he had discoursed at length on the free justification by faith and the forgiveness of sins, he then added that most certain confidence of the godly, by which they disregard dangers, swords, and death itself, and finally exult as victors even over the powers of hell. Moreover, when David seeks help from God in adversity, he is accustomed first to beseech God's mercy, so as to teach that we run to God in vain unless he holds us dear through his great mercy. But when we are firmly persuaded of the forgiveness of sins, it cannot be that we do not at the same time believe that we are protected by God, that God cares for us and that we shall be safe under his protection against all dangers. For there always comes to mind what Paul said: how can it be that he who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, will not also with him grant us all things? What then? He who has forgiven my sins, will he cast off care for me in future? He who has given me salvation in Christ, who has opened heaven to me, who has already brought me into possession of eternal life, will he not keep me safe and sound from the troubles of this life, as far as the reason of my salvation requires? He who conquered, overthrew, and trampled under foot sin, death, and Satan on my account, will he not put to flight the threats of my enemies, their attempts and their audacity? So we see that we must always begin with the forgiveness of sins, so that, this foundation being laid, we may then build up, so to speak, a great mass of hope, confidence, and courage against the assault of enemies, and with secure and fearless minds say with David: Thou art my hiding place.

units.la: Hæc etiam Dauidis verba nos docent Deum esse tutissimum piorum perfugium: quæ doctrina nobis in primis necessaria est. Quum enim hæc vita tot ærumnis & laboribus expósita sit, si semel hoc in animis nostris impressum fuerit, Deum esse nostrum perfugium, hæc certè vel sola cogitatio facilè absterget omnes præsentis vitæ molestias. Equidem autem, cedo, non statim hoc Dauidi af-sentiatur, in Deo certum perfugium nobis esse repositum, qui modò Dei naturam atten-tè considerauerit? Visne ad eum confugere qui sit potens, qui te amet, qui sit semper sui similis? Ergo ad Deum confugito: ille est enim summe potens & summe bonus, ille te summo amore prosequitur, ille denique perpetuò sibi cõstat, nec vlla vel illius potentiæ vel bonitati potest vnquam accidere muta-tio: ille est afflictorum solatium, inopum thesaurus, pereuntium salus, morientium vita, miserorum foelicitas. Quis ergo aliud sibi perfugium eligat? Nam (vt hanc Esaiæ similitu-dinem vsurpem) quemadmodum solemus, si-quando tempestas venerit & imbres vel grandines vrgeant, nos sub tectum recipere ad arcendam aëris iniuriam: ita cùm afflictionum nimbi tenebras ubique videntur offudisse, cùm hostes Ecclesiæ tonant, fulgurant, omnia permiscent: quid, cedò, nobis est in hac tanta calamitate faciendū? nónne ad Dei præsidium tanquam sub tectum tutissimum confugiendum est? Præclarè enim alibi Psal-tes: Qui habitat (inquit) in latibulo excelsi & in umbra Omnipotentis commoratur, ille liberabitur ab omnibus periculis: quemad-modum susè tractatur hoc argumentum toto illo Psalmo qui magnâ lucem affert huic loco quem nunc exponimus. Rursus sic alibi fideles canunt: Deus est nobis protectio & robur atque premente aduersitate auxilium præsentissimum. Propterea nihil timebimus, etiamsi loco moveatur, terra & montes ipsi in medium mare deuoluantur. In[?]fremant & turbentur undæ eius, tumultuentur gentes, motus concitent regna & tellus dato fragore defluat. Dominus exercituum stat à nobis, arx sublimis est nobis Deus Iacob. Magnifica vero vox & quæ debet magnam fidei lucem in animis nostris accendere. Ecquid enim timoris aut dubi-tationis erit nobis reliquum, si semel con-stituerimus Deum esse salutis nostrae praesi-dium firmissimum? Intueamur animo Da-uidem in hoc Dei latibulum confugientem, quoties fuit ab hostibus appetitus: Abscon-dit me, inquit, in tabernaculo suo in die adversitatis, occultabit me in abdito ten-torij sui. Videamus pium illum regem A-sam adversus Aethiopum, copias ad Domi-ni perfugium recurrentem. Contemplemur Iosaphatum consilij & auxilij humani prorsus inopem, oculos habentem in uno Dei prae-sidio defixos. Audiamus Ezechiam adver-sus Sennacheribi minas & impuri illius Rab-sacis blasphemias ad auxilium Dei[?]sancta pre-catione recurrentem. Quid pluribus opus est? abundat Scriptura praeceptis & exem-plis quae nos rebus adversis variè iactatos, quasi manu, ad Dei latibulum deducunt, u-bi securam tranquillamque vitam agere pos-simus.
units.tr: These words of David also teach us that God is the safest refuge of the godly, a doctrine especially necessary for us. For since this life is exposed to so many troubles and labours, if once it has been fixed in our minds that God is our refuge, this thought alone will certainly wipe away all the annoyances of the present life. But tell me, would not someone at once assent to David, that a sure refuge has been laid up for us in God, if he only considered carefully God's nature? Do you wish to flee to one who is powerful, who loves you, who is always like himself? Flee, then, to God: for he is supremely powerful and supremely good; he pursues you with the highest love; and finally he is constantly consistent with himself, nor can any change ever befall either his power or his goodness. He is the comfort of the afflicted, the treasure of the poor, the salvation of the perishing, the life of the dying, the happiness of the wretched. Who, then, would choose any other refuge? For (to borrow this comparison from Isaiah) as we are wont, when a storm comes and showers or hail press upon us, to take shelter under a roof to ward off the harm of the air, so when clouds of affliction seem to have spread darkness everywhere, when the enemies of the Church thunder, flash, and throw everything into confusion, what, tell me, must we do in this great calamity? Must we not flee to God's protection as to the safest roof? For the Psalmist has said admirably elsewhere: "He who dwells in the hiding place of the Most High and abides under the shadow of the Almighty will be delivered from all dangers," and this theme is treated at length throughout that whole Psalm, which throws great light on the passage we are now expounding. Again, the faithful sing elsewhere: "God is our protection and strength, a most present help in pressing adversity. Therefore we will fear nothing, even if the earth be moved and the mountains be cast into the midst of the sea. Let its waters roar and be troubled, let the nations tumult, let kingdoms be moved, and the earth melt with a crash. The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our high tower." It is a magnificent utterance, and one that ought to kindle a great light of faith in our minds. For what fear or doubt will remain for us, if once we have settled that God is the firmest protection of our salvation? Let us look with the mind upon David fleeing into this hiding place of God, as often as he was assailed by enemies: "He hides me, he says, in his tabernacle in the day of adversity; he will conceal me in the secret place of his tent." Let us see the pious king Asa, when the forces of the Ethiopians came against him, running back to the Lord's refuge. Let us contemplate Jehoshaphat, utterly destitute of human counsel and help, having his eyes fixed on God's protection alone. Let us hear Hezekiah, against the threats of Sennacherib and the blasphemies of that impious Rabshakeh, running to God's help with holy prayer. What more is needed? Scripture abounds with precepts and examples which, as if by the hand, lead us, tossed about in various adversities, to God's hiding place, where we may live a secure and tranquil life.

units.la: Quamobrem hoc Dauidis dictum nobis ante oculos perpetuo versetur, his praesertim temporibus, quibus hostes Euangelij maximum impetum in Ecclesiam faciunt. Eia ergo, confugiamus ad Dominum & cum Dauide, non tam corporis quàm animi voce exclamemus: Tu es latibulum nostrum, ô Domine. In hac tanta temporum acerbitate quem præter te inuocemus, cuius auxilium imploremus, ad cuius præsidium cõfugiamus habemus neminem. Tu vita nostra, tu sa- lus, tu nobis vnicum es perfugium. Ad te con- fugimus tanquam ad latibulum, ô Æterne, vt salus nostra aduersus vim hostium in tua po- tentia, & aduersus eorum crudelitatem in tua misericordia delitescat. Hæc & pleraque si- milia nobis in mentem veniant quoties ver- sabimur in huius loci meditatione. Nec eos sus eos imitemur qui vt res aducrsas effugiant, in re- bus terrenis sibi latibulum constituunt. Hic in humanis consiliis ac viribus sibi videtur egregie latere. Ille se totum abdit in ingen- tes diuitiarum aceruos, vt illis vndique in- uolutus tutò lateat. Alius aliud quoddam latibuli genus sibi comparat, atque ita ma- gna pars hominum se præclare saluti con- suluisse existimat. Qui similiter faciunt vt siquis à nemine se videri credat, modo si- bi ipse oculos obiectis manibus obtexerit. Atqui hoc non est non videri, sed non vi- dere. Quanto melius Dauid? Dauid, in- quam, sceptro potentissimo munitus, Da- uid fretus humanis viribus, stipatus magno militum numero, peritus rei militaris, & iam multis ac nobilissimis victoriis exornatus, ni- hilominus tamen exclamat: Tu es latibulum meum ô Domine: Non in regno, licet poten- tissimo, non in multis hominū millibus, non in sua virtute ac fortitudine, non in rerum gestarum gloriæ sibi latibulum perfugiúmque constituit, sed in Æterno. Nimirum longè aberat ab iis qui ad res humanas terrenásque adhærescunt. Quamobrem tantus hic error eripiendus est, atque ita statuendum, nusquam alibi quàm in vno Deo tutum nobis latibulum ac perfugium esse posse.
units.tr: Therefore let this saying of David always be before our eyes, especially in these times, when the enemies of the gospel make their greatest assault upon the Church. Come, then, let us flee to the Lord, and with David let us cry out, not so much with the voice of the body as of the soul: "Thou art our hiding place, O Lord." In such great bitterness of the times, whom else shall we call upon besides you, whose help shall we implore, to whose protection shall we flee? We have no one. You are our life, you our salvation, you alone are our refuge. We flee to you as to a hiding place, O Eternal One, so that our salvation may lie hidden against the violence of enemies in your power, and against their cruelty in your mercy. These and many similar thoughts should come to mind whenever we engage in meditation on this passage. Nor let us imitate them, who, in order to escape adversity, establish for themselves a hiding place among earthly things. One of these seems to himself to lie admirably hidden in human counsels and strength. Another buries himself entirely in huge heaps of riches, so that, wrapped up in them on every side, he may lie safe. Another prepares for himself some other kind of hiding place, and so a great part of mankind thinks it has splendidly provided for its safety. Those who act in this way are like someone who believes he cannot be seen by anyone simply because he has covered his own eyes with his hands. But this is not being unseen; it is not seeing. How much better was David! David, I say, fortified with the most powerful sceptre, David relying on human strength, surrounded by a large number of soldiers, skilled in warfare, and already adorned with many most noble victories, nevertheless cries out: "You are my hiding place, O Lord." He did not establish his hiding place and refuge in his kingdom, however mighty, nor in many thousands of men, nor in his own virtue and courage, nor in the glory of his deeds, but in the Eternal One. Doubtless he was far removed from those who cling to human and earthly things. Wherefore this great error must be torn away, and it must be established that nowhere but in the one God can we have a safe hiding place and refuge.

units.la: Sunt etiam reiiciendi qui idolorum auxilium implorant, & ab iis expectant præsidium salutis, ac nihilominus ea sunt impudentia, vt ad Deum recurrere videri velint.
units.tr: Those also must be rejected who implore the help of idols and look to them for the protection of their salvation, and yet they are so shameless as to wish to seem to be running to God.

units.la: Sed hoc vno Dauidis verbo refelluntur, cùm in Æterno suum latibulum & spem salutis politam esse profitetur. Nec enim Deus est eorum latibulum qui idolorum latebras sectantur, & vt per tenebricosas specus, i-ta per varios multiplicésque idololatriæ re-cessus aberrantes, veritatis lucem refugiunt.
units.tr: But this is refuted by the one word of David, when he professes that his hiding place and his hope of salvation are laid up in the Eternal. For God is not the hiding place of those who pursue the hiding places of idols, and who, wandering through the varied and manifold recesses of idolatry as through dark caves, flee the light of truth.

units.la: Nam hoc latibulum de quo loquitur Dauid, repositum est in vero Dei cultu, & in vera ipsius Ecclesia, quemadmodum ille i-pse satis explicat Psalmo 31. Quam ampla sunt, inquit, bona, quæ iis qui te metuunt reposuisti! Abscondes illos in latibulo faciei tuæ. Et in eo quem iam citaui loco: Hoc vnum postulaui à Domino atque etiam postulabo, vt habitem in domo ipsius cunctis diebus vitæ meæ: quoniam abscondet me in tabernaculo suo. Quibus verbis significat, in Ecclesia Dei & in puro eius cultu nobis aduersus improborum omnium conatus esesse delitescendum. Nec enim dubium est quin hoc latibuli vocabulo ad sanctum taberna-culum alluserit in quod, ante extructum ab Solomone templum, Israelitæ conueniebāt ad religionem exercendam: Ut enim tento-rio, ita summo Dei fauore undique fideles obteguntur. Quæ cum ita sint, quid mentis habent infœlices illi qui hoc tempore à vera religione metu hominum defecerunt? Me, inquis, præsens periculum exterruit, cū mors idetidem ante oculos versaretur. Quid? num idcirco fuit à latibulo discedendū quod ma-iora pericula imminerent? nonne potius eo magis te in ipsum latibulum intrudere, & illi ipsi penitus adhærescere debuisti? mirabā-tur homines: at tè Deus suo verbo cōfirmas- set[?]. In te impetu hominēs faciebant: at prōmptum erat Dei latibulum, in quod tuæ salutis curam coniceres. Eum deseruisti qui te de- sertum esse non est passus: qui te ex errorum tenebris, ex idololatria, ex ipsis inferorū fau- cibus eripuerat: qui te in sua Ecclesia, tanquā sub alarum umbra tuebatur, qui te verbo suo nutriebat, te paterno sinu fouebat, tibi quo- tidie rerum cœlestium æterna eque vitæ dul-cedinem in os quodammodo infundebat, assidua Euangelij prædicatione. Eum, ut vitæ consuleres, deseruisti qui solus tuæ vitæ au-thor, qui creator, qui conseruator fuit. O sal-laces mundi præstigias! O præposteras homi-num cupiditates qui vt viuāt, à vita deficiunt, & ne moriantur, in mediam mortem praeci-pites ruunt. An ergo te putas ex hostibus eua sisse qui in truculentissimorum hostium potestatem venisti? Districtos hominum gladios, crudelesque flammas horruisti, sed longe tibi peius accidit, cum incensæ peccati faces te intimum adurant: cum te Satan, caro, mundus, atque adeo horribiles inferorum impetus exterreant: denique tu tibi ipsi hostis es, cum te assidui conscientiæ stimuli confodiant, ac te miserum exagitet perpetua admissi peccati recordatio. Quamobrem (vos enim appello quos ipsa conscientiæ labes excruciat, quique admissum peccatum deflctis: ego, inquam, vna vobiscum flens ac dolens vos appello) redite tandem ad vos, vel potius ad eum a quo defecistis. Ille vobis manum adhuc porrigit, vos ad se revocat, vobis suum latibulum proponit, ut vos cō recipiatis. Deu reliqui-stis, sed ille non patitur vos esse diutius reli-ctos. Audite Patris clementissimi vocem, intuemini lucem exhibitam, recipite amplissimos Ecclesiæ thesauros, quos ille coram oculis vestris explicat, vobis offert, vobis tradit. Vestra fi-des & obedietia respondeat divinæ liberalita-ti, existimate vobis dictu quod Oseas vetere Israelis ecclesia copellans: Revertere, inquit, O Israel, ad Dominū Deum tuū: quoniam in iniquitate tua corruisti. Tollite vobiscū verba, & cōversi ad Deū illi dicite: Aufer omne iniquitatē, ō Domine. Hac ergo precatione usurpate quā vobis Oscas dictauit: Aufer nostram iniquitatē, Domine, ablue sordes pec-catorum nostrorū, sana vulnus quod nostra perfidia atq; ingratitudo nobis inflixit: sis nobis latibulum ac perfugiū aduersus horrore peccati & mortis, vt conscientia nostra in peccatorū remissione ac tuae misericordiae fiducia cōquiescat. Haec sunt quae debet perpetuo illis obuersari qui derelicto Dei latibulo, à puro ipsius cultu & ab Ecclesia hoc tempore defecerunt, vt se illuc, vnde egressi sunt, recipiat. Nos interim sapiamus tot exemplis nobis hodie propositis: agnoscamus infirmitatē nostrā, maneamus in Dei latibulo, petamus auxilium à Deo, ne qua vis, ne qua tempestas vnquā nos possit inde diuellere, & ipsos fratres qui lapsi sunt, tū precibus ad Dominū, tū sanctis cohortationibus, quoad eius fieri poterit, adiuuemus. Hoc autem loco iā attendāt ij quos Deus tot tantisq; beneficiis hodie prosequi-tur, qui sine labore, sine metu, sine periculo puram diuini verbi praedicationem habet in mediis vrbibus summo cum otio ac tranquillitate resonantem: qui dum alij tāquam tem-pestate iactati hāc & illāc incerti vagantur, ipsi in Dei latibulo tanquam in tutissimo portu foelices degunt, sedémque stabilem ac domicilium certum habent. Æstiment vt par est tantum Dei beneficium, colant eius liberalitatem, permaneant sub eius latibulo, & diuinas voces, quibus ipsorum aures. undique circunsonant, reuerenter audiant, attentè percipiant, sancte & diligenter exequantur. Hæc igitur omnia cõsideremus, ut merito possimus unà cum Dauide profiteri, Deum esse latibulũ nostrũ atq; perfugium. Quod proculdubio faciemus, si fructus qui inde cõsequentur, ita vt decet, expederimus.
units.tr: For this hiding place of which David speaks is laid up in the true worship of God and in the true Church itself, as he himself explains sufficiently in Psalm 31. "How great," he says, "are the good things which you have laid up for those who fear you! You will hide them in the secret place of your face." And in the passage I have already cited: "This one thing I have asked of the Lord, and will ask, that I may dwell in his house all the days of my life, for he will hide me in his tabernacle." By these words he signifies that we must hide ourselves in the Church of God and in its pure worship, against all the attempts of the wicked. For there is no doubt that by the word hiding place he alluded to the holy tabernacle, toward which the Israelites gathered to exercise their religion before the temple was built by Solomon. For as with a tent, so the faithful are covered on every side by the highest favour of God. Since these things are so, what are the minds of those unhappy men who in this time have fallen away from true religion through fear of men? "The present danger terrified me," you say, "when death was constantly before my eyes." What then? Was it for this reason that one ought to depart from the hiding place, because greater dangers threatened? Ought you not rather to thrust yourself the more into that very hiding place, and cling to it wholly? People marvelled; but God would have confirmed you by his word. Men were attacking you; but the hiding place of God was ready, into which you might have committed the care of your salvation. You deserted him who did not allow you to be deserted: who had snatched you from the shadows of error, from idolatry, from the very jaws of hell; who protected you in his Church as under the shadow of his wings, who fed you with his word, cherished you in his fatherly bosom, and poured into you, as it were, day by day the eternal sweetness of heavenly things by the constant preaching of the Gospel. You deserted him, in order to look after your life, who alone was the author of your life, who was its creator and preserver. O deceitful allurements of the world! O perverse desires of men, who, that they may live, fall from life, and that they may not die, rush headlong into the midst of death! Do you think you have escaped from enemies when you have come into the power of most savage enemies? You have dreaded the drawn swords of men and cruel flames, but it has happened to you far worse, when the torches of sin kindle you inwardly: when Satan, the flesh, the world, and indeed the dreadful assaults of hell terrify you; finally, you are your own enemy, when the constant goads of conscience pierce you, and the perpetual recollection of the sin you have committed harasses you in your wretchedness. Wherefore (for I address you, those whom the very stain of conscience tortures, who lament the sin you have committed; I, I say, weeping and grieving together with you, address you) return at last to yourselves, or rather to him from whom you have fallen away. He still stretches out his hand to you, calls you back to himself, and sets before you his hiding place, that you may take refuge in it. You have forsaken God, but he does not allow you to be forsaken any longer. Hear the voice of the most merciful Father, behold the light displayed, receive the most ample treasures of the Church, which he unfolds before your eyes, offers to you, and hands over to you. Let your faith and obedience answer to divine generosity, and take to yourselves what Hosea, calling back the ancient church of Israel, said to it: "Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have fallen through your iniquity." Take words with you, and turning to God say to him: "Take away all iniquity, O Lord." Therefore use this prayer which Hosea dictated to you: "Take away our iniquity, Lord; wash away the filth of our sins; heal the wound which our faithlessness and ingratitude have inflicted upon us; be to us a hiding place and refuge against the horror of sin and death, so that our conscience may rest in the forgiveness of sins and in confidence in your mercy." These are the things which ought constantly to present themselves to those who, having forsaken the hiding place of God, have in this time fallen away from his pure worship and from the Church, so that they may return to where they went out from. Meanwhile let us be wise in the light of the many examples set before us today: let us acknowledge our weakness, let us abide in the hiding place of God, let us seek help from God, lest any violence or any storm ever tear us from it; and let us help our brothers who have fallen, both with prayers to the Lord and with holy exhortations, as far as it can be done. But let those whom God today favours with so many and great benefits now give heed: those who have the pure preaching of the divine word resounding in the midst of their cities, without labour, without fear, without danger, in the greatest leisure and tranquillity; while others, as if tossed about by a tempest, wander uncertain hither and thither, they themselves dwell happily in the hiding place of God as in the safest harbour, and have a stable seat and a certain dwelling. Let them value, as is fitting, so great a benefit of God, honour his generosity, remain under his shelter, and reverently hear, attentively perceive, and holily and diligently carry out the divine voices which sound on every side around their ears. Let us therefore consider all these things, so that we may rightly be able, together with David, to profess that God is our hiding place and refuge. This we will undoubtedly do, if we work out the fruits which follow from it, as is fitting.

units.la: Addit enim noster vates: Seruabis me ab afflictione quæ si exprimas per tepus præsens, Seruas me (quod quidam faciunt) signifi-cabunt assiduam ac perpetuam Dei custodiam ergà suos. Atque ita erit gratiarum actio, qua vates agnoscit continuum erga se Dei præsi-dium, & sui conseruationem auxilio Dei so-lius acceptam refert. Sed omnino verba futu-ri temporis hic vsurpata vim magnã habent. Hinc enim colligi potest quanta sit eorum fiducia qui se in latibulum Dei receperunt, se cum affirmare non dubitêt sibi Deum per-petuò aduturum & se illius ope atque præsi-dio ab omni afflictione liberatum iri. Sed contra exoritur pontificiorum obiectio: Vnde tanta vobis arrogantia? Vnde tantus fastus, vt vos à Deo seruandos esse tam fidenter affirmare audeatis? Quid? num obsecro arrogans est, qui Deo credit? qui fidem habet Dei promissis? Sumne arrogantiæ insimulandus, si credo Deum seruare velle, quia promisit: seruare posse, quia Deus, quia Æter-nus, quia omnipotens est? Illéne sibi quippiam arrogat, qui suis atque adeò humanis omnibus terrenisque viribus diffisus, in uno Deo salutis fiduciam collocauit? Non dico: Seruabo me, sed d co[?] cum Dauide: Seruabis me, Domine. Sunt igitur arrogantes ij qui confidunt suisse meritis, operibus, satisfactionibus seruatum iri: longe vero absunt a suis ope[?] tam foedo illo arrogantiae crimine, qui ab Osea didicerunt se perditos quidem in seipsis, fiduciar[?] sed suam in Deo salutem esse. Iam ergo no- bis hanc Dauidis doctrinam accommodemus, & hoc tempore, cum Ecclesiae in toto propemodum orbe terrarum affliguntur, dicamus, certa, inquam, fiducia dicamus: Seruabis nos Domine: nobis miseris, perditis atque etiam indignissimis tantum hoc beneficium conferes: seruaturum enim promisisti: tibi Seruatoris nomen indidisti: nos in Ecclesiam tuam collegisti: fumus vasa misericordiae & salutis: nobis iam per Christum parta salus est atque redemptio. Seruabis nos, quia semper Ecclesiam tuam seruasti. Tu illam ex media Ægypti fornace exerto potentique brachio extraxisti. Tu Amalecitas, Chanaeos, Moabitas, Ammonitas, tu ipsum Babylonicae seruitutis iugum a ceruicibus Ecclesiae repulisti. Eadem perpetuo manet tua voluntas, eadem est semper tua potentia. Ergo seruabis nos. Haec & similia debent nobis idem occurrere, ne nos tristis rerum aduersarū facies deterreat, ac de fidei gradu deiciat. Neque tantum debemus esse certi de ge[?] nerali salute Ecclesiæ, sed Dauidis exemplo debet vnusquisque sibi accommodare generales promissiones. Itaque si me vrgeat peccatorum conscientia, si mihi lex Dei mortem & exitium minetur, si mihi admoneantur diuini iudicij faces, tum exclamabo, Seruabis me Domine. Rursus si quid periculi, si quid aduersi contigerit, idem perpetuo dicam. Hæc vna vox audietur: Seruabis me Domine. Quamobrem? nempe quia quæ generaliter Deus suis omnibus promisit, hæc mihi debeo priuatim etiam accommodare. Sed forte obiiciat aliquis, fideles nō semper à Deo seruari, cum sæpenumero in hostium manus incidant. Respondeo pios in media morte seruari, adeò vt cum maximè victi ac prostrati viden tur esse, tunc maiorem de hostibus victoriam reportent. Nec enim frustrà docuit Iohânes fidem esse piorum victoriam. Ergo quandiu vera fide dices, Seruabis me Domine: tandiu vincès, quicunque tandem rerum tuarū exi-tus esse videatur. Cæterum hinc admone-mur quèadmodum[?] sit intelligenda Dei erga nos custodia. Nec enim immunes sumus à periculis nec malorum & afflictionis expertes, sed seruamur ab afflictione, id est quanquam innumerabiles sunt nobis afflictiones sub-eundę, ita tamen premimur, ne opprimamur Deo nobis perpetuum auxilium salutémque conferente. Quod enim de se profitebatur Apostolus, id possunt fideles omnes merito dicere:In omnibus premimur, at non coar-ctamur:hæsitamus,at non prorsus hæremus: persecutionem patimur,sed in ea non defe-rimur:deiicimur,at non perimus. Et alio lo-co:vt morientes,inquit,& ecce viuimus.Præ- clara sanè sententia, vt quę nobis ponat ante oculos eorum conditionem qui mundo renun-tiantes se totos Dei cultui consecrarunt. Si e-nim cum militibus coparantur, qui sint,Apo-stolo teste,variis armorum generibus instruen-di,nū obscero ideo sunt milites, vt in umbra atq; otio perpetuo viuant? num ideo arman-tur,vt semper ignaui inertesque sedeant?no-bis saltem pudorem incutiat illa Poëtæ veteris exprobratio de Salmacidis spoliis sine sudore & sanguine. Si de morte, peccato atq; inferis triumphandū est,vincendum igitur:si vincendum,ergo pugnandū est:nisi præcesse-rit pugna,nō potest esse victoria(inquit Cy-prianus.) Sed præclarè nobiscum agitur qui Deo duce,auxiliatore,seruatore freti sumus. Enimuero ne,si id quidè liceat,nobis optan-dum fuerit vt rebus omnibus ad voluntatem nostram fluentibus, perpetua quiete perfruamur. Nā tum Dei potentia,iustitia, bonitas & imperuestigabilis sapientia refulgent ma-ximè,cum maxime instat atq; vrgent res ad-uersæ: ne quid dicā de piorum ita domandis cupiditatibus, ita exercenda fide, ita corō-nanda patientia. Quid quod præsentis dolo-ris acerbitas dulciore reddit futura à Deo liberationem? Scitum est enim quod aliquan- do Prosper discipulus Augustini dicebat: Dulcior fit salus cum dolor excruciat, & fa-nitatis amissae dulcedinem languoris amari-tudo commendat. Itaque cum hic a nostro vate doceamur a Deo nos seruari, meminerimus hanc esse piorum cōditionem vt eorum vita multis afflictionum telis proposita sit: quandoquidē non opus est salute, si nulla urgeat periculi necessitas: neque futurus est seruator, vbi non sint qui seruari debeant. Hoc ergo seruādi vocabulum satis nos admonet quot quantisque malis atque periculis vita nostra sit obnoxia. Quod etiam confirmant ea quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: For our poet adds: "You will keep me from affliction." If you render the verb in the present tense, "you keep me" (as some do), it will signify God's constant and unceasing guardianship over his people. The verse then becomes an act of thanksgiving, in which the psalmist acknowledges God's continual protection of himself and credits his preservation wholly to the help of God alone. But the verbs here in the future tense carry great weight. From them one can gather how great the confidence of those is who have taken refuge in God's hiding place, since they do not hesitate to affirm that God will always be present to them and that by his help and protection they will be freed from every affliction. The Papists object: "Whence this great arrogance in you? Whence this great pride, that you dare to affirm so confidently that you will be saved by God?" But what? Is he arrogant, I ask, who believes God? Who trusts in God's promises? Am I to be charged with arrogance if I believe that God wills to save me because he has promised it, and that he is able to save me because he is God, because he is eternal and almighty? Does he claim anything for himself who, distrusting all his own strength and all human and earthly resources, has placed his hope of salvation in God alone? I do not say, "I will save myself," but, with David, "You will save me, O Lord." Those are arrogant who trust that they will be saved by their own merits, works and satisfactions. Far removed from that foul crime of arrogance are those who have learned from Hosea that they are indeed destroyed in themselves, but that their salvation lies in God. Let us therefore apply this teaching of David to ourselves, and at this time, when the Churches are afflicted across almost the whole world, let us say, I say with certain confidence: "You will save us, Lord." To us, wretched, lost and even most unworthy, you will confer this benefit alone, for you have promised to save, you have given yourself the name of Saviour, you have gathered us into your Church, we are vessels of mercy and salvation, and salvation and redemption have already been won for us through Christ. You will save us, because you have always saved your Church. You drew it out of the furnace of Egypt with an outstretched and mighty arm. You repulsed the Amalekites, Canaanites, Moabites and Ammonites, and you tore the very yoke of Babylonian servitude from the necks of the Church. Your will remains the same forever; your power is always the same. Therefore you will save us. These and similar thoughts ought to come to us, so that the grim aspect of adverse circumstances may not frighten us or drive us from our footing in faith. Nor should we be certain only of the general salvation of the Church; following David's example, each one ought to apply the general promises to himself. So if the consciousness of sin presses on me, if the law of God threatens me with death and destruction, if the torches of divine judgment are brought before me, then I shall cry out, "You will save me, O Lord." Again, if any danger or any adversity befalls me, I shall say the same thing continually. This one cry will be heard: "You will save me, O Lord." Why? Surely because what God has promised generally to all his people, I ought to apply to myself also in particular. But perhaps someone will object that the faithful are not always preserved by God, since so often they fall into the hands of their enemies. I answer that the godly are preserved even in the midst of death, so that when they seem most overcome and prostrate, then they win the greater victory over their enemies. For John did not teach in vain that faith is the victory of the godly. So, as long as you say with true faith, "You will save me, O Lord," so long you will conquer, whatever the outcome of your affairs may appear to be. Moreover, from this we are reminded how the care of God for us is to be understood. For we are not exempt from dangers, nor free from evils and afflictions; but we are saved from affliction, that is to say, although countless afflictions must be undergone by us, yet we are so pressed that we are not crushed, God bestowing on us perpetual help and salvation. What the Apostle professed of himself, all the faithful can rightly say: "We are pressed on every side, but not crushed; we are perplexed, but not driven to despair; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but do not perish." And in another place: "As dying, behold, we live." This is a truly remarkable saying, since it sets before our eyes the condition of those who, renouncing the world, have wholly consecrated themselves to the worship of God. For if they are compared with soldiers, who, as the Apostle witnesses, must be equipped with various kinds of weapons, are soldiers, I ask, so that they may live in shade and perpetual ease? Are they armed so that they may sit forever idle and inactive? Let at least that old reproach of the poet about the spoils of Salmacis, won without sweat and blood, bring us shame. If we must triumph over death, sin and hell, then we must conquer; and if we must conquer, then we must fight; unless the battle has gone before, there can be no victory (says Cyprian). But we are dealt with splendidly, who have relied on God as our leader, helper and saviour. Indeed, even if it were permitted, we ought not to wish that, with all things flowing according to our will, we might enjoy perpetual quiet. For then the power, justice and goodness of God, and his unsearchable wisdom, shine forth most brightly when adverse circumstances press hardest and most urgently; not to mention how the desires of the godly are so tamed, their faith so exercised, and their patience so crowned. What is more, the bitterness of present pain makes deliverance from God sweeter in the future. For it is a fine saying which Prosper, the disciple of Augustine, once made: "Salvation becomes sweeter when pain torments us, and the bitterness of sickness commends the sweetness of health that has been lost." Therefore, since here we are taught by our poet that we are saved by God, let us remember that this is the condition of the godly, that their life is exposed to many darts of affliction; for there is no need of salvation if no pressing danger threatens, and there will be no saviour where there are none who must be saved. This word "saving" therefore warns us sufficiently of how many and how great evils and dangers our life is exposed to. The verses that follow also confirm this.

units.la: Me, inquit, liberationis caticis[?] circundabis, Hic liberandi verbum manifeste significat res aduersas periculorumque grauitate, quē-admodum alibi noster Psaltes: multa, inquit, mala iusto accidunt, sed illum Dominus ex-omnibus liberat. Nec leuiter praetereundum est circundandi vocabulum, quod arguit nos ab omnibus partibus vrgeri, donec auxilij diuini lux undique circunfusa tenebras afflictionum discutiat. Ac videte, obsecro, quàm egregiè crescat oratio: nec enim tantū Deus est nobis latibulum ac perfugium ad quod recurramus aduersus vim atque impetum hostium, sed nos etiā ab hostibus seruat atque liberat: nec rursus tantùm nos seruat, sed etiam facit, vt de victis prostratrisque hostibus triumphemus.Nam eò spectare caticum[?] ouationis nimis apertum est. Ita Domini ergà nos beneficia semper crescunt & in dies magis magísq; augentur,donec illis tandē cumulus accedat.Hæ sunt igitur nostrę partes, vt tot beneficiis exornati,Deo seruatori ac liberatori perpetuas gratias agamus & assiduis canticis nomen eius gloriámq; celebremus: inuoca me, inquit, die afflictionis, te libera-bo, tu vero meam gloria celebrabis.Sunt autem obseruandæ istæ phrases quæ sæpe occurrut in sacris literis, circumdabis me canticis liberationis:item,posuisti canticum in ore meo,& siquæ sunt similes quæ declarat Dei benefi-cia grato esse ac memori animo excipienda: totiesq; Deum nobis suppeditare decantandç suæ laudis argumentū quoties nos beneficiis exornat. Quid igitur de iis censendū est qui tot Dei dona,tot acceptas liberationes soe-da ingratitudine sepeliūt? Num ergo mirum videri debet si Deus toties à nobis offensus suam tandē liberalitatē quodammodo restrictioré esse patiatur?Atq; vt vetera relinquamus,exeplo sint Ecclesiæ toties iam ab hostibus Euangelij prostratæ atq; euersæ,toties à Deo,nõ sine multis miraculis instauratę:quę cũ tanta beneficia vel omnino non sentirent vel ingrate negligeret,nec propterea cum ad agendas Deo gratias,tum ad eius verbu reuerenter audiendū & ad melioris vitæ studium accenderentur, ecce noua atque adeo longe
units.tr: "You will surround me," he says, "with songs of deliverance." Here the word "deliverance" plainly signifies adverse circumstances and the gravity of dangers, just as our Psalmist says elsewhere: "Many evils befall the righteous, but the Lord delivers him out of them all." Nor should we pass lightly over the word "surround," which shows that we are pressed on every side, until the light of divine help, poured around us from every quarter, scatters the darkness of affliction. And see, I beg you, how splendidly the discourse grows! For God is not only our hiding place and refuge to which we may run against the violence and assault of enemies; he also saves and delivers us from our enemies; nor again does he only save us, but he also makes us triumph over our defeated and prostrate enemies.
