For it is quite clear that the song of victory aims at this. Thus God's benefits toward us are always increasing, and grow more and more, until at last they reach their full measure. Our part, therefore, is to be adorned with so many benefits and to give perpetual thanks to God our Saviour and Deliverer, and to celebrate his name and glory with continual songs: "Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me." Moreover, these phrases which often occur in Holy Scripture must be noted: "You have surrounded me with songs of deliverance," and "You have put a new song in my mouth," and any similar ones which declare that God's benefits must be received with a grateful and mindful heart, and that God gives us, as often as he adorns us with benefits, a matter for singing his praise. What then must be thought of those who bury so many gifts of God and so many deliverances received under a foul ingratitude? Ought it then to seem strange if God, so often offended by us, allows his generosity to be somewhat restrained? And, to leave aside older examples, let the Church serve as an example: so often already struck down and overthrown by the enemies of the Gospel, and so often restored by God, not without many miracles. Although at those times they either did not feel these great benefits at all or thanklessly neglected them, and were not on that account stirred up both to give thanks to God and to hear his word reverently and to pursue a better life, behold, a new and even far...

units.la: h.j. omnium grauissimâ calamitate, qua procul dubio Dominus nobiscū expostulat de præteritis offensis atque in primis de illa, quâ nûc exagito, beneficiorum acceptorum obliuione. Relipiscamus igitur, & cum assiduis precibus à Domino petimus Ecclesias instaurari, discimus à Dauide nos simul petere gratiarum a-ctionis & canticorum liberationis argumentum, vt erecto ac certo animo dicamus: Cir-cundabis nos canticis liberationis, id est, peccauimus, Domine, cum præteritarum liberationum memoria prope fuerit apud nos cōse-pulta: culpa agnoscimus, veniâ deprecamur: tuam paternâ ac solitam misericordiâ, tuum auxilium toties nobis exhibitū imploramus, atque tibi gratias acturos, tuâ virtutem, poten-tiam, bonitatè altissimâ voce & toto animo celebraturos esse profitemur. Nobis igitur ita potest accommodari fesus verborum Dauidis.
units.tr: This, the most grievous of all calamities, is the one by which the Lord without doubt reproaches us with our past offences, and above all with that forgetfulness of the benefits received which I am now censuring. Let us therefore repent, and with constant prayers ask the Lord to restore his Churches. Let us learn from David to seek at the same time the occasion for thanksgiving and the theme of songs of deliverance, so that with a confident and steadfast mind we may say: "You will surround us with songs of deliverance." That is: we have sinned, Lord, since the memory of past deliverances has almost been buried among us. We acknowledge our fault and beg for pardon. We implore your fatherly and customary mercy, and your help so often shown to us, and we profess that we shall give you thanks and celebrate your virtue, power and goodness with the highest voice and with our whole heart. So the words of David may be fitted to us.

units.la: Præterea videmus ab impiorum forte quàm longè distet piorum conditio. Nam piorum aduersæ res, & lacrymæ, tandem in lætitiam, & eorum fletus in cantica convertuntur: contra vero, profusa improborum gaudia (vt alibi docuit Solomo) desinunt in summos dolores atque cruciatus. Quamobrem ea nos cogitatio consoletur in mediis afflictionibus, tandem nos esse percepturos auxilium Dei, tandem nos esse laudes ipsius & gloriam celebraturos. Hoc significat cantici vocabulum vsurpatum à Dauide quod proprium est corum eorum qui præ ingenti lætitia, quantum more exultant: atque ita magis exprimit quanto animi ardore Deo gratias agere, & eius gloriam prædicare debeamus. Plerique enim Dei laudes canunt, sed id vix ore semi-aperto faciunt & tanquâ aliud agentes. Non etiam probandi sunt Pontificij qui non solùm homines, verùm etiâ ipsa propemodum idola, templis assiduo cantu persónantibus, obtundunt. Non enim solùm canedum, sed Deo, non idolis: Deo, inquam, nō sola voce, sed in primis animo canendum est. Atque hic verus est & rectus vsus musices, & eò sunt omnes nostri cantus referendi. Quò fit vt mirari satis nequeam, nec piorum magistratuum edictis, nec crebris Pastorum obiurgationibus profanas impurásque cantilenas nondum ab his locis exulare potuisse. Quid? num tua libido carnisq; cupiditas iam per se plus satis incensa, nouis adhuc iniectis illecebris inflammanda est? Tibine os & linguam Dominus idcirco dedit, vt vtrunque fœdis ac sordidis cationibus inquinares? Verum quid de lingua queror? Animum ipsum, ipsum, inquam, animum contaminatum esse oportet, cùm tot sordes ac tantam obscœnitatis colluuiem euomat. Impurissimi illi riuuli non possunt, nisi ex impurissimo fonte promanare. Si de otiosó verbo rationem reddituri sumus, quantò magis de ludicris, vanis, obscœnisque cantionibus? Quare audiamus Basilii affirmantem eos demum cætus esse recipiendos, qui nos possunt efficere meliores. Imitemur Dauide qui toties se no turpes affectus carnis, no molles inanesq; cantiunculas, sed Dei laudes & animo & voce & ipsis fidibus decantaturu esse pollicetur. Cum enim tanta hæc sit vis musices, vt res ipsæ quasi cætus dulcedine per aures adductæ in animos facilius influat, ad quid potius adhibeda fuerit quam ad res sacras diuinasq;, vt iis quotidie magis ac magis imbuamur? Ergo (vt ad Dauide nostrum redeamus) iā cātica cōparemus quibus summā Dei potentiam ac gloriā celebremus in Ecclesiarum instauratione refulgentem. Nunc quidē circundāt nos angustiæ dolores que in dies recrūdescentes, nunc nouæ quotidie afflictiones quasi certatim vndique concurrunt: sed erit tēpus (iam enim Dei miseri-cordia nobis ad bene sperandum signum aliquod videtur extulisse) erit, inquā, tempus cūm nos Dominus canticis liberationis circundabit: ille lacrymas nostras absterget, ille nostros gemitus nostrāq; suspiria cū lætissimis ac suauissimis cantibus, querelas nostras cum ingeniti gratiarū actione, commutabit. Hæc sunt quæ nobis proponere debemus vt Dauidis exemplum nobis accommodetur: cuius ea quæ sequuntur verba iam nobis expedenda sunt.
units.tr: Besides, we see how far the condition of the godly differs from that of the wicked. For the adversities and tears of the godly are at last turned into joy, and their weeping into songs. But on the contrary, the abundant pleasures of the wicked (as Solomon teaches elsewhere) end in extreme pains and torments. Therefore let this thought console us in the midst of afflictions: that at last we shall receive the help of God, and at last we shall celebrate his praises and glory. This is what the word "song", used by David, signifies. It properly belongs to those who leap for joy from great gladness, and so it expresses more fully with what ardour of mind we ought to give thanks to God and proclaim his glory. For most people sing God's praises, but they do so scarcely with their mouths half open, and as if they were doing something else. Nor are the Papists to be approved, who not only fill the temples with constant singing, but deafen them with the praise of men and almost of idols. For we must sing not only with the voice but above all with the mind, and to God, not to idols; to God, I say, and not with the voice alone. This is the true and right use of music, and to this all our songs should be referred. Hence I can hardly wonder enough that, despite the edicts of godly magistrates and the frequent rebukes of ministers, profane and impure songs have not yet been driven from these places. What? Is your lust and fleshly desire, already inflamed more than enough by nature, still to be kindled by new enticements? Did the Lord give you a mouth and a tongue for this, that you should defile both with foul and filthy songs? But why complain of the tongue? The mind itself, I say the mind itself, must be contaminated when it vomits up so much filth and such a flood of obscenity. Those most impure streams cannot flow except from a most impure fountain. If we are to render an account of every idle word, how much more of frivolous, vain and obscene songs? Let us therefore listen to Basil, who affirms that only those gatherings are to be admitted which can make us better. Let us imitate David, who, when he promises to sing, declares that he will sing not the base affections of the flesh, nor soft and empty little songs, but the praises of God, with his mind, his voice and the strings themselves. For since music has such great power that its sweetness, brought in through the ears, flows more easily into the mind, to what should it be applied more fittingly than to holy and divine things, so that we may be steeped in them more and more each day? Therefore (to return to our David) let us now prepare songs with which we may celebrate the supreme power and glory of God shining forth in the restoration of the Churches. Indeed, now distresses and pains that revive from day to day surround us, and new afflictions rush upon us from every side as if in competition. But a time will come (for already the mercy of God seems to have raised some sign for us to hope well) a time, I say, when the Lord will surround us with songs of deliverance. He will wipe away our tears; he will exchange our groans and sighs for the most joyful and sweetest songs, and our complaints for thanksgiving of a grateful heart. These are the things we ought to bring forward, so that David's example may be fitted to us. Now let us turn to the words that follow.

units.la: ver.8. Erudiam te & docebo te viam quam fis ingressurus: oculo meo tibi consulam.
units.tr: v. 8. I will instruct you and teach you the way you shall go; I will counsel you with my eye.

units.la: Postquam superiori precatiuncula docuit vates quanta animi fortitudine ac patientia res aduersas superare & quâta fiducia liberationem à Deo expectare debeamus, nunc ad peccatores sermone conuertit ut eos ad resipiscentiâ cohortetur. Hoc autem rectè cohæret cum eo quod paulo ante dicebat se futurum aliis pœnitentiæ exemplum, quemadmodum idem etiam profitetur. Pf.51. Docebo, inquit, peccatores vias tuas ut ad te convertantur. Nimirum hoc est certissimum veræ Dauidis pœnitentiæ argumen-tum, cum non tantum suæ resipiscentiæ, nō suę tantum salutis curâ habet, sed quantū in ipso est, aliorum etiam resipiscentia salutemq; procu-rat: vera siquidem pœnitentia non est otiosa neque sterilis, sed ubi semel in animis nostris est insita, tum se explicat & suos edit fructus ex quibus illa dignosci possit. Fructus autem pœ nitentiæ varij sunt atq; multiplices: producit enim dolore, suspiria, lacrymas, fletus, preces & peccati coram Deo confessionem. Atque illa quidem præclara: sed ubi ad homines ventum est, quandoquidem non tam perspicaces habemus oculos, ut ad interiores possint cogitationes penetrare, nihil est certe quod coram hominibus magis pœnitentia testetur, quam morum conversio & pristinæ vitæ in meliore mutatio.
units.tr: Having taught in the preceding little prayer with how much courage and patience we ought to overcome adversities, and with how much confidence we ought to expect deliverance from God, the prophet now turns his speech to sinners, to exhort them to repentance. This agrees well with what he said a little before, that he would be an example of repentance to others, as he also professes in the same way. Ps. 51: "I will teach transgressors your ways, that they may be converted to you." Certainly this is the surest proof of David's true repentance: that he cares not only for his own repentance and his own salvation, but, as far as lies in him, also procures the repentance and salvation of others. For true repentance is not idle or barren; once it has been planted in our minds, it unfolds and bears its fruits, by which it may be recognised. The fruits of repentance are various and manifold: for it produces grief, sighs, tears, weeping, prayers and the confession of sin before God. These are excellent, but when we come to men, since we do not have eyes so keen as to penetrate to inner thoughts, there is certainly nothing that repentance attests more before men than the conversion of manners and the change from the former life to a better one.

units.la: Quare nō sine causa Ioânes magnus ille præco pœnitentiæ in deserto exclamabat: ferte igitur fructum dignum iis qui resipuerint, quasi diceret, non satis est vos huc accedere vel ad audiendam doctrinam de pœnitentia vel etiam ad Baptismum ipsum suscipiendum: o-peræpretiū est veros fructus pœnitentiæ pro ferre.Etenim(ne longius ab illa præclara Io-annis cōcione discedamus)arborū similes su-mus.Omnis arbor non ferens fructū bonum exciditur,& in ignem abiicitur. Itaque nō sa-tis erit si sola folia producas, si vanam quan-dam refipiscentiæ speciem ostentes:fructus, fructus,inquâ,requirûtur.Cuius rei nō aliud de quâm à nostro vate petendum est exem-plum. Quantum enim dolorem ex admissis peccatis illum existimas persensisse? quot su-spiria ex intimo pe&ore duxisse? quot lacry-mas,fletus,preces coram Deo profudisse?Ve-runtamen ne illis quidem contentus, voluit suam refipiscetiam omnibus etiâ hominibus testatâ esse & in totius orbis terrarum ocu-lis quodámodo versari.Iam nos omnes com-pellat,nos admonet,nobis se duce,præuium, doctoremq; esse velle profitetur. Vos appel-lo, inquit, quotquot sub onere grauissimo peccatorû ingemiscitis, quotquot ad veram pœnitentiâ aspiratis:me,me pœnitete cospi-cite: vobis & doctrina & exeplo præluccebo: vobis rectam pœnitentiæ atque adeò verò sa-pientiæ viam comonstrabo.O præclarâ Da-uidis mutationem!qui antea peccati vinculis illigatus erat, nunc prodit liberatus à pecca-to,nunc ipsius peccati victor euadit:& quem hostem, fretus Dei misericordia, in se deui-cit,eúdem in aliis etiam profligare conatur.
units.tr: Therefore it was not without cause that John the great herald of repentance cried out in the wilderness: "Bring forth fruits worthy of those who repent." As if he were saying: it is not enough for you to come here, either to hear the doctrine of repentance or even to receive baptism itself; it is worth the effort to bring forth the true fruits of repentance. For (not to stray too far from that famous sermon of John) we are like trees. "Every tree that does not bring forth good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire." So it will not be enough if you produce only leaves, if you display some empty appearance of repentance: fruits, I say fruits, are required. For this matter we must seek no other example than from our prophet. For how great a grief do you think he felt for the sins he had committed? How many sighs did he draw from the depth of his heart? How many tears, weepings and prayers did he pour out before God? Yet he was not content even with these, but wished to show his repentance to all men also, and in some way to be set before the eyes of the whole world. Now he addresses us all, admonishes us, and professes that he wishes to be our leader, our forerunner and teacher. "I call you," he says, "all of you who groan under the heavy burden of sins, all of you who aspire to true repentance: look upon me, look upon me repenting. I will shine before you with both doctrine and example; I will show you the right way of repentance, and indeed of true wisdom." O remarkable change in David! He who before was bound by the chains of sin now comes forth freed from sin; now he becomes the conqueror of sin itself. And the enemy whom, relying on the mercy of God, he has subdued in himself, he also tries to overthrow in others.

units.la: .Quid nos autem, fratres? quàm obedientes, quàm attenti ad tam prǝclari ducis & doctoris vocē esse debemus? Ecce tibi rex summus atque potentissimus qui de throno illo regio descendit vt doctoris personam induat. Iam profecto cum Iustino Martyre cognoscimus quàm nō immerito Ethnicus ille optauerit, vt vel Philosophi reges essent, vel reges ipsi philosopharetur. Etenim ea demum est vera Philosophia quā noster hic vates profitetur. Audiamus igitur praestantissimū doctorem, & quēadmodum non verbo tātum, sed etiam exēplo docet: ita aequum est nō solum auribus doctrinā excipere, sed eā etiā obsignare ipsis vitae actionibus & morū integritate. Primum igitur discamus hunc esse verum poeni tentiae fructū, amare virtutē & peccatū odisse, neque id tantum in nobis, sed etiā in aliis, quod Dauidi nostro videmus vsuenisse. Cū enim alios docet & ad poenitetiam cohortatur, satis ostēdit se nō suae tantum, sed etiā alienę virtutis esse studiosum. Cōtrà verò qui vitiis sunt & carnis voluptatib dediti, nihil magis optāt quàm habere multos sibi similes, vt peccatorū foeditas peccantiū multitudine tegatur. Quò fit vt nō minus verè quā elegāter aliquando in haec verba exclamarit Augustinus: ô nimis inimica amicitiā, cùm dicitur, ea mus, faciamus & pudet non esse impudentē! Quod etiam Chrysostomus sentiebat cùm diceret inter eos qui insaniunt, insanum videri quisquis non insaniat. Ea nimirū est peccati lues, ut ab aliis ad alios quasi contagione celeriter manet atque diffudatur. Eo spectat quod ait, Solomo cum esse more peccatoribus, ut alios ad peccandi societate alliciant. Quanto igitur æquius est eum qui virtute colit, alios sanctis monitis in eandem mentem pertrahere, & quasi primus ex coeno surrexerit, sociis manum porrigere ut illi etiam emergāt? Adden-dum eodem est, nec poenitentia sine fide, nec rursus fidem sine charitate unquā esse posse. Ex quo efficitur ut cum poenitentia per fidem veras in animis radices egerit, tū charitas erga proximos eorumque salutis cura ac defi-deriū efflorescat. Hoc ergo praestemus neces-se est si Dauidis poenitentia volumus imitari.
units.tr: But what ought we, brethren, to do? How obedient and how attentive ought we to be to the voice of so distinguished a leader and teacher? Behold a king, most high and most powerful, who has come down from that royal throne to put on the character of a teacher. Now indeed we recognise with Justin Martyr how rightly that heathen man wished either that philosophers were kings or that kings would philosophise. For this is the true philosophy which our prophet here professes. Let us therefore listen to this most excellent teacher, and since he teaches not only by word but also by example, it is right that we should receive his teaching not only with our ears but also seal it in the actions of our lives and in the integrity of our conduct. First, then, let us learn that this is the true fruit of repentance: to love virtue and hate sin, and not only in ourselves but also in others, as we see our David did. For when he teaches others and exhorts them to repentance, he shows sufficiently that he is zealous not only for his own virtue but also for that of others. On the contrary, those who are given over to vices and to the pleasures of the flesh desire nothing more than to have many like themselves, so that the foulness of sins may be covered by the multitude of sinners. Hence Augustine exclaimed in these words, not less truly than elegantly: "O friendship most hostile, when one says, let us do it, let us act, and one is ashamed not to be shameless!" Chrysostom also thought this when he said that among those who are mad, whoever is not mad seems to be mad. Such indeed is the plague of sin: that it spreads quickly from one to another, as if by contagion, and is poured out. To this Solomon refers when he says that sinners are wont to entice others into the fellowship of sinning. How much more just, then, is it that he who cultivates virtue should draw others into the same mind by holy admonitions, and, as one who has first risen out of the mire, stretch out his hand to his companions so that they too may come up? It must be added to this that there can be neither repentance without faith, nor again faith without love. Hence, when repentance through faith has struck true roots in our minds, then love towards our neighbours and care and desire for their salvation blossom forth. Therefore we must do this if we wish to imitate David's repentance.

units.la: Iam propius attendamus ipsa Dauidis verba.
units.tr: Let us now attend more closely to David's own words.

units.la: Erudiam te, inquit. Non alienū erit fortase quærere, cur nō in hoc tantū loco, sed in aliis plerisque is sit Scripturæ usus, ut omnibꝰ verba faciens unū sæpissime copellare videa-tur. Nepe nos vult esse admonitos, siquidē in cohortationibus & reprehensionibus audien-dis proficere volumus, eas esse unicuique no-strū priuatim accommodandas. Ea.n.est natu-rae nostrae prauitas, ut quæ in genere dicūtur, si minus ea grata sunt, respuamus, nec ea nobis dicta esse existimemus. Dānentur vitia in Ecclesiastica cōcione, exagitetur ambitio, avaritia reprehēdatur: tū ambitiōsus aut avarꝰ hęc apud se: Nihil hoc ad me: telū istud aliū serit. rit. Ecce quo pacto sanctas obiurgationes quasi oppositio clypeo alio auertimus, ne in animos nostros possint penetrare. Te, te, inquam, ambitiose compello: teipsum moneo, te obiurgo, tibi Dei iudicium propono & ad summum eius tribunal te reum ago. Quamobrem in teipsum descende, mentem tuam introspice, excute omnes cogitationum latebras, explica vulnus illud tuum coram Dei maiestate, ora veniam, pete medicinam & ad spiritualem conscientiae valetudinem toto animo contende. Hic igitur est scopus ad quem spectat illud loquendi genus a Dauide & ab aliis sacris authoribus passim vsurpatum.
units.tr: "I will instruct you," he says. It may not be out of place to ask why Scripture so often speaks to one person, not only in this passage but in many others, when it seems to address everyone. Its purpose, I think, is to make us attentive. If we want to profit from exhortations and rebukes, they must be applied to each of us personally. For this is the perversity of our nature: if things are said in general and are not pleasing, we reject them and think they were not said to us. Vices are condemned in the sermon, ambition is attacked, avarice is rebuked, and the ambitious or greedy man says to himself: "This has nothing to do with me; that arrow is aimed at someone else." See how we turn aside holy rebukes, as if raising another shield, so that they cannot pierce our minds. You, you, I say, ambitious man, I address. I admonish you myself, I rebuke you, I set God's judgment before you and summon you as a defendant to his supreme tribunal. Therefore descend into yourself, look into your mind, search every hiding place of your thoughts, lay open that wound of yours before the majesty of God, beg pardon, seek the remedy, and strive with all your soul for the health of your conscience. This, then, is the aim toward which that manner of speaking, used by David and by other sacred writers everywhere, is directed.

units.la: Caeterum haec omnia egregie respondent inscriptioni huius Psalmi quemadmodum initio monuimus. Nec enim sine causa praefert nomen eruditionis, quum in hoc praesertim versu Dauid partes doctoris aperte suscipiat. Eo spectat verbum quo vtitur vates, quod significat intelligentem aliquem atque prudē-tē efficere eique praebere verae sapientiae cognitionem atque intelligentiam, qua de re quia iam aliquid diximus quum versaremur in epigraphes expositione, erimus hoc loco breviores. Tātum igitur hoc vnum dicemus, vniuersam mundi sapientiam damnari stultitiae, ne vana Philosophorum scripta nobis fucum faciant. Praeclare sane Paulus eos af-firmat cum se sapientes esse profiterentur, tum maxime stultos factos fuisse. Quid por-
units.tr: Moreover, all this agrees admirably with the title of this Psalm, as we noted at the beginning. It is not without reason that it bears the name of instruction, since in this verse especially David openly takes on the role of teacher. The verb the prophet uses points to this aim: it means to make someone intelligent and prudent, and to give him the knowledge and understanding of true wisdom. Since we have already said something about this when we dealt with the inscription, we will be briefer here. So we will say only this one thing: all the wisdom of the world is condemned as foolishness, lest the vain writings of the philosophers deceive us. Paul rightly asserts that when they professed to be wise, they became all the more foolish. Furthermore, what shall we say of the Scholastic and Papist teachers?

units.la: h.j. rò de Scholásticis ac Pontificiis doctoribus dicemus? eósne etiam stultitiæ insimulare au-debimus, qui sapientes, qui doctores ac soli Ecclesiæ magistri haberi volunt? Nempe nos homunciones magni illi viri cótracto supercilio, e summis suis cathedris despicient. Quare prodeat in medium Dauid præstantissimus ille Ecclesiæ doctor, ut eorum fastum & arrogantia retundat, eorúmq; coarguat ignorantiam quæ quidem eo maior est quòd eam non intelligat: adeóque bis sunt ignari qui nesciant se nescire. Cùm enim doctrinam de gratuita peccatorum remissione sapientiam atque intelligentiam vocet, cedò, quo nomine eos appellabit qui peccata non gratuito remittenda, sed humanis meritis & satisfactionibus expianda esse tradiderunt? Quare faccessat vana illa Pontificiorum doctorum ignorantia, ac potius amplectamur summam hac scientiam quā vates vel potius sacer Dei spiritus nobis proponit: Erudiam te, inquit, intelligentem te præstabo, docebo te viam quam sis ingressurus.
units.tr: Shall we dare to charge with foolishness even those who wish to be regarded as wise, as teachers, and as the only masters of the Church? Those great men will surely look down on us poor mortals from their lofty chairs with knitted brows. Therefore let David, that most excellent teacher of the Church, come forward to break their pride and arrogance, and to convict their ignorance, which is all the greater because they do not recognise it. Doubly ignorant are those who do not know that they do not know. For since he calls the doctrine of the free forgiveness of sins wisdom and understanding, tell me, by what name will he call those who have taught that sins are not forgiven freely, but must be expiated by human merits and satisfactions? Therefore let that vain ignorance of the Papist teachers depart, and let us rather embrace the supreme knowledge which the prophet, or rather the holy Spirit of God, sets before us: "I will instruct you," he says, "I will make you understand, I will teach you the way you are to go."

units.la: An etiam aliquid respondendum est ad improborum hominum conuitia quibus pio-rum simplicitatem & patientiam exagitant?ô vos, inquiunt, omnium stultissimos, qui reli-re & patria, spretis facultatibus & commodis, obliti cognatorum atque affinium & ad ex-teros longe profugientes infinita vitæ incom-moda perfertis! Imo potius, ô admirandam & mundo plane incognitam Dei sapietiam, quæ nostris mentibus lumen prætulit in tam crassis tenebris & in tanta hominum cæcita-te! Atenim,inquiunt,nónne summe est stul-titiæ ea tátùm videre quæ ante pedes sunt,ne què consulere in lōgitudinem?Cur ergo non ea quæ futura sunt prospicitis? cur si non de vobis,at salte de vestris liberis cogitatis? Ad quod ita paucis responsum esse volumus:Si si pietes eos esse existimát,qui longè in posterū prospiciunt,ad nos potius quā ad ipsos nomē sapientæ pertinere. Quid ita?nempe quia res illi præsentes,nos futuras intuemur.Nam qui mundum, qui terram, qui solam hāc præsen-tem vitam ante oculos habent,cosne [?] censeas ea prospicere quæ futura sunt? Quibus verò futura vita æternáque fœlicitas atque etiam ipsa æternitas ante oculos obuersatur, illos, illos,inquam rebus futuris,intetos esse meri-tó dixeris. Scitè proculdubió Chrysostomus eos qui mundi cupiditatibus implicantur,di-cebat puerorū esse similes, qui nucibus adeò detinétur,vt eas vel amplissimæ hæreditati li-bèter anteponant.Similiter ij quos Scriptura filios huius seculi appellat terrenis adeò nugis ac rebus caducis & momētaneis addicti sunt vt præ illis futuram hæreditatem rerúmq; cœlestium æternam fœlicitatem despiciant.
units.tr: Must we also reply to the insults of wicked men, by which they harass the simplicity and patience of the godly? "Oh, you most foolish of all," they say, "who, leaving home and country, scorning wealth and comforts, forgetting kinsmen and relatives, flee far away to strangers and endure endless hardships of life!" Nay rather, O wonderful wisdom of God, wholly unknown to the world, which has brought light to our minds in such thick darkness and such blindness of men! "But," they say, "is it not supremely foolish to see only what lies at your feet, and not to look far ahead? Why then do you not foresee what is to come? Why, if not for yourselves, at least do you not think of your children?" To this we answer briefly: if those are to be thought wise who look far ahead into the future, the name of wisdom belongs to us rather than to them. Why so? Because they have present things before their eyes, while we look to the future. For those who have before their eyes only the world, the earth and this present life alone, do you think they foresee what is to come? But those to whom future life, eternal happiness, and eternity itself are set before the eyes, these, I say, you would rightly call strangers to the things to come. Chrysostom wisely said that those entangled in worldly desires are like children, who are so taken with nuts that they would rather have them than a very large inheritance. Similarly, those whom Scripture calls sons of this age are so given over to earthly trifles and fleeting, transitory things that, for their sake, they despise the future inheritance and the eternal happiness of heavenly things.

units.la: Porrò hic locus egregiè cófirmat quod ait Paulus,Scriptura esse vtile ad doctrinā,redar-gutione & correctione. Nā & docet Dauid & redarguit & corrigit atq; cohortatur quèadmodum paulo post videbimus. Ex quo efficitur attentum ac docile animum a nobis praebendum, esse. Cum enim doctor & discipulus sibi mutuo referantur, necesse est, vbi extant doctores, ibi quoq; discipulos reperiri. Quare dada nobis est opera ne ad tanti doctoris vocem obdurescamus. Enimvero qui tot errores quibus abundat Ecclesia Romana ab ipso capite velit arcessere, reperiet profecto eos omnes manare ex hoc fonte, quod homines non se Scripturae discipulos, sed magistros: non se Scri-pturae subiectos, sed sibi Scripturam esse subiectam existimarint. Capitalis opinio, quae veram religionem commentis hominum atque horrenda idololatria videtur propemodum obruisse. Docebo te, inquit Dauid:ergo nostrae partes sunt audire, discere, obedire. Atque vt id magis dicas, considera quoties hic noster se discipulum attentum atque docilem praestiterit, cum saepe a Domino precatus est vt ab ipsius Spiritu doceretur. Itaque si vel ipse Dauid tam praeclare in rerum diuinarum cognitione versatus, nihilominus optabat a Deo doceri, quid nobis, obsecro, faciendum esse censemus? nobis, inquam, rudibus &, vt plurimum, ignaris earum rerum quibus salus nostra continetur? Audiamus igitur dulcissi-mam hanc Dauidis vocem: Docebo te. Quot olim Philosophi, quot sectatores humana-rum disciplinarum extitere, qui vt aliquid ad-discerent, traiecerunt maria, terrasque longinquas ac remotissimas summo labore pera grarunt? Nimirum illis discere nō labor erat, sed voluptas. Atqui omnes artes omnésque rerum humanarum scientiæ, si cum hac spirituali scientia conferatur, ne minimi quidem momenti instar obtinebunt. Ergo nos pudeat tam præclaram atque in primis necessariam scietiam nobis quotidie propositam & oblatam atque in mediis nostris vrbibus assiduè resonante, negligere. Quin potius Dauidi adeóque Dei Spiritui nos quotidie compellanti, respondeamus. Docebo te, inquit: Nos autem : discemus à te ô Domine : tuam vocem reuerenter audiemus, excipiemus, am plectemur : tua nos doctrina attentos & dociles tenebit. Hæc igitur nobis præstâda sunt si ita vt decet nobis hæc Dauidis verba sumus accommodaturi.
units.tr: Furthermore, this passage admirably confirms what Paul says, that Scripture is profitable for teaching, for reproof, and for correction. For David both teaches, reproves, corrects and exhorts, as we shall see shortly. From this it follows that we must bring an attentive and teachable mind. For since teacher and disciple are mutually related, wherever teachers are found, disciples must also be found. Therefore we must take care not to harden ourselves against the voice of so great a teacher. Indeed, whoever wishes to trace back to its head the many errors with which the Roman Church abounds will certainly find that they all flow from this source: men have thought of themselves not as disciples of Scripture but as its masters, not as subject to Scripture but as having Scripture subject to them. This is the chief opinion, which seems to have almost overwhelmed the true religion with the inventions of men and with horrible idolatry. "I will teach you," says David; our part, therefore, is to listen, to learn, and to obey. So that you may say this more fully, consider how often this man of ours showed himself an attentive and teachable disciple, since he often prayed the Lord to be taught by his Spirit. If David himself, so accomplished in the knowledge of divine things, nevertheless desired to be taught by God, what, I beg you, do we think must be done by us, who are unskilled and, for the most part, ignorant of those things on which our salvation rests? Let us therefore hear this most sweet voice of David: "I will teach you." How many philosophers of old, how many followers of human disciplines, have crossed seas and traversed distant and remote lands with the greatest toil to learn something? Clearly for them learning was not labour but pleasure. Yet all the arts and all the sciences of human affairs, compared with this spiritual science, will hold scarcely the least importance. Therefore let us be ashamed to neglect so excellent and so necessary a knowledge, which is set before us and offered to us every day and sounds constantly in the midst of our cities. Rather let us answer David, and so the Spirit of God, who addresses us every day. "I will teach you," he says. And we reply: "We will learn from you, O Lord; we will hear your voice reverently, receive it and embrace it; let your teaching keep us attentive and teachable." These things, then, must be done by us, if we are rightly to apply these words of David.

units.la: Iam quod addit non leuiter prætereun-dum est. Viam, inquit, tibi commostrabo & oculo meo te dirigam. Quæ per similitudinem dicta sunt. Quemadmodum enim qui viam aliquam incognitam atque difficilem ingrediuntur, opus habét duce ac præmonstrato-re, alioquin facilè à via aberraturi: ita nobis in hoc vitæ curriculo duce & moderatore opus est, vt rectà ad salutem nobis propositam ten dere possimus. Quem autem, cedò, potius quàm Dauidem nobis ad hac rem eligamus? ille peritus est, ille longo rerum vsu atque experientia exactè didicit quæ possit alios fideliter docere. Multi sunt huius viæ anfractus, multa diuerticula, quæ qui ignorabit, ille sanè tanquā per flexuosi cuiusdam labyrinthi errores inextrincabiles miser incertúsque vagabitur. Sed ne nos viæ difficultas deterreat, Dauid se ducem nobis fore profitetur. Quis autem vel fidelior desideret, vel peritior? Ille varias afflictiones multósque aduersariorum impetus, tanquā salebrosa loca, summa & ad mirabili Dei virtute superauit: ille salutis ac liberationis vias sæpe ab hostibus interclusas sanctissimis precibus aperuit: ille obiecta ab Satana carne & mundo scandala perspicacissima Dei prouidetia declinauit. Quod si in rebus lætis ac prosperis, tanquā in loco lubrico aliquando titubauit, statim erectus à Dei manu in viam rediit atque etiam (dictu mirabile) ex peccatis præteritis fortior, & ex ipsa infirmitate firmior effectus, totum vitæ præsentis spacium fœliciter peregit. Itaque merito potest & suo iure ita unumquęque nostrum alloqui, Viam tibi commonstrabo & oculo meo te dirigam. Si te, inquit, vexant hominum calumniæ, si hostium furores, si gladij, si flammæ te insectantur, si profugus ex patria per montes, per specus, per inculta desertaque loca longe vagaris, si ad Deum cum precibus ac lacrymis accessurus, si peccatorum veniam deprecaturus es: ipse tibi viam commonstrabo: illac mihi fuit sæpe transeundum: expertus te docebo. Sic igitur Dauid nobiscum agere videtur, adeo ut saluti nostrę pessime simus consulturi, nisi nobis hunc tam præclarum ac fidelem ducem sumpserimus. Multifariam enim hac in re peccari passim ab homi-nibus video. Alij enim vana sui consilij fi-ducia decepti, nec se à quopiam doceri, nec sibi viam commonstrari libenter ferunt. A-lij vero sibi duces assumunt quos sequantur, sed in illis eligendis graviter errant. Ita fit ut respuunt dum cæci(quemadmodum Christus ait)à cæ-cis ducuntur, ambo non tantum à recta via aberrent, sed etiam in foveam simul cadant.
units.tr: What he adds must not be passed over lightly: "I will show you the way," he says, "and I will guide you with my eye." These things are said by way of comparison. Just as those who enter an unknown and difficult road need a guide and one to point out the way, otherwise they will easily stray from it, so in this course of life we need a leader and governor, so that we may make straight for the salvation set before us. And whom, I ask, should we rather choose for this task than David? He is skilled; through long use and experience he has learned exactly how to teach others faithfully. This road has many twists and many byways, and whoever does not know them will wander wretched and uncertain, as through the inextricable errors of some winding labyrinth. But lest the difficulty of the road deter us, David promises to be our guide. Who could desire a more faithful or more skilful one? He overcame various afflictions and the many assaults of adversaries, like rough places, by the highest and most wonderful power of God; he often opened, by most holy prayers, the ways of salvation and deliverance that enemies had blocked; by God's most keen-sighted providence he avoided the stumbling-blocks that Satan, the flesh and the world put in his path. And if at times in happy and prosperous circumstances, as on a slippery place, he stumbled, he was at once raised by the hand of God and returned to the way; and (wonderful to tell) becoming stronger from past sins and firmer from weakness itself, he happily spent the whole span of his present life. And so he can rightly and with good reason address each of us in this way: "I will show you the way and guide you with my eye." "If," he says, "the calumnies of men vex you, if the fury of enemies, if swords and flames pursue you, if, a fugitive from your country, you wander far through mountains, caves, and wild and desert places, if you are about to come before God with prayers and tears, if you are about to beg pardon for your sins: I myself will show you the way; I have often had to pass that way, and having experienced it, I will teach you." Thus David seems to deal with us, so that we would be very poor counsellors of our own salvation unless we took up this so excellent and faithful guide. For I see that men err in many ways in this matter. Some, deceived by the vain confidence in their own counsel, bear neither to be taught by anyone nor willingly to be shown the way. Others indeed take to themselves guides whom they follow, but err grievously in choosing them. So it happens that, as Christ says, while the blind are led by the blind, both fall not only out of the right way but also into the pit together.

units.la: Hinc idolorum cultus, hinc vanæ ceremo-niæ, hinc denique profusa ad peccandum licentia, quòd homines spreta ac relicta divini verbi, ut ita dicam, Cynosura, eò se temere proripiunt quò à sua libine tanquam aliqua tempestate deferuntur. Quamobrem demus operam ut nostræ ignorantiæ atque infirmitatis conscij, nos ad Dauidis & cæterorum tum Prophetarum tum Apostolorum ductum applicemus, ne à Christo (quæ una est ad salutem via) unquam, ne tantillum quidem, discedamus.
units.tr: Hence come the worship of idols, empty ceremonies, and finally a loose licence to sin, because people, having despised and abandoned the divine Word, which is, so to speak, their Cynosure, rush headlong wherever their own desires carry them, like a boat driven by some storm. Let us therefore take care, aware of our own ignorance and weakness, to submit ourselves to the guidance of David and of the other Prophets and Apostles, so that we never, not even by a little, depart from Christ, who is the only way to salvation.

units.la: Non enim frustra vates meminit sui oculi: Te, inquit, oculo diri-gam: sed ut melius intelligamus opus hic esse summo labore ac diligentia. Nam cum necesse sit ei qui nobis viam præmonstraturus est, acerrimis oculis omnia lustrare, omnia intueri, atque in nobis perpetuo defixos oculos tenere, ut nusquam incurrere atque offendere possimus: quàm, cedò, intentos ipsi oculos habere debemus? Quanta à nobis & pro nobis adhibenda est diligentia? Certè cùm ita Dauid locutus est, aperte docuit nos in ea esse via in qua facile sit & labi & errare, vt ita nos redderet cautiores.
units.tr: The prophet does well to mention his eye: "I will guide you with my eye," he says. But this is so that we may understand better that great labour and diligence are needed here. For he who is going to show us the way must of necessity scan everything with the keenest eyes, look at everything, and keep his eyes fixed constantly upon us, so that we never stumble or go astray. How intently, then, ought we ourselves to keep our own eyes fixed? What care should we bring to bear, and for our own sake? Certainly, when David spoke in this way, he plainly taught us that we are on a road where it is easy both to slip and to wander, and he meant to make us more cautious.

units.la: Quinetiam ipsa Dauidis persona consideranda est. Cùm enim esset Propheta & doctor Ecclesiae, praeclarè officio fungitur dum oculos in vnumquemque coniicit, vt nos omnes dirigat ad ingrediendam virtutis viam.
units.tr: Moreover, the very person of David must be considered. For since he was a Prophet and a teacher of the Church, he discharges his office admirably when he fixes his eyes upon each one of us, so as to direct us all into the path of virtue.

units.la: Debemus quidem alij alios (id praecipiente Apostolo) admonere, reprehendere, hortari: sed quos Dominus instituit in Ecclesia vt caeteris praesint & eos ex Dei verbo doceant, atque moneant, illis profecto peculiaris haec cura & officium incumbit. Quocirca debent Ecclesiae Pastores ac Ministri saepe ante oculos habere hanc Pauli ad Ephesios Presbyteros adhortationem: Attendite, inquit, vos ipsos atque totum gregem in quo vos Spiritus sanctus constituit Episcopos. Quibus verbis significat Pastorum Ecclesiae hoc esse proprium, vt non suae tantùm, sed aliorum etiam salutis curam habeant. Huc pertinet nomen Speculatoris inditum Praefectis Ecclesiasticis, vt videre licet apud Prophetam cum hac gravi comminatione: Te, inquit Dominus, speculatorem constitui domui Israelis: audies igitur verbum ex ore meo & diserte monebis eos meo nomine. Cùm dixero impio, morieris:nec tu eum monueris,nec fueris dehorta-tus impium à via sua :peribit is quidem in sua iniquitate , sed sanguinem eius de manu tua requiram:hæc ille, quæ vtinam Ecclesiæ mi-niftri attentè audiant & ferio apud fe expen-dant:ne vel ignauia sponte torpeant, vel eo-rum diligentia langueat ingratitudine popu li aut etiã tarditate:vtinam,inquam, audiant ex Iuftino martyre negligentes non esse ne-gligendos. Nec vero vllo modo ferendi sunt quibus moleftũ est à suis Pastoribus admone ri.Præducet,inquiũt,ministri & pro cocione quantũ videbitur,vitia insectetur:me autè vt etiã moneat? me reprehedat?me iudicio Dei & eius minis propositis deterreat? coftet vni cuique fui facti ratio, nec de singulorum mo ribus Pastores inquirant. Nolo meam vitam discutiant,nolo me defixis assiduè oculis per petuò intueantur? Itáne tandem? Ergóne iubes speculatorem otiosum & clausis ocu-lis stertere? Quid quod Pastores Ecclesiæ Ἐπίσκοποι ab inspiciendo & obseruando no minantur? Cur etiam Apostolus commemo-rat fe non tantum publice, verumetiam per singulas domos Ephesios docuisse & per to-tum triennium nocte & die cum lacrymis vnumquemque monuisse? Num porrò extra officij fui fines egressus est, cum vnumquèq; Thessalonicensium, tanquam pater liberos hortatus est atque consolatus?Ecclesiæ mini-ftros cum medicis Paulus comparabat : quis autem adeo demens fuerit vt existimet hoc demum esse medici fidelis officium: de variis morborum generibus publicè & è suggesto copiose disserere, priuatorum autem morbos negligere nec vnicuique morbo conueniens ac necessarium remedium adhibere. Petrus Ecclesiæ Ministros, Pastores, nec immeritò, appellauit: Num verò bonum Pastorē & eo dignum nomine illum censeas, qui gregis vniuersi ita curā habeat vt de singulis ouibus & de vnaquaque nō sit solicitus? quid si vna aut altera relicto grege aberrarit? nēpe si tibi credat, eius obliuiscetur, eam perire sinet: Sed si Christum audiat, ad illā perget, vsque dum eā inueniat, & inuētā imponet in humeros suos gaudens. Queadmodū etiā cūm de veri Pastoris officio disserit, ait oues ab eo nominatim vocari. Ac ne lōgè à Pastoris similitudine recedamus: quis non cōmoueatur hac Domini per Ezechielē facta increpatione? Vę, inquit, Pastoribus Israëlis. Quãobrē obsecrō? Debilē oue, inquit, non cōfirmastis: ægrotā non sanastis: cōfractā non obligastis, propulsam nō reduxistis: perditam non quæsiuistis. Quibus verbis reshēc tota quā tractamus apertissimè definitur. Quorsum enim & numero singulari & varia illa distributione vsus est, si Præfectorū Ecclesiæ munus sola concione publica cōtinetur? Facessant igitur vana illa subterfugia & pareamus Apostolo præcipieti vt ser-monem exhortationis susferamus. Ne simus illorū similes qui Prophetis dicebant: Ne vi-deatis,ne cōtemplemini, Nec nos socios ad-iungamus ciuibus Anathoth interdicentibus Ieremiæ nc in nomine Domini prophetaret. Sētiamus potí spirituales morbos animi & à Basilio discamus obiurgationē esse animę curatione. Agnoscamus tot errores quibus in hoc vitæ curriculo sumus obnoxij, & postule mus, nedum recusemus. Pastorum nostro-rum oculis dirigi atque gubernari vt verbo Dei duce ac præuio rectam salutis viam con stanter persequamur, donec tandem ad fœ-licitatis metam nobis propositam peruenire valeamus. Sed iam redeundum est ad Da-uidem.
units.tr: Indeed, we ought to admonish, reprove and exhort one another, as the Apostle commands; but those whom the Lord has appointed in the Church to preside over the rest and to teach and admonish them from the Word of God, upon them this special care and duty certainly rests. Therefore the pastors and ministers of the Church ought often to keep before their eyes that exhortation of Paul to the elders of Ephesus: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers." By these words he signifies that it is the proper task of the Church's ministers to care not only for their own salvation but also for that of others. To this belongs the name of "watchman" given to the church rulers, as may be seen in the Prophet, with this grave warning: "I have appointed you, says the Lord, a watchman to the house of Israel; you shall therefore hear the word from my mouth and warn them faithfully in my name. When I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you do not warn him, nor speak to dissuade the wicked from his way, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand." These are his words. Would that the ministers of the Church would listen to them attentively and weigh them seriously in their minds, so that neither idleness makes them sluggish of their own accord, nor their diligence grows weak through the ingratitude or even the sluggishness of the people. Would that, I say, they would take to heart what Justin Martyr says, that negligent ones are not to be neglected. Nor indeed are those to be tolerated in any way who are annoyed to be admonished by their own ministers. "Let the minister," they say, "preach against vices from the pulpit as much as he likes; but that he should also admonish me personally, reprove me, frighten me from my sins with the judgment of God and its threats? Let each one give an account of his own deeds, and let the ministers not inquire into the morals of individuals. I do not want them to examine my life, I do not want them to keep their eyes constantly fixed upon me." Is that really so? Do you therefore command the watchman to be idle and to snore with his eyes shut? What of the fact that the ministers of the Church are called bishops [Episkopoi], from inspecting and observing? Why does the Apostle also record that he taught the Ephesians not only publicly but from house to house, and for three years night and day admonished each one of them with tears? Did he, moreover, go beyond the limits of his office when, like a father with his children, he exhorted and comforted each one of the Thessalonians? Paul compared the ministers of the Church with physicians. Yet who would be so foolish as to think that this is the whole duty of a faithful physician: to discourse at length, from the platform and in public, on the various kinds of diseases, while neglecting the illnesses of private individuals and not applying to each disease the fitting and necessary remedy? Peter called the ministers of the Church shepherds, and not without reason. But would you consider him a good shepherd, and worthy of that name, who takes such care of the whole flock that he is not anxious about each single sheep, or about any one of them? What if one or another has strayed from the flock? Surely, if it trusts you, you will forget it and let it perish. But if it listens to Christ, he will go after it until he finds it, and when he has found it, he will lay it joyfully on his shoulders. In the same way, when he discourses about the office of the true shepherd, he says that the sheep are called by him by name. And that we may not stray far from the image of the shepherd: who is not moved by the reproof the Lord gave through Ezekiel? "Woe," he says, "to the shepherds of Israel." Why, I ask? "You have not strengthened the weak sheep," he says, "you have not healed the sick, you have not bound up the broken, you have not brought back the driven away, you have not sought the lost." By these words the whole matter we are now treating is most plainly defined. For why would he have used the singular number and that varied enumeration, if the office of the rulers of the Church were confined to public preaching alone? Away then with those empty excuses, and let us obey the Apostle, who bids us to endure the word of exhortation. Let us not be like those who said to the prophets, "Do not see, do not look," nor let us join the citizens of Anathoth, who forbade Jeremiah to prophesy in the name of the Lord. Let us rather feel our spiritual diseases of the soul, and learn from Basil that rebuke is a cure of the soul. Let us acknowledge the many errors to which we are liable in the course of this life, and let us ask for, and not refuse, to be guided and governed by the eyes of our ministers, so that, with the Word of God as our leader and guide, we may steadily pursue the right path of salvation until at last we are able to reach the goal of happiness set before us. But now we must return to David.

units.la: vers.9. Nesitis sicut equus & mulus.
units.tr: Verse 9: "Be not like the horse and the mule."

units.la: Psalmum concludit excellentissima cohor tatione ad pœnitentiam (quæ est huius Psal-mi postrema pars.) Quia vero nihil tam con trarium est veræ pœnitentiæ quàm obdure-scere in peccatis, idcirco nos reuocat ab o-mni peruicacia & obstinatione. Atque vt id præstet facilius, petit à brutis animanti-bus similitudinem, à quibus quàm maxi-me nobis abhorrendum esse vel ab ipsa na-tura didicimus. Ergo, inquit, si vobis viam ad pœnitentiam munitam esse vultis, in pri-mis cauete ne nimia peccandi consuetu-do iam callum animis vestris obducat, a-lioquin brutorum potius estis quàm homi-num similes futuri. Annon videtis equos & mulos nunc frenis ac loris coercendos, nunc calcaribus vrgedos esse? At illi qui præ fracto atque pertinaci animo & quasi frenū mordentes in peccatis se obfirmarunt, viden tur hominem quodammodo ex homine su- stulisse, & esse non tantum brutis similes, verumetiam multò stupidiores.Hæc est sen- tentia huius loci: vnde nobis colligendum est quàm sit perniciosa obstinatio, quámque saluti nostræ inimica. Peruicaces autem & obstinatos eos appellamus, non qui ab infir- mitate carnis superati in peccatum aliquod prolapsi sunt, sed qui sibi placent in peccatis in iisque toti volutantur, quos non pudor, non metus, non obiurgatio, non ipsæ denique Dei comminationes, ipsa Dei iudicia possunt à peccando reuocare. Itaque cum Dauid Psalmo primo varios peccantium gra dus nobis proponit, eos recensèt qui sedent cum irrisoribus: nec dubium est quin eo no- mine illos significet qui ludibrio habet quas- uis admonitiones & iam longa peccandi co- suetudine obduruerunt. Iis autem postremum gradū tanquā desperatis hominibus assigna- uit. Eò refereda est ea similitudo quam sæpe veteres vsurparunt dum peccatū dixerūt esse leprę similimum. Nec enim tantum lögę ser pit peccati contagio (nisi mature occurratur) sed etiā vbi semel totū homine infecerit atq; corruperit, eum reddit adeo stupidū, adeo in duratum, vt sensum propemodum ipsum a- mißse misisse videatur. Cùm autem sacra historia causas commemorat quibus Dominus addu-ctus est vt Iudeos miserit sub iugum Babylo-nicum, meminit nominatim illorum peruica ciæ & obstinationis, dum quasuis admonitio-nes obiurgationesque, ipsos etiā Prophetas Dei nuntios præfractè despiceret. Quàm au-tè grauis est ista Ieremiæ obiurgatio qua in Iudæos obstinatos inuehitur? Percussisti,in-quit,eos,ô Domine,neque tamen propterea doluerunt: consumpsisti eos, sed noluerunt recipere disciplinā: indurauerunt vultus suos magis, quàm saxum, reuertíque noluerunt.
units.tr: The Psalm concludes with a most excellent exhortation to repentance, which is the last part of this Psalm. But since nothing is so contrary to true repentance as to grow hard in sins, he therefore calls us back from all obstinacy and stubbornness. And so that he may accomplish this more easily, he draws a comparison from brute animals, from which we have learned, even from nature itself, that we must shrink as far as possible. "Therefore," he says, "if you wish the way to repentance to be open to you, above all take care that the excessive habit of sinning does not now harden your minds with a callus; otherwise you will become more like brute beasts than like men. Do you not see that horses and mules must now be restrained with bridles and reins, and now be urged on with spurs? But those who, with a stiff and stubborn spirit, biting the bit as it were, have made themselves hardened in sin, seem in some measure to have put off the man, and to be not only like beasts but far more stupid." This is the meaning of this passage. From it we must gather how deadly obstinacy is, and how hostile to our salvation. We call those stubborn and obstinate not those who, overcome by the weakness of the flesh, have fallen into some sin, but those who take pleasure in sins and wallow wholly in them, whom neither shame, nor fear, nor rebuke, nor even the threats of God and the very judgments of God can call back from sinning. Thus when David in Psalm 1 sets before us the various degrees of sinners, he lists those who sit with the scornful; and there is no doubt that by this he means those who make a mockery of any admonitions and have grown hard through a long habit of sinning. To these he assigns the last degree, as to men already despaired of. To this belongs the comparison that the ancients often used when they called sin most like leprosy. For the contagion of sin not only creeps on slowly (unless it is met in time), but once it has infected and corrupted the whole man, it makes him so dull, so hardened, that he seems almost to have lost sense altogether. Moreover, when sacred history recounts the causes for which the Lord was led to send the Jews under the Babylonian yoke, it mentions by name their stubbornness and obstinacy, since they stubbornly despised all admonitions and rebukes, and even the Prophets of God, His messengers. How grave is that reproof of Jeremiah by which he inveighs against the obstinate Jews? "You have struck them, O Lord," he says, "yet they did not grieve; you have consumed them, but they refused to receive correction. They have made their faces harder than stone, and they refused to return."

units.la: Hæc ille:quæ si olim Iudeos ipsos prope trun-cis ftupidiores non mouerunt, saltem nos hodie moueant, ne illorum obstinationis sic cij in eadem etiam poenas incurramus. Quid ergo? Nempe ita statuendum est, nihil syn-cera admonitione melius, nihil obiurgatio-ne fideli vtilius esse posse. Sic enim Solo-mo: Qui aduersus increpationem, inquit, ceruices indurauit, subito conteretur: qui-bus verbis eleganter ad hanc Dauidis simili- tudinem videtur allusisse. Quinetiam ille ipse alio in loco,Increpatio,inquit,sapientis,auri obtemperati est veluti inauris ex auro facta. (Quibus inauribꝰ vtinā delectetur tū viri tū fœminæ, quos omnes video tatopere nimio ac vano cultui esse adeò deditos, vt nullæ hactenus cùm publicæ tum priuatæ admoni-tiones hunc morbū in dies ingrauescentem vel sanare potuerint vel coercere.)Ne autem obiurgationes parui faciamus, nobis propo- nendum est exemplum Dauidis, qui alicubi profitetur sibi gratissimas, nedum molestas fore piorum obiurgationes, eaque se perinde habiturū ac si ipsius caput vnguento suauissimo perfunderent. Quamobrem demus locum admonitionibus, iis praesertim quæ toties ab Ecclesiasticis Pastoribus inculcantur. Parcamus Dei verbo nobis toties proposito: obstinationem a nobis procul arceamus, & semper habeamus in memoria quod a veteribus dictū est: Peccare humanū esse, obstina-te peccare diabolicum. Audiamus excellentem illam vatis cohortationem ad Iudæos: Hodie, inquit, si vocem Domini audieritis, ne obdurate corda vestra. Quæ verba si Apostolus ad sua tempora accommodauit, idem etiam nos hodie nostro iure facere possumus. Ergo fratres, si vocem Dei jam tot annos in auribus vestris resonatē audiuistis, ne obdurate corda vestra. Si vos Dominus hoc tanto præ multis aliis honore dignatus est, ut apud Ecclesiæ suæ domicilium collocarit, ut pater-no fauore semper complexus sit, ut vos quasi passis alis fouerit atque protexerit, a vobis pericula, cædes, hostilesque impetus auerterit, vobis hactenus tranquillissima pace frui concesserit, vos denique omni bonorum genere cumularit: Ne, inquam, obdurate corda vestra: ne ad clementissimi Patris vocem obsurdescite : ne eius liberalitatem contemnite: ne committite vt vestris istis thesauris quos nec hostium potentia, nec conatus vllus eripere potuit, vestra vos ingratitudo spoliasse videatur.Sed vlterius etiam progrediendum est. Deus enim loquitur multis modis: loquitur verbi sui praedicatione: loquitur interiori voce sui Spiritus: loquitur suis etiam iudiciis, hac praesertim aetate, si vnquam alias. Et vero, quidni ita loquatur? quum enim dulcem ac paternam eius vocem audire neglexerimus, quid mirum si ter-ribilem iudiciorum vocem & audire cogi-mur & sentire? Hinc pestis vrget, hinc fa-mes & annonae caritas, hinc hostiles im-proborum minae solicitant: Quid dicam de ipsis anni temporibus adeo intempestiuis, vt aestas in hyemem propemodum videatur esse commutata? Ergo coelum ipsum & ter-ra, ipsaeque res omnes creatae vocem quodammodo mittere videntur & Deum nostris peccatis iratum denuntiare. Itaque si tot voces audierimus, ne obduremus cor-da nostra, ne simus sicut equus & mulus (vt ait noster vates) ne obstinate peccatis adhaerescamus, sed vera poenitentia ad Dei mi-sericordiam recurramus, ab eoque peccato-rum veniam deprecemur.
units.tr: These are his words. If they did not move the Jews, who were more stupid than stumps, let them at least move us today, lest by the same obstinacy we incur the same punishments. What then? We must hold that nothing is better than sincere admonition and nothing more useful than faithful rebuke. So Solomon says: "He who hardens his neck against rebuke will suddenly be broken," words in which he seems to have elegantly alluded to this likeness of David. Indeed, in another place he says: "The rebuke of a wise man, heard by an obedient ear, is like an earring of gold." (Would that men and women alike took pleasure in such earrings. I see that all of them are so given over to excessive and empty adornment that hitherto neither public nor private admonitions have been able either to heal or to restrain this disease, which grows worse every day.) Lest we make little of rebukes, we must set before ourselves the example of David, who somewhere declares that the rebukes of the godly are not only most pleasing to him but even unpleasant, and that he would receive them as if they were poured on his head as the sweetest ointment. Let us therefore give room to admonitions, especially those which ministers of the Church press so often. Let us spare the Word of God, so often set before us. Let us keep obstinacy far from us, and always bear in mind what the ancients said: "To sin is human; to persist in sin is devilish." Let us hear that excellent exhortation of the psalmist to the Jews: "Today, if you hear the voice of the Lord, do not harden your hearts." If the Apostle applied these words to his own time, we too may rightly do the same today. Therefore, brothers, if for so many years you have heard the voice of God resounding in your ears, do not harden your hearts. If the Lord has deigned to honour you with this distinction above many others, that he has placed you in the dwelling of his Church, has always embraced you with fatherly favour, has cherished and sheltered you as if with outspread wings, has turned away from you dangers, slaughter and hostile attacks, has allowed you to enjoy the most peaceful tranquillity until now, and has finally heaped upon you every kind of good, then, I say, do not harden your hearts. Do not grow deaf to the voice of the most merciful Father. Do not despise his generosity. Do not let your own ingratitude seem to have robbed you of those treasures which neither the power of enemies nor any attempt could snatch from you. But we must go further still. For God speaks in many ways: he speaks through the preaching of his Word, he speaks by the inner voice of his Spirit, and he speaks by his judgments, especially in this age, if ever in any. And indeed, why should he not speak thus? Since we have neglected to hear his sweet and fatherly voice, why should it be strange if we are compelled both to hear and to feel his terrible voice of judgment? Hence plague presses upon us, hence famine and dearth of food, hence the threats of wicked enemies trouble us. What shall I say of the seasons of the year, so unseasonable that summer seems almost turned into winter? So heaven itself and the earth, and all created things, seem in some way to send forth a voice and to declare that God is angry at our sins. Therefore, if we have heard so many voices, let us not harden our hearts; let us not be like the horse and the mule (as our psalmist says), nor cling obstinately to sin, but by true repentance let us return to the mercy of God, and from him beg pardon for our sins.

units.la: Cūm autem Dauid meminit brutorum animantium, id eo spectat vt improborū obstinatione[?] acriùs insectetur. Sic in Scriptura sæpissimè legimus sceleratos homines cum variis brutorum generibus comparari. Nunc enim vocantur canes, nunc leones,nunc serpentes atque viperæ & id genus:nepe vt ma- gis appareat quàm sit detestadum[?] peccatum quàmq; horribilis obstinatio peccandi. Nec eo quidem contenti sacri authores, sæpe im- probos ablegat infra ipsas bestias vt lóge in-seriori conditione esse videantur. Sic enim Ieremias:Ciconia,inquit,nouit sua stata tem-pora,hirundo obseruat tempus profectionis suæ:at populus meus non cognouit iudicium Domini. Quàm autem præclarè Esaias! Agnoscit bos Dominum suum,inquit,& asinus præsepe dominorum suorum:at Israel nō agnoscit,populus meus non intelligit. Atque hæc increpadi ratio plurimum potest ad excutiendum illum stuporem qui nobis ingenitus est. Nam perinde est ac si Scriptura ita cum hominibus agat: Quæna[?] est ista peruicacia?quæ stupiditas?nónne vos Deus rationis participes creauit ? Quî fit ergo vt peccatum vos ex sublimi rationis humanę solio infra ipsas bestias deturbarit ? Huc pertinet quod ait vates, Nescitis, inquit, sicut equus & mulus quibus non est intellectus : quasi dicat, Pudeat vos homines, vos ratione atque intelligentia præditos,esse bestiis similes : & rectè quidem : Enimuerò ipsa nos oris vultúsque species,ipsa corporis compositio,debet com-mouere. mouere.Nam caetera quidem animalia in ter ram prona humi perpetuò defixos habet o-culos:sed Deus,vt inquit ille,os homini sub-lime dedit,coelumque tucri,iussit, & erectos ad sidera tollere vultus. Quae si verissimè de omnibus hominibus dicta sunt, quantò ma-gis de iis qui caeteris praestare debent? At-qui Prophetae quos citauimus & ipse noster vates ad eos sermonem conuertunt qui pu-ram religionem profitebantur, quos bestia-rum esse similes perquàm indignum est. Quid? num oblitus es te ad imaginem Dei crea-tum esse, eamque peccato deletam in iis in-staurari qui verè in Ecclesiam colliguntur? Iam ergo omitto te rationis lucecum reli-quis hominibus esse praeditum : hoc vrgeo, quòd te Deus ad sui cognitionem vocauit, in Ecclesiam introduxit, verbi sui radiis il-lustrauit & in mente tua diuinam fidei lu-cem accendit, quae ipsius rationis ratio me-rito censeri debet. Tene ergo ad bestia- rum ignauiam stuporemque proiicies? fi- dem extinguës? hominem exues? absit ab homine fideli tanta caecitas, tantaque per-tinacia. Itaque, fratres', haec serio cogite-mus, ne in nos quadrare posset quod olim Ie-remias Israelitis exprobrauit. Qui fit, in- quit,vt populus ille Hierosolymitanus aucr-tatur auersione tam pertinaci? attendi & auscultaui, sed nemo erat quem peccati poe-niteret,vt diceret, quid feci? Sed potius quifque illorum cursum suum persequitur instar equi toto impetu in prælium ruentis. Hæc Prophetæ verba videmus egregie convenire cum hac Dauidis cohortatione. Nefitisfi-cut equus & mulus quibus non est intellectus: quorum maxillas freno inieCto coerces, ne inte impetum faciant. Aut(ut alij exponunt)'quos frenis ac lupatis constrictos cogis ad te ac-cedere. In summa nos admonet vates, ut nos ad Dei verbum attentos docilesque præbeamus & prompto animo ipsius iussis obsequamur, non quod in nobis situm sit animos nostros ad obedientiam Dei flectere (Semper enim manent hæ præclarae sententiæ: Converte me Domine & con-vertar: flecte cor meum ad testimonia tua: Circuncidet Dominus Deus tuus cor tuum: Auferam cor lapideum de carne vestra, & dabo vobis cor carneum:& permulti alij lo-ci eodem spectantes)sed quia Deus utitur e-iusmodi cohortationibus ceu instrumentis per quæ vim suam exerit & suum Spiritum in animos nostros infundit.
units.tr: Now when David mentions brute animals, he does so in order to attack the obstinacy of the wicked more fiercely. Thus in Scripture we very often read that wicked men are compared with various kinds of brute beasts. Sometimes they are called dogs, sometimes lions, sometimes serpents and vipers and the like, so that it may appear more clearly how detestable sin is and how horrible is the obstinacy of sinning. Nor are the sacred writers content even with this; they often place the wicked below the beasts themselves, so that they seem to be in a far inferior condition. For thus Jeremiah: "The stork knows its appointed times, the swallow observes the time of its going forth; but my people has not known the judgment of the Lord." And how admirably Isaiah says: "The ox knows its owner, and the ass the manger of its masters; but Israel does not know, my people does not understand." And this manner of rebuke has great power to shake off that stupor which is innate in us. For it is just as if Scripture were dealing with men in this way: "What kind of perversity is this? What stupidity? Has not God created you as partakers of reason? How does it come about, then, that sin has cast you down from the lofty throne of human reason below the very beasts?" To this pertains what the psalmist says: "Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding." As if he were saying: "Be ashamed, you men, endowed with reason and understanding, to be like beasts"; and rightly so. For the very appearance of our face and countenance, the very make-up of our body, ought to move us. For other animals indeed have their eyes always fixed on the ground, bent toward the earth; but God, as that poet says, gave man an upright face, and commanded him to look up at heaven and to raise his erect face to the stars. If these words are most truly said of all men, how much more of those who ought to excel the rest? Yet the prophets whom we have cited, and our own psalmist, turn their speech to those who professed pure religion, and it is most unworthy that they should be like beasts. What? Have you forgotten that you were created in the image of God, and that this image, destroyed by sin, is restored in those who are truly gathered into the Church? Now I set aside the fact that you are endowed with the light of reason, as other men are. This I press: that God has called you to the knowledge of himself, has brought you into the Church, has illumined you with the rays of his Word, and has kindled in your mind the divine light of faith, which ought rightly to be counted the very reason of reason itself. Will you then cast yourself down to the sluggishness and stupor of beasts? Will you extinguish faith? Will you strip off your humanity? Far be such blindness and such stubbornness from a faithful man. Therefore, brothers, let us consider these things seriously, lest what Jeremiah once reproached the Israelites with could be applied to us: "Why is it," he says, "that this people of Jerusalem has turned away with such stubborn aversion? I have listened and attended, but there was no one who repented of his sin, saying, What have I done? Rather, each of them pursues his course like a horse rushing with full force into battle." We see that these words of the prophet agree remarkably well with this exhortation of David: "Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding; whose jaws you restrain with bit and bridle, lest they rush upon you." Or (as others explain it) "whom you must constrain with reins and bridles to come to you." In sum, the psalmist warns us to show ourselves attentive and docile to the Word of God, and to obey his commands with a ready mind; not because it lies in us to bend our minds to the obedience of God (for those excellent sayings remain: "Turn me, O Lord, and I shall be turned"; "Bend my heart to your testimonies"; "The Lord your God will circumcise your heart"; "I will take away the stony heart from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh"; and very many other passages to the same effect), but because God uses such exhortations as instruments through which he exerts his power and pours his Spirit into our minds.

units.la: Reliquum est ut hanc Dauidis cohorta-tionem nobis ipsis applicemus. Sunt enim hodie plurimi qui aure & lingua tenus Christiani sunt, cum interim animos gerant religione ac pietate prorsus vacuos. Quos si admoneas, si reprehendas, si obiurges & propositis Dei iudiciis urgeas, perinde facias ac si absentibus loquâre: nam (quod mirere) & præsentes absunt & audientes non audiunt. Multis quidem frenis debet effusus libidinum noftrarũ impetus coërceri. Nam & ipsa religio & iudicia Dei & humanæ le-ges, ipse denique pudor debet frenare no-stras cupiditates. Sed multi sunt adeo per-uicaces, vt excussis quibusçunque frenis inomnia scelera præcipites feruntur. Quod si cum hominibus eiusmodi res Dauidi es-set, vereor profecto, ne longè etiâ vehemen-tiori increpatione uteretur. Non enim for-tasse diceret: Ne sitis sicut equus, sed ita potius: Saltem estote equo similes, qui etiam ferocissimus frenis tamen ac lupatis do mari solet, vos autem estis prorsus indomiti. Miror equidem inter eos qui Euangeli-cam doctrinam profitentur tam duros & obstinatos homines posse reperiri. Verbum enim Domini cum aqua sæpissime compa-ratur: videmus autem vel durissima saxa ab aquis continuis cauata & exesa quodammodo mollescere. Quales igitur esse debemus qui quotidianis assiduisque verbi Dei concionibus irrigamur? num erimus ipsis saxis duriores? nónne tot cohortationibus, tot monitis, tot obtestationibus molliemur? Quamobrem hoc à Deo votis ardentibus precemur, ut animos nostros flectat vi & efficacia sui Spiritus, ut corda lapidea in carnea convertat, ut denique duritiem il-lam à natura corrupta nobis insitam excutiat & animum promptum & obfequen-tem nobis ingeneret, vt sponte ac libenter piis iussis pareamus. Alioquin verendum est ne qui à dulcissima Patris misericordia flecti recusarint, tandem grauissima summi iudicis sententia fracti, dent poenas iustissimas suae obstinationis. Audiedum est enim quod sequitur apud Dauidem.
units.tr: It remains that we apply this exhortation of David to ourselves. For today there are very many who are Christians in ear and tongue only, while in the meantime they bear minds utterly empty of religion and piety. If you admonish them, if you reprove them, if you rebuke them and press upon them the judgments of God, you would be doing the same as if you were speaking to absent men; for (which is a wonder) they are present and yet absent, and hearing they do not hear. Indeed the headlong rush of our lusts ought to be restrained by many bridles. For religion itself, the judgments of God, human laws, and finally shame itself ought to curb our desires. But many are so stubborn that, with every bridle thrown off, they rush headlong into every kind of wickedness. If David had to deal with men of this kind, I truly fear he would use a far more vehement rebuke. He would perhaps not say, "Do not be like the horse," but rather: "At least be like the horse, which, though most fierce, is nevertheless usually tamed by bit and bridle; but you are altogether untamed." I am indeed astonished that among those who profess the Gospel doctrine men so hard and obstinate can be found. For the Word of the Lord is very often compared with water; and we see that even the hardest rocks, hollowed and eaten away by continual waters, somehow grow soft. What then ought we to be, who are watered by the daily and unceasing sermons of the Word of God? Shall we be harder than the rocks themselves? Shall we not be softened by so many exhortations, so many warnings, so many entreaties? Therefore let us pray to God with ardent prayers, that he may bend our minds by the power and efficacy of his Spirit, that he may turn stony hearts into hearts of flesh, that finally he may shake off that hardness implanted in us by corrupt nature, and may engender in us a ready and obedient mind, so that we may obey pious commands willingly and gladly. Otherwise it is to be feared lest those who refused to be bent by the most sweet mercy of the Father, at length broken by the most grievous sentence of the supreme Judge, pay the most just penalties for their obstinacy. For what follows in David must be heard.

units.la: ver.10. Multi dolores impiu manent, id est, cum qui reiecta poenitetia in sceleribus obduruit. Est autem redditio praecedentis similitudinis quę paulo fusius ab Solomone explicatur: vt, inquit, flagellum equo & frenum asino: ita virga & plagae dorso stultorum adhibendae sunt. Quae comminatio eo spectat ne nobis in vitiis blandiamur. Quemadmodum etiam Moses vt Israelitas à pertinacia & obstinatione deterreret: Circuncidite, inquit, praeputium cordis vestri & ceruices vestras ne amplius induretis: Quia Deus vester est Deus deorum & Dominus dominorū, Deus magnus, fortis & metuendus, qui personam non recipit, neque accipit munus. Nulla igitur ratio accommodatior est ad eos qui peccatis indormiùt excitandos, quàm fi sibi pro ponant summam Dei potentiam & grauissima supplicia quae tandem obstinatos manet. Si enim equi quantumuis restitantes admonentur calcaribus vrgentur, fi quantumuis feroces, impositis frenis coercentur: quanto magis praefracti & pertinaces homines Dei flagellis
units.tr: v. 10. Many sorrows await the wicked, that is, those who, having rejected repentance, have hardened themselves in their sins. This is a restatement of the preceding comparison, which Solomon explains more fully: "As a whip for the horse, and a bridle for the ass, so a rod is for the back of fools." This warning is meant so that we do not flatter ourselves in our vices. Moses too, to deter the Israelites from stubbornness and obstinacy, says: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart and your necks, and harden them no more; for your God is the God of gods and Lord of lords, a great, mighty and terrifying God, who shows no partiality and takes no bribe." So no argument is better suited to rousing those who sleep in their sins than to set before them the great power of God and the most severe punishments that await the obstinate in the end. For if horses, however restive, are urged on by spurs, and however fierce, are restrained by bridles, how much more will stubborn and headstrong men be tamed by the scourges and judgments of God.

units.la: Qui vi tiis indormiunt propositis Dei iudiciis sunt e citadi. gellis iudiciisque domabuntur. Quid ergo? nēpe debemus prōpto animo & alacri Deo tanquā sessori subiecti, nos sponte ad eius du ctum applicare, ne audiamus quod Saulo ali quando dictum est: Durum est tibi contrā sti mulum calcitrare: rursus cùm primùm habe nas adducet, statim parere atque obsequi, ne eius irā in nos & iudicia prouocemus. Nā(vt aliquando à nobis discedamus) quid cesemus hostibus Euangelij futurum esse? Certè non minus verè quàm eleganter Augustinus dice bat, de iis qui Dei volūtatem facere nolunt, fieri voluntatem Dei. Nimirum tāta est eius virtus, tanta sapietia, vt improbos cogat in- uitos & imprudentes contrā quam velint fa- cere. Idè enim illis quod equis ferocibus ac- cidit, qui modò restitant, modò se transfuer- sos agūt, modò cessim redeunt, & tamè cùm frenis tum calcaribus tandem cogūtur viam cōficere: ita sit sūmo & imperuestigabili Dei consilio, vt cùm maximè sibi videntur impro bi aduersari Deo, tum maximè seruiant Dei gloriæ illustrandæ, & (vt quidam ex propha-nis dixit) fata fugiendo in fata ruant. Quid e-nim aliud dicemus de Pharaone? Quid de Sennacheribo? de Nabuchadnezare, Balzaza re & aliis innumeralibus hostibus Ecclesiæ quos Dominus tanquā belluas immanissimas frenis impositis potentissimè repressit? Sic e-nim Dominus per Esaiā de feroci & exultan te Assyrio: quandoquidē, inquit, tuos impeEze.38 tus furoresque in me conuertisti, iniiciam frenum labiis tuis & retroagâ te ea via qua venisti. Ac prope totidem verbis aduersus Gog vaticinatus est Ezechiel. Chryfoftomus autem dicebat sceleratos homines eò bestiis deteriores esse, quòd bestiarum vnaquæque sibi peculiare vitium habeat(fi tamen vitium appellandû est)Sic enim leoni crudelitatem, porco ingluuiem tribuimus, similiterque de reliquis dicendum est:at homo omniû prope beftiarû habeat vitia,adeò vt & leone crude lior,& lupo voracior, & porco sordidior, & vulpe fallacior esse videatur.Scite Chryfofto mus:quid fi autem inter ipsos improbos aliqui reperiantur, qui omnium improborum vitia in fe habeant?
