Ecce infœlix hæc ætas atque miserrima quæ multos eiusmodi homines in lucem produxit, vel potius eorum tenebris ipsam pietatis, veritatis, humanitatisque lucem propemodum extinxit:quibus no ster vates non iam profecto diceret: Ne fitis vt equus & mulus : sed potius, ne fitis vt lupi, vt leones,vt tigrides,quanquam,cur illis hominibus potius quàm nobis irascimur. Nos ipsi fratres, ea vincula quibus constrictæ illæ belluæ à Domino tenebantur, ipsi, inquam, rupimus:peccata nostra habenas laxarût earum crudelitati. Quare ad Dominum conuersi iamiam ipsius auxilium imploremus: hostium nostrorum atque adeò tuorum, ô Domine, immanitatem coërce, furoresque reprime. Hanc tantam rabiem adamantinis tuorum iudiciorum vinculis constringe: intentos in Ecclesiam gladios retunde : denique tot tantisque nostris vulneribus summa tua misericordia medeatur. Hæc & pleráq; similia meditemur,hæc precemur in hac tanta temporum acerbitate & certò statuamus,hostiles impetus non perpetuò duraturos. Credamus enim Dauidi ita nostram infirmitatẽ sulcieti: Multi dolores impiũ manet. Si ad aliquod tempus, inquit, improbi omni terrenarum voluptatuum genere perfusi, exultant ac triumphos agunt , interim dum vos multis æerumnis doloribúsque pressi assidue gemitis: ne propterea animos abiici-te. Illucescet aliquando dies cum improbo-rum voluptas in dolorem , deliciæ in cruciatus & gaudia in lacrymas gemitúsque con-vertentur: atque ita experientia tandem con firmabit hanc sententiã esse verissimam:multos dolores impios manere. Quæ cogitatio debet fidem nostram & patientiã sustentare,ne vel impiorum prosperitas vano fulgore nobis perstringat oculos,vel eorum furor atq; crudelitas animos deiiciat. Quare(ut ad equi similitudinẽ redeamus)imponamus frenũ nostrę impatientiæ,n e nos extra rationis & officij cancellos abripiat. Intueamur animo futurũ improborũ exitium & iam ipsum nobis spe certissima representemus, Sciamus Deum esse summũ & æquissime iudicem, cuius quò maior est patientia, cò sunt iudicia grauiora. Ex altera parte nobis felicissimam piorum conditionem proponamus, vt ita magis magisque ad pietatis virtutisque studium incendamur. Sic enim uates: Sed, inquit, cum qui fidit Domino misericordia circumdabit. Hoc autem opponitur superiori sententiæ. Nam improbi quidem postquam per aliquod tempus inebriati fuerint mūdi & carnis voluptatibus, eas tādem cum summis doloribus euomunt: fideles autem postea quam multos dolores perpessi fuerint, tandem cumulatissima Dei misericordia perfruentur. Non quòd il-la pios vnquam deficiat, sed quia tum clarissimè elucescit, cū ex maioribus periculis liberātur. Nec verò negligendus est ordo qui à Dauide hic obseruatur cùm ait impios quidem, multos tandē dolores sensuros esse, pios verò circundatū iri summa Dei misericordia. Nā hæc coniunctio nos docet piorū liberationē coniunctam esse cum exitio improborum: quod etiā multis veteribus exēplis confirmari potest. Cedò enim, ecquādo ab Ægyptiorū iugo Israelitæ liberati sunt? cùm Pharao & ingens Ægyptiorū exercitus mirando Dei iudicio aquis summersus est. Ecquando Iudæi ex Babylonica seruitute redierunt? cùm profanus ille ac blasphemus Balsafar [?] iugula-tus, cùm Babylonij trucidati, cùm ipsa Babylon fuit ab hostibus expugnata. Itaque tunc simul Dei iustitia & misericordia reluxerunt. Extant permulta alia exem-pla quorum nos attenta consideratio ad pa-tientiam erudiet. Deus enim suo tempore sua iudicia edet, & Ecclesiae liberationem, cum obstinatorum hostium interitu coniunget. Cæterum cum Dauid nominat Dei mi-sericordiam, excludit omnem de meritis humanis opinionem, ut Pontificiorum hac in parte errores semel damnemus. Nam siquid boni habemus, siqua quies nobis concedi-tur, ipsa denique liberatio, ipsa salus non alio debet quam ad solam Dei unici seruatoris misericordiam referri. Verbum autem, circūdabit, quo vates utitur, expleta piorum significat & cumulatissimam fœlicitatem: eiq; respondet quod iam ante audiuimus cum diceret, se liberationis canticis fuisse a Deo undique circundatum. Hinc autem nascitur egregia consolatio, cum scimus nos, qui tot hostibus sumus expositi, non ex parte tantum protegi, neque nobis dimidium tantum & mancum auxilium a Domino porrigi, sed ex omnibus partibus nos esse ab illius misericordia & auxilio circundatos. Ex quo fit ut Psalmum hunc vates concludat hac præcla-ra ad lætitiam cohortatione.
units.tr: Those who sleep in their sins are roused by the judgments of God set before them, and they will be subdued by the scourges and judgments. What then? Surely we ought, with a ready and willing mind, to submit ourselves to God as our rider, and of our own accord to yield to his leading, lest we hear what was once said to Saul: "It is hard for you to kick against the goad." Again, as soon as he brings the reins, we should at once obey and comply, lest we provoke his anger and judgments against us. For (to leave this point for a moment) what will become of the enemies of the gospel? Surely Augustine spoke no less truly than elegantly when he said that of those who refuse to do the will of God, the will of God is done. Indeed, so great is his power and so great his wisdom that he compels the wicked, against their will and without their knowing it, to do the opposite of what they wish. For what happens to them is what happens to fierce horses: now they resist, now they turn sideways, now they back away, and yet, both by the bridle and by the spurs, they are at last forced to complete the journey. So it is by the supreme and unsearchable counsel of God that, when the wicked seem most of all to oppose God, they then most of all serve the glory of God to be displayed; and (as one of the profane writers said) by fleeing their fate they rush into it. For what else shall we say of Pharaoh? What of Sennacherib? Of Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, and the countless other enemies of the Church whom the Lord, as though they were most savage beasts with bits in their mouths, has mightily restrained? For thus the Lord speaks through Isaiah of the fierce and exulting Assyrian: "Because you have turned your raging and fury against me, I will put a hook in your lips and a bridle in your mouth, and I will turn you back by the way you came." Ezekiel prophesied almost in the same words against Gog: Ezech. 38. Chrysostom used to say that wicked men are worse than beasts, because each kind of beast has its own peculiar vice (if indeed it is right to call it a vice). Thus we ascribe cruelty to the lion and gluttony to the pig, and the same may be said of the rest; but man has almost all the vices of the beasts, so that he seems more cruel than a lion, more greedy than a wolf, more filthy than a pig, and more deceitful than a fox. Chrysostom spoke wittily. But what if among the wicked themselves there are some who have in them the vices of all the wicked? Behold this unhappy and most wretched age, which has brought many such men into the light, or rather has almost extinguished in their darkness the very light of piety, truth and humanity. To such men our prophet would now say not, "Be not like the horse and the mule," but rather, "Be not like wolves, lions, or tigers." Yet why do we rage against those men rather than against ourselves? We ourselves, brothers, have broken, I say, those chains by which the Lord held those beasts bound; our sins have loosened the reins for their cruelty. Therefore, turning to the Lord, let us now implore his help: O Lord, restrain the savagery of our enemies and, indeed, of yours, and check their raging. Bind this great madness with the adamantine chains of your judgments; blunt the swords aimed against the Church; and at last, let your great mercy heal so many and such great wounds of ours. Let us meditate on these things and many like them, let us pray for these things in this great bitterness of the times, and let us firmly hold that the hostile assaults will not last forever. For let us believe David, who thus strengthens our weakness: Many sorrows await the wicked. "If for a time," he says, "the wicked, drenched in every kind of earthly pleasure, exult and celebrate triumphs, yet you, who are constantly groaning under many hardships and pains, do not therefore lose heart. A day will dawn when the pleasure of the wicked will be turned into pain, their delights into torments, and their joys into tears and groans." And so experience will at last confirm that this saying is most true: many sorrows await the wicked. This thought ought to sustain our faith and patience, so that neither the prosperity of the wicked may dazzle our eyes with empty brilliance, nor their rage and cruelty cast down our spirits. Therefore (to return to the comparison of the horse) let us put a bridle on our impatience, lest it carry us away beyond the bounds of reason and duty. Let us look with the mind upon the coming ruin of the wicked, and let us present it to ourselves now with the most certain hope. Let us know that God is the supreme and most just judge, and the greater his patience, the heavier his judgments. On the other side, let us set before ourselves the most happy condition of the godly, so that we may be ever more and more inflamed with zeal for piety and virtue. For thus the prophet says: But, he says, the one who trusts in the Lord, mercy shall surround him. This is set against the preceding statement. For the wicked, after they have for some time been intoxicated with the pleasures of the world and the flesh, at last vomit them up with the greatest pains; but the faithful, after they have suffered many pains, at last enjoy the most abundant mercy of God. Not that this mercy ever fails the godly, but it shines most clearly when they are delivered from the greatest dangers. Nor is the order observed here by David to be neglected, when he says that the wicked indeed will at last feel many pains, but the godly will be surrounded by the great mercy of God. For this conjunction teaches us that the deliverance of the godly is joined with the destruction of the wicked, which can also be confirmed by many examples from antiquity. For tell me, when were the Israelites freed from the yoke of Egypt? When Pharaoh and the vast army of the Egyptians were sunk in the waters by the wonderful judgment of God. When did the Jews return from Babylonian captivity? When that profane and blasphemous Belshazzar was slain, when the Babylonians were slaughtered, when Babylon itself was taken by its enemies. Then, at the same time, the justice and mercy of God shone forth. There are very many other examples, the careful consideration of which will train us in patience. For God, in his own time, will bring forth his judgments, and will join the deliverance of the Church with the destruction of its obstinate enemies. Moreover, when David names the mercy of God, he excludes every opinion about human merits, so that we may once for all condemn the errors of the Papists on this point. For if we have anything good, if any rest is granted us, indeed deliverance itself and salvation itself, these ought to be referred to nothing but the mercy of God, the one Saviour. The word surround, which the prophet uses, signifies the fullness and most abundant happiness of the godly, and it corresponds to what we heard earlier when he said that he had been surrounded on every side by God with the songs of deliverance. From this arises an excellent consolation: since we who are exposed to so many enemies know that we are protected not only in part, nor is only half and incomplete help stretched out to us by the Lord, but that we are surrounded on all sides by his mercy and help. From this it follows that the prophet concludes this Psalm with this famous exhortation to joy.

units.la: verf.11. Gaudete in Domino, & exulta-te iusti : iubilate quotquot estis recto corde.
units.tr: verse 11. Rejoice in the Lord, and exult, you righteous; shout for joy, all you who are upright in heart.

units.la: Quæ conclusio aptissimè cohæret cum iis quæ in hoc Psalmo tractata sunt. Egit e-nim de gratuita peccatorum remissione, de
units.tr: This conclusion fits very well with what has been treated in this Psalm. For it has dealt with the free forgiveness of sins, and with

units.la: k.j. verae poenitentiae fructibus, de auxilio Dei pa-ternaque eius erga fideles misericordia, qui-bus omnibus recte conuenit haec postrema cohortatio: Gaudete, inquit, quasi diceret: si ex animo doctrinam a me traditam percepi-stis: si peccatorum remissionem vera fide am-plexi, vos totos Dei cultui vitaeque sanctimo-niae consecrastis: si de praesidio Dei certi in e-ius benignitate & clementia acquiescitis: Gau-dete, exultate, iubilate: sint animi vestri spiri-tuali laetitia perfusi. Hoc igitur sibi vult Da-uid in hoc loco. Et certe doctrinam de gra-tuita iustificatione appositè sequitur cohor-tatio ad gaudium: quod vel patet ex Apo-stolo, qui postquam disseruit de iustificatione fidei, in epistola ad Romanos, tum subiungit nos fide iustificatos pace habere erga Deum, quae proculdubio omnem laetitiam & cumu-latissimum gaudium comprehendit, Idem e-tiam Apostolus Galatas docebat gaudiu esse fructum Spiritus. Et Ioannes affirmat se doc-trinam Euangelicam nobis proponere ut gaudium nostrum sit plenum. Quinetiā cum Angeli natum Christum annuntiant Pasto-ribus, profitetur se gaudium magnum annun-tiare. Nepe quia in Christo remissionem pec-catorum & iustitiam atque adeo perfectam foelicitatem habemus. Recte igitur nosier vates Gaudete, inquit, iusti: nam eos compel-lat qui suam iustitiam in peccatorum remis-sione collocarunt & toti ad pietatis stu-dium dium & ad producendos veræ pœnitentiæ fructus aspirant. Nec vero superflua est repetitio qua utitur, Gaudete, exultate, iubi-late. Sic enim docet quam tardi simus ad percipiendum illud cœleste gaudium quod nobis proponit. Nam similiter facit ut siquem arctiori somno sopitum oppressumque & cui vanæ somniorum imagines illudunt, semel atque iterum, & sæpius etiam, si sit opus, excitare coneris, ut experrectus lucem aspi-ciat & a somniis ad res veras animum tradu-cat: sic etiam nos terrenis mundi deliciis in-dormientes & fallacibus huius vitæ gaudiis, tanquam somniis (ut Nazianzenus ait) delu-sos, vates noster semel, iterum, & tertio vi-detur ex hoc tam diuturno somno excitare, ut oculos ad spiritualem lucem aperiamus, & renuntiantes vanis gaudiorum ludibriis quæ sunt co-mundus, & caro ceu per somnium often-tant[?], veram firmamque lætitiam amplecta-mur, & ut ille dicebat, solidum gaudium gau-deamus. Hec eadē est ratio cur in Psal.33.pios sæpius ad gaudia catusq; cohortetur. Et Paulus ad Philipp. Gaudete, inquit, in Domino semper: iterū dico, gaudete. Nimirum ita sumus urgendi, cum ad percipienda vera gau-dia simus tardiores. Sed & aliud in Dauidis verbis obseruandum est. Videtur enim oratio crescere, siquidem eam propius inspicias. Gaudete, inquit, exultate, ouate. Atque ita videmus hac esse spiritualis gaudii naturam vt semper in nobis quasi certis gradibus augeatur, donec tandem perfectissimle seper mum & cumulatissimum euadat. Iam, ouandi verbum quàm sit ad rem præsentem accommodatum, quis non videt? Nobis enim initio propositum quā graue sit ac difficile certamen dum nobis aduersus terrores legis adversus Satanæ & inferorū impetus pugnandum est: nunc apprehensa Dei misericordia ac peccatorum accepta remissione tanquam victores exultamus. Atque id si Dauid videre potuit cum adhuc effet vmbris & ceremoniis legalibus inuolutus, quanto nos æquius est illud ipsum agnoscere, postquam Christus in carne exhibitus magnificū de mundo, carne, Satana deque ipsa inferorū potestate trium phum egit? Gaudeamus, igitur, fratres, exultemus, iubilemus. Annon enim animo intuemur profratum Satanam, mortem cuersam, peccatum deletum, ipsos rectores tenebrarū ipsas spirituales malitias potentissima Christi virtute profligatas, & à Christo (vt ait Apostolus) in sublime ascendente in triumphum ductas? Sed fortasse huic ad gaudium cohortationi intercedere atque obstare videantur illi propemodum continui dolores, illæ quotidianæ molestiæ quæ solent piorum vitam comitari. Cur enim (dicat aliquis) eos gaudere & exultare iubeas, qui in perpetuis lacrymis & squalore vitam agunt? Eósne gaudere qui exilio, qui egestate, qui malis omnibus bus oppressi afliduis laboribus ac miseriis iactantur? eos exultare, quos vincula detinent, gladij trucidant, flammæ absumunt: quos adeo mundus exosos habet, vt viuis, vitæ alimenta, mortuis, mortis honorem & sepulturam soleat denegare: in quorum perniciem ipsa propemodum elementa videntur conspirasse, cum nec aër spirantibus, nec mortuis terra ipsa concedatur? Huic obiectioni respondet piorum constantia qui se in mediis doloribus gaudere profitentur, quique (teste Apostolo) direptionem facultatum suarum cum gaudio accipiunt.
units.tr: the fruits of true repentance, with God's help and his fatherly mercy toward the faithful. This final exhortation fits all of these well. "Rejoice," he says, as if to say: if you have received the teaching I have handed down from the heart; if you have embraced the forgiveness of sins with true faith and have consecrated yourselves wholly to the worship of God and a holy life; if, certain of God's protection, you rest in his goodness and clemency: then rejoice, exult, shout for joy; let your minds be filled with spiritual gladness. This, then, is what David means in this place. Indeed, an exhortation to joy follows aptly upon the teaching of free justification. This is plain even from the Apostle, who, after discussing justification by faith in his Epistle to the Romans, then adds that we, justified by faith, have peace with God, which without doubt includes all gladness and the fullest joy. The same Apostle also taught the Galatians that joy is a fruit of the Spirit. John affirms that he sets forth the Gospel teaching to us so that our joy may be full. Moreover, when the angels announce the birth of Christ to the shepherds, they profess that they announce great joy: namely, because in Christ we have the forgiveness of sins, righteousness, and indeed perfect happiness. Our prophet rightly says, "Rejoice, you righteous," for he addresses those who have placed their righteousness in the remission of sins and who strive wholly for the pursuit of piety and for producing the fruits of true repentance. Nor is the repetition he uses superfluous: "Rejoice, exult, shout for joy." For it teaches how slow we are to grasp that heavenly joy which he sets before us. He acts as one who, when someone is sunk in a deep sleep and deceived by vain dream-images, tries to rouse him once, twice, and even more often if need be, so that, awakened, he may see the light and turn his mind from dreams to real things. So too, our prophet seems to rouse us, drowsing in the earthly delights of the world and deluded by the deceptive joys of this life as by dreams (as Nazianzen says), once, twice, and a third time, from this long sleep, so that we may open our eyes to spiritual light; and, renouncing the empty mockeries of joy which the world and the flesh display as if in a dream, we may embrace true and firm gladness and, as that man used to say, rejoice in solid joy. This is the same reason why in Psalm 33 he so often urges the godly to joys. And Paul to the Philippians: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice." Surely we must be urged thus, since we are so slow to grasp true joys. But there is also another thing to be noted in David's words. For the expression seems to grow, if you look at it more closely: "Rejoice," he says, "exult, shout for joy." And so we see that the nature of spiritual joy is such that in us it is always increased by certain steps, until at last it becomes most perfect and fullest. Now, who does not see how well the word "shout for joy" suits the present situation? For at first we must fight a struggle, so hard and difficult, against the terrors of the law and against the assaults of Satan and of hell; now, having laid hold of God's mercy and received the forgiveness of sins, we exult as victors. And if David could see this while he was still wrapped in shadows and legal ceremonies, how much more fitting is it for us to acknowledge it, since Christ has been manifested in the flesh and has triumphed magnificently over the world, the flesh, Satan, and the very power of hell? Let us rejoice, then, brothers, let us exult, let us shout for joy. Do we not, in our minds, behold the vanquished Satan, death overthrown, sin destroyed, the very rulers of darkness and the spiritual wickednesses put to rout by the most powerful virtue of Christ, and led in triumph by Christ as he ascends on high (as the Apostle says)? But perhaps those almost continual sorrows and those daily troubles which usually accompany the lives of the godly seem to stand in the way of this exhortation to joy and to oppose it. For why (someone may say) do you bid them rejoice and exult who live their lives in perpetual tears and squalor? Should those rejoice who are tossed about by exile, by poverty, who are overwhelmed by all kinds of evils, by constant labours and miseries? Should those exult whom chains hold, swords slaughter, flames consume; whom the world so hates that it is wont to deny the living the means of life and the dead honour and burial; against whose destruction the very elements seem almost to have conspired, since neither the air is granted to the breathing nor the earth itself to the dead? The constancy of the godly answers this objection, those who profess that they rejoice in the midst of sorrows, and who (as the Apostle witnesses) accept the plundering of their goods with joy.

units.la: Respondent ipsi Martyres in mediis flammis non gaudentes modò, sed etiam canentes & (vt ad Dauidis verbum redeamus) tanquam parta de hostibus victoria feliciter ouantes. Etenim quidni gaudeant fideles? num quia mundus ceu perpetuus hostis eos insequitur. At potius hæc fuerit maxima gaudij ratio cum ita appareat eos haudquaquam ad mundum pertinere. Sic enim Christus: si ex mundo, inquit, fuisset mundus quod suum est amaret: quia vero ex mundo non estis, sed elegi vos ex mundo, propterea odit vos mundus. O felix & votis omnibus exoptandum odium! o dulces labores qui nos electos à Deo, nos Deo charos, nos Dei filios esse testantur! Ergo iam mundus nos odio prosequautur, quandoquidem nos amat Deus: nos mundus reiiciat, quandoquidem à Deo recipimur: sæuiat mundus, pugnet, insectetur, excruciet, morte denique afficiat, cùm in Deo nostro pacem tranquillitatem, vitam, salutemque certissimam habeamus.
units.tr: The martyrs themselves answer it, not only rejoicing but even singing in the midst of the flames, and (to return to David's word) exulting joyfully, as if victory had been won over enemies. For why should the faithful not rejoice? Is it because the world pursues them as a perpetual enemy? Rather, this should be the greatest ground for joy, since it so clearly shows that they do not belong to the world. For thus Christ says: "If you were of the world, the world would love what is its own; but because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you." O happy hatred, and to be desired by all prayers! O sweet labours, which testify that we are chosen by God, dear to God, sons of God! Therefore let the world now pursue us with hatred, since God loves us; let the world reject us, since we are received by God; let the world rage, fight, harass, torment, and finally put us to death, since in our God we have peace, tranquillity, life, and most certain salvation.

units.la: Num obsecrò, potest ille non gaudere, non exultare, non triumphum agere, cui sacer Dei spiritus in animo certitudinem electionis obsignauit? Credo ac persuasum habeo mihi Deum es-se patrem: me à Deo electum: Christum pro mea salute sanguinem illum pretiosis-simum fudisse: Christum mea peccata de-leuisse: Christum pro me mortis imperium aboleuisse: me futurum tantæ victoriæ par-ticipem: mihi cœlum patêre, mihi salutem à Christo comparatam, mihi fœlicitatem æternam in cœlis esse repositam, me iam fide ac spe certissima in cœlis cum ipso Chri-sto, cum Angelis, cum Patriarchis, Apo-stolis, martyribus, denique cum infinito fi-delium numero confidere. Non igitur gau-deam? non exultem? non triumphem? i-mò iam vitæ futuræ dulcedine, præsentis vitæ acerbitas dolorêsque superentur: & ij mœrores quos hîc momento temporis pa-timur, infinitis æternîsque gaudiis ac re-rum futurarum certissima expectatione ob-ruantur. Non sunt (inquit Paulus) ea quæ præsenti tempore perpetimur, paria futuræ glorię in nobis retegendæ.Quæ cùm ita sint, affiraffirmamus Dauidé recté nos ad gaudedum cohortari, quamuis multæ nobis molestiæ idem tidem suscipiendæ sint. Etenim longé cedunt dolores corporis spirituali cōsolationi: quæ vt in animis nostris alatur, opus est assidua precatione. Præclarè enim Paulus ad Thessa lonicenses: Semper, inquit, gaudete: indesi-nenter orate: precatione perpetui gaudij nu-tricem & alumna esse significans. Enimuero non agit vates de vanis illis gaudiis quæ pas-sim homines solent ex rebus terrenis & cadu cis percipere: Gaudete, inquit, in Domino. Nō vobis propono carnis delicias & voluptates: sed ita vos gaudete velim, vt in Deo, in rebus sanctis, in rerum sacrarum suauissima cogitatione gaudeatis: non enim ambitiosos aut vo-luptarios, sed iustos ac sanctos homines alloquor, qui sunt recto corde: id est, quorum ani mus est integer & quorum pura est confcien tia. Ex his igitur apparet quinam homines proprie gaudere dicantur, nempe iusti & qui sunt recto corde. quemadmodum etiam alibi, lætamini, inquit, iusti in Domino. Quanquā igitur sibi lætari videntur filij huius seculi & in mediis voluptatibus exultare, tamé, si rem propius spectes, nunquam illi gaudent. Extat apud Chrysostomum egregia disputatio, qua confirmat solos sanctos gaudere posse: im- probis vero gaudiū non esse tribuēdum. Sem per enim auari, semper ambitiosi, semper vo- luptarij desiderant: & quò magis vel diuitiæ
units.tr: Indeed, I beg you, can he fail to rejoice, fail to exult, fail to triumph, to whom the holy Spirit of God has sealed in the mind the certainty of his election? I believe and am persuaded that God is my Father; that I have been chosen by God; that Christ shed that most precious blood for my salvation; that Christ has blotted out my sins; that Christ has abolished the dominion of death for me; that I shall be a partaker of so great a victory; that heaven lies open to me; that salvation has been obtained for me by Christ; that eternal happiness is laid up for me in heaven; and that now, by the most certain faith and hope, I rest in heaven with Christ himself, with the angels, the patriarchs, the apostles, the martyrs, and finally with the infinite number of the faithful. Shall I not rejoice then? Shall I not exult? Shall I not triumph? Indeed, let the sweetness of the future life overcome the bitterness and pains of the present life; and let those sorrows, which we suffer here for a moment of time, be overwhelmed by infinite and eternal joys and by the most certain expectation of the things to come. "The sufferings of this present time," says Paul, "are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed in us." Since these things are so, we affirm that David rightly exhorts us to rejoice, although many troubles must be undertaken by us at the same time. For bodily pains yield far to spiritual consolation, which, in order to be nourished in our minds, requires constant prayer. For Paul writes splendidly to the Thessalonians: "Rejoice always," he says, "pray without ceasing," indicating that prayer is the nurse and foster-mother of perpetual joy. Indeed the prophet is not speaking of those vain joys which men commonly derive everywhere from earthly and fading things. "Rejoice," he says, "in the Lord." I do not set before you the delights and pleasures of the flesh; rather I wish you to rejoice in this way, that you may rejoice in God, in holy things, in the most sweet thought of sacred things. For I address not ambitious or pleasure-loving men but righteous and holy men, who are "upright in heart," that is, whose mind is sound and whose conscience is pure. From these things, therefore, it appears who are properly said to rejoice, namely the righteous and those "who are upright in heart"; just as elsewhere he says, "Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous." Although, therefore, the sons of this age seem to themselves to rejoice and to exult in the midst of pleasures, yet, if you look at the matter more closely, they never truly rejoice. There is an excellent disputation of Chrysostom, in which he maintains that only the holy can rejoice, and that joy is not to be attributed to the wicked. For the covetous are always desiring, always the ambitious, always the lovers of pleasure; and the more either riches increase or honours are enlarged, the greater the lust for riches and honours becomes.

units.la: k.iiij. crescunt vel honores augentur, eo fit maior diuitiarum honorumq; cupiditas. Nunquam au-tem expletur cupiditatis sitis: ne quid dicā de perpetuo metu in quo versantur & auari & ambitiosi & quotquot rebus terrenis addicti sunt. Crescentibus enim diuitiis, simul crescit metus ne quis eas casus auferat: ita ut quo maiores sunt diuitiæ, eo maiore esse metu necesse fit. Quamobrem verissime dixit Solomo, Cor impij in risu dolere: ut etiam Propheta affirma-uit nullam esse pacem impiis, sed eos instar maris assiduis perturbationum fluctibus agitari. Scita profecto similitudo: nunc enim impij leuissi-ma mundi & carnis aura inflati, vanis gaudiis ita efferuntur, ut sibi videatur ad cœlum usq; pertingere: nunc aduerso rerum successu ita depres-si sunt deiectique eorum animi, ut a desperatione, tanquam a profunda quadam voragine absorbeatur. An etiam multis confirmandū est quæ leuia sint, quam incostantia gaudia improborum? Cuius rei no alij testes quam ipsi improbi citandi sunt. Hoc enim agnoscebat ille apud Comicum, qui cum præ gaudio apud se non esset, mori optabat, ne gaudiu illud vita con-taminaret aliqua ægritudine. Quocirca non abs re Solomo: Finis, inquit, gaudij improborum est luctus. Statuamus igitur verum gaudium non alibi quam in piorum animis posse reperiri: improborum vero gaudia indigna esse quæ gaudia nominentur: quod facile poterit intelligi si proborum & improborum gaudia mutuò inter se comparentur. Nam il-li in Deo, hi vero in rebus terrenis gaudent: illorū animus vera & solida laetitia perfundi-tur, horum caro laetitia exterius tantum aspĕrgitur. Illi in mediis doloribus exultant, hi in mediis gaudiis dolent atq; cruciantur. Illorū perpetua, horū fluxa & caduca est laetitia. De-niq; illorū gaudia semper augetur, donec tan-dem illis æterna fœlicitas tanquā cumulus ac-cedat: horū vero spes in desperatione, vita in morte æternā, gaudia momentanea in perpe-tuos dolores cōuertūtur. Facessat igitur vanę mundi carnisq; bladitiæ: neq; nobis improbo-rū gaudia fucu faciant. Sed audiamus potius Dauide affirmante eorū demū esse laetari qui in Domino laetatur, qui iustitię & pietati stu-det & quorū animus integer est & vacuus o-mni hypocrisi atq; simulatione. Itaq;, fratres, interiore animi integritate colamus & recta sanaq; cōscientia retineamus, quę veri gaudij sedes est atq; domicilium. Nec eos imitemur qui hoc tēpore Euangelio renunciarūt & mūdi insana gaudia cruci Christi prætulerūt. Qui, si verū fateantur, dicet se intus in animo cru-ciari infinitis doloribus. Danda igitur est o-pera vt cor nostrum sit rectum, vt Dauid lo-quitur, atque ita verę ac spiritualis lætitiæ par-ticipes esse possimus. Cùm autem Propheta doceat, cor hominis natura peruersum esse, petamus à Deo vt peruersitate nobis insitam à natura, corrigat suo Spiritu, vt ita illius gratia & beneficio, ex animis rectis, recta opera proficiscantur. Hæc sunt quæ ex postrema Dauidis cohortatione colligere debemus.
units.tr: k.iiij. As riches increase or honours grow, the desire for riches and honours grows with them. The thirst of desire is never satisfied, not to mention the constant fear in which the miserly, the ambitious, and all who are given over to earthly things live. For as riches increase, fear increases with them, that some chance may take them away, so that the greater the riches, the greater the fear must necessarily be. Therefore Solomon spoke most truly: "The heart of the wicked grieves in laughter." As the Prophet also affirmed, there is no peace for the wicked, but they are tossed like the sea by the constant waves of disturbance. A fitting comparison indeed. For now the wicked, puffed up by the lightest breeze of the world and the flesh, are so elated by empty joys that they seem to reach up to heaven; now, when things go against them, their spirits are so cast down and dejected that they are swallowed up by despair as by some deep whirlpool. Or need I confirm with many examples how light and inconstant the joys of the wicked are? No witnesses are to be summoned for this but the wicked themselves. For that man in the Comic poet acknowledged it, who, beside himself with joy, wished to die, lest some sorrow should stain that joy with his life. Hence Solomon, not without reason: "The end of the joy of the wicked is grief." Let us therefore establish that true joy can be found nowhere but in the hearts of the godly, and that the joys of the wicked are unworthy of the name of joy. This can easily be understood if the joys of the good and of the wicked are set side by side. The former rejoice in God, the latter in earthly things. The mind of the former is flooded with true and solid gladness; the flesh of the latter is only sprinkled on the outside with gladness. The former exult in the midst of sorrows; the latter grieve and are tormented in the midst of pleasures. The gladness of the former is perpetual, that of the latter fleeting and perishable. Finally, the joys of the former constantly grow until at last eternal happiness comes to them as a crown; but the hope of the latter ends in despair, their life in eternal death, and their momentary joys are turned into everlasting pains. Let the vain frivolity of the world and the flesh depart, and let not the joys of the wicked make us their dupes. Rather let us listen to David affirming that those alone rejoice who rejoice in the Lord, who are devoted to righteousness and piety, and whose heart is sound and free of all hypocrisy and pretence. Therefore, brothers, let us cultivate integrity of heart within and keep a right and clean conscience, which is the seat and home of true joy. Nor let us imitate those who in this age have renounced the Gospel and preferred the mad joys of the world to the cross of Christ. If they were to confess the truth, they would say that they are inwardly tormented in their souls by endless sorrows. Care must therefore be taken that our heart be upright, as David says, so that we may be partakers of true and spiritual gladness. Since the Prophet teaches that the heart of man is perverse by nature, let us ask God to correct, by his Spirit, the perversity implanted in us by nature, so that by his grace and kindness right works may come forth from upright hearts. These are the things we ought to gather from David's closing exhortation.

units.la: Cùm autem multæ ac variæ doctrinæ nobis in hoc Psalmo propositæ fuerint, curemus ne illarum memoria nobis effluat, sed eas potius assidua cogitatione recolamus. Itaque (est enim illarum summa aliqua facienda) cùm illi demùm sint fœlices qui vera fide peccatorum remissionem amplexi sunt: agnoscamus peccata nostra, & eorum vero sensu perculsi, ad Dei misericordiam in Christo plenè nobis exhibitam recurramus, vt illius perfectissima iustitia induti, coram Dei oculis iusti reputemur. Hæc autem nostra per Christum iustifi-catio instar arboris feracis producat suos fructus, atque in primis animi puritatem atque integritatem, excussa illa hypocrisi quæ solet in animis nostris delitescere. Cùm verò ea sit, naturæ nostræ stupiditas, vt ægrè ad peccatorum confessionem adducamur, nunc saltem cùm sentimus Domini ferientis manum graviter in nos depressam, cùm his temporibus tot tantaque vulnera nobis inflicta sint, redeant in memoriam peccata præterita, eorumque veniā à Domini misericordia petamus: verásque lacrymas & gemitus ex intimo pectore proficiscentes coram paternis Dei oculis effundamus. Ne vanas excusationes pecca-tis nostris prætexamus, sed serió & ex animo fateamur innumerabiles offensas quibus in[?] Dei in nos prouocauimus. Tum vera fide re-missione peccatorum nobis oblata in Christo recipiamus, atq; sentiamus Deum nos passis ma-tribus in dilectissimo filio complectetem[?]. Illi igitur preces assiduas offeramus, illi salute tū animi tū corporis commendemus, ab illo, his praesertim difficilimis temporibus, ope expectemus: ad illū unū tot malis passim inundatibus tanquā ad portū tutissimū velis remisque cō-tendamus. Ille sit nobis perfugiū, latibulū & salus. Ac iam fidei certissimis oculis die illum intueamur, cum Dominus non tantū nostri priuatim, sed tot fuarū[?] Ecclesiarū[?] misertus, nos omnes mirabili fauore prosequetur, cum Turcas & omnes hostes Ecclesiae, divina virtute superatos fractosque cernemus, cum de-nique solēni gratiarū actione, tēpla, domus, vici, plateæ, loca deniq; omnia undique personabunt. Quamobrem hunc nostru vate, ceu doctore praestantissimū audiamus, eum ceu fidelissimū duce ac praeuiū sequamur, ei docenti, monenti, hortantique, pareamus. Excutiamus omne contumaciam, nec simus earū bestiarū similes quae sunt ad obsequium frænis & cal-caribus adigedæ. Iam spōte & alacriter viam illam conficiamus, quā ipsō Dei spiritu duce sumus ingressi. Horreamus ea iudicia quae in probos & obstinatos manent. Aspiremus ad eā summi Patris misericordia, quae pios ac fi-deles circundat atque obtegit. Confidamus Deo, Deo, inquā non hominibus cōfidamus, in mediis afflictionū procellis, ut fidē nostrā nulla mundi, nulla Satanæ tēpestas unquā e-vertat. Quod si[?] nos ad aliquod tēpus multis doloribus ac molestiis exercet Dominus, hac tristitiam interioribus gaudiis, tanquam fomentis abhibitis, leniamus. Neque nos detineat vana mūdi & carnis lætitia, sed iustitiam sectātes gaudeamus in Æterno, qui ut nostræ iustitiæ, ita solidi gaudij æternæque fœlicitatis firmissimum est fundamentum. Atque ut suauissima consolatione assiduē perfruamur, eam animi & conscientiæ puritate foueamus.
units.tr: Since many and varied teachings have been set before us in this Psalm, let us take care that their memory does not slip from us, but rather recall them by constant meditation. Therefore (for their sum must be grasped in some way): since those alone are blessed who have embraced the forgiveness of sins with true faith, let us acknowledge our sins, and, struck by their true weight, let us flee to the mercy of God fully displayed to us in Christ, so that, clothed in his most perfect righteousness, we may be counted righteous before the eyes of God. Let this justification of ours through Christ, like a fruitful tree, bring forth its fruits, and above all purity and integrity of soul, the hypocrisy that is wont to lurk in our hearts being shaken off. Since our nature is so dull that we are scarcely brought to confess our sins, let us now at least, when we feel the hand of the Lord striking heavily upon us, and when so many and great wounds have been inflicted on us in these times, call to mind our past sins and seek their pardon from the mercy of the Lord; and let us pour out true tears and groans, rising from the depths of the heart, before the fatherly eyes of God. Let us not put forward vain excuses for our sins, but seriously and sincerely confess the countless offences by which we have provoked God against us. Then let us receive, with true faith, the forgiveness of sins offered to us in Christ, and let us feel that God embraces us with open arms in his beloved Son. To him therefore let us offer constant prayers; to him let us commend our safety, of soul and of body; from him, especially in these most difficult times, let us expect help; to him alone, as to the safest harbour, let us make haste with sails and oars amid the many evils that everywhere flood in upon us. May he be our refuge, our hiding place and our salvation. And now with the most certain eyes of faith let us look forward to that day when the Lord, having mercy not only on each of us but on all of his Churches, will show us his wonderful favour; when we shall see the Turks and all the enemies of the Church overcome and broken by divine power; when at last, in solemn thanksgiving, temples, houses, villages, streets and every place will resound on all sides. Therefore let us hear him as our most excellent teacher and prophet, let us follow him as our most faithful guide and leader, and let us obey him as he teaches, warns and exhorts. Let us cast off all obstinacy, and let us not be like those beasts which must be driven to obedience with bridles and goads. Now let us willingly and eagerly complete that path upon which we have entered under the leading of God's own Spirit. Let us shrink from those judgements that await the wicked and the obstinate. Let us aspire to that mercy of the highest Father which surrounds and covers the godly and faithful. Let us trust in God, in God I say, and not in men, so that no storm of the world or of Satan may ever overturn our faith in the midst of the tempests of affliction. And if the Lord exercises us for a time with many sorrows and troubles, let us soothe this sadness with inner joys, applied as a comfort. Let not the vain gladness of the world and the flesh detain us, but, pursuing righteousness, let us rejoice in the Eternal One, who is the firmest foundation both of our righteousness and of solid joy and eternal happiness. And that we may constantly enjoy this most sweet consolation, let us cherish it by purity of soul and conscience.

units.la: Faxit autē Dominus cuius misericordiam imploramus, cuius certissimis promissionibus nitimur: cuius solius potentiam nostrorum hostium viribus, sapientiam dolis, clementiam crudelitati opponimus, denique cuius ob nomen gloriosissimum & veritatē sanctissimam tot mala, tot exilia, tot cædes, multos jam annos perpetimur: faxit, inquam, summus ille Deus ad cuius pedes provoluti peccatorum veniam & collapsarum Ecclesiarum instaurationem supplices petimus, ut votorum compotes jamjam in ipso gaudeamus, exultemus, triumphemus, & cum ore, tum synceris animis, summa illius beneficia perpetua gratiarum actione celebremus. Amen per Chri-stum.
units.tr: May the Lord, whose mercy we implore and on whose most certain promises we rely, grant this; he alone, whose power we set against the might of our enemies, whose wisdom we set against their tricks, and whose clemency we set against their cruelty; and for whose most glorious name and most holy truth we have endured for many years now so many evils, so many exiles, so many slaughters. May he, I say, that highest God, at whose feet we lie prostrate, suppliantly seeking the pardon of sins and the restoration of the fallen Churches, grant that, having obtained our desires, we may rejoice, exult and triumph in him, and with our mouths and with sincere hearts celebrate his greatest benefits with perpetual thanksgiving. Amen, through Christ.

units.la: LAVS DEO
units.tr: PRAISE TO GOD
